# The Engineer Factory

## How India Priced Its Engineers by the Hour, and What AI Does to That Bargain

---

## A note on how this book was made

This book was researched, drafted and checked with the help of an AI model made by Anthropic. The same company's products, Claude Code and Claude Cowork, appear in sources discussed in Chapter 19, which deals with AI coding tools and the Indian software industry. Readers should weigh what the book says about AI with that in mind. The products are described there as the sources describe them, and the book makes no claim about them beyond what those sources say. Much of what Chapter 19 describes happened after the AI model's training ended; those passages rest on documents read in October 2026, not on the model's memory.

The work followed a fixed method. A register of sources was compiled first, and every chapter was drafted only from research dossiers built on that register. Each chapter was then checked by a separate pass that re-opened the sources behind every quotation, number, date, name and causal claim, corrected or softened what did not hold, and logged the result. A revision pass removed repetition and contradictions across chapters. The checking logs, the source register and the data files are kept in the book's public repository.

## A note on sources

No one was interviewed for this book. Every person who speaks in it does so through a published or archived record: a memoir, an oral history, a company filing, a court judgment, a parliamentary record, a government report, a scholarly study, or a newspaper or magazine report. The notes give the source and, where one exists, the page.

Some people appear only under names given to them by others. Where a reporter or a scholar used a pseudonym, the book uses the same one and says so where the person first appears. No character in the book is a composite, and no scene, thought or line of dialogue has been invented.

Gaps in the record, such as a report that could not be located or a date on which sources disagree, are recorded in the notes rather than in the text. Quotations are exact and kept short. Where a source could be read only in summary, the book paraphrases it rather than quoting. Figures published by companies, by the industry's lobby group Nasscom, or by consultancies that sell to the firms they count are labelled as theirs. Disagreements between sources are shown rather than resolved where the evidence does not settle them. Material published after mid-2025 was checked against the live source in October 2026, and the notes say so.

Ordinary workers speak less often in this book than its subject deserves. The published record of Indian software work is dominated by founders, executives, officials and scholars; the accounts of trainees, testers, call-centre agents and engineers who never became prominent are few, and most are anonymous or pseudonymous. Where such accounts exist, the book uses them and labels them. Where they do not, the gap is part of the story.

Rupee amounts are converted to US dollars at the average rate for the year in question, and Indian fiscal years, which run from April to March, are written in the form FY2023-24. Cities are given the names in use at the time, with the current name at first mention in each chapter.

# Prologue. The joining date (2026)

On Thursday 6 February 2025 a 24-year-old trainee at the Infosys training campus in Mysuru, whom the reporter who told her story for *The News Minute* called Gayatri (not her real name), received an email summoning her to a meeting the next day.[1] The email concerned the assessment held at the end of her training, which she had failed a month earlier. It said: 'You are required to maintain confidentiality, hence do not discuss this, or share this calendar with anyone.'[2] 'I was devastated after receiving the email,' she told the reporter. Her seniors, she said, had explained that such an email meant she would be asked to leave.[3]

The next morning, according to her account, security staff at the campus entrance took her electronic devices and her bag, as they did with the other trainees summoned that day. She was taken into a cabin, where a member of the human resources staff asked her to sign a 'mutual separation agreement'.[4] The report says she was coerced. The agreement itself said the opposite: 'You have knowingly and voluntarily chosen to enter into this agreement and have not been forced or pressured in any way to sign it.'[5] She signed. 'I signed it unwillingly. I did not want to quit the company. They wasted two and a half years of my career. It was my dream job,' she said.[6]

What followed took a few hours. The company took back the trainees' laptops, put them on a bus to their accommodation and told them to leave the premises by 5 pm that day.[7] Gayatri, the report says, had no time to arrange travel, so she booked a hotel for the night before going home to Andhra Pradesh.[8] The separation payment Infosys offered was one month's salary, which the reporter put at Rs 25,000.[9] Another trainee, given the name Raju, described the day in six words: 'We were thrown on the road.'[10] A third, given the name Rishi, aged 25, said he had waited nearly two years to be onboarded and had been removed after four months: 'I regret joining the company, they have traumatised me.'[11]

The two and a half years she spoke of had begun with success. Gayatri graduated in 2022 and in the same year cleared Infosys's interview for the post of system engineer, the company's entry-level job for new graduates.[12] Then nothing happened. In the reporter's words she 'was left hanging for nearly two years' and was onboarded in October 2024 'only after numerous emails and a legal intervention'.[13] From July 2024 she and others in her position took part in online 'pre-training', for which they were not paid. 'Pre-training was unheard of earlier,' she said.[14] The unpaid sessions and assessments ran for four weeks in July and six weeks in August, before any of the graduates was an employee.[15]

The offer had mattered beyond her. 'My parents and teachers were very proud when I got the offer letter from Infosys,' she told the reporter. After she failed the test three times, she said, her parents asked whether she had cheated in her college exams.[16] Her own summary of what the termination did was brief: 'The termination has taken away all my self-esteem and confidence.'[17]

This book is about the system that made her offer letter worth waiting two years for. For half a century India built a machine for turning young people into software engineers: colleges that taught them, companies that hired them by the thousand and trained them on campuses like the one at Mysuru, and an export trade that paid for it all. Her story shows that machine from the bottom, at the moment when it seemed to need fewer of the people it had been built to produce.

## The waiting

Gayatri was not alone, and her wait did not begin with her. In October 2022 *Business Today* reported that freshers placed by Accenture, Infosys, Wipro and HCLTech were seeing their joining dates pushed back, in some cases into the following year.[18] One graduate told the magazine that the company had postponed the date again two days before joining: 'I had packed my bags and booked all tickets to move to the new city.'[19] By June 2024 the Nascent Information Technology Employees Senate (NITES), a union of IT workers based in Pune, claimed that more than 10,000 graduates were still waiting for joining dates from Wipro, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Zensar and LTIMindtree, a figure no company confirmed.[20]

Infosys's case is the best documented, because NITES took it to the government. On 20 August 2024 the union complained to the Union Ministry of Labour and Employment about more than 2,000 campus recruits from 2022 who had not been onboarded.[21] According to NITES, Infosys issued about 2,000 offer letters on 2 and 3 September with joining dates in October.[22] Infosys told the state's labour department that the union's allegations were 'patently false' and that the graduates had already received joining dates.[23]

The recruits arrived in Mysuru that October.[24] *Republic Business* reported that most had joined under the National Apprenticeship Training Scheme, a government programme for on-the-job training, which would matter later.[25] Trainees told the reporter that the pass mark had risen to 65 per cent from 50 per cent in earlier years, and that the syllabus had grown, to 200 hours of material by one magazine's account.[26] A trainee given the name Rohan said the earlier batches had been treated leniently: 'The fact that they made it difficult for us shows that, since the beginning, they never wanted to hire us.'[27] By the report's count, which is not a company figure, of 930 who joined in one October intake, 160 passed at the first attempt and 140 at the second.[28]

## Two accounts

Infosys's account deserves to be stated at its strongest. In a statement quoted in the report and by *Deccan Herald*, the company said that all freshers, after foundational training at Mysuru, are expected to clear internal assessments. 'All freshers get three attempts to clear the assessment, failing which they will not be able to continue with the organisation, as is also mentioned in their contract,' it said, adding that the process had been in place 'for over two decades' and ensured 'a high quality of talent availability for our clients'.[29] On this view the test is quality control, in a training system that, later chapters argue, the firms built because colleges did not teach what they needed. In a later round the termination email listed what the company had provided: 'additional preparation time, doubt-clearing sessions, several mock assessments and three attempts'.[30] Infosys offered those let go help with finding other work, courses through the training firms NIIT and UpGrad, and a route into its business-process arm.[31]

The trainees and the union saw a company reducing a batch it no longer wanted. *Outlook Business* reported that termination rates at the assessment had risen from under 10 per cent to between 30 and 40 per cent, and unnamed current Infosys employees told the magazine that 'an excess of resources and fewer projects' lay behind it.[32] The two accounts are not simply opposed: the process could be old, as the company said, and the bar could have been raised, as the trainees said. Alagunambi Welkin, general secretary of the Union of IT and ITES Employees, said that companies hire large numbers 'as a result of poor decision making by the management' and, when money is short, 'sack the employees instead of taking accountability'.[33]

Even the number let go is disputed: Infosys said about 300 in February, the report estimated 400, and NITES, in its complaint to the Labour Ministry, said about 700.[34] The departures did not stop. By one count in the financial press, about 35 more trainees went in March, 240 on 18 April and 195 later that month, almost 800 since February.[35]

The state did not agree with itself. On 13 February 2025 the Union Labour Ministry directed Karnataka's Labour Department to take 'urgent necessary actions to resolve the dispute'.[36] But the Karnataka department, according to an unnamed source quoted by the financial news site Moneycontrol, concluded that no layoff had occurred at all: 'They were all apprenticeship trainees, not employees.'[37] If that was right, the law on retrenchment did not apply. NITES then complained to the skills ministry that the apprenticeship law itself had been broken, and no outcome has been reported.[38] Whether the trainees were wronged in law is unsettled. What is clear is that two levels of the Indian state disagreed about whether this was a labour question at all.

## The same years, from the top

From the top, the same years looked like growth. In February 2026 Nasscom (the National Association of Software and Service Companies), the industry's lobby group, reported that India's technology industry would earn $315 billion in the year to March 2026, up 6.1 per cent, with 5.95 million direct employees after 135,000 net additions.[39] Its president, Rajesh Nambiar, acknowledged that jobs were growing more slowly than revenue, 2.3 per cent against 6.1, a gap he called a non-linearity.[40]

That word, in this book's reading, names the bargain on which the whole industry was built, at the moment it began to come apart. For half a century Indian software firms sold, above all, the time of their engineers. A firm that sells time can grow only by selling more of it, so revenue rose with headcount, and the factory had to keep hiring graduates like Gayatri by the tens of thousands. Colleges, training campuses and offer letters were all arranged around that fact. A non-linearity is the opposite: revenue rising faster than the number of people needed to earn it. A gap of 2.3 per cent against 6.1 is small, but it runs against the logic of everything that came before. Artificial intelligence tools press on the bargain at its centre, because what they promise to shrink is the time it takes to write and test code, and that time is exactly what was being billed.

The largest firm shows how unsettled the picture still is. In April 2026 K. Krithivasan, chief executive of TCS, said the company had made 25,000 offers to freshers for the coming year and that clarity on demand would lead to more hiring, and by the end of September, by the company's figures as reported, about 24,000 freshers had joined in the year's first two quarters.[41]

The factory, then, had not stopped. The waits that Gayatri and thousands of others endured began in 2022, in what the report called the 2022 lull in the IT industry.[42] Infosys's annual reports to the American regulator mentioned AI in general terms before then, but did not mention AI code generation until the one for the year to March 2024, filed in June 2024.[43] So the first answer to the obvious question, whether artificial intelligence caused all this, is that the waits began about two years before AI code generation appeared in Infosys's own account of the risks to its business. That does not make the question smaller. On this evidence the bargain was already under strain when the tools arrived, and the tools work on the very hours the bargain sold. How much they have added since is weighed in Chapter 19, and it is the question that makes the history worth telling.

## The question

The question this book asks is how India came to build software engineering, as an education and as a profession, and what AI does to what was built. Gayatri's offer letter was the product of a long chain of decisions, made in planning offices and boardrooms, in classrooms, on export contracts that priced Indian programmers by the hour, and in visa offices abroad. The training campus where her career ended is one of the last links. It exists because colleges and companies spent decades arguing over who should teach the engineer what the job required.

The chain starts long before there was an industry, in two research institutes where computers were scientific instruments and nobody yet thought of programming as a job. In 1955, the computer scientist V. Rajaraman records in his history of Indian computing, only a few dozen scientists and engineers in India knew about computers; by 2010 more than 2.4 million people were employed in computer-related jobs.[44] Between those two numbers lies a bargain that held for half a century: India came to train its engineers by the hundred thousand and sold their time to the world. Gayatri's offer letter was a promise that the selling would go on. Whether it does, now that machines can shorten the hours themselves, will decide what the next offer letter is worth, and whether a joining date comes with it.



# Part I: Before software (1940s-1977)

# Chapter 1. The statistician's machines (1931-1966)

In February 1959 a small team of physicists and engineers in Bombay (Mumbai since 1995) finished assembling a computer, and then had to stop work on it. The machine stood in the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR), which had been working on it since 1955. It held 2,700 vacuum tubes and drew around 18 kilowatts, and the institute had no suitably air-conditioned room in which to run it.[1] 'Unfortunately, owing to the lack of air-conditioning facilities, the work had to be suspended till almost the end of 1959,' its designer, R. Narasimhan, wrote a few weeks after the machine finally entered service.[2] Testing began only in mid-November, with an auxiliary air-conditioning system brought in for the purpose, and the computer was commissioned for routine work in the third week of February 1960.[3]

The men who built it had learned as they went. When the project began, the team numbered about six, most with a master's degree in physics and a specialism in electronics. Narasimhan described them in 1999: 'Except for one member (namely, myself), none had been outside India, and none of the participants in the project, including myself, had any experience in either using a computer or operating one, let alone building one.'[4] Their machine would later be named TIFRAC, and Narasimhan would call it 'the first fullscale electronic digital computer designed, built, and operated in India'.[5]

A year's delay for want of an air conditioner is a small story, but it holds much of what follows. India's first computers were acquired, and in one case built, by a handful of scientists working for the state. They were limited less by ideas than by things that had to be paid for in foreign currency or manufactured at scale: machines, spare parts, cooling, memory. And the most lasting thing they produced was not hardware. It was a small group of people who now knew how computers worked.

The state had already named the value of such people, though not with computers in mind. In March 1958, while the TIFR team was still wiring its machine, the Government of India adopted a Scientific Policy Resolution. It declared that 'Science and technology can make up for deficiencies in raw materials by providing substitutes, or, indeed, by providing skills which can be exported in return for raw materials.'[6] The resolution was about science in general. Beyond it, notes V. Rajaraman, a computer scientist who later wrote a history of Indian computing, 'there was no government policy on computers'.[7] Read with hindsight, though, the sentence describes, decades early, the bargain on which India's software industry would be built: not machines, but skills, sold abroad in return for what the country lacked.

Two institutions, in two cities, took two different routes to the first computers. In Calcutta (Kolkata since 2001), the Indian Statistical Institute (ISI) bought its machines, first from Britain and then from the Soviet Union. In Bombay, TIFR decided to build one. By the mid-1960s both had arrived at the same place. ISI's attempt to build a machine of its own failed, and TIFR, having built TIFRAC, chose to buy an American computer to replace it.

## Computers before machines

The Indian Statistical Institute was founded in Calcutta in 1931 under Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis.[8] In its early decades the word 'computer' meant a person: Mahalanobis designated some of the institute's statistical staff as computers, and they calculated and tabulated its large sample surveys, beginning with those of the jute crop.[9] By late 1951 the institute had two new models of IBM tabulators, the punched-card machines then used for counting and sorting large volumes of records.[10]

What turned this into a demand for electronic computers was national planning. Mahalanobis helped set up the National Sample Survey in 1950, a continuing household survey that produced data on a scale no team of clerks could tabulate quickly.[11] The historian Nikhil Menon argues that the decision to plan India's economy from the centre, and the 'explosion of official statistics' that came with it, provided the justification for the pursuit of computers; ISI's influence culminated in its effectively authoring the Second Five Year Plan of 1956-61, a plan with an emphasis on heavy industry in the public sector.[12] India sought computers for planning and development, not for military use.[13] A plan of that size, built from survey data, needed arithmetic that a room of clerks with tabulators could not supply quickly enough. That, more than any interest in the machines themselves, is why a statistician became India's first buyer of computers.

Mahalanobis first saw an electronic computer at Harvard in 1947.[14] By 1953 ISI's computing laboratory, opened three years earlier under the engineer S.K. Mitra, had built an analogue computer from Second World War surplus parts that could solve simultaneous linear equations in up to ten variables.[15] An analogue machine represents numbers as physical quantities such as voltages, rather than as digits, and it could not do the general-purpose arithmetic that planning required. Mahalanobis suspected that it would not be adequate.[16] He wanted a digital computer, and India could not make one.

## A Cold War shopping trip

For four years Mahalanobis tried to buy an American machine. Between 1950 and 1954 he held informal talks in Washington about acquiring a UNIVAC, a machine famous in American popular culture, on which he had been fixed since the 1940s; the best American machines would cost a million dollars.[17] The talks failed. One reason, Menon found, was a secret dispatch sent from the US Embassy in Delhi to the State Department in 1953, which described Mahalanobis as a Soviet sympathiser.[18]

He turned east. In February 1954, at a lunch hosted by Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, Mahalanobis pressed the Soviet ambassador, Mikhail Menshikov, for help with a computer, arguing in effect that the Soviet Union could hardly object to sharing what the Americans already knew.[19] That spring and summer he travelled through Geneva, London and Prague to Moscow, writing about computers to his colleague Pitambar Pant as he went.[20] In Moscow he, Mitra and a delegation of Indian scientists visited the Institute of Precision Mechanics and Computer Engineering, which was building a computer with the backing of Nikita Khrushchev, and Mahalanobis persuaded the Soviet authorities to supply India with a machine.[21] Some eight months after the Menshikov meeting, according to Kris Gopalakrishnan and his co-authors, the Soviet Union and the United Nations agreed to fund India's purchase of a digital computer, which they identify as the British HEC-2M.[22]

## A computer without support

The first electronic digital computer to work in India was British, and it came on hard terms. Mahalanobis ordered it from the British Tabulating Machine Company (BTM), which sold keypunches, sorters and mechanical calculators in India. 'BTM agreed to sell a computer to the ISI in 1954 though without any technical support,' Rajaraman writes. 'The ISI was to install and maintain the machine using its own scientists and engineers.'[23] BTM would not install and maintain a single machine in India, he later explained, since only one was coming to the country.[24]

So ISI sent two engineers, Mohi (Monimohan) Mukherjee and Amresh Roy, to England in December 1954 to watch the machine being made. The Hollerith Electronic Computer Model 2M had been designed by A.D. Booth at Birkbeck College in London and was assembled in BTM's workshop, and the two men gathered there the knowledge they would need to install and keep it running.[25] It cost 18,500 pounds sterling, paid by the Government of India, which lent it to ISI.[26] It reached Calcutta in 1955 or early 1956.[27] Its memory, a rotating magnetic drum, held 1,024 words, and it had to be programmed in binary machine code through punched cards.[28] 'Around a dozen people learnt to program the computer which was used for some statistical calculations,' Rajaraman writes.[29] It also handled requests from the Planning Commission, the National Sample Survey and other scientific institutions, and, in his words, it 'was found to be a very difficult machine to use'.[30]

The dozen people who learned to program it make up most of India's computing profession in the mid-1950s. 'In 1955 only a few dozen scientists and engineers in India knew about computers,' Rajaraman writes.[31] There were no courses to take. What they knew came from watching machines being assembled abroad and from operating manuals.

## The URAL and the Russian manuals

Mahalanobis started looking for a second machine, and the obstacle was money from abroad. It was difficult to get funds, Rajaraman notes, 'particularly foreign exchange funds'.[32] A computer had to be paid for in dollars or pounds, not rupees. The solution again came from the Soviet side. A URAL-1, a first-generation vacuum-tube machine that could perform about 12,000 operations a second, was ordered in 1958 with United Nations assistance.[33] Eight Russian engineers installed it.[34] 'All the manuals were in Russian and the ISI engineers learnt Russian to enable them to maintain the machine,' Rajaraman writes.[35] When it was unveiled in Calcutta in December 1958, the *Times of India* reported that it could calculate 600 times faster than a single man.[36]

With two working computers and a group of people who could program and maintain them, ISI was, in Rajaraman's phrase, 'the de-facto National Computer Centre' of India in 1958.[37] Its users included universities, the atomic energy establishment and defence laboratories, among them Andhra University, the Indian Institute of Science in Bangalore (Bengaluru since 2014), the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) at Kharagpur and TIFR.[38] India had taken a British machine with no support and a Soviet one with eight engineers and Russian manuals, because its attempt to obtain the American machine it wanted had been hampered by Cold War suspicion. Non-alignment allowed it to buy from both sides, but on terms the sellers set.

Expertise was so thin that Mahalanobis went looking for it in odd places. In February 1959 Morton Nadler, a 37-year-old American engineer, flew from Prague to Calcutta to take a two-year contract at ISI.[39] Nadler, who had joined the Communist Party in 1936 and renounced his US citizenship after the American embassy seized his passport in 1950, had worked at Czechoslovakia's Institute of Mathematical Machines and, by Menon's account, was under suspicion of espionage by both the American and the Czechoslovak authorities. Disillusioned with communism, he could neither leave Czechoslovakia easily nor go home, and Mahalanobis's offer gave him a way out.[40] His lectures at ISI in the spring of 1959 became a book, *Topics in Engineering Logic*, and in 1960 he left for the French computer maker Bull.[41]

## Bombay decides to build

The physicist Homi Bhabha founded TIFR in Bombay in 1945.[42] Computing work began there in 1954, and towards the end of that year TIFR decided, as Narasimhan put it, 'to design and build a fullscale, general purpose, electronic digital computer using contemporary technology'.[43] Narasimhan led the project, with Bhabha's 'acceptance and active support'.[44] He had an engineering degree from the College of Engineering, Guindy, in Madras (Chennai since 1996), and had spent 1948 to 1954 in the United States on a part-loan scholarship from the J.N. Tata Endowment.[45] With no one who had built a computer, the team worked in two stages: first a small pilot machine, to try out circuit and logic designs and to train the team on the job, and then a full-scale computer.[46]

The pilot was completed in 1956 and kept running for about a year.[47] Design of the full-scale machine began early in 1957, and its final assembly was completed in February 1959.[48] It was a stored-program machine with a memory of 1,024 forty-bit words held in ferrite cores, tiny magnetic rings that each stored one bit, and it could add two numbers in 45 microseconds.[49] The team made that memory with their own hands. P.V.S. Rao, a member of TIFR's computer group, described how they strung the matrix together themselves, threading hair-thin enamelled wire through magnetic cores less than a millimetre across, held in Plexiglass frames.[50]

They did not work entirely alone. 'The TIFRAC control logic design benefited crucially through design details kindly made available by the ILLIAC team,' Narasimhan wrote in 1999, referring to the computer group at the University of Illinois.[51] Mahalanobis could not buy an American computer in Washington; Narasimhan was given American design details, scientist to scientist.

## A name, and a verdict

The machine entered routine service in February 1960, and when Nehru inaugurated TIFR's new building in 1962, he named it TIFRAC.[52] It ran until early 1964, by the end working two shifts a day.[53] Its users were TIFR's own scientists, the Atomic Energy Establishment and some universities, and the analysis of TIFR's cosmic-ray air-shower experiments, Narasimhan wrote, would not have been feasible without it.[54] Its storage was too small to attempt a compiler, the program that translates instructions written in a human-readable language into machine code.[55]

Narasimhan's judgement of his own machine was unsentimental. The pilot, he wrote in 1999, had been close to the state of the art in 1954, and the 1957 design not very far behind it. But by the time it was commissioned in 1960, TIFRAC was 'an obsolete first generation machine'.[56] The second generation of computers, built with transistors, needed production know-how that only large manufacturers had.[57] A research institute could build one machine. It could not build the next generation, and it could not build many.

What TIFRAC left behind was people. The computer section had grown from about half a dozen members to some two dozen, with a 'hard core of specialists' who could design digital equipment and a group that had learned to maintain complex electronic systems.[58] And, in Narasimhan's words, 'many of the computer users in India, handling sophisticated and advanced computational techniques, had their first introduction to programming through the use of TIFRAC.'[59]

## The first to leave

Some of those people left. Between 1959 and 1962 about half a dozen of the scientists who had designed and built TIFRAC took visiting appointments at American universities. Three of them settled permanently in the United States; others came back.[60] Narasimhan himself spent the early 1960s as a visiting scientist at the Digital Computer Laboratory of the University of Illinois.[61] Three people are not a brain drain. But the pattern would recur at much larger scale. India trained engineers at public expense, often on projects that could not employ them for long, and the United States offered the next stage of their careers.

## From building to buying

The engineers who went to America also helped TIFR decide what to do next. Because some of its staff now knew American machines at first hand, TIFR could set up an expert committee, chaired by Narasimhan, to compare the large commercial systems on offer. It recommended the CDC 3600, of which only one was then in operation, at its maker's plant in Minneapolis.[62] Rajaraman calls it 'a bold decision'.[63] The machine was bought for $1.5 million, with funds from the United States Agency for International Development that Bhabha persuaded the Government of India to arrange.[64] Installed in mid-1964, it ran from October that year as a National Computation Centre, maintained and operated by TIFR staff once the manufacturer's early support ended, and over 150 institutions from across India used it for more than a decade.[65] In the first year users had the machine free of charge. The only demand on them was that they write and debug their own programs, and to help them TIFR's staff programmers ran 'many short courses on programming'.[66]

So the institute that had built India's first computer bought an American one with American aid money, on the recommendation of the man who had led the building. Narasimhan saw no contradiction. Once second-generation machines required production know-how that only large manufacturers had, he judged, TIFR was 'wise' to look to the world market.[67]

## The end of building, for now

ISI tried once more. In the early 1960s it set out to build a transistorised computer jointly with Jadavpur University in Calcutta. The machine, called ISIJU, was completed in 1966, but in Rajaraman's words 'It was not a successful project as the computer was unreliable and did not have appropriate software.'[68] Menon counts 15 digital computers in India by the end of 1964.[69] The state still had no policy on computers; a national committee on electronics was appointed only in 1963, under Bhabha, after the 1962 war with China.[70] In the autumn of 1965 the Planning Commission opened its own computer centre in Delhi, an IBM 1620 bought with a Ford Foundation grant of Rs 2.3 million (about $462,000), run 'open shop' for outside users.[71] The planners who had once queued for time on ISI's machines now had one of their own, made by IBM.

## Two explanations

Why did these beginnings not lead to an Indian computer industry? Narasimhan's answer was the economics of manufacturing: a research group could build a first-generation machine, but only large manufacturers could build the second generation, and build it in numbers.[72] A different answer comes from Dwaipayan Banerjee of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, in *Computing in the Age of Decolonization* (2026). As its publisher and reviewers describe it, the book argues that India's attempt to build a self-reliant computing industry was blocked, chiefly from outside, by Cold War politics, trade imbalances and the monopolies of American corporations, and also by the preference of India's technocratic elite for profitable technical services; Angela Saini quotes its judgement that by the mid-1960s IBM's dominance of Indian computing was 'nearly absolute'.[73] Tracie Farrell reports that it contrasts IBM with Control Data, the maker of TIFR's CDC 3600, which in the book's words, as she quotes them, was 'treating Indian researchers as peers'.[74] The record of the 1950s fits parts of both answers.

## Coda: from building machines to teaching people

By 1966 the experiment of the 1950s had reached its end. ISI's own machine had failed, TIFRAC had been retired, and the best computer in the country was American. What remained was the people who had learned their trade on TIFRAC and the URAL, and the users who had learned to write their own programs on the CDC 3600. The resolution of 1958 had spoken of skills that could be exported in return for what India lacked. In 1966 nothing was being exported, but the one thing India's first computers had reliably produced was exactly those skills. The country had learned that it could make computer people more easily than it could make computers.

The next step was to train more of them, in classrooms rather than workshops. Chapter 2 tells how a new campus at Kanpur, in Uttar Pradesh, became the place where India first taught computing as a subject, and where the engineer factory began.


# Chapter 2. Kanpur, 1963 (1946-1978)

In July 1963 a chartered DC-7 landed at a military airbase in Kanpur, a large city on the Ganges in Uttar Pradesh. In its hold was an IBM 1620, a small transistorised computer of a model common in American universities.[1] It was bound for the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) at Kanpur, which was then three years old. At the institute, in the historian Ross Bassett's words, 'a group of young Indian men muscled the machine into place'.[2] Waiting for it was Harry Huskey of the University of California at Berkeley, who had consulted on the pioneering American computer ENIAC and had worked with Alan Turing in England.[3]

The machine had been planned before there was a building to put it in. Its delivery date had been set by the earliest moment that a room could hold it.[4] The computer room was still unfinished. 'This is monsoon season, by the way, in the middle of July,' Huskey recalled for the Computer History Museum in 2006, and the crated machine was set down in about an inch of water.[5] Because the 1620 had been paid for with American aid under a 'buy America clause', it was built for 60-cycle power, while India's supply ran at 50 cycles. It took telegrams to IBM and a converter found in Germany before, 'in about three weeks', the machine was running.[6] With two colleagues from Princeton, Forman Acton and Irving Rabinowitz, Huskey showed it to the institute's Board of Governors in late August.[7] V. Rajaraman, who joined the Kanpur faculty that year and later wrote a history of Indian computing, calls it the first computer with a FORTRAN compiler in any Indian educational institution. A compiler is software that translates a program written in a high-level language such as FORTRAN into the machine's own instructions.[8]

Once it ran, the three Americans began an informal course for twenty-five first-year students, chosen for the purpose. After their ordinary classes, the students 'would stay long into the night programming the computer'.[9]

Kanpur was not the first place in India with a computer, although Huskey came to remember it that way. 'So I think our computer center was the first such in India,' he said.[10] The Indian Statistical Institute and the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research had working machines years earlier (Chapter 1). Kanpur was the first place where a computer was put at the centre of an engineering education, where every student was required to program, and where computer science was first taught as a subject of its own. It was also, from its first graduating year, a door to the United States. This is where the factory's raw material begins: an engineer trained in English, to an American standard, on American machines, and therefore exportable. The education was built to serve India, and a large share of its best products went to America.

## The standard of MIT

The engineering colleges the British founded in India had a limited purpose: to prepare Indians for subordinate posts under British rule.[11] The idea of something grander came from a British scientist. In 1944 A.V. Hill, a Nobel laureate who was advising the government of British India, noted that India had no institution like the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), and recommended one or two technical institutes 'of the highest possible standing'.[12] A committee chaired by N.R. Sarker proposed four in 1946, spread across the regions of India, to train students to the standard of MIT.[13] The first Indian Institute of Technology opened at Kharagpur, west of Calcutta (Kolkata since 2001), in 1951, with help from the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union and UNESCO.[14]

For the next four, the government gave each institute a single foreign patron. The Soviet Union supported Bombay (Mumbai since 1995), which opened in 1958; West Germany supported Madras (Chennai since 1996), opened in 1959; the United States took Kanpur, opened in 1960; and Britain supported Delhi, which began in 1963.[15] For a while the IITs were different experiments under one name. Madras built a curriculum heavy with practical training in manual skills such as blacksmithing and woodworking, and its first computer was a surplus analogue machine that had belonged to an American university.[16] At Bombay the first director said in 1961 that he had turned down a Soviet Ural-I computer because it cost too much.[17] The common belief that the IITs were modelled on MIT is therefore half right. MIT was the standard the planners named, but four of the five early institutes had non-American patrons. Kanpur came closest to the American model, and it was the American model that won.[18]

The turn to America predated Kanpur. Before the Second World War between one and two thousand Indian students a year studied in Britain, and at most 208 in the United States. In 1944 the government of British India began paying for Indian students at American universities, and by 1949-50 there were 1,680 Indian students in America and fewer than 700 in Britain.[19] Bassett's larger argument is that the alignment was chosen, not imposed. An Indian technical elite educated in America built ties with American firms, universities and, at times, the American government, and kept them through the worst years of relations between the two states.[20] Kanpur was that elite's most important project.

## A director reads a book

By 1958 India and the United States had informally agreed that America would help build the IIT at Kanpur. Delays meant that the institute opened in 1960 without American help.[21] Its first director, P.K. Kelkar, was an electrical engineer with a 1936 doctorate from the University of Liverpool. He had taught at the Victoria Jubilee Technical Institute in Bombay and had been chief planning officer for IIT Bombay, working closely with its Soviet sponsors.[22]

In a memoir written after he retired, and never published, Kelkar described the moment his thinking turned. He read the proceedings of a 1957 conference of American engineering deans, which described how their schools were reorganising teaching around 'engineering science': a common scientific foundation beneath the separate branches of engineering.[23] The volume's other theme was the computer. One contributor called it 'the embodiment of a new attitude toward the utilization of ideas', which would become, like the library, the intellectual hub of a university.[24] Another, Gordon Brown, the dean of engineering at MIT, defined the modern engineer as someone who 'builds mechanisms to program, to control or to compute with lightning-like speed'.[25]

The engineering-science model had won in America partly because engineering schools wanted military research funding. Its rhetoric, Bassett argues, was broad enough to appeal to Kelkar, an idealist who had come to engineering through physics.[26] The computer was central to his plan from the start. Even before any American programme was in place, he planned to buy an IBM machine with American funds and to have physicists at Delhi University train his faculty to use it.[27]

Kelkar also brought with him a connection that would matter later. In the late 1950s, at the Victoria Jubilee Technical Institute, he and F.C. Kohli, an MIT-trained control engineer working for Tata Electric, had started a master's course in control engineering. Brown, the MIT dean, had been one of Kohli's professors.[28]

## Arrival at Kanpur Central

The first hundred undergraduates arrived in July 1960.[29] The institute had no campus of its own. Abhay Bhushan, who holds roll number 60001 and so counts as Kanpur's first student, later wrote a three-part account of those years. He remembers arriving at Kanpur Central station with a few coins in his pocket and being collected by truck with other boys from all over the country.[30] They lived in a hostel borrowed from the Government Central Textile Institute in Gwaltoli, and attended classes and laboratories at the Harcourt Butler Technological Institute.[31] Fewer than seventy lived in the hostel, two to a room; the food, from a contractor, was by his account generally poor.[32] The first classes on the new campus were held in its workshop building in 1963.[33]

Not one of the hundred who started was a woman. When students put on plays, boys took the women's parts.[34] The absence was so ordinary that it shaped the language of the people describing the place. Peter Fay, a Caltech historian who taught at Kanpur from 1964 to 1966, described the last two undergraduate years as professional training in the branch of engineering 'which the boy or the boy's father has chosen'.[35]

Entry was by a common examination taken across India.[36] Teaching was in English, and Fay reported that only a fraction of the students were thoroughly comfortable in it. The English paper in the entrance examination had a pass mark set deliberately low, so as not to exclude promising engineers, and the first-year English course had largely become a language course.[37] Bhushan's first-year teachers, he wrote, had been borrowed from the colleges of Uttar Pradesh and taught by memory and rote, even in mathematics; in the second year new teachers arrived, many with doctorates from the United States, Canada and Britain.[38]

## Influence, not power

American help arrived after the students. In January 1961 MIT sent three professors to India, and their report proposed a consortium of American universities with MIT informally at its head.[39] Later that year the two governments and nine universities, among them MIT, Caltech, Princeton, Berkeley and Purdue, agreed to set up the Kanpur Indo-American Program, known as KIAP. Stanford was asked and declined.[40] Early in 1962 the US Agency for International Development (USAID) contracted with the nine through an agent, and American faculty began to arrive.[41] The programme was meant to last ten years.[42] It ended in 1972.[43]

Fay's report from Kanpur is the fullest contemporary description of what this meant on the ground. The Americans were contract employees of the aid agency. They lived in houses it rented for them, drew flour, sugar and Scotch from the commissary in New Delhi, and were paid in dollars through their home universities.[44] At their peak there were about thirty of them; by 1966 there were twenty, and falling.[45] They sat on the committees that appointed faculty, but without a vote, and were often not even consulted on promotions. Where an Indian could head a department, an American did not.[46] They also held periodic morning meetings of their own, to which their Indian colleagues were not invited. Fay's examples of what came up there include equipment 'lying in the rain at Delhi airport waiting for customs', and how to get out of Kanpur in a hurry during 'the fighting last September, when the city was blacked out and Americans in the Punjab were all ordered to Delhi', the war with Pakistan of September 1965. In his own case, he added, the problem was leaving without abandoning 'a four-foot Benares brass tray'.[47]

A first-year student from Delhi told Fay that he had chosen Kanpur over the IIT near his home because 'you Americans run this one'. Fay replied that he sometimes wished they did. 'For the fact is we have influence; we do not have power.'[48] He was frank about the hurry the arrangement imposed: 'For we have always been in a hurry. The program is to run for only ten years, and individuals never stay for more than two.'[49]

Influence still bought a great deal. Drawing on a 1972 dissertation by Kim Patrick Sebaly, Bassett estimates that the American contribution to Kanpur, in equipment and visiting faculty, was twice what the Soviet Union gave Bombay or West Germany gave Madras, and three times what Britain gave Delhi.[50] By November 1965 more than $4 million of equipment and books had been ordered from the United States. Fay judged that Kanpur was 'already the best equipped engineering and science school in India', and that this had helped it attract faculty.[51] The student thought the Americans ran Kanpur; Fay thought they had influence and not power; Bassett reads the alignment as chosen by Indian elites for their own ends. All three can be true at once: the money and the model were American, the appointments and the institution were Indian.[52]

## Learning on the fly

Kelkar chose most of his permanent faculty from among Indians with American doctorates, many of them recruited while they were working or teaching in the United States.[53] By 1966 Kanpur had about seventy-five faculty at assistant professor level or above. All but four were under forty. All held doctorates or equivalent degrees: over half from the United States and Canada, a dozen from Britain or elsewhere in Europe.[54]

The people who would run the computer centre came by the same route. H.K. Kesavan, who had a doctorate from Michigan State and had been a professor at Waterloo in Canada, arrived in January 1964 to head electrical engineering, and in May became the first head of the computer centre. Rajaraman had arrived in 1963, with a master's from MIT and a doctorate from Wisconsin in analogue computation. Two of Kesavan's former colleagues at Waterloo, H.N. Mahabala and T.R. Viswanathan, followed.[55] None of them had been trained as computer scientists, because almost nobody had. Rajaraman and Mahabala obtained their computing education, in Bassett's phrase, 'on the fly, without formal training'.[56] The first teachers of computing in India were electrical engineers who taught themselves, and then taught others.

## Switching it on

Among the students who took to the machine was Ravi Sethi, a first-year in the autumn of 1963. In a recollection published in 2021 in *The Spark*, a student magazine of the 1960s revived by IIT Kanpur alumni, he describes taking an evening course from Acton after the midterm examinations, and being one of six students selected to operate the 1620. He remembers being authorised to switch it on as an event in itself.[57] Programs were punched on cards, one line of code to a card. From the blinking lights on the console, the students learned to tell when a program had fallen into a loop. Rabinowitz once challenged Sethi to write a program that would copy a deck of cards and fit on a single card, which meant six instructions or fewer. The machine needed its generators running, and then its air conditioning, before it could be turned on. Sethi spent the following summer working for Huskey on a compiler.[58]

By February 1964 the 1620 was running twenty-four hours a day, and by April the centre was open to students around the clock.[59] Undergraduates worked there as programmers. Among them were Sethi, who later became a senior manager at Bell Labs; Jayadev Misra, later head of electrical engineering at the University of Texas at Austin; and Raj Kanodia, who would help connect MIT to the ARPANET.[60]

From the spring of 1964 every student at Kanpur was trained in computing.[61] Rajaraman describes it as a compulsory course in programming and numerical methods for all engineering students, and claims it as a first in India.[62] Kelkar, speaking at Berkeley in 1968, described the effect: 'we soon became aware of the compelling power of the computer. It exercised a unique fascination over the minds of not only post-doctorals, but also freshmen'.[63]

The faculty moved quickly to make the subject a discipline. An M.Tech programme in computers followed in the mid-1960s, which IIT Kanpur's own account calls the first time computer science was offered as an academic discipline in India.[64] The institute's catalogue for 1969 listed a full range of undergraduate and graduate courses, including software engineering, information theory, hardware design and image processing.[65] Rajaraman published an introductory textbook, *Principles of Computer Programming*, in 1969, and later texts on FORTRAN and COBOL.[66]

## Missionaries

The three Americans who set up the 1620 saw their job as spreading the gospel of computing across India. They lectured at research institutes and universities including the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, IIT Madras and the Indian Statistical Institute, and gave a special session for fifteen members of the Planning Commission.[67]

Their lasting contribution was a ten-day course for people from institutions that might one day use computers. Huskey opened it to scientists, engineers and teachers from across India rather than restricting it to Kanpur's own faculty.[68] The course taught programming, numerical methods and computer logic, in a variant of FORTRAN called FORGO, with hands-on laboratory sessions.[69] Each course had about fifty or sixty participants, and it ran three or four times a year.[70] By August 1965, 600 people from fifty institutions had taken it, from other IITs, engineering colleges, national laboratories, government agencies and private firms.[71] Indian faculty kept it going after the Americans left; Rajaraman says it ran until 1975 and trained over 1,500 people.[72]

The Kanpur faculty taught the course, as Bassett puts it from Mahabala's recollections, 'with an almost religious sense of mission', in many cases driving to the railway station ten miles away themselves to collect participants, while their wives cooked the meals.[73] Kelkar's claim at Berkeley in 1968 was that 'there is hardly a computer installation where there is nobody who had been to Kanpur at least once.'[74] The claim cannot be tested, but it was not far-fetched. A government committee later counted thirty computers in the whole of India in 1965, and a course that had trained 600 people by August of that year had reached a large part of the small world of Indian computing.[75]

## A dead crow on the world market

The 1620 was a good first machine, small, simple and needing little staff, but within a year Kanpur had used up its capacity.[76] It had cost roughly $320,000 before IBM's 60 per cent educational discount.[77] The institute's second computer was a much bigger purchase: an IBM 7044, which arrived in 1966 and made Kanpur home to one of the most powerful computers in India.[78]

How it was paid for matters to the rest of this book. The 7044's list price was $3 million. IBM gave Kanpur its standard educational discount, and also 'allowed it to pay in rupees', which Bassett calls 'a major concession to a country for which foreign exchange was precious'.[79] The money came from the Government of India.[80] Foreign exchange was the binding constraint on Indian computing for the next quarter-century. A machine bought in rupees escaped it.

The concession had a cost. The 7044 had been introduced in 1961 as a stopgap while IBM developed its System/360, and by 1969 IBM was phasing it out. Neither IBM India nor its American parent helped the institute obtain new software.[81] Kanpur students had been learning FORTRAN II, which the student newspaper, *Spark*, called 'almost a dead crow on the world market'.[82] The response was the first of many Indian adaptations to old hardware. In 1970 Kanpur undergraduates wrote what Bassett calls 'the first compiler written in India', which brought features of newer versions of FORTRAN to a machine never designed for them.[83] KIAP ended in 1972 with no second phase, and with no American money for a replacement Kanpur kept its 7044 until 1979.[84]

Other IITs fared worse. At Bombay a Soviet Minsk II computer, delivered through UNESCO in 1965, stood in storage for two years while the Soviet Union and UNESCO negotiated who would pay for the technicians to install it; it began working in January 1968, running a Soviet programming language rather than FORTRAN.[85] Madras overtook Kanpur by a different route. In 1971 West Germany agreed to give IIT Madras a computer, and Mahabala, who had moved there from Kanpur, persuaded the Germans to buy an IBM machine. The IBM 370/155 inaugurated at Madras in November 1973 was the most powerful computer in India.[86]

Kanpur's enthusiasm was not the national mood: Indian unions called computers 'job eaters', and the government did not study the question seriously until the late 1960s.[87] What connected Kanpur to the wider country was IBM. A 1974 survey counted 217 computers installed in India: 65 per cent made by IBM, 13 per cent by the British firm ICL and 11 per cent by the Indian public-sector firm Electronics Corporation of India Limited (ECIL).[88] 'Simultaneity is not causality,' Bassett writes, 'but an American-oriented program of engineering education in India and an American computing firm did reinforce each other.'[89] Kanpur taught people to program IBM machines, and IBM sold the machines they programmed.

## The road out

Kelkar and the Americans who designed KIAP had meant to build an Indian institute that would train engineers to solve Indian problems. The students partly defeated that aim by making Kanpur what its name already implied: 'the Indian MIT', and a step towards the American one.[90] In 1965-66 almost 7,000 Indians were studying in the United States, and at MIT in 1966 only Canada sent more students than India's eighty-two.[91] For its best undergraduates Kanpur was often only a step towards the best American graduate programmes, while its own graduate courses drew mainly students from further down India's educational hierarchy.[92]

Law made the step permanent. Before 1965 national quotas severely restricted permanent Indian immigration to the United States, and Indian engineers could study in America but were generally not allowed to stay and work. In 1965, the year of Kanpur's first graduating class, President Lyndon Johnson signed a law that abolished the quotas and made it much easier for Indians to settle.[93] Sixty-six of Kanpur's first hundred students graduated that May.[94] Bhushan went to MIT on a research assistantship.[95] An email list of the first batch showed that roughly a third were living in the United States in 2005.[96] The most thorough study of IIT emigration, made at Bombay by S.P. Sukhatme, found that slightly over 40 per cent of the institute's electrical engineering graduates of 1973 to 1977 had ended up abroad, the great majority in the United States.[97] No comparable figure exists for Kanpur.[98]

Kanpur's graduates reached the centre of American computing within a few years. On 14 June 1971 the ARPANET's Network Working Group issued Request for Comments 176, a protocol document. Its four authors were listed as A. Bhushan and R. Kanodia of MIT, Robert Metcalfe of MIT, later the inventor of Ethernet, and Jon Postel of UCLA.[99] Bhushan chaired the working group that defined the File Transfer Protocol, a standard still used to move files between computers.[100] Two of the four names on that document had learned to program on a 1620 in Kanpur. In 2008 Bassett examined the faculty of the ten American computer science departments ranked highest in 1993. Thirty-eight had taken their first degree in India, ten of them from IIT Kanpur. It was, he wrote, 'enough to fill a good-sized department'.[101]

## Twenty seats

Until 1978 computing at Kanpur lived inside electrical engineering. That year the institute created a bachelor's degree in computer science, the first at any IIT.[102] Rajaraman, who led the effort, recalled that the senate had 'grudgingly allowed 20 students' into the programme, because it did not think computer science was mainstream engineering.[103]

Admission to every IIT seat was by rank in the Joint Entrance Examination. In 1978 over 100,000 students sat it for about 1,500 places.[104] The highest-ranked candidate chose any seat at any IIT, the next chose from what remained, and so on down.[105] Arjun Malhotra, later a co-founder of the computer firm HCL, described the arithmetic to the Computer History Museum in 2018. Sitting the examination in the mid-1960s, he wanted one of the 30 places in IIT Kharagpur's electronics department and told himself that with 'a rank of 30 or less, then no one can take my first choice away from me'. He came 32nd, and got in because candidates ranked above him chose other courses.[106] In 1978 the students' choice was decisive. 'Students and their parents were very apprehensive about this new programme,' Rajaraman recalled in 2018. 'The greatest surprise came when the JEE results were declared and the B.Tech programme closed at an AIR of 40,' AIR being the all-India rank.[107] About half of India's top forty candidates had chosen a subject the senate had not considered mainstream engineering. The other IITs, Rajaraman writes, were surprised, and all of them started degrees in computer science.[108] Ten years later Kanpur's fourteen computer science seats were filled by rank 38.[109]

Where those students went is documented for the first class. Nineteen graduated in 1983. In 2007 Bassett traced seventeen through an alumni website. One had died. Of the other sixteen, fourteen lived in the United States, one in the Czech Republic and one in India.[110] Nine had doctorates and five held faculty posts in American computer science departments. Six lived in the San Francisco Bay Area, and at least three had founded companies. One, Rajeev Motwani of Stanford, was an early academic mentor to Larry Page and Sergey Brin in the work that led to Google.[111] Some Kanpur teachers, frustrated by the outflow, tried to stop it by refusing to write recommendation letters for students applying to American graduate schools. Bassett calls the attempt futile.[112]

## The road to industry

Kanpur never had a computer industry of its own, unlike MIT and Stanford, each of which seeded one nearby.[113] Its influence on Indian software ran through people.

The first of them was Kohli, Kelkar's old colleague from Bombay. Kelkar persuaded him to sit on Kanpur's electrical engineering selection committee and to visit the institute regularly. Kohli got his practical introduction to computing on Kanpur's 1620, and took computing back to Tata Electric in Bombay.[114] When the Tata group set up a computing business, Kohli moved to head it.[115] In the early years of what became Tata Consultancy Services, Mahabala spent his summers there as a consultant, and Kohli often hired Kanpur's master's graduates in computing.[116]

The second was N.R. Narayana Murthy. He had studied electrical engineering at the University of Mysore, meaning to become a hydroelectric engineer, and then took a master's degree at Kanpur, where he got 'hooked' on computing.[117] In his own account the turn came after a breakfast-table talk by a visiting professor from Princeton; within months he was running simulations through the night on the 7044. 'It was a macho thing to make the six tape units rotate fast.'[118] Each of the twelve students in his graduate class, he told the Computer History Museum in 2018, had four or five job offers from companies that had installed IBM 1401s. He took a job at half the salary with Jashwant Krishnayya, an MIT-trained professor at the Indian Institute of Management in Ahmedabad who had come to Kanpur to recruit engineers with computing skills, because Rajaraman advised him that he would learn how a time-sharing system worked.[119] It is the first price for programming skill in this book: a class of twelve choosing among some fifty offers. Murthy later joined Narendra Patni, whose firm was one of the first in India to get computing work from American companies, and left it in 1981 to found Infosys with colleagues.[120] Kanpur gave Murthy the ability; men like Patni and Kohli, already connected to American business, gave that ability its commercial force.[121]

The third large firm of the period has no Kanpur connection at all. Wipro was built by Azim Premji, a Stanford-educated electrical engineer who turned his family's cooking-oil business towards computers.[122] Kanpur was one route into the industry, not the only one.

## Coda: from the classroom to the state

In 1972 the American programme ended, and Kanpur's computer was already old. Kelkar had left two years earlier to direct IIT Bombay.[123] The government in Delhi had created a Department of Electronics in 1970 and was setting out to have India's computers designed and built in India by a public-sector company.[124] The state wanted machines made at home. Kanpur had already made the thing India would one day sell to the world: an engineer trained in English, to an American standard, on American machines. For now, many of the best of them left.


# Chapter 3. Self-reliance and its limits (1962-1977)

On 18 July 1968 the government of India called a special meeting of its Standing Labour Committee in New Delhi to discuss a single subject: automation. It was one of the tripartite bodies in which government, employers and trade unions argued out labour policy.[1] For this session the Ministry of Labour also invited workers' and employers' representatives from the Life Insurance Corporation (LIC), the State Bank of India, the railways and the oil companies, organisations that would not normally have had a seat at the table.[2] The machines that had brought them there were computers, and there were not many of them. The country had 30 computers in 1965 and 88 in 1968.[3]

The workers' side asked for something close to a ban. Their statement, as the government later printed it, argued that 'since the country had an enormous volume of unemployment and was short of technological and capital resources the general orientation of policy should be against automation'. Exceptions could be allowed where there was a real compulsion, but until guidelines were agreed there should be a freeze, and employers who had already installed automatic machinery should be asked to stop using it.[4] The employers replied that some concerns had become so large and complicated that computers were a necessity, that automation created more employment across the economy in the end, and that fears of large-scale displacement were unwarranted because automatic processes had been introduced in only a few establishments.[5] The Labour Minister of Maharashtra proposed a tripartite sub-committee, with experts, to draw up national guidelines.[6]

The meeting ended without agreement. Summing up, the Labour Minister said there was no consensus, that the government would bear the different views in mind, and that the existing procedure for screening computer imports would continue. In the meantime the government went on allowing automation 'on a selective basis'.[7]

The argument in that room did not end in 1968. It set a machine that could do part of the work of salaried office staff against the jobs of those staff, and it asked who should bear the cost and who should keep the gain. The employers said growth would absorb the people displaced. The workers said a poor country could not afford to make them redundant. Nearly six decades later the same argument returned, over software that could write software, and the office workers whose jobs were in question were the programmers whose industry this book follows. The book comes back to it in its last chapter.

Between the war with China in 1962 and the general election of 1977, the Indian state tried to do two things with computers at once. It wanted India to design and build its own, as a matter of national self-reliance. And it wanted to stop computers from taking the jobs of the country's organised clerical workers. Both aims grew out of scarcity: of foreign exchange, which India needed to buy machines abroad, and of jobs, which the computer seemed to threaten.

## Repainted machines

Before 1970, V. Rajaraman, the historian of Indian computing, writes, there was no government policy on computers beyond the 1958 Scientific Policy Resolution.[8] The rule that mattered was about money. 'Foreign companies were permitted to manufacture and sell computers provided foreign exchange was not required. Computers were not considered a priority area that deserved foreign exchange outflow.'[9]

IBM found a way to work within that rule. It had had a commercial outlet in India since 1950 and began manufacturing in 1963, making punched cards at a factory in Bangalore (Bengaluru since 2014) and, at Kurla in Bombay (Mumbai since 1995), the model 029 key punch (a machine for punching data onto cards) and other unit-record equipment.[10] The key punches were exported to IBM branches in South-East Asia, and the foreign exchange they earned paid for imports of used, disassembled IBM 1401 computers.[11] Around 1965 many 1401s were being replaced in America and Europe by IBM's new System/360, and IBM could import the old machines at a low inter-company price. In Bombay they were dismantled, their worn parts replaced, and then reassembled, painted and rented to Indian customers.[12] The government licensed IBM to recondition 68 of them over three years, from 1968 to 1970. IBM had applied to recondition System/360s instead.[13] Its British rival ICL ran the same trade from a plant in Poona (now Pune), exporting card equipment and using the proceeds to sell its systems in India.[14]

By 1970 the 1401 was the most popular computer in India, with about 80 installations. Indian Railways had more than a dozen; most Tata group companies and the big textile firms had them; the first computer at Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) was a 1401. For smaller firms IBM ran data centres in the major cities.[15] ICL, by comparison, had 48 of its 1901A machines assembled by the public-sector Bharat Electronics between 1965 and 1975.[16]

The machines were not cheap. The annual rental for a high-end 1401, with four tape drives and two disks, was about Rs 850,000, some $113,000 at the 1970 exchange rate.[17] The devaluation of the rupee in 1966 gave IBM a windfall, because its rentals were quoted in dollars.[18] IBM 'was in fact accused of profiteering', since rentals in America were much lower. Its defence was that the rental included free maintenance and the services of a systems engineer who analysed the customer's needs, designed the software and even helped with programming: IBM was selling a computing service, not renting a machine.[19] In that arrangement the engineer's time had no price of its own. It came bundled into the rent of the machine. The industry that grew up later would turn the arrangement round, and sell the time itself.

That service is where many Indians learned the trade. Rajaraman, who is not uncritical of IBM's prices, credits it with recruiting and training very good technical and sales staff. 'A whole generation of maintenance engineers and programmers were trained and nurtured by IBM. In short IBM set a bench mark for professional operations in India.'[20]

The state was already moving against the trade in repainted machines. By the early 1970s the new Department of Electronics had declared in its annual report that 'no further manufacturing programmes based on the renovation of 'As is' machines will be accepted in future as a matter of national policy'.[21] The question was what would replace them.

## A plan for 500 computers a year

The 1962 border war with China persuaded the government that electronics and communications mattered for defence and for long-run industrial growth. In 1963 it appointed a committee on electronics under Homi Bhabha, the chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission.[22] The committee's report was ready by 1966, but Bhabha was killed in an air crash before formally submitting it.[23] It was presented to the government only after his death, and a committee under Vikram Sarabhai was set up in 1966 to carry out its recommendations.[24] The central ones were a Department of Electronics in the central government and an Electronics Commission with wide financial and executive powers.[25]

The committee's computer subcommittee was chaired by R. Narasimhan, head of the computer group at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) in Bombay.[26] It projected India's needs for ten years ahead. One very large computer would be imported for a national facility. Three to five medium-large machines would be imported and run as Regional Computer Centres, shared like power utilities. All smaller computers would be made in India from Indian components, about 500 a year for ten years.[27] Its report argued that 'attaining self-sufficiency in systems engineering and fabrication is of fundamental importance from the point of view of the defence and security of our country'.[28]

In 1970 the plan was debated at a National Electronics Conference at TIFR, attended by people from universities, companies, government, laboratories and the armed forces.[29] Rajaraman, then on the faculty of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kanpur, argued that India lacked a home market large enough to build up in the textbook order, from components to circuits to systems. India should go backwards, design systems first and import the components, and pay for the imports with exports. 'Foreign exchange can also be earned by software export,' he said. In his history of 2012 he added: 'However, my comment was not taken seriously.'[30]

The chairman of the conference, Sarabhai, who had succeeded Bhabha, took a larger view. In his concluding remarks he called computing 'far more fundamental, of wider significance than any other field of electronics', and of 'particular relevance to our developing country where resources are scarce'. Multinational companies had a contribution to make, but not, he said, at the cost of a major national effort.[31] On that thinking the government started a computer division at the Electronics Corporation of India Ltd (ECIL), a public-sector company set up at Hyderabad in 1967 under the Department of Atomic Energy to commercialise electronics developed at the atomic research centre at Trombay.[32]

## The gatekeeper

The Department of Electronics (DoE) was established in 1970 and the Electronics Commission, by most accounts, in 1971. M.G.K. Menon, the director of TIFR, became secretary of the department and chairman of the commission.[33] Narasimhan later described the two big decisions that followed. The first was to develop and manufacture small and medium computers in India, so that within a set time most of the country's needs in that range could be met from Indian production. The second was to centralise all computer purchasing through global tenders.[34]

The DoE also became the gate through which every imported computer had to pass. In 1970 responsibility for import licences for computers was transferred to it as a 'single window clearance', and it drafted rules that judged each request by its essentiality, whether an equivalent machine was made in India and how much foreign exchange it needed.[35] The rupee was not convertible and the trade balance was permanently in deficit, so that 'obtaining foreign exchange for import of equipment required elaborate justification'.[36] The quadrupling of oil prices in 1973 made foreign exchange scarcer still. Unless the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) or a foreign government was paying, clearance to import a computer usually took one to three years.[37] The delays hurt universities, laboratories, industry and especially companies that wanted to import computers in order to export software.[38]

Foreign policy closed other doors. During the 1971 war with Pakistan the United States, which favoured Pakistan, embargoed exports of electronics and computers to India. India's first nuclear test in 1974 brought a further embargo on advanced electronic equipment, including high-end computers and scientific software.[39]

Private Indian firms, several of them already making electronic calculators, wanted to build computers. The DoE kept delaying the policy that would set the rules for them, partly because many components and peripherals would have to be imported and partly to protect the ECIL programme it was funding.[40] In the meantime, Rajaraman writes, the DoE 'became very unpopular' as legitimate requests from universities, government science departments and industry were 'inordinately delayed'; and 'no private Indian company was allowed to manufacture computers'.[41]

## A cottage industry in Hyderabad

ECIL's computer division was headed by S. Srikantan, who had designed the Trombay Digital Computer 12 (TDC-12) at the atomic research centre. It was a 12-bit real-time machine, similar in design to the PDP-8 made by the American firm Digital Equipment Corporation, and it was commissioned at Trombay in 1969.[42] ECIL had no commercial computer of its own on which to develop software, so it sent much of the work out to TIFR, IIT Kanpur and the Indian Institute of Management at Ahmedabad; with ECIL's own engineers, they produced an operating system, an assembler and BASIC and FORTRAN compilers.[43] The TDC-12 was followed by the TDC-312 in 1974, the 16-bit TDC-316 in 1975 and, in 1978, the Micro 78, built around a microprocessor.[44]

Between 1971 and 1978 ECIL sold 98 computers.[45] A TDC-316 cost Rs 3 million, about $360,000 at the 1975 rate.[46] ECIL had shown, in Rajaraman's judgement, that computers could be made in India from local components with imported chips and peripherals. 'It however worked more like a cottage industry', because its volumes were small. Most of its machines went to atomic energy establishments, government departments and universities that depended on government grants and were 'constrained to buy' from it. 'Only 4 machines were sold to the private sector.' The machines were overpriced and short of software.[47]

ECIL's most important work was hidden from view. The Air Defence Ground Environment System (ADGES), a chain of radar stations along India's borders to detect hostile aircraft, could not be bought abroad without revealing sensitive information to foreign vendors. TIFR designed the system and its software. Each installation used three ruggedised TDC-316s and cost Rs 30 million; 25 were deployed by the Indian Air Force between 1969 and 1984, and the income sustained ECIL's other development work.[48] Besides the 98 machines sold commercially, 75 ruggedised TDC-316s went into this project.[49] 'In the published literature this important contribution of ECIL is not mentioned,' Rajaraman writes.[50]

The most lasting product was people. ECIL trained 'over a thousand engineers in designing systems and developing systems software', and many of them later joined private computer makers and software companies to lead groups there.[51] For an Indian engineer in the 1970s who wanted to build computers rather than operate them, ECIL was one of very few possible employers.

## The clerks' case

The computer met its strongest opposition not in factories but in offices. The labour movement already had a template for dealing with new machines. In 1957 the 15th Indian Labour Conference had adopted a Model Agreement on rationalisation, which promised no retrenchment and no loss of earnings for existing workers, an equitable sharing of the gains among the community, the employer and the worker, and prior consultation with the unions before new equipment was installed.[52] Automation in new process industries and in manufacturing aroused little opposition. Computers in offices, the government's Committee on Automation later found, 'evoked serious misgivings among the employees'.[53]

According to that committee, the issue gained national attention because of the 'unilateral decision' of LIC's management, in the mid-1960s, to introduce a computer. The All India Insurance Employees' Association started an agitation, and the central trade union organisations took up the wider question of automation.[54] The unions' case, as the committee summarised it, was that automation was 'a painful luxury, and ... a labour saving device which has no place in a developing economy marked by labour surpluses and scarce capital resources'. They held that the loss of jobs, existing and potential, was built into any scheme of automation, and that using an expensive computer for routine office work was a misuse of a costly tool.[55] The employers answered that automation was simply an advanced stage of mechanisation, indispensable for industrialisation and better management.[56]

The dispute reached Parliament.
