On 24 November 1966, the day before the insurance employees' one-day token strike against the computers, the Finance Minister, Sachindra Chaudhuri, told the Lok Sabha that LIC had decided on computers in 1964 and installed the first at Bombay in November 1965. The switch would take some three years. '383 jobs would disappear but the very process of computerisation would create 225 new jobs.' The net loss of 158 was, he said, insignificant beside the 1,500 or so new jobs LIC created every year, and no one would be retrenched.[57] Four months later George Fernandes, then a member of the Lok Sabha, asked how many computers LIC had installed, at what cost, and how many employees had lost their jobs. The Minister of State for Finance, K.C. Pant, answered that one computer, made by IBM, had been installed at Bombay, and that no one had lost a job.[58] When another member asked whether the computers would harm the corporation's capacity to create jobs, and whether that was wise, the new Finance Minister, Morarji Desai, replied: 'It will be an unwise policy if we do not do this.'[59]

The tripartite meetings did not settle the matter. The Indian Labour Conference discussed automation in July 1966 and agreed that the Model Agreement should apply. The Standing Labour Committee returned to it in May 1967 and could not agree on clerical automation at all.[60] Union conventions in 1966 and 1967 demanded an immediate ban.[61] The one safeguard the government had, a requirement that any import using foreign exchange be cleared by the Labour Ministry, barely touched the problem. Most new computers were assembled in India, not imported, so they escaped screening. Between 1967 and 1971, 94 computers were introduced in India and only five proposals were referred to the Labour Ministry.[62] IBM's way around the foreign-exchange rule was also, in practice, a way around the labour rule.

## Inside the computer rooms

The Committee on Automation, which grew out of the July 1968 meeting, produced the best surviving picture of where India's computers were and who worked around them. By August 1971 it counted 140 computers in the country: 10 in government departments, 39 in public-sector undertakings including the railways, 55 in private firms and 36 in research institutions, technical institutes and universities.[63] Bombay alone had 35, a quarter of the total.[64] Nearly all were new. 'As many as 124 of the 140 computers in India have been installed only since 1965,' the committee wrote.[65]

Most did office work. Payroll, billing, invoices and financial statistics dominated, partly because these jobs had already been partly mechanised on punched-card machines.[66] The railways used their computers for wagon movements and accounts; the State Bank of India reconciled some 70,000 inter-branch transactions a day; Delhi Cloth Mills and Calico Mills used linear programming to choose the cheapest blend of cotton.[67] The committee heard the charge that some firms bought computers as status symbols, 'to keep up with the 'Joneses''.[68] When it asked 40 public and private organisations why they had installed computers, most named better service, faster tabulation and better management decisions. Only five named a reduction in labour costs.[69]

The committee's case studies show how the work changed hands. Computer departments created new posts, many at higher grades: systems analysts and programmers above all. Punch-card operators and machine operators were moved into the new sections, and much of the computer staff was recruited from inside the organisation and trained. Several existing employees, the committee found, 'got the benefit of better jobs and better pay', while the pay of the remaining clerks did not rise.[70] Some clerical workers now had to work second and third shifts to keep the expensive machines busy, 'a practice associated usually with blue-collar jobs'. Union representatives told the committee that computerisation had put clerical staff under more strain, requiring greater speed and fixed schedules.[71]

The question of jobs was harder to measure than either side admitted. A works study team in Maharashtra, looking at six establishments, followed 741 employees displaced by computers: 531 were given other jobs, 93 were retrained for the computer section, 71 were absorbed elsewhere in the organisation and 46 in expansion.[72] Almost nobody was sacked. The unions' point was that this was not the whole story. In one unnamed establishment studied by the committee, the staff on branch clearance and government accounts fell from 380 in November 1966 to 304 in January 1970, while the volume of work rose; the old methods would have needed 516 people for the 1970 volume.[73] The committee concluded that although there had been no direct retrenchment, the immediate effect of the computer was a fall in the demand for clerks, because vacancies left by natural wastage were filled by surplus staff rather than new recruits.[74] It was the next generation of clerks, not the present one, who lost.

Few managements asked their workers first. Of 42 units for which the committee had information, 35 had introduced a computer without prior consultation, and only seven had consulted their unions.[75] 'No instance was brought to our notice in which a proposal to instal a computer was dropped due to disagreement with union.'[76]

## The Committee on Automation

The committee was set up by the Ministry of Labour in July 1969 under R. Venkataraman, a member of the Planning Commission, and finished its work under the economist V.M. Dandekar. Its members included industrialists, an economist, a computer specialist and two members whose notes to the report speak for labour.[77] It was candid about its limits. It was 'greatly handicapped because of the inadequacy of available data', had found no comprehensive study of the effects of automation in India, and relied on questionnaires, case studies and oral evidence.[78]

Its recommendations, signed on 18 May 1972, tried to give each side something.[79] Computers in education, research, government statistics and defence should be allowed, with protection for existing staff.[80] Commercial and industrial users, public or private, and expressly including consultancy services, should be examined case by case.[81] Where possible their needs should be met from shared computer service centres, since a computer facility was 'in the nature of a public utility' and should preferably be in the public sector.[82] And 'all use of computers by commercial and industrial establishments ... should be subject to a prior agreement with the workers'.[83] A firm wanting a computer would write a Justification Report setting out the jobs to be computerised, the expected benefits and the likely effects on employment and pay. Experts chosen jointly by management and workers would assess it, and disputes would go to a National Bipartite Machinery of employers and unions.[84] The committee urged that India's needs in hardware and software be met 'as far as possible from indigenous sources', which would save foreign exchange and create jobs.[85]

Every member signed, but three explanatory notes show how far apart they remained. Satish Loomba wrote that in a capitalist economy automation served profit, so Indian workers had to oppose it in general; he agreed to the recommendations 'as a practical policy at the present juncture'.[86] G. Ramanujam warned that automation could reduce employment: 'It can rob labour of its personality, creative effort, sense of achievement and drag down work itself to boredom.' He signed because of the prior-consent safeguard and the public-sector computer centres.[87] The industrialists Naval H. Tata, Babubhai M. Chinai and B.D. Somani argued from the report's own figures that the effect on employment would be negligible, a couple of thousand people over a decade or more even if half the country's large companies installed computers, enough 'to dispel the exaggerated apprehensions entertained by some sections of the trade unions'. They too signed.[88]

How far the recommendations were applied is not clear from the record. Rajaraman, writing as a participant in the period, judges that the committee 'prescribed in 1972 strict controls' and that its report 'constrained the introduction of computers in banks, insurance companies and many private companies'. He attributes its hostility partly to the 1401s themselves: small machines used for payroll, accounts and stores, which vocal white-collar workers saw as labour-saving devices.[89] In 1975 Parliament's Public Accounts Committee added its own caution: in a country with large-scale unemployment the use of computers for labour-saving work 'may not be desirable or may even be detrimental'.[90] The DoE had to move cautiously.[91]

## Training the state's own

The state that restricted computers also trained people to use them, and much of the education of these years ran through its institutions rather than through universities. IBM had trained the first generation of programmers and maintenance engineers on its rented 1401s, ECIL its thousand systems engineers, and IIT Kanpur ran short programming courses for people from other institutions until 1975.[92]

The DoE's largest training venture was the National Centre for Software Development and Computing Techniques (NCSDCT) at TIFR, set up in the mid-1970s with money from the DoE and UNDP and directed by Narasimhan from 1975 to 1985.[93] Narasimhan saw the training of enough software engineers as a major challenge. 'Formal educational channels are wholly inadequate to cope with a demand of this magnitude,' he wrote. NCSDCT's answer was a one-year evening course in computer science, held at the Victoria Jubilee Technical Institute in central Bombay and linked by telephone lines to the PDP-10 computer at TIFR. Preference went to people already working in software, employers were persuaded to pay, entry was by a fairly rigorous test, and classes took 60 to 80 students at a time, taught largely through self-study, assignments and imported textbooks.[94]

The DoE built other institutions too. The National Informatics Centre, founded in 1975, set up a large computer centre in New Delhi for central government data processing.[95] Regional Computer Centres followed: at Poona in 1974, with an ICL mainframe offering cheap computer time to students and software exporters; at Jadavpur University in Calcutta (Kolkata since 2001) in 1977, where students in eastern India had free access to a Burroughs mainframe; and at Chandigarh.[96] In 1976 the DoE created the Computer Maintenance Corporation (CMC) to maintain imported computers and, foreseeing IBM's departure, the machines IBM would leave behind.[97] These bodies employed engineers and programmers on government terms. Of NCSDCT's successor, Rajaraman notes that a core group of its scientists 'later became leaders in the profession'.[98]

## A small door marked export

One DoE decision of these years mattered more than its authors could have known. Rajaraman records that, 'recognizing the potential of software export', the department allowed computers to be imported exclusively for software export, and that the first policy paper on this was published in 1974.[99] It was the idea Rajaraman had put to the 1970 conference, turned into an import rule: a computer could be justified if it earned foreign exchange by producing software for foreign clients. TCS, the Tata group's computer services unit, used the rule to import a mainframe and earn foreign exchange from programming work done for clients abroad.[100]

What matters here is the mechanism. In a decade when almost every computer import was suspect, the one sure justification was export earnings, and the export that India could make was programming. The machine was to be paid for with the time of the people who programmed it. That is the first form of the bargain this book follows.

## Four explanations

The record agrees on what happened between 1962 and 1977. It disagrees on why India did not build a computer industry. Rajaraman's verdict is that 'as a poor country with a low demand for computers it was strategically incorrect to try to design computers starting at the component level during 1970-1980 and hope to be completely "self-reliant"'.[101] Narasimhan had argued that building second-generation computers required production know-how that only large-scale manufacturers had or could command.[102] The historian Dwaipayan Banerjee's 2026 history of Indian computing, as its publisher and reviewers describe it, blames Cold War politics, trade imbalances, the monopolies of American corporations and the technocratic elite's preference for profitable technical services; one reviewer, Nikhil Menon, sums up the outcome as 'reliance, not self-reliance'.[103] The Committee on Automation's records add a fourth force. Organised clerical labour made the computer politically costly in exactly the sectors, insurance, banking and the railways, that would later be among its largest users.[104] These explanations do not exclude one another. The state was at once an obstacle and a builder, and both roles appear in the same documents.[105]

## Coda: 1977

In 1975 Indira Gandhi declared a state of emergency after a court ruled her election invalid; civil rights were suspended and opposition leaders arrested. The emergency ended in 1977, and in the general election that followed the Congress party lost power for the first time since independence. A coalition led by the Janata Party formed the government, with Morarji Desai as prime minister.[106] Ten years earlier, as Finance Minister, Desai had told the Lok Sabha of LIC's computer: 'There is going to be no retrenchment on this account.'[107]

The change reached computer policy quickly. M.G.K. Menon was replaced as secretary of the DoE, and in 1978 the government at last announced a minicomputer policy.[108] The same year IBM left India.[109]

The self-reliance programme had produced fewer than a hundred commercial computers and more than a thousand trained engineers. The labour settlement had made the office computer something a firm had to justify to its workers. And the import rules had left one opening. In the summer of 1970, when the Committee on Automation took evidence in Bombay, one of the delegations in front of it came from a small Tata unit that called itself a consultancy, and among its members was F.C. Kohli.[110] The clerks' unions had made the computer hard to justify at home. Kohli's unit would justify it by selling the work abroad.


# Chapter 4. Tata's experiment (1968-1978)

In January 1975 the Computer Society of India held its annual convention at Ahmedabad. Its president that year was F.C. Kohli, a power engineer who ran Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), a small computer-services company in Bombay (Mumbai since 1995) owned by the Tata group. In his presidential address, as he quoted it himself more than thirty years later, Kohli told the delegates: 'Many years ago, there was an industrial revolution. We missed it due to reasons over which we had no control.'[1] The new revolution, in information technology, was one 'which requires the capability to think clearly. This we have in abundance.' He went on: 'We have an opportunity to participate in this revolution on an equal footing; we even have the opportunity to be leaders.'[2]

It was a large claim to make in a country with a few hundred computers, most of them IBM's.[3] Getting permission to import another one could take between one and three years.[4] The company Kohli ran had begun as a bureau doing bank reconciliation, payroll and accounts for Tata companies and other Indian firms, and by its own later account its revenue passed $1 million in 1976.[5]

In the decade behind that speech, a data-processing unit set up to serve one business group found something it could sell abroad: the work of Indian programmers, done partly in Bombay on machines the company had to fight to import, and partly on the premises of American clients. A second, smaller venture sent American documents to Poona (now Pune) to be typed onto tape. Neither firm set out to create an export industry. The rules on foreign exchange, the scarcity of computers and the shape of the American market pushed both of them towards one.

## Half-hour slots

The people who did the early work are known mainly through the memories of men who later ran the companies, but the memories are specific. S. Ramadorai joined TCS in 1972 and became its chief executive in 1996. In 2008 *The Economist*, drawing on him and other long-serving staff, described the computers of his early years as bulky and temperamental, in need of assembly, installation and constant repair. 'You had to work with your own hands,' a colleague recalled.[6] Jayant Pendharkar, later the company's chief marketing officer, remembered a new computer arriving in three truckloads.[7] Programmers booked half-hour slots on the Burroughs terminals, and the magazine adds that 'One hour's computer time cost more than a programmer earned in a month.'[8] Seturaman Mahalingam, later the chief financial officer, worked on an early offshore project in Feltham, outside London, and posted his instructions to the programmers in Bombay twice, a day apart, in case one postbag went astray. A telephone call from London to Bombay, the magazine adds, would be interrupted every few minutes by the operator, checking that the caller wanted to keep talking.[9]

In Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1972, Narendra Patni and his wife, Poonam, tested a business of their own in their apartment. Dinesh Sharma, a journalist and historian of the industry, writes that they made the living room stand for the United States and the bedroom for India.[10] At the end of the decade Nandan Nilekani, as he recalled for the Computer History Museum, was interviewed with puzzles by N.R. Narayana Murthy in a small cabin at Nariman Point in Bombay and hired on the spot for Patni's software division. The firm's Data General computer was often idle at night, 'and for those of us who had grown up sending these cards, to have a terminal where you could do whatever you wanted was unbelievable luxury.' He worked all night on it, learning, and part of the job was teaching the customers who had bought the machine.[11]

The magazine's comparison of an hour of computer time with a month of a programmer's pay holds the economics of the decade in one line. The machine was dear and the programmer was cheap. The business that grew out of these years would be built on the difference.

## A bureau for the group

TCS began as a computer centre for the Tata group's own companies. The likeliest reading of the record is that the centre existed, with an IBM 1401, by late 1967, and that the company built on it was constituted as Tata Consultancy Services in 1968.[12]

The founding staff came from management schools and statistics more than from engineering. Sharma names three graduates of MIT's management school who had worked as interns with the Tatas, Lalit Surajmal Kanodia, Nitin Patel and Ashok Malhotra, and a fourth founding member, Yashpal Sahni, a postgraduate of the Indian Statistical Institute.[13] The Tata group's tribute to Kohli says that he recruited the most promising engineers, chartered accountants, and science and mathematics postgraduates.[14] Whatever the industry later became, its first company was not staffed only by engineers, still less only by graduates of the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs).

The work was the work of a service bureau: bank reconciliation, payroll and accounting.[15] A profile of Kohli in *MIT Technology Review*, based on interviews with him, adds two jobs: reconciling transactions between the branches of a nationalised bank, and producing Bombay's telephone directory.[16] These were the standard uses of a commercial computer in India at the time. The Committee on Automation, appointed by the Ministry of Labour to study what computers would do to jobs, noted that one of the important uses of the State Bank of India's computer was to reconcile inter-branch transactions, about 70,000 of them a day.[17] Most Tata companies already rented IBM 1401s, so a Tata bureau that sold computing to Tata companies was doing, inside the group, what IBM did for its clients.[18]

## The control engineer

Faqir Chand Kohli came to computers through electric power. Born in Peshawar in 1924, he took a physics degree at Government College, Lahore, and in 1946, 'before the partition', as he put it, went on a scholarship to Queen's University in Canada to study electrical engineering.[19] He worked for about a year at General Electric, took a master's degree at MIT on a scholarship, and learned load dispatch, the scheduling of power stations' output across a grid, at the New England Power Company.[20] In 1951 he came back to India and joined Tata Electric in Bombay, which wanted to set up what he called 'the first load dispatch in India'.[21]

Ross Bassett, a historian of technology who interviewed Kohli, describes him as an MIT-trained control engineer, a specialist in the regulation of systems, which was one of the fields from which computing grew.[22] Kohli's ties to IIT Kanpur gave him his practical introduction to computing, and he brought digital computers into Tata Electric's system control in the late 1960s.[23] In 1973 he became the first Indian to sit on the board of directors of the IEEE, the international but American-oriented society of electrical engineers.[24]

The Tata group's chairman, J.R.D. Tata, asked him to take on the new computer company.[25] In 1969 he moved from Tata Electric to TCS as general manager, succeeding Kanodia.[26] In 1974, according to the *Technology Review* profile, the director of TCS died and Kohli succeeded him.[27] He stayed for three decades. In 2020 he corrected an interviewer who dated his retirement to 1996: he had worked until 1999, when he was seventy-five.[28]

## Machines on a budget

The company's first machine was a rented IBM 1401, in place from September 1967. The first it bought, on the likeliest reading, was an ICL 1903, made by the British firm International Computers, in use from 1971.[29]

How it bought the ICL is the best story in the *Technology Review* profile, and it rests on that profile, which drew on Kohli's own account. According to the profile, the machine, never used, had belonged to a government-owned insurance company where a labour union had blocked its installation, calling it a monster that would eat jobs. TCS bought it for a fraction of its original price.[30] If the story is accurate, it connects the two halves of the Indian argument about computers. A union's veto in one public enterprise produced a cheap computer for a private firm, which would come to use machines like it for work that displaced no Indian clerks, because the clients were abroad.

New machines were harder to get than old ones. Every import needed a licence from the Department of Electronics (DoE), and the delay, V. Rajaraman, the historian of Indian computing, writes, 'particularly hurt companies which wanted to import computers for software export.'[31] Old machines had been the way round the problem. Sharma writes that IBM and ICL had imported used computers until an audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General led the government to rein them in and give the DoE control of the matter.[32]

## Up, but not running

The domestic market could not keep the company going. 'TCS was up, but it wasn't running,' Kohli told the *Technology Review*. The company struggled, and took on management-consulting work to stay afloat.[33]

Near the end of his life Kohli told a simpler story. In an interview for the Computer History Museum in January 2020, when he was ninety-five, he said: 'First few years it was built only on exports. People didn't understand.'[34] Asked about strategy, he said that he had built strong links with the engineering colleges, starting with IIT Kanpur, so that people knew about the company: 'There was no question of my going for business. The people came to us, "Could you do this for us?"'[35] The better evidence points the other way. The company's own histories list domestic bureau work as its first business,[36] and Sharma found that Kohli, courting Burroughs, visited the United States at least nine times between 1972 and 1974.[37]

A second witness, from outside TCS, confirms how thin the Indian market was. Murthy, who later founded Infosys, had worked for a French company in Paris in the early 1970s. Within a couple of years of his return he started a firm to write software for Indian customers. Within seven or eight months, he told the Computer History Museum, he realised 'that there was no domestic market in India for software. There were hardly any computers in India'. He closed the firm and set out to learn whether his market would have to be global, 'a market particularly in the United States'.[38] His is a founder's retrospective, but it comes from a different firm and points the same way.

## Burroughs

TCS tied its fortunes to Burroughs, a computer maker based in Detroit and, in Kohli's words, the 'number two computer company at that time'.[39] TCS became Burroughs' exclusive agent in India, in a relationship formed in 1973-74.[40]

In the account Kohli gave the *Technology Review*, Burroughs wanted a healthcare software package to sell with its new computers, and TCS had no Burroughs machine in India to write it on. Its programmers wrote the software on the ICL and built a filter, a program that converted it to run on Burroughs hardware. The job made Burroughs a large repeat client.[41] Other accounts give other first jobs: Sharma describes operating-system work for a new series of Burroughs mainframes, and Rajaraman the conversion of software written for other makers' computers.[42] The Tata group's own timeline counts the conversion of a hospital-accounting system for a Detroit client in 1973 as the first recorded case of offshore software delivery, which is the company's claim about itself.[43] Sharma lists the clients who followed as the Detroit Police, the City of Detroit, the State University of New York and several banks.[44]

Whichever account is closest, the work had a pattern that would last. Programmers in Bombay wrote code for machines they could not see, and the code was carried to the United States to run. Software was the one product a computer-starved country could make without many computers of its own, so long as it had one machine to write on and a way to move the result.

The partnership spread beyond services. In 1975 Tata and Burroughs formed a company to manufacture computers in Bombay. They also set up a separate software unit, Tata Burroughs Limited, which, with TCS, remained India's top software exporter for a long time.[45] TCS also looked well beyond Detroit. The company lists a project for an electric utility in Iran in 1971 and one for a British housing society, done for Burroughs, in 1974.[46] Rajaraman says TCS 'actively scouted for programming work' in Iran, Switzerland, South Africa and Canada as well as the United States, and that it 'was able to demonstrate that software services export from India was feasible and profitable'.[47] In 1976, according to the Tata group, Kohli received an award as a leading exporter from the Engineering Export Promotion Council.[48] The Tata group's tribute to Kohli adds that customers valued the company's quality of service at a low cost, the more so after the 1973 oil crisis.[49] That is the company's own statement of the cost advantage on which the industry would be built.

## Programmers on site

Not all the work could be done in Bombay. William Aspray, an American historian of computing, writes that Burroughs asked TCS to send programmers to the United States to install systems software for Burroughs customers, and he treats that request as the birth of India's software export business.[50] A manufacturer installing machines at its customers' premises needed programmers there, and TCS supplied them. The practice came to be called, derisively, 'body shopping', and once TCS had succeeded, other Indian firms began to offer the same service.[51]

How TCS charged Burroughs or its American clients in the 1970s, by the person-month, the hour or a fixed price for each job, is not shown by any contract or rate card that has come to light.[52] The conversion and package work suggests fixed deliverables; the installation work on site suggests time-based billing. So it cannot be said that billing by the hour began here. A review of Ramadorai's own history of the company says only that the arrangement with Burroughs let TCS do part of the development work in India and part at client locations abroad.[53] The industry's first exports combined two things: code written at home and people's time spent at a client's site. Chapter 6 follows how the second came to dominate.

## Data by air

The second experiment was smaller, and in one way it went further. Narendra Patni had studied at MIT and, according to Bassett, worked with the computer pioneer and entrepreneur Jay Forrester, doing consulting work and taking part in his business ventures.[54] Patni formed Data Conversion Inc., the forerunner of his later Patni Computer Systems, to convert paper records into data on paper and magnetic tape.[55] After the test in the Cambridge apartment, a team of data-entry operators was hired in Poona, two dozen by Sharma's account, twenty by another.[56] The work was keying American documents onto tape in India and sending the tapes back. It was an early form of the offshore 'process' work that would fill the back offices of the 1990s, and it began two decades before them.

Patni then moved into software, forming Patni Computer Systems with his brothers Gajendra and Ashok, both graduates of IIT Delhi, in the late 1970s. It began by reselling minicomputers made by the American firm Data General and then wrote software for Data General's customers.[57] In August 1977 Patni hired Murthy to head its software division. By the time he arrived, he recalled in 2018, the Patnis had 'also started a business to develop software for export to the United States'.[58] The division's staff by the end of the decade included Nilekani and Kris Gopalakrishnan; in 1981 Murthy and six colleagues left to found Infosys.[59]

## Who did the work

The profession at this stage was defined by the task, whether systems programming, conversion or data entry, rather than by a degree. TCS's recruits included chartered accountants and science and mathematics postgraduates as well as engineers; the operators in Poona needed typing, not engineering; and the people who joined Patni's software division at the end of the decade had a year or so of experience each.[60] Most of those in India who could already program had been trained by IBM, the public-sector Electronics Corporation of India, Kanpur's short courses or the state's software training centre in Bombay.[61] TCS drew on these pools and trained its own staff on the job. Kohli said in 2009 that the company had judged early on that technology became obsolete 'in less than 24 months', so that its staff would need continuing education.[62] His view of the raw material, as he put it in 2020, was simple: 'Indians are capable of doing a lot of things. And only thing is they have to receive some training.'[63]

## Three readings

Three explanations of this decade can be drawn from the record, and they are not exclusive. The first is the founders' own. Kohli saw the potential of the technology, recruited the best people and, in 1975, told the profession what India could become. The Tata group's tributes tell the story this way, and so, mostly, did Kohli.[64] It is a self-description, and Kohli himself resisted its strongest form. When the Computer History Museum's interviewer called him the father of the industry, he replied: 'Father is a misnomer.' He was, he said, the father of his three children, and that was all. Then he added: 'I did set up the computer industry in this country, and that is that. People know it.'[65] The second reading, which Rajaraman's and Aspray's accounts support, is that the export industry was a by-product of import controls and foreign-exchange rules: firms exported because exports were the price of getting machines, and because there was too little demand at home.[66] The third is Bassett's. What mattered, he argues, was the pairing of an American-style engineering education, at Kanpur and elsewhere, with men such as Kohli and Patni who had American training and American contacts.[67]

The record bears on two claims that recur in histories of the industry. The first is that TCS was India's first software company. It began as a bureau selling computing to its own group, as IBM's data centres in the big cities already did for smaller firms. As a firm that exported software services it was among the first, with Patni's venture beside it.[68] The second is that the first offshore development centre in India was opened by Texas Instruments in Bangalore (Bengaluru since 2014) in 1985 (Chapter 8). Software written in Bombay for Burroughs in 1973-74, and data keyed in Poona from 1972, show Indian firms doing work for foreign clients in India more than a decade earlier, though without satellite links and not in a centre owned by a foreign company.[69]

## Twice the value

The rule that turned scarcity into an export business took shape in the early 1970s. The DoE allowed computers to be imported exclusively for software export. Rajaraman had told a conference in 1970 that foreign exchange could also be earned by software export.[70] Its working is clearest in TCS's own purchase of a Burroughs computer in 1974. The machine cost $340,000. With Indian tariffs TCS paid more than twice that.[71] *The Economist* itemised the tariff at 101.25 per cent: import duty, auxiliary duty, countervailing duty and a levy to help pay for the war in Bangladesh.[72] The government let the machine in on one condition. In the *Technology Review*'s words, 'Kohli had to commit to exporting twice the value of the machine over a five-year period.'[73]

On the machine's price alone, that meant at least $680,000 of earnings abroad in five years, or about $136,000 a year. The size of the commitment shows against the national figures. In 1977, by a contemporary West German estimate, the whole of India's software exports came to about Rs 10 million, roughly $1.1 million, and the firms named as reaching markets abroad were TCS and the Operations Research Group of Baroda (now Vadodara).[74] In 1980, Aspray writes, twenty-one Indian firms were exporting about $4 million a year, mostly by sending people to client sites.[75] One import licence could commit a single firm to earning abroad, each year, more than a tenth of the whole country's software exports in 1977.

A firm in Bombay had few ways to earn that money. It could not sell computers, which it could barely import. It could sell the work of its staff, as code written in Bombay or as programmers sent to the client. The machine was the dear part of the business and the programmer the cheap one, and the obligation could be met only by selling the cheap part abroad. Each new computer had to be paid for with engineers' work sold abroad, and each addition to the stock of machines meant more people whose time would pay for them. This is the bargain the rest of the book follows, written down for the first time in an import licence: a computer priced in the future labour of Indian programmers.

The rule was not watertight. Aspray concludes that by 1980 most of the hardware imported into India was being used for domestic purposes, not for producing software exports.[76] But for TCS, and for the firms that copied it, the condition fixed the shape of the business.

## 1978

The decade closed with a break. The Tata group dates the end of TCS's partnership with Burroughs to 1978.[77] The reviewer Rashmi Bansal writes that Ramadorai's history of the company presents that year as the gravest test TCS had faced, because Tata Sons formed a formal joint venture with Burroughs and left TCS to fend for itself.[78] The same year IBM, which had installed most of India's computers and trained many of its programmers, left the country, and the government at last let private Indian companies make minicomputers (Chapter 5).[79] India had fewer than 1,000 computers.[80] In 1979 TCS sent Ramadorai to the United States to open its first overseas office. Free now to work with other computer makers, it had to find its own customers.[81] What it offered them was what the export licence had already taught it to sell: the time of its programmers.



# Part II: Bodies and wires (1977-1991)

# Chapter 5. The year IBM left (1973-1984)

Some time in 1977, a group of senior executives from International Business Machines (IBM) went to see India's new minister of industry. They had already been to the top. The prime minister, Morarji Desai, had heard them out and told them to see the minister, George Fernandes.[1] The meeting, as the science journalist Dinesh C. Sharma later wrote, turned out to be decisive.[2]

'IBM was very cocky,' Fernandes told Sharma in 2006, in the only account of the meeting that survives. The executives, he recalled, told him they had refused to accept what the French president, General Charles de Gaulle, had told them about diluting their equity. His reply, as he remembered it: 'if you think the General succumbed to you, I am telling you that I am not succumbing to you. You get out.' And then, for emphasis, he added that yes, he had said it: you get out.[3]

On 1 June 1978 IBM closed its Indian operations.[4] The company that had brought most of India's computers into the country, rented them out, maintained them and trained the people who ran them was gone.

What India lost, and what it gained, was not what either side expected. A rule written to save foreign exchange pushed out the largest foreign computer firm. A licensing policy then let a handful of small Indian companies build computers from imported chips. Because those companies were not allowed to import software, they wrote their own, and the engineers who did that work became, by the account of the period's leading participant-historian, the skilled programmers India later sold to the world. The hardware itself did not last.

## The renting business

IBM had sold its machines in India since 1950.[5] From 1965 it built a business on key punches made in Bombay (Mumbai since 1995) and exported, whose foreign-exchange earnings paid for used IBM 1401 computers, which IBM refurbished, repainted and rented to Indian customers with maintenance and help with software included.[6] The rents drew charges of profiteering, but V. Rajaraman, the historian of Indian computing, also credits IBM with training a whole generation of India's maintenance engineers and programmers (Chapter 3).[7] The model gave IBM about two-thirds of the 217 computers counted in India in 1974, and by Sharma's later estimate about 80 per cent of the market.[8]

The same model made IBM a target. Sharma calls it IBM's 'As is' policy, and judges that it 'kept the technology in Indian market one or two generations behind the latest'.[9] He dates the government's pressure to 1967, when the Electronics Committee under the physicist Vikram Sarabhai wanted IBM to stop importing old machines and leasing them to government departments at inflated rents.[10]

## Forty per cent

The legal hinge was a law about money. In 1973 India amended the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA). Its purpose, in Rajaraman's words, was 'to conserve foreign exchange', and under it foreign companies 'except those considered essential were to dilute equity to 40% and take an Indian partner'.[11] Any company with more than 40 per cent foreign equity had to obtain fresh approval from the Reserve Bank of India to continue operating.[12] FERA was one more of the devices, like import licences and export obligations, by which the Indian state rationed its dollars.

Two years later Parliament added a charge of its own. After the Comptroller and Auditor General raised questions about IBM's dealings with the Railways, the Public Accounts Committee of Parliament, chaired by Hirendra Nath Mukherjee, opened 'a full-scale enquiry into the functioning of IBM' in November 1975.[13] The committee found, as Sharma reports it, that IBM had 'defrauded the country of enormous revenues by resorting to various unfair practices like transfer pricing under the garb of inter-company billing system, misuse of import entitlements'.[14] Transfer pricing here meant setting the price at which IBM's own affiliates sold machines to its Indian arm, which decided how much foreign exchange left the country. 'IBM was found to dump used and obsolete mainframe computers in India at inflated prices,' Sharma writes of the same enquiry.[15]

IBM bargained. Rajaraman says it first refused to dilute, 'as it was not its global policy'. It then proposed a manufacturing unit, wholly owned and wholly for export, whose earnings would pay for computers imported for sale in India, and offered to invest 26 per cent of its profit in a research centre in India.[16] Sharma describes the offer in more detail. IBM would split its Indian business in two. Card manufacture and the data centres would go into one company with 60 per cent Indian equity, as FERA required; the export factory would be the other, fully owned. 'But it was not willing to dilute its equity in its marketing and maintenance business', which Sharma calls its core business.[17]

IBM, Rajaraman writes, was 'very confident that it would be considered "essential"'. It had over 150 installations in India, at the Railways, the Planning Commission, textile and petrochemical companies, and many research laboratories and educational institutions. 'IBM's data centres were widely used and its service was excellent'.[18] The Department of Electronics (DoE) still hoped for a negotiated solution. Then, in March 1977, the government changed.[19]

IBM's British rival made the other choice. ICL diluted its equity, formed International Computer India Manufacturing Ltd (ICIM) with an Indian partner, and in 1977 began making a computer series called the ICL 2900 in India.[20] It shows that a foreign computer firm could stay on FERA's terms, and so that leaving was at least partly IBM's choice. It does not show whether anyone in Delhi wanted IBM to stay.

## The minister

The 1977 election ended thirty years of continuous Congress rule. A coalition led by Morarji Desai took office.[21] George Fernandes was made minister of communications and moved very soon afterwards to industry, replacing Brij Lal Verma.[22]

He brought a history with him. 'As a trade Union leader in Bombay,' Sharma writes, 'Fernandes had led anti-computer agitation of workers in the 1960s'.[23] The man who now held IBM's file had been on the other side of the union campaigns against office computers. During the election campaign he had said that India did not need 'foreign technology for making brassieres and tooth paste'.[24] He was also pressing Coca-Cola to share its secret formula if it wanted to stay in India.[25]

In his 2006 interview Fernandes gave two reasons for his stand. One was IBM's attitude in the meeting. The other was that, in his view, IBM's computers 'were taking away jobs of Indian workers'.[26] The second reason ties the exit to the long Indian argument about automation and work.

Sharma's own verdict is careful. The audit, the parliamentary enquiry, the FERA rules and pressure from the Department of Electronics had already made it hard for IBM to stay, and Fernandes's arrival was the last nail in the coffin. 'The file on IBM and Coca Cola came to him as FERA cases, and he took the decision based on recommendations of the FERA committee. It was well within the purview of policy and law, but helped Fernandes score a political brownie point'.[27] What the minister did, in Sharma's view, was to shut the window in which IBM and Coca-Cola might have renegotiated.[28] By 1978 Coca-Cola, IBM, Mobil and Kodak had quit India or applied to do so.[29]

## Who left whom

Whether IBM was thrown out or chose to go has been argued ever since. Rajaraman's account is that it chose to leave rather than give up control: 'After prolonged negotiations the government was unwilling to relax FERA for IBM. Consequently IBM decided to withdraw from India in 1978'.[30] Sharma's is that FERA only eased an exit whose real cause was a power struggle between a multinational and the government.[31] A report written at the time points the same way. In April 1978 the West German trade weekly *Computerwoche* wrote that specialists thought the Electronics Commission might have brought on the confrontation deliberately, accusing IBM of making excessive profits from outdated machines and of largely blocking the local development of new systems. IBM replied that it had proposed replacing its 1400 series in 1970, and again in 1972, and that the government had taken up neither plan.[32]

Shiv Nadar, a founder of one of the Indian firms that grew in IBM's absence, gave a third account to Knowledge at Wharton in 2006. When the interviewer began to say that Fernandes had evicted IBM in 1977, Nadar cut in: 'IBM wasn't evicted. The real story was different.' In his account the government had ruled that if a product was made in India, its source code had to reside in the country. Equity dilution, he said, did not hurt companies much, but the source-code requirement did. 'That was the main reason why IBM decided to leave India, as did Coca-Cola'.[33] No other source mentions such a rule for computers; Coca-Cola's secret formula was certainly an issue, and Nadar may have run the IBM and Coca-Cola cases together.[34]

The fourth account is expulsion. The historian Dwaipayan Banerjee's 2026 history of Indian computing is described by its publisher as treating IBM's departure as a decisive expulsion, one act in a project of technological independence, and a reviewer summarises it as saying that IBM was 'eventually expelled in 1977 by the union-backed Janata Party'.[35] Fernandes's own words support that reading at the level of political intent.[36] The accounts agree on most of the facts. The rule made IBM's way of doing business in India impossible unless it gave up control of its core business; IBM would not; the minister closed the door loudly. 'Expelled' and 'chose to leave' describe the same event from opposite sides.

## June 1978

The unwinding was quick. In April 1978 *Computerwoche* reported that IBM, which under FERA could have kept only 40 per cent of its Indian subsidiary, against the company's worldwide policy, would end all its activities in India by the end of the year.[37] The refurbishing work in Bombay stopped. The computers IBM had rented out 'were sold to the customers at their book value which was almost zero'.[38] A group of former IBM employees formed a company called International Data Machines (IDM) and took over the card factory and the data centres.[39]

Maintenance went to a state company that had been waiting for it. The Department of Electronics had set up the Computer Maintenance Corporation (CMC) in 1976, Rajaraman writes, 'to maintain imported computers foreseeing such a contingency'.[40] It had cost Rs 53 million to establish,[41] about $5.9 million at the 1976 average exchange rate.[42] IBM sold CMC the spare parts for its 1401s and other machines at a nominal price, and CMC took over the maintenance of IBM's installations across the country.[43] Indian users, *Computerwoche* reported, were soon paying much more for data processing, and CMC was said to be using its new monopoly to charge fees even higher than IBM's.[44]

What happened to IBM's people is disputed. Rajaraman's account is smooth: 'Most employees of IBM joined CMC. There was thus no disruption of operations of computers'.[45] The trade magazine Dataquest's chronology says that T.B. Finn, who became IBM India's general manager in 1976, laid off a third of the workforce within four months, and concludes that IBM had already made up its mind to leave.[46] A 2018 report in the Deccan Chronicle on a reunion of former IBM India staff in Mumbai, forty years after the exit, said there had been around 150 employees at the end, and that many had been left with almost nowhere to go. Some went back to their home towns to look for work, some found jobs, and some started businesses.[47] One of them, K.R. Naik, laid off by IBM, later worked for ORG Systems, one of the Indian computer makers that grew in IBM's place, and helped organise the reunion.[48]

When IBM left there were fewer than 1,000 computers in India, and software exports were, in Rajaraman's word, insignificant.[49]

## The Sondhi policy

The new government reviewed the electronics industry. A committee chaired by Mantosh Sondhi, with Biswajit Nag as its secretary, found 'long delays in importing computers due to the cumbersome procedures of the DoE'. It proposed simpler procedures, and it proposed that private companies be allowed to make computers.[50] In 1978 Nag became secretary of the Department of Electronics.[51]

The minicomputer policy that followed opened a door but kept a hand on it. It favoured what it called systems engineering companies, which need not make their own processors or peripherals. Small entrepreneurs were preferred for dedicated machines for data entry, accounting, invoicing and typesetting. Foreign collaboration was in general not allowed, though foreign equity of up to 40 per cent was permitted in special cases. Every manufacturer needed a licence. Production was capped at Rs 20 million in value,[52] about $2.4 million at the 1978 average rate,[53] and there was a limit on the number of machines. Only the public-sector Electronics Corporation of India Limited (ECIL) would be allowed to make 32-bit computers, the larger machines of the time.[54]

One clause carried the labour settlement of the previous decade into the new one. The policy 'would continue to be restrictive in allowing use of computers in areas where labour displacement was likely to be involved'.[55] The state that let private firms build computers still limited where those computers might replace clerks.

Rajaraman's judgement on the policy is double. It 'did not completely free the industry from the "licence-permit raj"', but it let private companies into a field that had been reserved for the state.[56] Many licences went to traders who never made anything. The firms that did manufacture, by his list, were DCM Data Products in Delhi, ORG Systems in Baroda (now Vadodara), Hindustan Computers Limited in Delhi, PSI Data Systems in Bangalore (Bengaluru since 2014), Wipro in Bangalore, Patni Computers in Pune, IDM in Bombay and Zenith Computers in Bombay.[57] Two of them left founders' and institutional accounts detailed enough to show what the work was like.

## An attic in Delhi

Shiv Nadar and his colleagues were engineers in the calculator division of Delhi Cloth Mills (DCM), a textile company. The calculators had moved from digital circuits to chips, and the more advanced chips went into programmable calculators, which Nadar later called the forerunners of personal computers. A few of the engineers thought they could build a computer.[58]

The state, in Nadar's telling, was not only an obstacle. The government's Electronics Commission 'was interested in making entrepreneurs out of executives and engineers. They asked us to write a report' saying they could build an eight-bit machine, and they did. 'Youthful exuberance and age were on our side'.[59] They launched Hindustan Computers Limited (HCL) in August 1976, two years before IBM left. Getting permission to make computers was the hard part. They could not expect a licence themselves, so they found a partner that had one, the government of Uttar Pradesh, and formed a joint venture. 'Interestingly, our toughest challenge was not designing or making computers but getting the government's approval to produce them'.[60]

The money came from the founders, who had first set up a company to sell calculators from their own savings and used its earnings for HCL. In 1975 six of them, among them Nadar and Arjun Malhotra, pooled Rs 175,000 in a calculator-trading company, Microcomp, most of which went on buying an office in Bombay. Once they had the licence they incorporated Hindustan Computers Limited with equity of Rs 2 million (20 lakh), about $223,000 at the 1976 average rate. A quarter came from the Uttar Pradesh government, and the 49 per cent meant for the public was taken up by Microcomp.[61]

The people were young. 'I was 31, and I was the oldest,' Nadar said. When candidates came for interviews, the founders told them first to consider the size of the company they were joining. 'We offered a monthly salary of Rs. 2,000,' he said, a sum 'more than what Citibank was paying at that time. Otherwise, how do you get someone to work in an attic with a bedroom, a table and a chair?'[62] Rs 2,000 a month was about $223 at the 1976 average rate.[63] It is the first salary this book can document for a job in an Indian computer company, and it is worth holding in mind. The export trade that followed was built on the gap between a rupee salary like this one and the dollar price the same skill could fetch abroad. Each hire added 5 per cent to the company's overheads, Nadar said, so they judged each one closely. They took five students from the Indian Institute of Management in Calcutta (Kolkata since 2001) and told them that if they did things right they should become entrepreneurs themselves. 'Did any of them become entrepreneurs? No one did'.[64]

HCL's engineers wrote software as well as building hardware. Before they could build their computer they had to create the system software that made the parts run together.[65] In the 1980s they wrote a relational database, which they called Genesis, and Nadar insisted they wrote it 'from scratch'.[66] HCL's first computer, the HCL 8/C of 1977, was meant to replace IBM 1401s, Malhotra recalled for the Computer History Museum. Because 1401 users were used to punched cards, HCL sold separate data-entry machines that recorded onto floppy disks. To ride out power cuts, the computer was wired to a truck battery that held its state through a cut, and a maintenance engineer had to call every two weeks to top up the battery's distilled water.[67]

Nadar's view of IBM's departure is the opposite of the nationalist story. 'If IBM had stayed on, we would have grown faster. See, IBM was fundamentally creating the market for computers in India.' After IBM left, HCL had to create the market by itself, and 'At that time no one saw the computer as a necessity. It was a convenience'.[68]

## Vegetable oil and the 8086

Wipro's road into computers ran through a university. In the late 1970s Wipro Products made vegetable and refined oils.[69] It decided to move into computers, and in July 1979 it signed a consultancy agreement with the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) in Bangalore, through the institute's consultancy centre, worth about Rs 1.4 million (14 lakh),[70] about $172,000 at the 1979 average rate.[71] On 5 October 1979 the institute's registrar wrote to Ashok Narasimhan, Wipro's general manager for finance and planning, that the institute had 'undertaken a project for the design and development of microprocessor-based minicomputer systems' for Wipro, with the know-how to be handed over 'in another fifteen months'.[72]

Sridhar Mitta, who joined Wipro as research and development manager in 1980, explained in 2019 why a company like his could now enter the business at all. The world, he said, was moving 'From the expensive vertically integrated systems where computer vendors had to develop components' themselves towards 'more open and cheaper, horizontally integrated systems', in which a maker could buy sub-systems and peripherals from different vendors and put them together.[73] A microprocessor bought from Intel could be the heart of a machine designed in Bangalore.

Buying even the tools was hard. N.J. Rao, who ran the institute's Digital Systems Lab, recalled that in 1979 Intel released a development system for its new 8086 processor. 'It would have been really difficult for a company to import the Intel Microprocessor Development System,' he said. 'So IISc procured it'.[74] The university served as a way round the import licence. The Wipro team worked out of Rao's lab. Azim Premji, Wipro's chairman, said the institute set up a committee 'to advise us on what computer we should make'.[75]

The Wipro Series-86 came out in 1981. It used the Intel 8086 processor and Intel's Multibus, a standard set of connections for plugging circuit boards into the machine, and its operating system was licensed from Sentinel Computer Corporation, an American firm. A team at the institute's Centre for Electronics Design and Technology, led by Kishore Babu, designed the case.[76] By Mitta's account the first year's revenue was Rs 20 million (2 crore),[77] about $2.3 million at the 1981 average rate.[78] The new company moved to its first office at 45 Dickenson Road in Bangalore.[79] Forty years later Premji told the institute's convocation that 'it would be quite accurate to say that the Wipro IT business was born in IISc',[80] a founder's tribute on a ceremonial day.

The Wipro story also names some of the first employees, which founders' stories rarely do. Y. Narahari, then an engineering undergraduate at the institute and later the chair of one of its engineering divisions, remembered that Victor Jayakaran, from the Digital Systems Lab, was one of Wipro's first hires. 'Out of the first few employees of Wipro, several were trained in this lab,' he said. 'IISc students were given an opportunity to work for a start-up like Wipro'.[81] Many of the institute's graduates joined Wipro in its first two years, among them Vallab Kulkarni, Srikant Seshadri, Anand Talwai and Ravi Bail.[82] Narahari himself was offered a job at Wipro early in 1982. He chose instead to stay for a master's degree in the institute's School of Automation.[83]

## Programmers made by scarcity

Rajaraman's description of what these firms did is the core of this chapter. They 'designed their systems from scratch using imported microprocessors, support chips, peripherals, and local components'. They 'designed and fabricated printed circuit boards, mounted and soldered all the components and tested the systems'.[84]

Then came the constraint that turned hardware makers into software writers. 'As software could not be imported they had to develop operating systems, device drivers, compilers and application programs. UNIX was the operating system of choice as it was easily available'.[85] Unix, developed by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie at AT&T in 1969, was itself written in C, a high-level programming language, and because American regulators did not allow AT&T to market it, versions circulated almost freely. The one developed at the University of California at Berkeley was popular, and Indian minicomputer makers modified and adopted it.[86] A committee of the Reserve Bank of India chaired by Rangarajan, which recommended that every bank computerise its back offices, made Unix the standard operating system for bank computers.[87] The banks' demand, Rajaraman writes, was large 'and could not be ignored'.[88]

His conclusion follows. 'Thus during 1978-1984 a large number of systems programmers in India became experts in UNIX development and usage. They also adopted C widely as UNIX was written in C. This expertise came in handy when India entered the software services export market in the late 80s'.[89] Systems programmers write the software closest to the machine: operating systems, compilers that translate programs into machine instructions, and the drivers that let a computer talk to its disks and printers.

The only reference Rajaraman gives for this passage is a personal communication in 2012 from Vinay Deshpande, an engineer of the period. It is a participant's judgement, not a count.[90] A second participant, independent of that source, makes the same link. Malhotra said that HCL wrote its own operating systems and compilers 'because we technically weren't allowed to import software unless it was in source code form', and that this was 'why UNIX became so popular in India over time'.[91] He states the rule more precisely than Rajaraman: software could come in, but only as source code. The claim is plausible and partly evidenced.

The new firms also drew people from the state, among them engineers trained at ECIL.[92] After 1978, Rajaraman writes, 'ECIL found it difficult to compete with these companies and lost many of their designers to the private sector companies'.[93] In his account the years from 1978 to 1984 saw 'considerable local design and development'. Firms 'designed mother boards and device drivers, modified the UNIX OS and wrote compilers from scratch', and competition drove prices down.[94] The profession was being built from three directions at once: IBM's former staff moving to CMC, IDM and the Indian makers; ECIL's engineers moving to private firms; and new graduates from IISc, the IITs and the management institutes taking jobs in attics and converted offices. The universities began to respond in the year IBM left, when IIT Kanpur started India's first undergraduate degree in computer science; a national panel proposed a new Master of Computer Applications degree in 1980, and the private training company NIIT was founded in 1981 (Chapter 7).[95]
## Screwdrivers

The 1978 policy did not end the permit system. Infosys, founded in 1981 to sell programming abroad rather than build computers, found the import rules as hard as HCL had found the manufacturing rules: by N.R. Narayana Murthy's later account, a licence to import a single computer took about three years.[96] In 1981 the Electronics Commission appointed another committee under Rajaraman, which 'recommended liberalization of import of computers for genuine exporters'.[97] The trade was still tiny.[98] Nor had the argument about computers and jobs gone away. Seven years after Fernandes told IBM that computers took Indian jobs, the bank unions, who read the Rangarajan committee's push to computerise as a warning sign, observed 1984 as an 'anti-computerization year' (Chapter 8).[99]

The period ended with a new prime minister and a new policy. Indira Gandhi was assassinated in 1984 and Rajiv Gandhi succeeded her.[100] He had organised the computerisation of the 1982 Asian Games in Delhi, using locally made DCM terminals, and had heard there, in Rajaraman's account, the private makers' complaints about the rules that hampered them.[101] That year's computer policy, announced on 19 November,[102] let any manufacturer make 32-bit machines and removed the limits on numbers.[103] It also allowed assembled boards, with their microprocessors and interface electronics already mounted, to be imported, and cut the duty on them.[104]

Rajaraman saw what that meant for the engineers who had been soldering their own boards. 'It changed manufacturing to assembly and system integration.' Imported boards were cheaper and more reliable than boards made in India from local parts and imported chips. 'Thus local manufacturing of boards slowly disappeared'.[105] Within two years the growth of computers went up by 100 per cent and their cost fell by half, and the old guard called the new kind of production 'screw driver' manufacturing.[106] A friend of Rajaraman's described his own job as a consultant to Indian PC makers: finding firms in Taiwan, Singapore and Hong Kong to supply motherboards, disk drives, monitors, power supplies, cables and cases, and timing the deliveries to local 'manufacturers' who assembled them, 'put their labels on them' and printed a manual.[107] The ideal of self-reliance, the cornerstone of the Bhabha Committee's report, was in Rajaraman's words 'truly and completely buried'.[108]

He found one failure larger than the rest. 'The only major failing was not investing enough resources to develop a local integrated circuit manufacturing industry.' Indian engineers could design large integrated circuits for Texas Instruments and other foreign firms, 'but had no foundry to fabricate them in India'.[109] A committee on semiconductors had reported in 1973, and nothing tangible was done until 1978; even then, he writes, the investment was too small.[110]

What India kept was the skill of making computers work. The engineers who had written operating systems and compilers because software could not be imported, and the graduates trained to design business systems, were about to find a market abroad. The same 1984 policy that ended board-making recognised software as an industry, cut the customs duty on computers imported for software export, which had been over 100 per cent, and made one more change that would shape the next decade. 'Sending engineers abroad to develop and maintain software for clients at their sites and profits earned thereby was recognized as "software export"'.[111] By FY1990-91 software exports, insignificant when IBM left, had reached $131.2 million on the estimate of Richard Heeks of the University of Manchester.[112] Rajaraman dates the start of that trade to these years and gives it the name the industry used, 'body shopping'.[113] India had tried to make its own computers and was now assembling other people's. What it would sell instead was an engineer's time, and from 1984 an Indian engineer's hours at a client's desk abroad counted as an Indian export.


# Chapter 6. Body shopping (1978-1991)

In 1990 a computer programmer from Bombay (Mumbai since 1995) went to California on a B1/B2 visa. He had been hired by the Indian computer company Hindustan Computers Limited (HCL) and sent to its offices in Palo Alto. In 1995 the American magazine *Multinational Monitor* told his story under a name it made up, 'Rajesh Ahuja (not his real name)', and that pseudonym is the only name the record gives him.[1] The magazine described the visa he travelled on as one 'intended for foreign consultants to work in the United States for relatively short stints'.[2]

The work was not at HCL. Ahuja 'worked anywhere HCL sent him, at whatever company he was subcontracted to', and he was 'required to work overtime without extra pay'.[3] Most of his time in America was spent at Sun Microsystems in Mountain View. 'I shared a two-bedroom apartment and a car with three other programmers, and got $40 a day for expenses,' he told the magazine. His salary, about $800 a month, was paid into his bank account in India, and he called it 'all savings'.[4] HCL had rented an apartment complex for its programmers, and one person handled 'all the paperwork, transportation and living arrangement for 160 of us'.[5]

He knew the terms were hard and said he did not like them. He accepted them for a reason he put plainly: 'All my life I have dreamed about coming to the United States and being able to go to New York and Disneyland, and listen to bands like the Rolling Stones.' He would have two years of it, and his flight was paid.[6]

The magazine recorded one more figure, and it is the reason this programmer opens the chapter. 'For Ahuja's services, Sun paid HCL $50 an hour, about half of which remained with HCL.'[7] When the assignment ended he went home for what he meant to be a short visit. He then learned, by the magazine's account, that HCL 'had not bothered to renew his visa', and he could not go back. 'That's typical of them,' he told the magazine.[8]

The arithmetic that follows is this book's, not the magazine's. At a working month of 160 hours, $50 an hour comes to about $8,000 billed to Sun each month. Ahuja's salary and a thirty-day expense allowance together came to about $2,000, with the apartment, the shared car and the flights on top. The magazine's own statement is narrower: about half the hourly fee stayed with HCL.

Ahuja's year in California stood for a whole trade. Through the 1980s, most of what India sold abroad as 'software' was the time of programmers like him, working on clients' computers in clients' offices. The firms that sent them priced that time by the hour or the month, and the founders of one small company spent most of the decade doing the same work.

## A name the trade gave itself

The trade's own name for the business was not flattering. V. Rajaraman, the historian of Indian computing, defines body shopping as 'sending software engineers to client sites abroad to develop software', and the historian William Aspray notes that the service came, derisively, to be called by that name.[9] Richard Heeks, a British researcher who did fieldwork in Indian software firms from the late 1980s, was more exact. In the Indian context, he wrote, 'the combination of onsite and programming work has come to be known as "body shopping"'.[10] The work was done at the client's site (onsite), and it was programming rather than analysis or design. Both halves mattered. Later scholars, among them Carol Upadhya of the National Institute of Advanced Studies in Bangalore (Bengaluru since 2014), used the word both for the industry's whole early model and, for the 2000s, for agencies that placed engineers abroad and took a cut of their pay. This book uses it in Heeks's wider sense.[11]

The model was older than the decade. Dinesh Sharma, a journalist and historian of the industry, writes that Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) and Patni Computer Systems had been sending staff to customer sites in the 1970s, and that this 'became a dominant way of doing software business in the 1980s'.[12] By 1980, by Aspray's count, twenty-one Indian firms exported about $4 million of software a year, and the industry was mainly a body-shopping one.[13] Heeks's series gives the same $4.0 million for 1980.[14] When the Americans first noticed the trade is disputed, and no source names a first contract, but TCS had programmers in the United States by 1974.[15]

The early firms clustered in Bombay, around Nariman Point and later the Santa Cruz Electronics Export Processing Zone (SEEPZ), until at least the mid-1980s.[16] An office in Bombay, though, was often only where the contracts were signed. Heeks's 1988 survey found that 65 per cent of export contracts were carried out wholly at the client's site. Counting the work itself, just under three-quarters of export development took place overseas and a quarter in India. That was true even of firms in the export zones, which had been set up as bases for work done in India.[17]

## Why ship people

Why would a country export programmers rather than programs? The sources give the same answer from different angles. Sharma's is the simplest. Indian firms did not have the hardware, the software tools or the basic infrastructure for serious export work, so 'the best way to leverage it was go to the customer site and work there using their computers'.[18]

Heeks turned the point into an explanation of the whole industry. Because the work was done onsite, he wrote, it needed no purchase of hardware or software by the Indian company and no technology infrastructure in India. Firms had chosen 'a path of almost "inputless" exports which requires only a contact overseas, a little finance, and the names of some local programmers who can be hired if a contract is forthcoming'. Such a path could be followed 'relatively independent of government policy measures, particularly those on imports, because no imports are needed'.[19]

That last clause links body shopping to the import rules. India rationed foreign exchange, and so it rationed imported machines. N.R. Narayana Murthy, a founder of Infosys, told the Computer History Museum that before 1991 a licence to import a computer took years of visits to Delhi (Chapter 9 gives his account).[20] He also recalled banks that did not understand what software was and would not lend against it, no venture capital, a wait of years for a telephone line, and the need for the Reserve Bank of India's permission even for a day's business trip abroad.[21] Before 1984, Rajaraman adds, customs duty on computers imported for software export 'used to be over 100%'.[22]

Computers stayed scarce. India had fewer than 1,000 of them in 1978 and 80,000 in 1990.[23] Against that background, a programmer on a plane was the cheapest export India had. The interviewer at the Computer History Museum, David Brock, put it to Murthy that despite these obstacles Infosys had got going quickly 'because you could send your colleagues to go work in the U.S. at customer sites'. Murthy answered, 'Yeah.'[24]

Policy was the push. Heeks's interviews found a pull as well. Indian managers liked onsite programming because it 'produces quick revenue for low investment', which suited a business culture wary of risk in uncertain times.[25] Sharma calls it simply 'a high margin business'.[26] The workers pulled too. 'Many Indian staff also want to work overseas and, if denied the opportunity by one company, will simply join another which will send them abroad.'[27] Ahuja's dream of New York and the Rolling Stones was not unusual. It was one of the things the business ran on.

## The minicomputer route

The firms that did this work had come to it by several roads. One ran through the American computer makers that replaced IBM in India after 1978. These minicomputer firms found the Indian market small and slow, and to keep their operations viable they began using local engineers to write software for the machines they sold locally. They found, in Sharma's words, 'that not only were Indian engineers cheaper but the quality of software they wrote was very good', and they began using them for customers back home.[28]

Narendra Patni, whose company sold Data General minicomputers in India, described how his firm's software business began. 'There was a lot of business exchange, and we started doing software work for them including operating systems. That's how our software stream started.'[29] The engineers who did such work are rarely heard in the record. One who is, through a note he sent Sharma in 2006, is K.R. Trilokekar, who joined ORG Systems in 1978. ORG, a division of the Ambalal Sarabhai group, distributed Sperry's mainframes in India. 'We developed P1024 protocol, which Sperry used in its mainframes worldwide,' Trilokekar recalled. 'We also developed several systems software products for them.'[30] His is a reminder that the trade was not only coding to other people's designs. Some Indian engineers wrote the systems software that sat at the heart of American machines.

The largest road ran through Tata. TCS had learned its trade in the 1970s on work for the American computer maker Burroughs, and the two firms' joint software company, Tata Burroughs, was renamed Tata Unisys in 1986.[31] Sharma reports that these two Tata companies 'accounted for nearly 70 per cent of exports through body shopping'.[32] The World Bank's table of top exporters, from data gathered by the National Association of Software and Service Companies (Nasscom), the industry's lobby group, and published in 1994, shows how far ahead they stayed. TCS's exports were Rs 1,754.8 million and Tata Unisys's Rs 560.0 million. The next firm, Digital Equipment (India), had Rs 317.8 million.[33]

Below these few firms, the industry was tiny. Over three-quarters of Indian software companies had fewer than twenty-five professionals, and about 95 per cent had software revenue under $100,000. Some, the World Bank noted, were in the business of renting out programmers abroad and operated with 'a one-room office, telephone and fax'.[34] So many start-ups took this road for a simple reason. A new firm founded by someone who had left a big company could trade on that person's contacts. It could not so easily overcome the barriers of technology, skills and finance, and so it began with onsite programming, where there were few economies of scale. Selling anything else took patience: a few firms had spent two or three years on export marketing before winning a first order.[35]

## Seven founders and an apparel package

Infosys was one of those start-ups. After a first company of his own, Softronics, had failed for want of computers in India, Murthy joined Patni Computer Systems in Bombay as general manager of software and visited the United States many times.[36] Patni, he recalled in an earlier museum interview in 2018, sold Data General computers in India, wrote application software for Indian customers and exported software to the United States, and he built a group of 'about 100 youngsters' there.[37] Among his colleagues were Nandan Nilekani and Kris Gopalakrishnan, young engineers with a year or a year and a half of experience. When he left to try again, he told them he was 'convinced that there's going to be a great future for a company that develops bespoke software for a large market like the U.S.'[38]

The company was incorporated in July 1981 as Infosys Consultants Private Limited.[39] Its 1999 filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission says it was founded by seven people: Murthy and six software professionals.[40] They had, Murthy said in 2018, 'lots of hopes, lots of dreams, some confidence, but no money', and what carried them was 'a deal with our client who gave us a reasonably good advance'.[41] The founding is usually remembered for a small sum: Sudha Murty, Murthy's wife, has said she gave him Rs 10,000 of her savings of Rs 10,250 to start it, keeping Rs 250 back, and that she saw it as a risk because his previous venture had failed.[42] At the 1981 average exchange rate that was about $1,150.[43] The story is told often. What the company did next is told less.

Murthy described the first customer to the Computer History Museum. It was an American firm, Data Basics, which sold a software package to apparel and shoe companies, among them Jockey and Reebok. Most of its customers ran the package on small 16-bit minicomputers, the Data General NOVA or the DEC PDP-11. Infosys proposed to move it to a 32-bit Data General MV/8000 and later to an IBM 4381 mainframe, so that Data Basics could sell to bigger companies. 'It was a godsend for us,' Murthy said.[44] The job was a port, the rewriting of an existing program to run on different machines: exactly the kind of conversion work that the World Bank would later list as typical of Indian contracts.[45]

The clearest record of where the founders spent the 1980s is the management section of that 1999 filing. It reads like the biography of a body shop. 'From 1981 to 1987, Mr. Nilekani was in the United States managing the marketing and development efforts of Infosys.' K. Dinesh, from 1981 to 1990, 'managed projects for Infosys in the United States'. S.D. Shibulal, from 1981 to 1991, 'worked for Infosys in the United States on projects in the retail and manufacturing industries'. From 1987 to 1994 Gopalakrishnan managed 'all projects at the U.S.-based KSA/Infosys', a joint venture with the American consultancy Kurt Salmon Associates.[46] Three of the seven founders, in other words, spent most or all of the decade working in America, and a fourth ran the projects of an American-based joint venture for the last part of it.
