Nilekani's own recollection matches the filing. Murthy, he said, opened an office in his flat in Poona (now Pune), and 'we all went abroad, so he was the only guy here. We were all sitting in Florida or somewhere doing some programming work for a company which was a client'. 'Essentially from 1981 to 1987,' he said, 'I was in the U.S. working on various projects for Infosys for clients in the U.S.' His explanation was the one Sharma and Heeks gave: 'in the early days when the technology was not there yet, we had to actually go and do this work physically.'[47]

The same filing describes Infosys as one of the pioneers of a different model. 'The Indian offshore development model was initiated in the mid-1980's', it says, as a way of dividing a project between a facility in India and the client's site.[48] That is the company's own claim, made to investors. The founders' careers show that for most of the decade the Infosys model, like everyone else's, was onsite. By the early 1990s Infosys was twelfth in the World Bank's table of exporters, with exports of Rs 120.6 million.[49] In 1994, Murthy recalled, the whole company, perhaps 200 people, could still meet in its canteen.[50]

## Selling hours

How was this work priced? The question matters to the argument of this book, which is that the Indian industry was built to sell engineers' time rather than finished products. The best sources for the 1980s converge on an answer, though none of them is a contract.

The first is a World Bank study by Nagy Hanna, published in 1994, which drew on Nasscom data and on surveys of foreign buyers made in 1991 and 1992. It described Indian export growth as coming mainly from contract programmers doing low-level work, '"body-shopping" or "manpower contracts" in which the overseas buyer typically buys "hours" and not a total project or product'. It went on: 'Typically, programmers are contracted out to work for a client at an agreed hourly or monthly rate for six to eighteen months.' The jobs were data conversion and coding, such as moving systems from batch processing to online processing, or converting code to run on Unix.[51] The contracts were 'short in term, low in risk, low in value added, and low in investment', and they made up '70-80 percent of the industry's export revenues'.[52]

The second is Heeks's survey work, and it measures something different from his onsite figure: not where contracts were done but how they were billed. 'During the period 1988-1998,' he wrote, 'at least 65% of export contracts were solely for programming work billed on a "time and materials" basis, with programming figuring strongly in the remaining one-third of contracts.'[53] Time and materials is the contract term for billing a client for staff time at agreed rates, plus expenses. The rate could be set per hour, per day or per person per month. The opposite is a fixed-price contract, where the supplier promises a result for a set sum and carries the risk if it takes longer.

The third is Ahuja's case, a single documented price: $50 an hour, billed by HCL to Sun in 1990.[54]

A fourth, from inside HCL, is a recollection. Arjun Malhotra, one of its founders, told the Computer History Museum in 2018 that he was sent to HCL's new office in Sunnyvale, taken in 1989, to wind down the company's attempt to sell its own computers in America. He laid off the hardware team, but the American software companies whose compilers and databases his engineers had been adapting for HCL's machines asked for the work to continue and offered to pay for it. That gave him 'a nice positive cashflow, because they were paying me $45+ an hour in those days. I'm going back to 1989.' He thought he had 'about 10, 15, maybe 20 people' there, and he dated HCL's services business from it: 'That is how HCL Technologies started.'[55] His figure is close to the $50 an hour that Sun paid HCL for Ahuja.

Together these sources support the claim that Indian software exports were priced by time and not by product, at least from 1988 and very likely through the decade. Two limits apply. For the years before 1988 the evidence is the World Bank's general description, written in 1994. And the time was sold by the hour or by the month; only Ahuja's case documents a true hourly rate, with Malhotra's recollection beside it.[56]

Why did Indian firms not sell products instead? Heeks's answer, written in 1998, was that the barriers to packaged software were higher than those to services. Indian firms were far from the foreign markets they wanted to serve and found it hard to follow changing needs. Software multinationals could spend 40-50 per cent of their annual revenue on selling and marketing packages, and experience suggested that 'only about 1-5% of software packages succeed'. Neither government policy nor managers' attitudes favoured such high-risk, long-term bets.[57] Some firms did custom work cheaply in the hope of selling the result as a package, but such 'packages' often became platforms for more custom work.[58]

The pricing had consequences that Heeks spelled out. A firm that sold time could grow only by selling more of it: in custom services, 'earnings are directly proportional to the number of people working in the industry'.[59] This is the bargain the rest of this book follows. Revenue rose with headcount, so a firm that wanted to grow had to keep hiring, and every hour of work it saved was an hour it could not bill. The time it sold was also the cheapest part of the job. Citing a 1991 study by Bhatnagar and Jain, Heeks wrote that 'Coding is the lowest paid part of the software development process, earning only 10-15% of total project revenue'.[60] Foreign buyers knew what they were paying for. A survey of 150 American and European hardware and software firms, cited by the World Bank, ranked Indian software services as having 'the lowest labor cost after China'. Citing a separate 1991 study of European attitudes, the report also noted 'a low perception of Indian software skills in OECD markets', particularly in project management, and observed that programmers who returned from onsite work had gained little or no experience of managing large projects.[61] The pattern lasted. In the nine months to December 1998, Infosys earned 63.7 per cent of its revenue from time-and-materials contracts and 36.3 per cent from fixed-price ones.[62]

## The policy catches up

The government did not invent body shopping, but in the 1980s it began to recognise it. The shift was slow. Looking back in 1994, Murli Menon, editor of the Indian magazine *C&C*, wrote that 'In 1984, the government still believed in self-reliance, indigenisation and protection of the domestic [computer] industry'.[63] Yet the computer policy of that year counted the work of engineers sent to clients' sites abroad as software export (Chapter 5). The state now counted the body shop as an exporter.[64]

With machines easier to obtain, some firms began working from India on clients' systems, though high telecommunications costs held this back.[65] Two foreign arrivals showed what the alternative could look like: Citibank's software unit at SEEPZ, inaugurated in 1985 as Citicorp Overseas Software Limited (COSL), which by the year to March 1990 was India's third-largest software exporter and even sold a banking product, priced as a thing rather than as hours, and the centre that Texas Instruments set up in Bangalore with its own satellite link to Dallas, which Heeks called 'the first proper offshore software facility' (Chapter 8 tells TI's story).[66]

The World Bank saw better data links as the way out of body shopping and the brain drain.[67] In the 1980s, though, TI and COSL were exceptions. An estimate by Rakesh Basant and Uma Rani, cited by Upadhya and Vasavi, shows how rare they remained: in 1990-91, '90 per cent of Indian software and service export revenues came from onsite work and only 5 per cent from offshore'.[68] Heeks traced the persistence of onsite work into the 1990s to clients' distrust of unknown Indian suppliers, their focus on cost, projects too small to be worth sending offshore, the need for face-to-face contact and the shortage of experienced managers in India.[69] Even in the year to March 1998, more than half of software services export earnings still came from onsite work.[70] Pratap Chatterjee, the *Multinational Monitor* reporter, wrote in 1995 that until about two years earlier most Indian software exported to the United States had been produced on American soil.[71]

## Who went

The people who went were, overwhelmingly, young men. Heeks found that 'Only some 10% of Indian software developers are female'. Women faced particular obstacles, because the work often meant unsocial hours and, above all, going overseas. One manager described onsite programming to him as 'the young, single man's game'. Yet the women Heeks interviewed felt that software offered 'a more relaxed and less discriminatory atmosphere than many other Indian employment options'.[72]

The papers they travelled on are thinly documented for the decade. Heeks wrote that only when American rules tightened in the 1990s were Indian workers channelled into temporary work visas, 'rather than student or training or even tourist visas as in the past'.[73] Ahuja's B1/B2 visa fits that description.[74] The work visa that later defined the trade, the H-1B, belongs to Chapter 13.

The firms invested in the people they sent, and they tried to keep them. Sharma describes the routine: firms 'had to hire the right people, train them for a brief while, send them to American clients to execute projects and then they would come back'.[75] Not all came back. The World Bank observed that 'once the personnel are abroad, the temptations to remain abroad are strong', and that the cost of endlessly training replacements had to be set against low profit margins.[76]

Some firms used the courts. Chatterjee described a programmer whom TCS had brought to San Francisco. When she tried to move to another company, TCS 'sued to enforce her contract, which called for her to pay more than $30,000 to the company if she quit'. The firm's lawyer, the magazine reported, said TCS had sued sixteen former employees successfully and had won her case too.[77]

Ahuja's $800 a month in 1990 is the earliest known figure for the pay of an Indian programmer sent abroad.[78] In the 1990s the US Department of Labor found Indian firms paying their programmers in America '$15,000 a year plus housing and travel', against '$70,000 plus benefits' for an average American counterpart.[79] Chatterjee wrote in 1995 that a good software engineer in California could earn $100,000 a year while the best in India earned $10,000.[80] Infosys's 1999 filing, citing the consultancy Software Productivity Research, put the average Indian software wage at about 15 per cent of the American rate.[81] The gap was the business. It explains both why clients bought Indian hours and why Indian programmers wanted to be the ones sent to sell them.

Many stayed abroad for good. The World Bank estimated that migration of graduates from 'premier institutions like the IITs' was 'as high as 50 percent', and that nearly 60 per cent of computer science graduates of IIT Bombay and IIT Madras left the country for study or jobs.[82] It placed part of the blame on the trade itself: 'The orientation of the sector toward renting out programmers for the export market has led to the ubiquitous problem of "brain drain"'.[83]

## The ledger

By the numbers the decade was a success. Heeks's series, compiled from his own research and the trade magazine *Dataquest*, shows exports rising from $4.0 million in 1980 to $131.2 million in the year to March 1991.[84] The World Bank calculated that exports grew by 35 per cent a year between 1987 and 1991, against 21 per cent for the industry as a whole.[85] The number of firms with sales above $1 million rose from fifteen in 1990 to forty-four in 1992.[86] The exporters had also organised. Nilekani was a co-founder of Nasscom, and Murthy was its president from 1992 to 1994.[87]

The headline numbers overstated what India kept. They were gross foreign-exchange earnings. Net of the foreign exchange spent on Indian workers' travel and living allowances abroad, on marketing, on profits sent home by multinationals and on imported hardware and software, earnings were estimated at about 40 per cent of the gross.[88] The estimate, made in the late 1990s, covers more than travel, but it qualifies the case for the trade. An industry valued as a source of foreign exchange spent much of what it earned abroad, and a good part of that went on the costs of sending people there.

How to judge the decade is a matter of interpretation, and the sources allow three readings. Heeks headed his section on the trade 'Body shopping prison'. In that reading body shopping was low-value labour export that built few higher skills, lost the best people to emigration and left India's industry stuck at the bottom of the work.[89] Heeks also offered a second reading in the same paper: 'Some have therefore been able to use onsite "body shopping" services as a stepping stone to better things.'[90] He set out a possible path from exporting labour, to exporting services done in India, to exporting products, and found support for the first step among individual firms though little in the industry as a whole.[91] The third reading is about policy. Body shopping was a rational answer to import controls and scarce foreign exchange, and it outlived them because clients and managers liked it.[92] Heeks's own summary was that much of India's export growth may have come from the industry's 'dogged following of the low-risk, low-barrier first path'.[93]

## A warning in 1994

The World Bank's study named a risk in the model that this book returns to at its end. Among the drawbacks of body shopping it listed this: 'Demand for these skills is likely to be eroded by tools that automate many of these tasks.' Cheaper countries, it added, were entering the low end of the trade.[94] 'Globally,' the report went on, 'a long-term decline in demand for routine or low-level programmers has been forecasted.'[95] Heeks, four years later, also named 'automation from new technology' as one of the things that could hurt this kind of export.[96] He noticed a trap in it. Clients would let work go offshore only when it was tightly specified, and tightly specified work was exactly what automated software tools could do.[97]

These warnings did not come true in the decades that followed. The tools of the 1990s did not erode the demand for Indian programmers. Exports kept growing fast, reaching $1,650 million in the year to March 1998.[98] The epilogue of this book returns to them, and to the caution they suggest about any forecast that machines will soon do the work.

## Making programmers

Body shopping changed what a software education in India was for. Heeks found that '85% of workers in Indian software exports are programmers', although the average software project needed less than half its labour from programmers.[99] The industry hired, and the colleges supplied, people for the lowest stages of the work. The trade also drew them away from everyone else. The World Bank estimated that software export needs could 'cannibalize' other sectors 'by taking almost one-half of all new computing course graduates from government-initiated courses'.[100]

The 1980s had shown that India could sell its programmers' time abroad, and that the time sold best when there was plenty of it. The next chapter asks who made those programmers: the new degrees, the private institutes that sold computer courses to anyone who could pay, and the private engineering colleges whose fees became a political fight.


# Chapter 7. The training economy (1980-1995)

In 1971 Vinod Kumar Bansal, a newly qualified mechanical engineer from Banaras Hindu University, went to work for JK Synthetics in Kota, an industrial town in Rajasthan. He was already helping neighbourhood students prepare for the entrance tests for engineering courses. In the early 1980s, according to a 2023 book by Pradip K. Saha about the education company Byju's, he began teaching eight students sitting around his dining table, and in 1983, when his company shut down, he started teaching full-time.[1] Some of his students got into the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs), and, as Saha tells it, word spread that '"Bansal sir" had a magic touch'. Parents in Kota sought his help, and then parents from outside Rajasthan. Bansal Classes, as a named institution, dates from 1991.[2] By 2023, on Saha's figures, Kota had more than 150 coaching institutes and about 200,000 students, and more than 1.1 million candidates competed for 17,385 IIT places.[3]

Bansal's dining table stood at the narrow top of a much larger market. In the fifteen years after 1980 the public universities could not grow fast enough to make the people the software trade needed, and three other suppliers grew up beside them, each with a hand from the state. A government panel invented a new degree. Four state governments let private trusts open engineering colleges that charged their students the cost of their education and, the courts later found, sometimes more. And private companies began to sell programming in four-week and twelve-week courses, and from 1987, through franchises, in smaller towns.

This book reads that market as a bet on hours. The export trade sold engineers' time abroad by the hour. A family that paid for a coaching class, a capitation seat or a course in COBOL was buying a claim on hours its child might one day bill. The training companies sold the hours of teaching that made the billable hours. And the courts, in deciding what a college might charge, decided who could afford to place the bet.

## A degree for commerce graduates

The state saw the shortage coming. In 1980, V. Rajaraman, the historian of Indian computing, later wrote, the Electronics Commission 'foresaw the problem of scarcity of human resources for the emerging computer industry'.[4] Rajaraman, then the Kanpur professor who had built India's first academic computer science programme, was a member of the Commission, and he chaired the Panel on Computer Manpower Development that it set up.[5]

The panel made two proposals. The first was to expand undergraduate computer science at the IITs and other engineering colleges. The second, which Rajaraman called novel, was a new postgraduate course, the Master of Computer Applications (MCA).[6] It was aimed at the large number of Indian students who took three-year B.Sc degrees in physics, chemistry and mathematics, or B.Com degrees in commerce and economics. These degrees, in Rajaraman's words, 'do not prepare a student for a profession which requires specific skills'.[7] The panel felt that 'India needed a large number of persons to develop business/management information systems for use in organizations both in India and abroad'.[8] The phrase 'and abroad' is worth noticing. In 1980 the state's manpower planners already had foreign employers in view.

The curriculum combined three subjects: computer science 'with emphasis in software engineering and systems analysis', mathematics for operations research and statistics, and management science, so that graduates could talk to managers in their own language. It included 'a semester of actual system design in an organization', a placement in a working office.[9] Where a B.Tech in computer science trained people to design hardware and software, the MCA trained them to design software for business. The government decided at first to fund ten institutions in full to run it.[10] Rajaraman published his curriculum proposal in *CSI Communications*, the journal of the Computer Society of India, in October 1981.[11]

Three decades later Rajaraman judged his own creation generously. 'The availability of well trained MCAs was one of the contributing factors for the rapid growth of software services industry in India,' he wrote.[12] That is the designer assessing the design. The first firm count of MCAs in his history comes from much later: about 7,000 graduated in 1998.[13]

The other half of the panel's plan ran into the narrowness of the elite system. In 1978, the year IIT Kanpur opened the first undergraduate computer science course at any IIT, more than 100,000 students sat the entrance examination for 1,500 IIT places in all.[14] The other IITs soon started computer science degrees of their own, but IIT places stayed scarce, and the World Bank later estimated that as many as half of their graduates emigrated.[15] Rajendra Pawar, a co-founder of the training company NIIT, recalled the position in 1981 this way: 'there were a handful of people coming out of the IITs, but they were not the ones writing programs.'[16]

## 'A bold decision'

The decisive change came from the states. In the Sixth Five-Year Plan (1980-85), according to a 2010 paper from the National University of Educational Planning and Administration, quoted by the journalist Thomas Manuel, the central and state governments were 'finding it difficult to expand technical education', and 'a few state governments', especially Karnataka, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh, 'took a bold decision to permit private registered societies and trusts to establish and run technical institutions on a self-financing basis'.[17] Self-financing meant that the students paid.

The official count of colleges shows how fast the decision worked. In the academic year 1980-81 India had 149 engineering and technology colleges. Five years later, in 1985-86, it had 242, an increase of 62 per cent. Growth then slowed: there were 289 colleges in 1990-91 and 337 in 1994-95.[18] The great expansion of engineering colleges came after 1996 (Chapter 12). The surge of the early 1980s was the first, smaller rehearsal for it.[19] These are counts of institutions, not of students.[20]

New colleges needed teachers, and the people who could teach computing were the people the industry wanted most. In 1985 the Department of Electronics set up a committee under S. Sampath, which 'suggested training teachers in Computer Science for the colleges which were being newly established'.[21] The difficulty did not go away. A World Bank study of 1994 listed 'the scarcity of teachers and trainers, particularly in public education institutes' among the causes of the shortage of software staff.[22] It also blamed the trade's habit of 'renting out programmers' for shortages of teaching staff as well as for the brain drain.[23]

## Four weeks of BASIC

Outside the degree system, a different kind of supplier appeared. NIIT was founded in 1981 by Pawar and Vijay Thadani.[24] In a 2022 interview with the magazine *PCQuest*, Pawar recalled the state of computer education when they began: 'At that time, it was non-existent. But the manufacturing industry was already anticipating a problem of talent shortage.' NIIT, he said, 'was born out of that threat'.[25]

The timetable he remembered is precise. 'The first two courses that NIIT announced in 1981 were one, an entry level BASIC. It was a 4-week programme, 5 days a week and 2 hours a day.' The second was a longer programme: 'Entry level COBOL, for 12 weeks.'[26] BASIC was a simple teaching language. COBOL was the language of business data processing, and Pawar called it 'state of the art' at the time. NIIT also taught FORTRAN, the scientific language, to engineers and scientists.[27] Forty hours of BASIC was not an education in computer science. It was an introduction to a trade.

The curriculum grew with its customers. NIIT ran a course for company executives called 'How to buy a computer', and added systems analysis, design and databases. It made an arrangement with the company of Edward Yourdon, whom Pawar called 'the father of software engineering', to teach Yourdon's structured methodology, and Pawar recalled that 'TCS was a very big participant'.[28] Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), a far older firm, was buying training from a company that had existed for only a few years. But the core of the business stayed where it began: 'quite clearly the largest need was for people who could write programs.'[29]

NIIT's growth came from franchising. Rajaraman dates the start of its franchise model, 'to spread their courses to smaller towns in India', to 1987.[30] Pawar described it as an invention: 'We found like-minded entrepreneurs in cities and motivated them to go back to their towns and set up an NIIT centre.' He recalled that 'at its peak (there were thousands)' every centre had the same look and feel, and that the *Far Eastern Economic Review* 'talked of it as the McDonald's of education'.[31]

The franchisees were small businesspeople, and a 2002 profile in the trade magazine *Dataquest* named some of them. Pratap Agarwal, who had worked as a software engineer in the United States, opened a single NIIT centre in Chandigarh in 1988 and said that by 2002 he ran more than sixty. Others opened centres in Dehradun in 1990 and Faridabad in 1992; the Faridabad franchisee, Captain Virendar Singh, had worked in human resources at TCS and Wipro. Ludhiana followed in 1993 and Amritsar in 1994.[32] The same profile reported that in 1988 the magazine *Asiaweek* had called NIIT 'the biggest computer trainer this side of the Suez'.[33]

NIIT was not alone. Aptech, founded by Atul Nishar in 1986 according to a 2014 profile in *Outlook Business*, was the other company that, on that profile's account, 'defined the space' with NIIT. Looking back, that profile described the 1980s and 1990s as years of queues of students waiting to sign up for multi-year computer courses.[34] Rajaraman called Aptech and NIIT 'pioneers' of 'non-formal training in software development and computer use', which 'also provided the much needed human resources'.[35]

None of these companies has published its enrolments or fees for the 1980s. The best independent picture comes from the World Bank's 1994 study by Nagy Hanna, which reviewed the trade in the early 1990s, drawing on industry surveys. It found that 'an estimated 1,000 proprietary organizations turn out about 80,000 trainees annually from courses ranging from two weeks to two years.' Fees ran from Rs 800 for two months to Rs 8,000 for a one-year course, roughly $25 to $250 at the 1993 exchange rate.[36] The verdict on quality was harsh. 'Industry specialists estimate that 98 percent of the training organizations are below standard,' Hanna wrote, and 'Few of the graduates find employment'. Only ten to fourteen of the larger organisations offered good programmes. Between them they trained about 40,000 people a year, some 30,000 of them in basic two-year programmes meant to qualify them for entry-level programming jobs.[37]

The study also gave the private trade's share. The proprietary organisations, it said, 'now produce almost 85 percent of the programmers and 40 percent of the systems analysts', and the large ones had been doubling their capacity and output over the previous few years.[38] If that estimate is right, by the early 1990s the typical Indian programmer had not been trained by a university at all. He, or less often she, had been trained by a company that sold courses, often in a franchised centre in a provincial town.

The state tried, late, to bring some order to this market. The Department of Electronics created a scheme called DOE Accreditation of Computer Courses (DOEACC), under which accredited private institutes taught standard courses, from basic programming, the 'O level', to a master's-level qualification, the 'C level'. Hanna called the scheme 'recently-developed' in 1994 and saw in it 'flexibility for recycling graduates from various fields into information technology'.[39] Recycling graduates from other fields was exactly what NIIT, Aptech and the MCA had been doing for a decade.

## What the employers found

The people who came out of this system went into a job market that was short of them and suspicious of them at the same time. Hanna's study found that in India 'the demand for trained software personnel far outstrips the supply, and the shortage is a major constraint to the industry's expansion'. The shortage placed a heavy training burden on firms and caused high staff turnover.[40] The same study warned that manpower forecasts made by the Department of Electronics and others were unreliable for lack of basic data.[41]

Yet employers trusted few of the public institutions. Only 275 industrial training institutes, polytechnics, colleges and universities were qualified and supported to run computer training. Most of them were short of teachers, equipment and books, and had weak links with industry. In 1991 the number of MCA graduates rose by 50 per cent, yet only 5 per cent were hired by software exporters. One large software house considered students from only thirty universities.[42] The MCA was producing graduates, but few of its graduates were going to the exporters.

The large firms trained their own. The World Bank reproduced, from a background paper written by the National Association of Software and Service Companies (Nasscom), the industry's lobby group, a short account of in-house training at TCS, which had just completed twenty-five years. TCS said that it recruited able graduates from leading institutions and turned them into systems professionals through a demanding initial training programme. Its corporate training centre in Bombay (Mumbai since 1995) had run 6,000 programme days in the previous year, about 120,000 person-days of training, and the company said it spent 7 to 8 per cent of its revenue on training.[43] Hanna judged that large firms did 'a satisfactory job' of in-house training, while small and medium firms did very little, for fear that trained staff would leave for better-paid jobs.[44]

The World Bank's remedy for the shortage was more of what the 1980s had already produced. It proposed 'recycling graduates in other disciplines into software engineering', inviting multinationals and non-resident Indians into computer education, and building 'centers of excellence in IT education on the lines of IITs'.[45]

## A seat with a price

Mohini Jain, a student from Meerut, was told by the management of Sri Siddhartha Medical College in Tumkur, in Karnataka, that she could join its medical degree course in the session beginning in February or March 1991. The management asked her to deposit Rs 60,000 as the tuition fee for the first year and to furnish a bank guarantee for the fees of the years that followed.[46] That was about $2,600 at the year's exchange rate.[47] The Supreme Court later recorded what happened next in a single sentence: 'The petitioner's father informed the management that it was beyond his means to pay the exorbitant annual fee of Rs.60,000 and as a consequence she was denied admission to the medical college.'[48] She also alleged that the college had asked for a further 'capitation fee of rupees four and a half lakhs', that is Rs 450,000. The management 'vehemently denied the same'.[49]

Mohini Jain wanted to be a doctor, not a programmer, but her case belongs in a book about software because of what the judges had to describe in deciding it. By 1991 a seat in a professional college in southern and western India, in engineering as in medicine, had a price, sometimes several prices, and the states had written them into notifications under the same laws. Within a year a larger bench of the Supreme Court heard private engineering and medical colleges from four states say that the ruling in her favour would force them to shut.[50]

## Regulating a surge

The states that opened the door to private colleges also tried to police what came through it. In Karnataka an ordinance of 1983 against capitation fees was replaced by the Karnataka Educational Institutions (Prohibition of Capitation Fee) Act, 1984, which took effect from 11 July 1983.[51] A capitation fee was a payment for admission, over and above tuition, and the laws defined it broadly. Maharashtra's Act of 1987, which received the governor's assent on 13 April 1988, defined it as 'any amount, by whatever name called', in excess of the fees the government had prescribed or approved.[52]

Maharashtra's legislators explained themselves in the preamble. Capitation, they wrote, 'is on the increase in the State', and 'this undesirable practice has been contributing to large scale commercialisation of education which is not conducive to the maintenance of educational standards'. They called it 'this evil practice'.[53] Tamil Nadu passed its own Act in 1992, and Andhra Pradesh already had one, from 1983.[54] Each of the four states that had licensed the private colleges thus also had a law against what the colleges were doing.

National policy said the same thing in two minds. The National Policy on Education of 1986, as the Union government quoted it to the Supreme Court, declared that 'the commercialisation of technical and professional education will be curbed', and in the next sentence promised that 'An alternative system will be devised to involve private and voluntary effort in this section of education'.[55] Maharashtra cited the first half of this in its preamble.[56]

In 1987 Parliament gave the All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) statutory powers.[57] Its functions read like a list of the problems of the 1980s. The Council was to 'make forecast of the needed growth and development in technical education', the manpower planning of the 1980 panel now written into law. It was to 'fix norms and guidelines for charging tuition and other fees' and to 'take all necessary steps to prevent commercialisation of technical education'.[58] Its definition of technical education did not name computer applications or software, and a technical institution was 'an institution, not being a university'.[59] On the text of the Act, then, the franchised courses of NIIT and Aptech fell outside the regulator's reach unless the government notified otherwise. In the early 1990s, Hanna found, the government was 'considering regulating the proprietary training organizations and setting quality standards, but nothing has been done up to now.'[60]

The regulator also came after the surge it was meant to discipline: the number of engineering colleges had already risen from 149 to 242 before the Act was passed.[61] By 1992 the government's Programme of Action admitted an urgent need to strengthen the AICTE. It asked the Council to work towards a 'realistic fee structure' based on the actual cost of education, to encourage private participation in technical education, and to add a 'penal clause' to its own Act to curb malpractices.[62] The Union government told the Supreme Court that the AICTE was approving new engineering colleges on the condition that they collect no capitation fee, and that under its guidelines an unaided college could recover about 70 per cent of the cost of a student's education in fees, against 20 per cent in a government institution.[63]

## Three prices for one seat

The fees on paper were set by the states. In Maharashtra the government prescribed a uniform fee of Rs 6,500 a year in private unaided engineering colleges, raised to Rs 8,500 in 1991 (about $375 at that year's rate). In 1992 it raised the fee only for students from outside the state, to Rs 17,000. The government filled 90 per cent of the seats in private engineering colleges with its own nominees and left 10 per cent to the managements.[64] In Andhra Pradesh the permitted fee in private engineering colleges for 1991-92 was Rs 10,000 a year.[65] These were the official fees. Capitation payments, by their nature, were rarely recorded.

The clearest record of how a seat was priced comes from medicine, in the notification at the centre of Mohini Jain's case. On 5 June 1989 Karnataka fixed the fees that private medical colleges could charge. Students admitted to 'Government seats' paid Rs 2,000 a year. Other Karnataka students could be charged up to Rs 25,000. 'Indian students from outside Karnataka' could be charged up to Rs 60,000.[66] The same course, in the same college, had three prices, and the highest was thirty times the lowest.

The colleges defended the scale. Their counsel told the Court that the students who paid more belonged to a different class: those on government seats were 'meritorious' and the rest were not. The association of private medical colleges argued that they received no aid from the central or state governments, that a five-year medical course cost them about Rs 5 lakh (Rs 500,000) per student, and that because 40 per cent of the seats paid only Rs 2,000, the cost had to fall on the rest. The fees, on this argument, were not profit but recovery of cost.[67]

The bench of two judges, Kuldip Singh and R.M. Sahai, rejected this entirely on 30 July 1992. In Justice Kuldip Singh's words: 'Capitation fee is nothing but a price for selling education. The concept of "teaching shops" is contrary to the constitutional scheme and is wholly abhorrent to the Indian culture and heritage.'[68] 'Education in India has never been a commodity for sale,' he added.[69] The judgment named the social effect plainly. Capitation brought 'a clear class bias': 'A poor student with better merit cannot get admission because he has no money whereas the rich can purchase the admission.'[70] The Court held that the right to education flowed directly from the right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution. The Rs 60,000 charged to outsiders was 'not tuition fee but in fact a capitation fee', and a private college run with government recognition should be prohibited from charging more than the government's Rs 2,000 from any student.[71]

The case concerned a medical college, but its reasoning applied to every recognised private professional college, and the engineering colleges understood that at once.

## Hyderabad, 1992

What the private engineering colleges did when the law left them room is recorded in the judgment that followed. Andhra Pradesh had 'a number of private engineering colleges', the Supreme Court noted. Until the academic year 1992-93 all their seats were filled by the convenor of the state's common entrance test. The managements had no say in admissions and were allowed only to charge a fee 'relatively higher than the fees charged in the Government Engineering Colleges'.[72] On 15 April 1992 the state inserted a new section, 3-A, into its Act. The colleges took it to mean that they could admit half their students 'according to their choice, irrespective of merit, so long as they have qualified in the entrance test'.[73] The Court's comment was dry: 'It is obvious that such a stand meant collection of capitation fee as much as they could.'[74]

'There was an uproar among the student and teaching community against such admissions,' the judgment continues. The government told the colleges on 26 July 1992 not to admit anyone until rules had been made. By then the colleges said they had already filled their half. The convenor, for his part, had allotted students to only half of each college's seats, 'thereby sending an explicit signal that the colleges were free to fill up the rest on their own'.[75] The colleges then charged the same Rs 10,000 fee to both halves. 'Thus they have reaped a double advantage,' the Court observed.[76]

The students admitted in this way were the rank and file of the training economy, and the judgment records them only as a class. Their counsel, Shanti Bhushan, argued that 'they were innocent parties and had obtained admission in a bona fide belief that their admissions were being made properly'. By the time the Supreme Court ruled they had been studying for months.[77] The Court let them stay. It ordered the colleges to charge 'the 50% "free students"', for the rest of their course, only the fee of the university engineering colleges, which it called the 'government fee', and to pay the balance already collected that year into the government's account within six weeks or lose their recognition and affiliation.[78]

## The free seat and the payment seat

The larger question reached a bench of five judges in *Unni Krishnan, J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh*, decided on 4 February 1993. The petitioners, Justice B.P. Jeevan Reddy wrote, were 'running medical/engineering colleges in the States of Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu', and they said that if *Mohini Jain* was followed 'they will have to close down; no other option is left to them'.[79]

Both sides put their case in strong terms. The colleges argued that the law of supply and demand should be given free play, and that 'only when there was profit motive that persons with means would come forward to open more and more schools and colleges'. At the least, they said, a citizen had the right to set up 'a self-financing educational institution, which institution might also be described as one providing cost-based education'.[80] Against them stood, among others, the Indian Medical Council and the AICTE itself. Their argument, as the headnote summarised it, was that 'a capitation fee did not cease to be a capitation fee just because it was called as cost-based education or by calling the Institution concerned as a self-financing Institution'.[81] The Union government took a middle line. Private institutions could not be forced to charge only government fees, it argued, and 'It would be unrealistic and unwise to discourage private initiative' in providing education.[82]

The Court partly overruled *Mohini Jain*. It agreed that a right to education flowed from the right to life, but held that its content was limited by what the state could afford. Citizens could not 'demand that the State provide adequate number of medical colleges, engineering colleges and other educational institutions to satisfy all their educational needs'.[83] The right to free education ran to the age of fourteen. Above that, private colleges without state aid could charge more than government colleges, within a ceiling, but 'commercialisation of education' was still not allowed.[84]

To give this effect the Court wrote a scheme, to apply from 1993-94. It covered every private professional college, defined to include 'colleges of engineering and colleges and institutions imparting technical education including electronics, computer sciences'.[85] At least half of the seats in each college were to be 'free seats', filled by the government or university on merit at the government fee. The rest were 'payment seats', filled by those prepared to pay a fixed higher fee, but still in order of merit. 'There shall be no quota reserved for the management or for any family, caste or community which may have established such college.'[86] All admissions would run through one state notification for each kind of college.[87] The payment half, in effect, was to pay for the free half.

The scheme was a compromise between the market reading and the commercialisation reading of the 1980s. It accepted that private colleges would charge their students much more than the state did, and it tried to keep merit as the rule for deciding who could pay. It governed admissions to private professional colleges for the rest of the period this chapter covers, and for some years after. On 31 October 2002 eleven judges of the Supreme Court, in *T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka*, held that the scheme 'was not correct' and overruled it, leaving unaided colleges to fix their own fees, though still without capitation fees or profiteering (Chapter 12).[88]

## Who paid

The question of who could enter the new profession has a partial answer in the legal record, and the answer is those whose families could pay. Karnataka's notification charged an outsider thirty times what a government-seat student paid for the same medical course.[89] The Andhra colleges filled half their engineering seats at their own discretion, and the Court found it 'not possible to investigate or verify for what consideration those admissions were made'.[90] A family that wanted an engineering seat in the south or west, and could not win one on merit in a government college, could buy one. Mohini Jain's father, in the one sentence the record gives him, said that he could not.[91]

The training companies offered a cheaper door. Their courses cost from a few hundred to a few thousand rupees, and in the World Bank's phrase they recycled graduates from other fields into computing.[92] They were also, on Hanna's evidence, a gamble: most institutes were below standard and few of their students found jobs.[93] The franchise spread the gamble to towns like Chandigarh, Dehradun and Ludhiana, where local entrepreneurs opened centres under the NIIT name.[94]

By the mid-1990s the training economy had made software a career that could be bought, at every price from a two-month course at a franchised centre to a payment seat in a private engineering college. Each purchase was a bet that the hours a graduate would one day sell would repay the hours bought to make the graduate. *Unni Krishnan* had settled who could place the larger bet, and on what terms. Whether it paid would be settled by the trade.


# Chapter 8. Satellite and permit (1984-1991)

On a day in 1985 that he called memorable when he wrote about it in 2013, the journalist Janardhan Roye found his Ambassador car stuck behind a bullock cart outside his office on Miller Road in Bangalore (Bengaluru since 2014). The cart was heavily laden, and it was struggling up the steep slope at the gate of an office block called Sona Towers. Traffic piled up and horns blared until security staff came to the aid of the cart's driver.[1] The people in the neighbouring offices, he recalled, were less interested in the traffic than in the wooden boxes being unloaded.[2]

The boxes were addressed to the Bangalore office of Texas Instruments (TI), the semiconductor company from Dallas. They held the equipment for a two-way satellite link between India and the United States, for data transmission and software development.[3] Among the onlookers, Roye recalled, was Sam Pitroda, the engineer who led the government's telecommunications research centre, C-DOT, and who was often to be seen at its offices on the floor above Roye's. When the contents of the boxes became known, Roye remembered him shaking his head and smiling: 'This can happen only in India.'[4] The building's owner, the Sona Group, tells the same story of a satellite dish arriving by bullock cart.[5]

The dish was small by later standards. Roye gives its capacity as 64 kilobits a second, and he described the antenna as 'like a whale surfacing'.[6] What made it remarkable was not its speed but its permission. Until then, telephone networks and overseas links had been a government monopoly, run by a department whose staff were civil servants. TI's dish was a private line out of the country, approved by the state.[7]

The years from the computer policy of November 1984 to the first Software Technology Parks of 1990 and 1991 were the years of Rajiv Gandhi's government and its immediate successors, and they are often remembered as the moment India's information technology industry began. The record supports a narrower claim. The permit regime was loosened in pieces, and much of what changed was paperwork: duties, licences and the definitions of what counted as an export. The changes that moved software work into India, rather than sending Indian programmers abroad to do it, were mostly about telecommunications, and they came late and slowly. A satellite dish on a bullock cart is a fair emblem of both halves.

## The permit, loosened

Rajiv Gandhi had learned what computers could do at a sporting event. When the Asian Games were held in Delhi in 1982, he, the son of the prime minister, Indira Gandhi, and in the account of V. Rajaraman, the historian of Indian computing, 'an amateur electronics buff', was given overall charge of organising them. He decided that computers should draw up the schedules, keep the event records, announce the results and do the clerical work. Locally made DCM computers served as terminals at the venues, connected to a Hewlett-Packard server, and software engineers of the government's National Informatics Centre wrote the whole system in six months. The computerisation of the Games was, in Rajaraman's words, 'a resounding success', and it brought the centre's director general, N. Seshagiri, close to Rajiv Gandhi.[8] Organising the Games also brought him into contact with the private computer makers, who told him of their difficulties with 'myriad rules and regulations'.[9] After Indira Gandhi's assassination in 1984 he became prime minister, with Seshagiri as an informal adviser.[10] Rajaraman describes him as a man of the post-independence generation who 'was open minded regarding private enterprise'.[11] The new computer policy followed within weeks. Dataquest's chronology dates it to 19 November 1984.[12]

Its effect on hardware was to turn Indian computer making into assembly. For exporters it did three things. It recognised software as an 'industry', which opened the way to bank loans and duty exemptions. It cut the customs duty on computers imported to write software for export, which, Rajaraman writes, 'Earlier it used to be over 100%'. And it counted engineers sent to work at clients' sites abroad as software exporters.[13]

The policy also carried a promise. According to a World Bank study of 1994 by Nagy Hanna, the government announced its Computer Policy Plan in November 1984 and 'expected software exports to reach US$258 million (or 0.5 percent of the world market) by 1990'.[14] It was a target built, the Bank thought, on 'limited but alluring data' about the world market.[15]

Two years later, in December 1986, came the Policy on Computer Software Export, Software Development and Training; in the Bank's account, 'A major reform in computer software' followed its adoption.[16] Its terms show how far the old logic of foreign exchange still governed the trade. A firm could import a computer duty-free to write software for export, but it had to 'earn 250% of the cost of the imported computer within 4 years'. Where no foreign exchange had been spent, for example 'a non resident Indian bringing a computer with his earnings', the obligation fell to 150 per cent.[17] The rule descends from the bargain Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) had struck over its Burroughs machine in the 1970s: the state would allow imports if they paid for themselves in dollars.

Two clauses pointed somewhere new. 'Software developed in India could be exported using communication systems such as satellite and cable.' And the state-owned Computer Maintenance Corporation's (CMC's) network of IBM mainframes, called Indonet, was opened to exporters at a concessional tariff.[18] Foreign capital was eased too. From 1986 foreign firms could own all of an export-oriented software project, though they were still held to 40 per cent of firms selling software in India.[19] That 40 per cent was the figure that had driven IBM out in 1978. It was now waived for anyone who exported.

The historian Dinesh Sharma sums up the effect of the two policies cautiously. Imports of hardware and software were liberalised, 'though the actual import of hardware still took time'. Bringing software under the Open General Licence, the list of goods that could be imported without a separate permit, meant that 'New software packages and tools started becoming available'.[20] The World Bank was less kind about the system that administered all this. In its account, policy had 'fundamentally focused on ways to make export figures rise', while 'troublesome delays exist for import of computers and spare parts'. 'On the positive side,' it concluded, 'it has pushed firms into exporting. On the negative side, this pushing has been short-term oriented'.[21]

## The dish

TI's link required a negotiation inside the government before it required a bullock cart. Rajaraman, who had served on the government's Electronics Commission, records it briefly. 'The DoE negotiated with the Department of Telecommunication (DoT) in 1985 to allow Texas Instruments (TI) to set up a dedicated satellite communication link to its centre at Dallas, USA.' Over that link, he adds, TI's Bangalore centre sent the software tools it developed to Dallas.[22] The Department of Electronics (DoE), headed by scientists and engineers since 1970, promoted computing; the Department of Telecommunications ran the telephones.[23] Rajaraman judged the result 'the first step in breaking the monopoly of the DoT in communications', with far-reaching consequences for offshore development centres and, later, the Software Technology Parks.[24]

The World Bank added a detail. TI 'obtained a private Intelsat Business Service earth station so that its programmers can communicate with other TI operations using satellite links'. The special measures and approvals TI won, the Bank wrote, 'helped make India more attractive' to other foreign firms, among them Hewlett-Packard, Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC), British Telecom, Philips and Westinghouse.[25] Richard Heeks of the University of Manchester, who studied the industry through fieldwork in India, reported that 'TI was known to have cut through many red tape barriers, particularly on imports', and that its arrival was 'constantly reported in the home and international media'.[26]

The date is disputed by a year. TI's own milestone list puts the start of its Indian operations in 1985, the year of the negotiation and of Roye's bullock cart; Heeks dates TI's arrival to 1986. The likeliest reading is that TI arrived in 1985 and its satellite link was working by 1986.[27]

TI's claim to have been first is narrower than the one often made for it. In 1985, its press release says, TI became 'the first multinational to establish a software design center in India and the first to install and use a satellite dish for exporting software'.[28] The World Bank's account of the private earth station supports the second half. The first half needs care. Citibank had set up a software unit in the Santa Cruz Electronics Export Processing Zone (SEEPZ) in Bombay (Mumbai since 1995) in 1984, and it was inaugurated as Citicorp Overseas Software Limited on 28 October 1985; in its early years it wrote software for the bank's own use in America and other regions.[29] What TI had first was the private line.

What TI did with it was not the work most Indian exporters did. Its Bangalore engineers wrote software tools, in Rajaraman's account.[30] From 1989, according to the company, the centre designed mixed-signal integrated circuits, chips that combine analogue and digital functions, and built libraries for computer-aided chip design; by 2005 its Bangalore engineers had filed close to 300 patent applications.[31] Rajaraman notes the irony that Indian engineers 'could design large scale integrated circuits, including combined analog and digital systems for TI and other overseas companies but had no foundry to fabricate them in India'.[32] TI showed that a multinational could put design work of a high order in India, which was a different thing from Indian firms doing it.

Heeks thought TI's arrival helped settle the industry in Bangalore rather than Bombay, a shift whose causes Chapter 10 examines.[33] Roye quotes C.S. Murali of the Indian Institute of Science on the dish: 'It turbocharged the IT revolution'.[34] Vijay Chandru, a scientist whom Roye also quotes, argues that Bangalore had been a technical city well before the multinationals came.[35]

## The wires that were missing

The dish mattered because the ordinary wires were so poor. 'In 1982 there was a waiting time of over 2 years to get a land line telephone connection,' Rajaraman writes. Telephones were run by a government department whose staff were civil servants and whose budget was part of the national budget, which in his account meant low investment and poor service.[36] Under Rajiv Gandhi two reforms followed. The telephones of Bombay and Delhi were handed to a public company, Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd (MTNL), with 'operational autonomy'. A second company, Videsh Sanchar Nigam Ltd (VSNL), was set up in 1986 to run overseas communication.[37]

The more visible change came from C-DOT. Formed in 1984 under Pitroda, it was given the task of designing small digital telephone exchanges that could survive rural India's poor power supply and its temperatures of 45 degrees in summer and below freezing in winter. C-DOT 'recruited a highly motivated group of engineers', and they produced a rugged exchange 'in a record time of 3 years'.[38] Alongside it spread the public call office, a telephone booth with a microprocessor that printed the cost of each call so that an attendant could collect it. Because a booth cost little to set up, many small entrepreneurs opened them in towns, villages and on highways. 'Every nook and corner of India was connected within 5 years,' Rajaraman writes. 'The power of microcomputer was visible to all'.[39]

None of this gave a software exporter a cheap line to a client in New Jersey. The overseas gateways stayed with VSNL, and the history published by Software Technology Parks of India, the agency that later took over the parks, records that data links carried a substantial cost.[40] In 1994 the World Bank still listed poor communications links among the industry's weaknesses.[41] It argued that faster, more open data services 'would open major opportunities for off-shore software services activities in India, thereby reducing dependence on body-shopping (on-site delivery of services) and the consequent brain-drain'.[42]

The numbers show how little the policies of 1984 and 1986 had moved the work. Heeks found that in 1988 about 65 per cent of export contracts were carried out wholly at the client's site abroad.[43] Sharma records that after 1986 some firms began 'remote software development', working from India on clients' machines, 'But still there were impediments such as high telecom costs'.[44] What India sold, in other words, was still mostly engineers' time, billed where the client was. The dish and, later, the parks would change where those hours were worked. They did not change what was being sold.

## Fifty counters

Inside India, the most important computer of the decade sold railway tickets. The project matters to this book for what it did to clerks.

The argument over computers and jobs was still live in 1984. When the Reserve Bank of India's Rangarajan committee recommended that every bank do its back-office work by computer, the growth of computing in the banks was, in Rajaraman's words, 'a red flag to the trade unions', and they observed 1984 as an 'anti-computerization year'.[45] Dataquest's chronology adds that in 1984 the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh declared an 'Anti Computer Year' in protest against the bank proposal, with 1 March observed as Anti-Computer Day.[46] The unions were also bargaining. A biographical note on Suresh Dhopeshwarkar, a bank union leader, held by the Indian Labour Archives, records that in 1983 his union 'reached the first ever agreement on computerisation to meet the new challenges'.[47] The state itself had been cautious. The minicomputer policy of 1978 had said it would 'continue to be restrictive in allowing use of computers in areas where labour displacement was likely to be involved'.[48]

The railways faced a problem of scale that no one could solve by hand. In 1984, Rajaraman writes, Indian Railways handled 'over 5 million passengers travelling in over 600 long distance trains with around 50,000 reservation requests'. Passengers stood in long queues. 'Clerks kept numerous ledgers, one for each train', and juggled between them as passengers changed their minds.[49] CMC proposed a computerised system. The railways accepted. The project began in 1984, and 'by 1986 a reservation system was developed and implemented at the New Delhi booking office. It had 50 counters and customers could go to any counter to get a reservation done for any train'.[50] The official audit of the system, by the Comptroller and Auditor General, gives an exact start for a smaller first step: the pilot, called IMPRESS, 'was launched on 15 November 1985' at New Delhi. The government dates the introduction of the reservation system proper to 1986.[51]

To the public, Rajaraman writes, it was 'almost a miracle'. Instead of waiting hours and running from counter to counter, a passenger could get a confirmed reservation within 30 minutes, book connecting and return journeys, and cancel for an immediate refund.[52] For the clerks the change came in the evening's accounts. 'The counter clerks were also happy,' Rajaraman writes, 'as they could reconcile the collected cash against issued tickets with the help of the computer within 30 minutes after closing time whereas in the manual system it used to take at least two hours.'[53] And they kept their jobs. 'There was also no reduction of staff; in fact there was an increase as more counters were operated with more clerks working simultaneously.'[54]

The mechanism is worth stating because the book returns to it. Demand for reservations had been held down by the queues. When the computer let any counter sell a ticket on any train, the railways opened more counters and needed more clerks to staff them. The machine raised each clerk's output, and the extra output was absorbed by demand that had been waiting. Whether that pattern holds for a new technology depends on how much demand is waiting, and that question runs through the last part of this book.

The system ran on a cluster of DEC VAX minicomputers, with terminals at the counters, and was written in FORTRAN. 'The entire software effort was by Indian software engineers', Rajaraman writes, with no foreign consultants involved.[55] He also claims it was the first such transaction system in the world to run on a VAX cluster.[56] Its effect on opinion he does not doubt. 'There was an attitudinal change among both the general public and the white collar workers about computerization', and some bank unions accepted the computerisation they had opposed.[57] He groups the reservation counters with the public call offices and the first electronic voting machines, used in a by-election in Kerala in 1982. Together, he writes, they 'changed the perception of policy makers and the general public about computers and their relevance to India'.[58]

## The Cray that did not come

The decade's best-known story about computers and national pride concerns a machine India did not get. It is usually told as a simple sequence: the United States refused India a Cray supercomputer, so India built its own. The record is more tangled.

In 1984 the Ministry of Human Resource Development gave the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) in Bangalore Rs 500 million, about $42 million at the rate Rajaraman uses of Rs 12 to the dollar, to set up a Supercomputer Education and Research Centre.[59] A national committee visited two companies in the United States and one in Japan and chose a Cray Y-MP. Cray signed a contract to install it at the institute by 1989, and 'Cray was confident of getting a licence to export the computer'. A team led by a US State Department official visited the institute and agreed conditions for its use.[60] Rajaraman, who chaired the centre from 1982 to 1994, 'participated in the entire exercise'. He records the outcome flatly: 'The US government did not give an export licence to Cray before the date specified in the contract'.[61] IISc cancelled the order and bought other machines instead, among them a Control Data Cyber 992 mainframe and, in 1992, an Indian-made parallel computer.[62] 'The denial of Cray was a blessing in disguise', Rajaraman concluded, 'as the money saved was used to buy state-of-the-art powerful parallel computers'.[63]

A second sale, for weather forecasting, was argued over in public in the United States. After the *Christian Science Monitor* reported the planned sale in December 1986, it printed on 8 January 1987 a reply from Dean Churchill, a meteorologist at the University of Washington who studied the monsoon. He thought that 'acquisition of a Cray or Cyber supercomputer might not solve the problem' of forecasting it, because of the lack of observations over the Indian Ocean and the gaps in scientific understanding.[64] That sale appears to have gone ahead in a smaller form: a Cray X-MP/14 was reportedly imported in October 1988 for the National Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasting.[65] If so, India was both denied one Cray and sold another.

In 1986 the Science Advisory Committee to the Prime Minister, chaired by the chemist C.N.R. Rao, set up a committee under Rajaraman on designing high-performance computers. It was formed, he writes, 'as a consequence of the difficulties encountered by India in buying supercomputers from the USA and Japan', and it proposed 'a mission mode project to build parallel computers with a speed of a giga-flop or above'.[66] A parallel computer divides a problem among many processors working at once; a gigaflop is a billion arithmetic operations on fractional numbers a second. In 1988 the DoE set up the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC) at Pune with Rs 300 million, about $22 million at that year's average rate, to build such machines. 'The project was successfully completed in 1991.'[67]

C-DAC was not alone. Between 1985 and 1992 the National Aeronautical Laboratory in Bangalore built FLOSOLVER for fluid dynamics, the Defence Research and Development Organisation built PACE in Hyderabad, and the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre built ANUPAM in Bombay.[68] The popular version, in which a single refusal leads straight to a single Indian supercomputer, owes much to later journalism; a 2017 web feature on C-DAC and PARAM, for example, says that the effort began when 'the US stopped the export of a Cray supercomputer'.[69] The defensible version is that American export controls, among other difficulties, pushed the government to fund parallel computing, and that several laboratories were already working on it.

What the episode produced, besides machines, was people. All these projects, Rajaraman writes, 'generated a large pool of engineers adept in designing and programming parallel computers'. Around ten IISc students earned doctorates in the field.[70] C-DAC also built a chip, called GIST, that let personal computers display most Indian scripts.[71]

## Laboratories as schools

The state projects of these years taught more people than they sold products. Most were paid for partly by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), and the pattern began with chip design. In 1984 the DoE used UNDP money, and a much larger sum of its own, to set up centres for computer-aided design (CAD) at two of the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs), at Kanpur and Bombay, at IISc and at Jadavpur University. 'Many scientists went abroad to get trained in the design and use of CAD tools', Rajaraman records, and came back to build tools of their own and teach short courses for industry. They had little choice: 'During the mid 80s the US Government had banned the export of CAD tools in electronics to even educational institutions in India.'[72] The same model ran the Knowledge Based Computer Systems programme from 1985 at five institutions, which worked on parallel computers, medical expert systems and the recognition of Indian scripts and speech.[73]

The longest-lived of these programmes was a network. In 1986 the DoE obtained four years of UNDP funding for Education and Research in Computer Networks (ERNET). It linked the five IITs, IISc, the National Centre for Software Technology (NCST) in Bombay and the DoE 'for exchange of email and other documents', and it was meant to train people in networking.[74] 'ERNET also brought the Internet to India under the leadership of S.Ramani of NCST, Mumbai,' Rajaraman writes, and after the project ended it became the internet provider for India's educational and research institutions.[75]

In all of them the money bought machines and sent scientists abroad, and the scientists came back, mostly to public laboratories and universities, and trained others. Rajaraman's summary is that by 1990 'a good foundation had been laid' in computer-aided design, parallel computing, networking and software engineering.[76] The published accounts do not say where the people they trained went next: into public research, to TI and the export firms, or abroad. The wider supply of engineers grew in the same years: recognised engineering and technology colleges nearly doubled in number between 1980-81 and 1990-91, by the statistics ministry's count.[77]

## The lobby and the department

The industry organised itself in these years. The Manufacturers' Association for Information Technology (MAIT) was founded in 1982, and the National Association of Software and Service Companies (Nasscom), the software firms' lobby, in 1988, with 38 members.[78] Rajaraman thought Nasscom 'fortunate in employing Dewang Mehta as its President in 1991. Mehta was a superb lobbyist for software companies'.[79]

The department the lobby dealt with changed character at the same time. From 1970 to 1988, Rajaraman writes, the DoE had been headed by technocrats and treated as a scientific department, like Atomic Energy and Space. In 1989 'A difference of opinion between two technocrats in the DoE' led to its being taken over by 'a generalist bureaucrat' of the Indian Administrative Service (IAS), and it ceased to count as a scientific department.[80] Yet he credits the generalist who followed. N. Vittal, an IAS officer who took over the DoE in 1990, was in his account 'dynamic and more business savvy' than his predecessors, and 'instrumental in setting up STPs and obtaining a host of fiscal concessions to the software industry by persuading the bureaucrats of the Ministry of Finance'.[81]

## The parks

The Software Technology Parks turned TI's privilege into a public service. Their stated purpose, in the World Bank's words, was to give small and medium firms 'an opportunity to enter the international software export market'.[82] Rajaraman describes what they offered: 'buildings, work stations and continuous uninterrupted power supply', and satellite links through which firms could 'develop software on the computers of their overseas customers from access terminals located in their respective premises'.[83] The World Bank adds a 'single window' for government clearance of imported equipment.[84] 'As the investment required to set up a company in STP was low,' Rajaraman writes, 'this initiative allowed many small entrepreneurs to enter the software services export business.'[85]

Rajaraman says 'The first STP was established in Bangalore in 1990'.[86] By the World Bank's dates Pune came first, in August 1990, two months ahead of Bangalore, followed by Bhubaneswar in December 1990, Hyderabad in February 1991, and Thiruvananthapuram, Gandhinagar and Noida in July 1991.[87] Software Technology Parks of India itself was registered on 5 June 1991.[88]

When the World Bank looked at the parks, about 160 companies had been approved to join, with estimated exports of $7.28 million by 1994, and it judged that 'it may be too early to judge' whether they would live up to expectations.[89] Rajaraman, writing with hindsight, put the parks beside the breaking of VSNL's monopoly and cheaper satellite links as the changes that 'allowed many entrepreneurs to enter the software export business'.[90]

## Half the target

By the end of the decade the export trade had grown fast from a small base. The World Bank's table of the industry shows software exports rising from $24 million in FY1985-86 to $128 million in FY1990-91, the year to March 1991.[91] These, like the other series of the period, count gross earnings, as Heeks warned, before the foreign exchange the trade spent abroad.[92] Even gross, the trade in FY1990-91 was about half of the $258 million that the government had expected by 1990 when it announced its policy in 1984.[93]

That gap is the best test of the claim that Rajiv Gandhi started India's information technology revolution. The strongest case for it is real. The policies of 1984 and 1986 came under his government, Rajaraman ties them to what he learned at the Asian Games, and the telephone reforms taken 'Under the leadership of Rajiv Gandhi', which created MTNL and VSNL, came in the same years as C-DOT's exchanges and the call offices that showed Indians what a microprocessor could do.[94] Roye's account of Bangalore in 2013 repeats the popular version, in which the business climate 'dramatically changed' once Rajiv Gandhi became prime minister.[95]

The case against is also documented. The export trade had begun in the 1970s, and the private computer industry that made his reforms possible had been opened by the policy of 1978, after IBM left. Heeks's series shows no sharp break at 1984. Exports grew by 99 per cent in 1982, 35 per cent in 1983 and 39 per cent in 1984, and by 9 per cent in 1985, 40 per cent in 1986 and 39 per cent in 1987.[96] The trade the policies counted as exports was still mostly programmers working abroad, and the share done in India rose only slowly. Sharma places 'The real breakthrough in software exports' after 1991, 'with the advent of the Software Technology Park scheme'.[97] The World Bank's reading is harsher still: the policies pushed firms to export, but in a 'short-term oriented' way, 'without any specific focus or direction on building sustainable competitive advantage and capabilities'.[98]

A third reading, which the evidence here supports best, puts the weight on infrastructure. The decisive changes were the ones that let work stay in India: TI's private link, negotiated in 1985, VSNL in 1986, the parks in 1990 and 1991. They came in pieces, across several governments, pushed by a technocratic department and then by a generalist one.[99] Rajiv Gandhi's government began that process. It did not finish it.

The permit, the old system of licences and obligations, was loosened between 1984 and 1986 but not abolished; a computer imported duty-free still had to earn back two and a half times its cost in dollars. The satellite, which could make an Indian office part of a foreign company's network, was in 1990 still a privilege granted case by case. By the time the first parks were registered, Rajiv Gandhi was out of office. His party lost the election of 1989, and the coalition that replaced it fell in 1990.[100] He was assassinated during the campaign for the election of 1991.[101] The government that took office after that election inherited a country, in Rajaraman's words, in 'a near default economic situation'.[102]



# Part III: The export machine (1991-2008)

# Chapter 9. 1991 (1990-1997)

On 24 July 1991 Manmohan Singh, a professional economist who had been finance minister for about a month, rose in the Lok Sabha to present the budget for the year to March 1992 (FY1991-92). He began with a dedication to Rajiv Gandhi, the former prime minister, who had been assassinated during the election campaign that spring.[1] Then he described what the new government had inherited. 'The new Government, which assumed office barely a month ago, inherited an economy in deep crisis. The balance of payments situation is precarious.'[2] India had borrowed from the International Monetary Fund in July 1990 and again in January 1991, and its foreign-exchange reserves had still fallen sharply. 'We have been at the edge of a precipice since December 1990 and more so since April 1991,' he said. 'We have not experienced anything similar in the history of independent India.'[3]

On his second page he gave the number that made the crisis concrete. 'The current level of foreign exchange reserves, in the range of Rs.2500 crores, would suffice to finance imports for a mere fortnight.'[4] Rs 2,500 crore was Rs 25 billion, about $1.1 billion at that year's average exchange rate.[5]

On page 20 of a speech that ran to thirty-one pages, the minister came to software. It got one paragraph. 'Our software industry has made considerable progress in recent years. However, there is still a vast unexploited potential for growth. It is time we make all-out efforts to capture the overseas software market.' To that end he proposed to extend to software exports the income-tax concession under section 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, which gave a deduction for profits from exports. 'With this concession, the exports of this industry should register rapid growth.'[6] Eleven pages later he closed by quoting Victor Hugo, that 'no power on earth can stop an idea whose time has come', and named the idea as India's emergence as a major economic power. 'Let the whole world hear it loud and clear. India is now wide awake. We shall prevail. We shall overcome.'[7]

The prediction came true. Software exports, by one count, rose from $128 million in the year to March 1991 to $1,759 million in the year to March 1998, an average of about 45 per cent a year.[8] That growth, and the date at which it began, has made 1991 the most famous year in the story of Indian software. Founders date their industry's take-off from it, and a common view holds that the industry is a product of the liberalisation that began that summer. On the documents, 1991 changed money: the exchange rate, the right to spend foreign currency, and the right to raise capital. It did much less to change the work itself, which was still mostly sold by the hour or the month, and much of it still done at the client's site abroad. It also changed, more quietly, who was recruited into the work and how.

## A fortnight of imports

Singh traced the crisis to deficits at home and abroad. The central government's fiscal deficit was more than 8 per cent of gross domestic product in 1990-91. External debt had reached about 23 per cent of GDP, and debt service took 'about 21 per cent of current account receipts in 1990-91'. These strains, he said, 'were stretched to a breaking point on account of the Gulf crisis last year'.[9] V. Rajaraman, the historian of Indian computing, puts it more bluntly. India 'was about to default on foreign loans', and it was bailed out by the IMF on conditions that included devaluing the rupee and opening the country to foreign investors.[10]

The response came in stages. The rupee was devalued on 1 and 3 July 1991. The budget speech described those 'exchange rate adjustments' and a liberalised system of import licences as 'the beginning of a transition from a regime of quantitative restrictions to a price based mechanism'.[11] Annual averages show the size of the change: about Rs 17.5 to the dollar in 1990 and about Rs 25.9 in 1992.[12]

On foreign capital the minister turned a long tradition around. 'After four decades of planning for industrialisation, we have now reached a stage of development where we should welcome, rather than fear, foreign investment. Our entrepreneurs are second to none. Our industry has come of age.' Foreign equity of up to 51 per cent in high-priority industries would get prompt approval.[13] He also promised full statutory powers to the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), transferring to it powers then held by the Controller of Capital Issues and the government, so that it could regulate the stock exchanges.[14]
