The software paragraph sat inside this argument about foreign exchange. Two paragraphs after it, Singh extended the same logic to professionals generally. Their 'scientific, technical and professional skills, knowledge and experience' had, he said, 'an increasing capacity to earn foreign exchange for the country'.[15] In July 1991 software entered national economic policy as a way to earn dollars. It was not described as an industrial capability to be built for its own sake. That framing was continuous with the export obligations of the 1970s and 1980s, when firms were allowed to import computers only if they promised to export.

## What came before July

The reforms did not create the infrastructure on which the next decade's offshore work would run. The Software Technology Parks (STPs), government-run sites that offered exporters shared satellite earth stations and a single window for official permissions, had opened at Pune, Bangalore (Bengaluru since 2014) and Bhubaneswar in 1990, and the body that ran them, Software Technology Parks of India, says it was registered as an autonomous society on 5 June 1991, seven weeks before the budget.[16] The economists Gaurav Khanna and Nicolas Morales date the setting up of satellite links in the parks to 1992, which they say began 'negating the need for some kinds of on-site work'.[17] The parks were planned before the reforms and began to matter after them.

The government's export targets had a longer history of disappointment. Nagy Hanna, in a World Bank study published in 1994, recorded that it had set targets of $400 million by 1992 and $800 million by 1995.[18] On Rajaraman's figures exports were $225 million in 1992-93 and $734 million in 1995-96; the $800 million mark was passed only in 1996-97, when exports reached $1,100 million.[19] The targets were missed, and then the trade overtook them.

## Fifty visits to Delhi

The best-known account of what 1991 did for software comes from N.R. Narayana Murthy, who founded Infosys in 1981 with six colleagues.[20] In an oral history recorded for the Computer History Museum in Bangalore in January 2020, he said 'there is absolutely no doubt that for an industry to take off and demonstrate rapid growth you need the blessings of the government'. He dated his industry's growth from 1992 and credited the reforms of 1991 with three changes.[21]

The first was the end of licensing for computer imports. Before it, he said, 'it would take us fifty visits to Delhi and about three years of elapsed time before we got a license to import a computer of about 300,000 US dollars'.[22] The second was convertibility on the current account, the freedom to buy foreign currency for trade and travel. 'Before that, if I wanted to travel abroad even for a day, I had to apply to the Reserve Bank of India (the Central Bank), wait for about 15 days, get the permission and then travel.' He told of a fellow entrepreneur who had permission for two days in Paris and one in Frankfurt. A prospect moved, so he spent one day in Paris and two in Frankfurt, and reported this honestly on his return. 'He promptly got a show cause notice from the Reserve Bank!'[23]

The third change concerned the stock market. Until then an official in Delhi, the Controller of Capital Issues, decided whether a company could offer shares to the public and at what price. In Murthy's words, 'That government officer had no idea what the capital markets were'. The controller priced issues on past performance, so most were at par, the shares' face value. 'Therefore, most entrepreneurs were uncomfortable about going public because they gave away a lot of their equity and raised very little money.' When the office was abolished and companies could set their own prices with their bankers, Murthy said, 'that made life so much easier for us and the industry took off'.[24]

Rajaraman, drawing on Murthy, adds that convertibility let firms 'send software engineers to clients' sites at short notice'.[25] He also credits the devaluation, which, he writes, 'enabled Indian software companies to be competitive in selling their services', and a run of smaller concessions that followed it, from ten years' freedom from tax on export earnings to private satellite links to overseas customers; multinationals could now own their Indian companies outright.[26]

Murthy is an interested witness, a founder whose company went public under the new regime. But the three changes he names have something in common. None of them changed what Indian firms sold. They changed what it cost a firm to move people and money across borders and to raise capital at home. For a business that sold the time of programmers, many of whom worked at clients' sites abroad, the right to send an engineer to America at short notice, without a fortnight's wait for the Reserve Bank, was close to the heart of the business.

## Only 64 brilliant young engineers

Four months after the budget, on Tuesday 26 November 1991, Infosys took half a page in the Bombay (Mumbai since 1995) edition of the *Times of India*. Above a photograph of a crowd on a city street, with crosshairs on the face of one young man, the headline read: 'Only 64 brilliant young engineers are destined to conquer the world of software. Find out if you are one of them this Saturday.'[27]

The advertisement shows in unusual detail how the profession was assembled in these years. It asked for 'young male/female engineers in any discipline (or science graduates plus MCAs)', the last being holders of the Master of Computer Applications degree. The firm wanted people who had been 'among the top 10 rank holders in their discipline' with 'an aggregate score of 65%. Nothing less will do.' Then came the line that matters most to the argument of this book: 'Ideally we expect you to have up to one year of work experience in any field of engineering. A computer software background is not essential.'[28]

Infosys was buying general ability and proposing to make programmers of it. The advertisement described the conversion. Training, it said, would be 'on live and simulated projects using our in-house facilities', which it listed as two IBM AS/400 minicomputers, a VAX 3400 and several Unix machines running Oracle. Recruits would share the experience of two holders of doctorates from the Indian Institute of Management who were dedicated to training. 'Training at Infosys, as some of our past recruits have discovered, is like doing your post graduation and being paid for it.'[29] A World Bank study three years later would recommend exactly this kind of conversion. Infosys was already doing it, and selling the training as a reason to join.

The pay was stated plainly. 'You will join us as a Software Engineer Trainee and will be initially based at Bangalore. The gross annual pay package is Rs.45,000 plus.' After twelve months' probation the trainee would be confirmed as a software engineer, and 'The best can expect to earn a gross annual compensation of Rs.57,000 on completion of the one year training period.'[30] Rs 45,000 was about $2,000 at the 1991 average exchange rate, and Rs 57,000 about $2,500.[31] A separate box offered a higher starting salary to engineers with one or two years in the software industry; the figure is illegible in the surviving copy.[32]

The rest of the page sold a life. 'The job is transferable, so you can look forward to jet setting not only in India, but all over the world.' The recruit would join a team of 400 people drawn from all over India. The firm said it had offices in Bangalore, Delhi, Bombay, Atlanta, Boston and Paris, a joint venture with the American consultancy Kurt Salmon Associates, and clients that included General Electric, Reebok and Polo Ralph Lauren. Forty engineers in Bangalore, it said, were working on a large project for Reebok UK. Under a heading promising fast promotion without a change of employer, it claimed that people who had joined as software engineers had risen to be vice presidents within six years.[33] Of Bangalore it said: 'The garden city, as it is called, has a quaint ambience of its own.'[34]

The selection was compressed into a weekend. Candidates were to come to the Leela Kempinski hotel in Bombay at 9 a.m. on Saturday 30 November, with their bio-data and certificates. After an initial screening on qualifications came 'a round of brain teasers, IQ and aptitude tests'; a box of tips warned that the test had sections on arithmetical reasoning and analytical skills. Those who did well would be interviewed on the Sunday, and the successful were guaranteed an appointment letter on the Monday. The heading over that promise read: 'Your girlfriend is sure going to miss you next Monday'.[35] Despite 'male/female' in the call, the page seems to have imagined its reader as a young man. Senior professionals were invited to see Nandan Nilekani or K. Dinesh, two of the founders, at the same hotel.[36]

How many came is not documented. A 2017 article on a business website, which reproduced the advertisement, says Murthy recalled about 1,500 people turning up and a crush at the hotel, but it gives no source for the recollection, and it misreads the Rs 57,000 as Rs 52,000.[37]

## Seventy thousand applications

By the end of the decade the Saturday test at a Bombay hotel had become a national sorting machine. Infosys's registration statement for its American share listing, filed in February 1999, described it. The company focused its recruiting 'on the top 20% of students from engineering departments of Indian schools' and chose them through tests and interviews, selecting 'on the basis of their ability to learn as well as their academic achievement'. In the year to March 1998 it received about 70,870 applications, tested about 21,350, interviewed about 5,800, made about 1,790 offers and saw about 1,300 accepted. A faculty of 33, twenty of them with master's degrees or doctorates, ran fourteen-week training courses for new recruits.[38]

The numbers say something about the education that fed the industry. Fewer than one applicant in fifty became an Infosys employee. The test, not the degree, did the sorting, and the firm's own course, not the college, taught the work. The same filing gave the national picture as an argument for investors: according to the National Association of Software and Service Companies (Nasscom), the industry's lobby group, the number of software professionals had grown from about 56,000 in the year to March 1990 to about 200,000 in the year to March 1998, and India had more than 1,800 engineering colleges and technical institutes training about 68,000 graduates a year in information technology.[39] Other counts, Rajaraman's among them, differ by source and definition.[40] The firm itself grew from about 480 IT professionals in the year to March 1994 to about 2,200 in the year to March 1998.[41]

The selling point to clients was price. Rajaraman writes that 'The salary of software engineers in India was about 20% that of an equivalent western engineer.'[42] The Infosys filing, citing the consultancy Software Productivity Research, put the average Indian software wage at 'approximately 15% of the average U.S. rate'.[43] A sharper comparison, which Khanna and Morales quote from a 1992 study, is that in 1989 'an Indian computer professional earned about $5486, whereas Microsoft was offering $40,000 plus relocation benefits and a green card'.[44] The trainee's Rs 45,000 in 1991 was well below even the 1989 figure, though the two are not the same measure.

## Going public

Infosys had meant to sell shares to the public in 1991. Murthy said in 2020 that he had wanted to list within ten years of founding, as American companies did. The assassination of Rajiv Gandhi in May 1991 and the arrival of the reforms led the firm to wait. In 1992 the stock market was shaken by what he called 'a huge stock exchange scam', the securities scam associated with Harshad Mehta, and on 6 December 1992 a mosque, the Babri Masjid, was demolished. Each time, Murthy recalled, the firm was advised to wait.[45]

'So, we went public on 24th of February 1993. It was a very tough time. We barely managed it. Nobody had any idea what a software company was.' Infosys was, he said, the second software company to go public, after Mastek in December 1992. The offer ran from 24 to 27 February, but the shares were listed only in June. 'It opened pretty well at about 50 percent premium.'[46] The company's 1999 filing says that in 1993 it raised 'approximately $4.4 million in gross aggregate proceeds' from its initial public offering, and it names the Bangalore Stock Exchange.[47]

The listing mattered to Murthy for reasons beyond the money. He said that from the start the company would give its accounts to any journalist, and that going public was meant 'to convince the decision makers of our customer organizations in the U.S. that we were a transparent company'. From 1995 it voluntarily prepared accounts under American accounting rules.[48] A firm that sold its engineers' time to American corporations was also selling trust, and a public listing was a way to show it.

## The hotel rooms

In May 1995 Infosys's largest customer came to renegotiate. Murthy's account of the episode, in the same oral history, shows in detail how the trade was priced. General Electric (GE) had chosen four Indian firms, Infosys among them, after a presentation to Rajiv Gandhi's government in the 1980s. Infosys began working for GE in 1990. GE renegotiated its contracts every five years, and by 1995, Murthy said, it 'formed about 25 percent of our revenue'.[49]

'They sequestered the vendors in different rooms at a five-star hotel in the city. They would go from room to room and would negotiate to get better and better terms.' The talks ran over a Thursday and a Friday. 'All other competitors of ours were ready to sign on the dotted line.' Infosys would not cut its price. Murthy said he told GE that 'if we reduced our prices to them we would have to reduce prices to our other customers too', and that lower prices would leave less money for pay, tools, technology and productivity.[50] Infosys withdrew and handed the work over to competitors, and, he recalled, 'my colleagues were unhappy with me'.[51]

The company's filing tells the same story without naming the client. In 1995 Infosys 'chose to reduce significantly the services provided to its then-largest client rather than to accept the price reductions and increased Company resources sought by such client'.[52] That client's share of revenue fell from 21.5 per cent in the year to March 1996 to 6.7 per cent in the year to March 1997. Total revenue still rose by 48.8 per cent, to $39.6 million, in the year to March 1997.[53]

The episode shows who held the power in a trade sold by time. The buyer set the terms in a hotel, room by room, and played its suppliers against one another. A supplier could refuse only if it had other buyers, and Infosys, on its own account, did. Murthy's further claim, that Infosys long charged more than its Indian rivals, is taken up in Chapter 11.

What was being priced was mostly time. In the year to March 1996, 76 per cent of Infosys's revenue came from time-and-materials contracts, under which the client pays for hours or months worked, and 24 per cent from fixed-price contracts. In the year to March 1997 the split was 63 per cent and 37 per cent.[54] In its 1999 filing the company said it was 'seeking to increase the proportion of projects that are undertaken on a fixed-price, fixed-time frame rather than a time-and-materials basis'. Its reason was that such projects offered 'the Company the potential benefit of enhanced margins for projects that are performed efficiently'.[55] Under time-and-materials, a firm that finished faster billed less. Under a fixed price, it kept the saving. The filing added that 'The Company's policy is to decline or discontinue projects that do not offer the potential to meet the Company's profit margin targets.'[56] Selling time also meant that revenue could grow only as fast as the number of engineers billed, which is why the recruiting machine had to keep running. That is the bargain the rest of this book follows. The question of who keeps the gains when work is done faster, the client or the supplier, returns at the end of the book, when the tools doing the work faster are machines.

## Onsite, offshore and the visa

The reforms did not bring the work home quickly. On Nasscom data reported by Khanna and Morales, 'The fraction of on-site work went from 90% in 1988 to 66% in 1995 and 56% in 2000', measured as a share of software revenue.[57] Richard Heeks, a researcher at the University of Manchester who studied the trade through the 1990s, found that 'by 1997/98, it was still true that more than half of all software services export earnings came from onsite work'.[58] Other series, which count exports or development effort rather than revenue, differ by a few points but agree on the direction and the pace.[59]

Two forces pushed it towards India. One was the satellite links. The other was American visa policy, whose shift of 1993 Chapter 13 describes. The H-1B visa, created in 1990 for workers in 'specialty occupations', required the employer to pay the greater of the wage paid to its other employees in the job or the prevailing wage for the occupation. Its cap was set at 65,000 a year. 'In the early years, the cap was never reached', but by the mid-1990s it 'started binding'.[60] Heeks dates the main change to 'the arrival of the Clinton administration, partly in response to the desire of local labour unions to halt or reduce the use of foreign workers in the US'. Indian workers 'were channelled into taking temporary work visas (rather than student or training or even tourist visas as in the past)', and the changes 'pulled a number of Indian companies out of their complacency about onsite work'.[61]

The leading firms built a method around the shift. Rajaraman calls it the Global Delivery Model and, citing Murthy, says Indian software companies invented it. In his description, the part of a project that needed face-to-face work with the customer, typically 20 to 30 per cent of the time, was done at the client's premises. Coding and testing, 70 to 80 per cent of the time, was done in India, in secure areas set aside for a single client and joined to it by a dedicated satellite link.[62] The time difference became an asset: India's working day fell in the American night, so bugs reported at the end of an American shift could be fixed by morning.[63] Murthy said in 2020 that he 'formalized' the model in the late 1980s and early 1990s, aiming at 'only about 20 percent of our effort at customer site'.[64]

Infosys's 1999 filing described the mechanics as the firm practised them: a small team at the client's site and a much larger one in India, with the client's systems linked by satellite to as many as four Indian centres. 'By pursuing this model, the Company completes approximately 80% of its project work at its offshore software development facilities in India.'[65] At any time about 15 per cent of its professionals were working at client sites abroad. In December 1998, 231 of its people in the United States held H-1B visas and 111 held L-1 visas, which were open only to employees who had worked for the company for at least a year.[66]

That 80 per cent was the leading firm's account of its own work at the end of the decade. The industry as a whole still earned more than half its export revenue onsite.[67] The model described where the best-organised firms were going, not where the trade already was.

To persuade distant clients that people they never saw would do the work properly, the leading firms also collected certificates of process, and by 1999 Infosys described itself as 'Certified under ISO 9001, TickIT and at Level 4 of the Capability Maturity Model', a five-level grading of software development; Chapter 11 follows how such certificates were sold.[68]

## Not only the reforms

Two series of export figures cover the decade, one compiled by Subhash Bhatnagar and one by Heeks from his own research and the trade magazine *Dataquest*. They differ by up to about a tenth in some years, but both show growth of between about a quarter and two-thirds a year, faster from 1993 than in 1990-93; the data appendix sets them side by side.[69]

Not all of the growth came from policy. Rajaraman lists the decade's 'fortuitous circumstances' alongside policy: the millennium bug, the conversion of European banking software to the euro, and 'a technically savvy influential Indian diaspora in the USA'.[70] The millennium bug, or Y2K, already brought Infosys 23.3 per cent of its revenue in the year to March 1998.[71]

On the diaspora he writes that 'The "brain drain" of the 60s and the 70s became "opportunity gain" in the 90s'. Indians in senior posts at American companies gave Indian firms 'small contracts at the beginning which grew as the companies delivered good quality software applications'.[72] He offers no data for the claim.

Foreign firms came too, beginning with a Tata joint venture with IBM, which had left India in 1978, that Rajaraman dates to 1992.[73] On his dating, American Express, Oracle and GE Capital International Services followed between 1994 and 1997, and in Bangalore engineers at Texas Instruments designed a signal-processing chip, Ankur, announced in 1997 and 'entirely designed in India'.[74] Chapter 15 follows these foreign-owned centres.

The boom was concentrated. Heeks estimated that by 1998 there were 400 to 500 active software export firms, most of them small firms with a single contract. The top five firms earned more than 40 per cent of all exports and the top twenty about 70 per cent.[75] It was concentrated in place as well. Of 558 software companies whose headquarters *Dataquest* recorded in 1998, 152 were in Bangalore, 122 in Bombay, 93 in Madras and 86 in Delhi.[76] By the close of the period, Rajaraman writes, 'the voice of NASSCOM was strong and it got the ear of the government'.[77]

## What 1991 changed

There are three ways to read the years after the crisis, and the evidence supports parts of each.

The first is the founders' reading. Murthy credits the reforms with the industry's take-off. The export series gives him only partial support: growth was already fast in the late 1980s, slowed in the first years of the decade, and quickened again from 1993.[78] The reforms that mattered most to software were the ones Murthy named, about money and movement: devaluation, convertibility, the end of licensing for imports, and the freedom to price a share issue.

The second is a reading of continuity. The leading firms, the business of sending programmers to clients' sites, the duty-free import regime for exporters and the Software Technology Parks all predated July 1991. The budget's own contribution to software was a tax concession, and it justified that concession as a way to earn foreign exchange.[79] The onsite series and the Infosys contract split show that where the work was done, and how it was sold, changed only slowly. Heeks's verdict in 1998 was that much of the growth 'may have come from its industry's dogged following of the low-risk, low-barrier first path', the export of labour.[80]

The third reading looks to America. Khanna and Morales argue, using an economic model, that the prospect of American jobs through the H-1B visa drew Indian students into engineering, and that those who could not get visas because of the cap stayed home and staffed the Indian industry.[81] On this reading, American demand and American immigration law shaped the Indian profession at least as much as Indian policy did. It is an argument from a model, calibrated on data.

What none of the readings disputes is the change in who did the work. In 1991 a firm of 400 people advertised for sixty-four engineers of any discipline, promised to make them programmers, and paid them about $2,000 a year. By 1998 the same firm was testing more than twenty thousand applicants a year and hiring fewer than one applicant in fifty. Its recruits were trained in a company faculty, worked to documented processes, and spent most of their time in India while their clients slept. The advertisement of 1991 had told them where they would start. 'Say cheers to Bangalore', it said.[82] The next chapter follows them there.


# Chapter 10. Bangalore (1947-2010)

In the early 1970s the journalist Janardhan Roye used to see a young engineer named Vinay Deshpande working long hours in a basement. The basement belonged to the Classic Building on Richmond Road in Bangalore (Bengaluru since 2014), and the firm that occupied it was called, in Roye's spelling, Processors Systems India. One evening Roye went down to see him. Deshpande was holding a soldering iron over a circuit board. He looked up, smiled, and explained that he was putting together 'hi-tech firmware, bound for the US'.[1]

Roye wrote the scene down forty years later, in 2013, in an article about how Bangalore had become a technology city. He dated it to about twelve years before the day in 1985 when Texas Instruments' satellite equipment arrived at Sona Towers by bullock cart. He thought Deshpande typical of the engineers of the 1970s, who worked quietly on their own or alongside the government's industrial, defence and science laboratories.[2] His point is one the rest of the evidence supports. Bangalore was building electronics for American customers before any American software company had an office there.

In November 1991 Infosys advertised for sixty-four young engineers to start their careers in Bangalore.[3] There are three answers to why the software trade gathered in that city. The first is older than the trade. Bangalore was a city the Indian state had filled with engineers, laboratories and colleges in the forty years after independence. The second is a set of decisions by firms, some of them about engineers and some of them about landlords. The third is a policy that made the city's software parks a kind of export enclave, with their own power and their own links to the world, and that required each firm in them to earn back its Indian wage bill one and a half times in exports every year.[4] That rule tied what a firm had to sell to what its engineers cost. What the enclave did for the rest of Bangalore is the hardest question.

## The state's city

N.R. Narayana Murthy, the founder of Infosys, gave his own account of the city's origins in an oral history for the Computer History Museum, recorded in Bangalore in January 2020. 'Right from 1947 when we got independence,' he said, 'the government of India decided to locate its defense oriented high-tech companies in Bangalore, which was away from the border with Pakistan and with China.'[5] He added a reason of geography: the city lay about 250 miles from the Arabian Sea and about 200 from the Bay of Bengal, so that a plane coming to bomb it would be shot down first. That was why, in his telling, Jawaharlal Nehru and his cabinet made Bangalore a defence-oriented, high-technology place.[6] That is Murthy's explanation; no cabinet record of it has surfaced.

The institutions themselves are not in doubt. Murthy named the Electronics and Radar Development Establishment (LRDE), a defence laboratory; Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL); and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL). His interviewer added the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), and Murthy agreed that space research came 'in the late '70s'.[7] A social scientist studying the city's poor, Supriya RoyChowdhury, describes the same city from another angle. In the decades after independence Bangalore was known as 'a garden city of retirees' bunglows [sic], and for a significant public sector presence', with central and state government enterprises set up from the early to mid-1950s and 'premier scientific research institutions' founded by the central government. 'The city's development in the first four decades was closely aligned with the development of the state sector,' she writes.[8]

The city's growth followed the same timetable. A research group at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) reports that Bangalore's population grew by 76 per cent between 1971 and 1981, a rise it attributes to the public-sector industries and defence establishments of the 1970s. Between 1991 and 2001, the decade of the software boom, growth was 38 per cent, and the urban agglomeration's population at the 2001 census was 5.7 million.[9] Software did not make Bangalore big. It arrived in a city that the public sector had already made large and full of engineers.

The private technology community grew inside that public one. Vijay Chandru, a former professor of computer science at IISc who later founded a life-sciences company, told Roye: 'Bangalore was a tech city well before the arrival of the MNCs (multi national corporations)'.[10] He called it 'the original Beantown', after Boston, and said that from the 1960s 'a host of engineers were engaged in creating hardware and software solutions' for avionics, defence, telecommunications and weather forecasting, mostly in the public sector.[11]

The education half of the story sits in the same institutions. When Wipro, then a maker of vegetable oils, decided to make computers in 1979, its research team worked inside the Indian Institute of Science's Digital Systems Lab, on equipment the institute could import more easily than a company could, and several of its first employees had trained there.[12] The computer business of a company that later sold programmers to the world began in a university laboratory.

## A flat in Pune

The software trade did not start in Bangalore. Richard Heeks of the University of Manchester, who studied the industry from the late 1980s, wrote in 1998 that it began in Bombay (Mumbai since 1995), 'in the business district around Nariman Point in the late 1970s'. When prices and commuting times rose, part of the industry moved north to the Santa Cruz Electronics Export Processing Zone (SEEPZ), and Bombay remained the centre of the trade 'until at least the mid-1980s'.[13] Then its firms began to run short of people, partly because programmers were leaving for jobs abroad, and the city's high prices and poor quality of life told against it. Firms, foreign investors and would-be founders began to compare Bombay with other places.[14]

Murthy's account of one such comparison turns on housing law. Infosys was founded in Pune in 1981. 'We pretty soon realized that Maharashtra was not the best place to have a startup,' he said, because of the state's tenancy laws.[15] A tenant who had lived in an apartment for seven years could not be made to leave and could claim it as his own. 'With the result, most landlords in Maharashtra refused to give an apartment on rent because of this fear. Unless you were a big company, unless you gave some big bank guarantee, etcetera, etcetera. But no startup could do that.'[16] The founders wanted a state where the law was 'fair between the landlord and the tenant', and Karnataka was one. So the choice narrowed to Madras (Chennai since 1996), in Tamil Nadu, or Bangalore.[17]

They chose Bangalore, Murthy said, 'because of the availability of engineering talent'. Part of the reason was the defence public sector. The other part was education. In the 1970s and 1980s, he said, 'when there were very few engineering colleges in the country, Karnataka had a disproportionately higher percentage of engineering talent and engineering students in the country.'[18] A later study put the regional supply in numbers. Writing in 2001 for a Stanford University conference on India's economy, the scholar of Silicon Valley AnnaLee Saxenian reported a finding that 60 per cent of India's computer science graduates came from three southern states, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, and that the industry was concentrated there 'largely because of their concentration of engineering manpower'.[19] The private engineering colleges described in Chapter 7 were part of that supply.

## Beer, climate and perception

A common answer to the question of why Bangalore won is that companies liked the weather. The evidence makes this partly true but incomplete. Heeks gave the most systematic answer, using a model of how software firms choose locations. He found three factors at work in the mid-1980s and a fourth that took over later.[20]

The first was labour. Bangalore was seen to have 'abundant labour that could be drawn from its long-standing research laboratories, educational institutes and public sector electronics firms', among them IISc and the Indian Institute of Management.[21] The second was quality of life. Bangalore had a reputation 'for a good climate and social life', and IT workers were quickly drawn into the city's social life and its 'pub culture'. Heeks recorded a semi-serious club of senior industry managers, the Beer-drinkers Association of Information Technology, whose members met to discuss strategy on condition that each drank at least six mugs of beer in the evening. Bombay, by contrast, had 'a long and troubled history of both communal and labour relations strife'.[22] The third was infrastructure. 'You could get across town in a matter of minutes in a car,' where Bombay's peak-hour traffic could take hours, and Bangalore promised plentiful power and water.[23]

Heeks added a caution from his interviews: 'the perception of these factors as much as their reality has coloured locational decisions'.[24] Some insiders gave the weather more weight. C.S. Murali of IISc, quoted by Roye in 2013, listed policy, skilled workers and the public-sector giants and then, 'above all', the city's 'inviting salubrious climate and cosmopolitan character'. Murthy, asked what had made Bangalore a hub, began with 'a pretty salubrious climate' and put engineering talent second.[25] Both named skilled people too. As the main reason for Bangalore's rise, the climate story is mostly false; as one reason among several, it is true.

The infrastructure advantage was the least durable of Heeks's factors. By 1998 a rival city was advertising Bangalore's traffic as its weakness. By 2005 the concentration of technology production had brought fast-rising wages and worsening congestion, and Bangalore's engineering salaries were among the highest in India, yet firms kept clustering there rather than moving to cheaper places.[26]

## Twenty-five rules

Heeks treated the arrival of Texas Instruments (TI) as 'a key event in Bangalore's history'. Once TI 'set up operations in 1986, it was the first proper offshore software facility, using satellite-based telecommunication links, and this was constantly reported in the home and international media'. The company was also 'known to have cut through many red tape barriers, particularly on imports'. From then on, he wrote, the Bangalore 'snowball effect' began.[27]

Saxenian put a number on the red tape. Citing an interview given in 1996 by N. Seshagiri, a former additional secretary in the Department of Electronics, she wrote: 'When Texas Instruments set up the first earth station in Bangalore in 1986, for example, the process involved removing or breaking 25 different government rules.'[28] Without such links, she added, Indian firms 'had no alternative to providing contract programming on-site', at the customer's premises and usually in the United States.[29]

Other multinationals followed TI, and they explained themselves in terms of skill and risk. One American employer in Bangalore, in an interview of 1996 cited by the researcher Balaji Parthasarathy and quoted by Saxenian, said: 'we came here because of the skills. We expanded because of the skills.' The risks of distance, of the satellite link, the telephones and the flights, 'were offset by the costs'.[30]

Some of the work was hard engineering. TI's Bangalore centre began by designing tools for chip design. Its engineers went on to design a digital signal processing chip, announced in 1997 under the code name Ankur, Sanskrit for seedling, which V. Rajaraman, the historian of Indian computing, says was designed entirely in India and widely used in disk drives and instruments.[31] It became a standard.[32] Oracle opened a software development centre in Bangalore in 1994.[33]

By 1998 the snowball could be counted. A Dataquest survey of 558 Indian software companies, reproduced by Heeks, found 152 with headquarters in Bangalore, against 122 in Bombay, 93 in Madras, 86 in Delhi, 34 in Hyderabad and Secunderabad, 27 in Calcutta (Kolkata since 2001) and 22 in Pune.[34] Heeks warned that the table understated Bombay, which was still home to several of the largest firms. But since the mid-1980s, when Bombay had led on numbers, Bangalore had grown at its expense and had come to be called India's 'Silicon Plateau'.[35]

## The parks and the bargain

The state that had built Bangalore's laboratories now built its export infrastructure too. Bangalore's Software Technology Park (STP) opened in October 1990.[36] An STP was in effect an export processing zone for software. Firms in it received five years' exemption from tax, guaranteed access to high-speed satellite links and reliable electricity, ready office space, duty-free imports of equipment and permission for full foreign ownership, 'in exchange for a sizable export obligation'.[37]

The obligation puts the book's bargain into the language of regulation. A park firm had to earn, net, 150 per cent of the value of its imported hardware within four years, and 'a net amount equal to 150% of their wage bill on an annual basis'.[38] Every year, then, a firm's Indian payroll had to come back one and a half times over in foreign exchange. The rule measured exports against the cost of the people who produced them. On its arithmetic, every engineer a park firm hired raised the exports it owed, and a firm that sold time could earn more chiefly by billing more people's time. That is the bargain the rest of this book follows: India sold engineers' time, and revenue grew with headcount.

From January 1995 park firms could sell a quarter of their output in India, and from 1999 half.[39] By 1998 the scheme had spread to 25 parks at various stages of planning, besides the government's own, and some were private ventures. The Information Technology Park in Bangalore was a partnership of the Karnataka government, Tata Industries and a consortium of Singapore firms.[40]

The parks moved work from America to India, slowly. The share of Indian software exports earned at clients' sites abroad fell through the 1990s but was still more than half in 1998.[41] By 1995, 435 companies were registered under the scheme, accounting for more than 16 per cent of exports.[42]

Karnataka's numbers grew fastest. According to the state's development report of 2007, cited by RoyChowdhury, the number of software export companies in Karnataka rose from 13 to 1,154 between 1991 and 2003, and the state's software exports from Rs 5.6 crore (Rs 56 million, about $2.5 million) to Rs 12,350 crore (Rs 123.5 billion, about $2.65 billion).[43] In the second half of the 1990s Karnataka was, she writes, the only state to grow faster than 8 per cent a year.[44]

## What the work paid

The economics behind the cluster were simple, and Saxenian set them out without ornament. 'India's greatest asset is a large, educated, English-speaking workforce that is willing to work at relatively low wages.' In 1994, she wrote, 'wages for software programmers and systems analysts in India were less than one-tenth of those for their US counterparts, and lower even than other developing countries like Mexico'.[45]

Low wages meant low revenue per worker. On the figures Saxenian used, the industry employed about 180,000 people in 1998, and annual revenue per employee was $15,000 to $20,000, against about $100,000 per employee in Israel and Ireland.[46] Revenue per head is the bargain's own measure: a firm that sold time at a low price could grow only by adding heads. Wages rose fast from their low base: the National Association of Software and Service Companies (Nasscom), the industry's lobby group, estimated that software pay rose 21 per cent a year in the late 1990s.[47] That eroded the cost advantage that had brought the work. Ashank Desai, chairman of Mastek, a leading Indian software company, said in 1999 that Indian firms were finding it 'difficult for them to compete only on one differential', which was cost.[48] The largest firms, among them Wipro and Infosys, were seeking bigger contracts, often on a turnkey basis, in which the firm delivers a finished system. 'Rather than competing on the basis of hourly productivity,' Saxenian wrote, 'they aim to accumulate intellectual property.'[49]

For the programmers, the city was often a waiting room for America. Those who worked abroad for Indian firms were 'paid their salaries in rupees and provided with minimal allowances for housing and expenses', and some called the business 'resume selling'.[50] 'Many thus aspire to work for foreign companies,' she wrote, 'not only for the relatively high wages but also for the opportunity be transferred overseas.'[51] By 1999 Indians were receiving the largest share of the H-1B temporary work visas that the United States issued.[52]

Behind them came a large training system. By Nasscom's count, Indian colleges and polytechnics trained more than 67,000 computer science professionals a year, and another 200,000 people enrolled each year in the private software training institutes that had multiplied in the 1990s.[53] Bangalore drew on that system and on the colleges of the three southern states that supplied most of the country's computing graduates.

The gap between those who got the jobs and everyone else stayed wide. Writing in 2013, Roye reported that the average software professional in Bangalore, outside the call-centre trade, earned Rs 50,000 a month, which he put at about $1,000, more than eight times the state's monthly income per head of Rs 6,000.[54] The figure is a journalist's unsourced estimate, but it points the same way as the evidence of a decade earlier: fast-rising pay for a skilled minority in a poor state.

## Cyberabad

In November 1998 the chief minister of the neighbouring state of Andhra Pradesh, the 48-year-old Nara Chandrababu Naidu, inaugurated a building called CyberTowers near Madhapur, on the edge of Hyderabad. It was to be the centrepiece of a planned Hi-Tech City. 'Until now, the world has heard of the twin cities of Hyderabad-Secunderabad,' he said. 'From today, the world will know of the triplet cities of Hyderabad-Secunderabad-Cyberabad.'[55]

*Business Today*'s cover story the next month, written by an economist based in Hyderabad, set the challenge in context. Hyderabad had once been called the nation's second capital, and public-sector firms such as Bharat Heavy Electricals and the Electronics Corporation of India had set up there in the 1970s. But 'the late 1980s saw Bangalore overtaking Hyderabad' as South India's most dynamic and corporate-friendly city.[56] Naidu's answer was to court the largest names in software. 'When Naidu got Microsoft's CEO, Bill Gates, to locate its R&D centre at CyberTowers, he made sure no other company could ignore the city.'[57] Oracle, BaaN, Tata IBM, Satyam, Wipro and others were already there.[58]

Hyderabad's pitch was aimed at Bangalore's weak point. J.A. Chowdhury, a director of the Software Technology Parks of India and, in the magazine's words, a key player in Naidu's Project Cyberabad, put it bluntly: 'Hyderabad is preparing for the future. Other cities will be left behind when traffic-congestion and urban chaos overtakes them.'[59] He described the city as a 'knowledge hub'. It had the first Indian Institute of Information Technology, research institutes, defence laboratories and six universities, so that the supply of computing skills matched the demand.[60] 'Infotech professionals would like to live close to work so that they can work early morning or late into the night,' Chowdhury said, and the magazine added that housing could always be found within ten minutes of the workplace.[61] The magazine, making Naidu's case, also cited a Nasscom survey of IT professionals that scored Hyderabad 3.40 out of 4 for the availability of qualified people and 3.20 for quality of life, but only average for climate, commuting and its educational facilities.[62]

The same article recorded doubts. Drinking water was short. Large parts of the city had 'grown haphazardly'. V.K. Bawa, one of its best-regarded urban planners, had drawn up a plan in the 1970s that no government had implemented, and he complained: 'The model of Hyderabad's development is regressive; it does not conform to modern concepts of urban growth.'[63] The whole project depended on one politician. If Naidu won the next state election, due in November 1999, the direction was clear. 'If he loses, the imponderables are many.'[64]

Saxenian saw in Naidu something larger than one city's ambition. While the central government had begun liberalisation, she wrote, 'the state governments have pioneered some of the most far-reaching policy innovations in the IT sector', and Naidu had made 'e-governance', the use of computers to deliver public services, his signature.[65] His campaign set off competition from his neighbours. Karnataka's new government announced plans to upgrade its 'overburdened roads', and Tamil Nadu and Kerala drew up IT policies of their own.[66] By 2001 software employment was concentrated in Karnataka (Bangalore), Andhra Pradesh (Hyderabad), Tamil Nadu (Chennai), Maharashtra (Bombay) 'and areas surrounding Delhi'.[67]

## The enclave

The sharpest contemporary warning about the cluster came from Saxenian herself, in a paper that asked whether Bangalore was 'the Silicon Valley of Asia'. The comparison, she answered, was 'not only misleading but also distracts attention from the deeper challenges and opportunities that IT affords the Indian economy'.[68] Most IT development already took place in parks 'insulated from the day-to-day challenges of doing business in India by dedicated communications links, private power sources, and liberal rules for investment and taxation'.[69] The insulation answered real shortages. In 1997 India had 18.6 telephone lines per 1,000 people, against 55.7 in China, and a new connection took more than twelve months to arrive.[70]

Its cost was disconnection. 'Professionals in IT enclaves could become better connected, both economically and socially, to distant regions than to the rest of the Indian economy.'[71] The policy of the day, she concluded, 'risks accelerating the growth of IT as a small, modern enclave in a poor and backward economy'.[72]

## The road not taken

Saxenian did not think the enclave was the only possible Bangalore. India, she wrote, 'already has the design capabilities' to build products of its own. 'However India lacks the environment needed to support experimentation with the application of these skills to new markets.'[73] Her example was the Simputer, a very low-cost mobile computer priced at under Rs 9,000, about $200 by her conversion, built by a Bangalore team from IISc and Encore Software.[74] Encore was the company of the same Vinay Deshpande whom Roye had seen with a soldering iron on Richmond Road.[75] Her prescription was a level field, in which products and services sold at home would 'enjoy the same tax benefits as those currently enjoyed by software export units'.[76] A regime built to earn foreign exchange had made it easier to sell software abroad than at home.

## Three readings

The evidence supports three readings of what happened in Bangalore, and they are not exclusive. The first is a story of agglomeration. A city filled with public-sector engineers and laboratories attracted a few early movers, TI, Wipro and Infosys among them, and the cluster fed itself as employees left to found firms nearby.[77] On this reading Bangalore's software industry was the delayed return on forty years of state investment in defence, science and engineering education.

The second reading is Saxenian's, that Bangalore depended on cheap skill and an export regime, and that its best engineers were drawn towards America.[78] TI's chip showed that the capability was real. Revenue per worker showed how little of it was being used. What filled the parks at the end of the 1990s was routine work done at great volume, as hundreds of American and European companies outsourced 'coding, maintenance and Y2K solutions' to Indian firms.[79]

The third reading is about the city. The industry created a well-paid professional economy with private power, private links and few ties to the city's poor.[80]

## K.S. Garden

What did the boom do for the people of Bangalore who did not write software? The most careful answer comes from RoyChowdhury's study of six slums in the inner city, on J.C. Road close to Lalbagh, which she calls the central commercial hub of the city. She surveyed 300 households and held focus groups.[81] She begins with the transformation. The city had 'become the icon of India's information technology revolution'. Real estate prices soared. The large campuses of the public-sector firms became 'shadows of a past': much of their land was put up for sale, units closed, and their permanent workforces were 'downsized and contractualized'.[82]

The new economy grew, she writes, 'through the expansion of capital intensive rather than labour intensive industries, as well as skill-based industries, which offered limited scope of employment, and only to technically skilled personnel'.[83] The poor found work in construction and in the export garment trade, at low wages, and in new service jobs: driving the cars and vans of call centres and outsourcing firms, guarding and cleaning malls and supermarkets, waiting at tables. Whether in factories or services, that work remained 'in the casual/contract mode with no security of service, insurance or pension'.[84] 'In Bangalore, nearly one million poor live in slums,' she reports, and about a third of slum dwellers lived below the poverty line, on less than Rs 2,500 a month, which she converts as $55.[85]

The IT economy reached one of her slums, K.S. Garden, in a particular way. It had the lowest poverty ratio of the six. Families in its better-paid occupations, from skilled trades to permanent jobs in public bodies, could send their children to private English-medium schools or to computer training.[86] 'About 50 youths in the slum had managed to get some kind of computer training. Of these, some 25-30 women were working as receptionist in small offices, or showrooms, at cash counters in small super markets.'[87] They had left the low-paid work of their parents. But the gain was fragile. In the focus groups, 'even those with some computer training frequently remained unemployed or only partially employed', and where someone had found a foothold, 'a connection through family or network had worked in most cases'. RoyChowdhury's conclusion is plain: 'there had not been any systemic or policy based effort to incorporate the urban underclass into the city's growing economy'.[88] In the same slum, coolie labour and domestic service still accounted for 52.3 per cent of households surveyed.[89]

Roye's article of 2013 names two individuals, both young women from the villages and towns around the city. Anusaya, from Immadihalli village, worked at an ice-cream kiosk in a shopping mall in Whitefield, one of the new technology districts, for Rs 6,000 a month, about $100 by Roye's conversion. 'I work here in the day, go to evening college,' she told him. 'The money I earn meets some of my family expenses and funds college fees.'[90] Ramya Gowda, from Malur, worked at a doughnut counter. 'I got this job because I learnt English and have finished school,' she said. 'This is a part time job. I'd like to study more, especially computers, and work in a big company like Yahoo!'[91] Neither was a software engineer. Both were working at the edge of the economy that software had built, and both described education, English first and computers next, as the way in.

Roye recorded what the corridors had replaced. The campuses of Whitefield, Electronic City and the Outer Ring Road stood largely on what had been farmland or swamp; many farmers on the city's edge had sold their land; the city had fewer trees, lakes and open spaces, and was by his account the third most expensive in India.[92] He ended the article in a bar on Lavelle Road, where a young software worker from Thanisandra told him: 'Seriously uncle, the city has arrived!'[93]


# Chapter 11. Y2K and Nasdaq (1995-2002)

At twenty past six on a Tuesday morning in late 2000, a correspondent for *Business Today*, R. Sukumar, stood on a street in BTM Layout, a growing neighbourhood in south Bangalore (Bengaluru since 2014), opposite a restaurant called Udipi Garden. He was waiting for a company bus. It was one of the buses that carried close to 4,000 people a day to the campus of Infosys Technologies on Hosur Road, and he had been told that many of its staff lived nearby. Staff from outside the south, he learned later, often clubbed together in threes or fours to sub-let a flat or house in neighbourhoods like this one.[1] On the bus, almost everyone was young and almost nobody talked. People read newspapers, one young woman read what looked like a technical book, and a few at the front fell asleep. The company discouraged its junior staff from riding motorcycles to work, because Hosur Road was so dangerous.[2] The crowd was more mixed than he had expected: many from the south of India, as he had assumed, but also faces from the west, the north and the north-east.[3]

The bus reached the campus at a quarter past seven. Sukumar had visited in the summer of 1995, when it had one office block, one canteen and one small gymnasium. Now it covered 50 acres and had five office blocks, three canteens, a branch of the old Bangalore eating house Mavalli Tiffin Rooms, a coffee bar, a pizza outlet, a swimming pool, a sauna, a medical centre and a small golf green.[4] It also had a three-storey training centre, built for Rs 23.6 crore (about $5 million), where every batch of new engineers went through a three-month course. The whole campus, the magazine reported, would eventually cost Rs 320 crore, about $71 million. Its chief financial officer, T.V. Mohandas Pai, showed off a building whose curved walls, he said, had taken more than 4,000 equations to get right.[5] The cars that drove in a little before eight were mostly small Marutis and Santros. Everyone paid market prices for food in the canteens.[6]

The magazine had named Infosys the best employer in India, and its article was written in that spirit.[7] But its numbers were specific. The share price had risen from Rs 63.75 in early April 1996 to Rs 7,160 on 15 December 2000. Of the company's 7,925 employees at the end of September 2000, 7,853 had been offered stock options, creating, the magazine reported, '1,773 rupee millionaires and 213 dollar millionaires'.[8]

Five and a half years earlier this firm had walked out of a negotiation with its largest customer and lost a quarter of its business. In between, the leading Indian services firms turned a way of organising work into something they could certify, sell and list on an American stock exchange. A programming error in old American software, the millennium bug, brought them inside the largest companies in the United States. Then the market that had made their employees rich turned and fell.

## A quarter of the revenue

In May 1995, in the telling of N.R. Narayana Murthy, the company's co-founder, Infosys alone among the Indian suppliers of General Electric (GE) refused its demand for lower prices and handed its GE work to competitors (Chapter 9).[9]

Two lessons can be read in the company's later filings. The first was about dependence. When Infosys registered its shares with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in February 1999, its largest client provided 10.5 per cent of revenue in the year to March 1998, and it had about 130 clients.[10] The same document listed among the causes of uneven results 'the size, timing and profitability of significant projects'.[11] By the year to March 2002 the largest client provided 6.1 per cent of revenue and the five largest together 24.1 per cent. In both filings the company described its mix of work as chosen 'in an effort to avoid service or client concentration'.[12] The second lesson, in Murthy's own account, was about price. He said in 2020 that 'at least until 2007, 2008, probably 2009, Infosys always got 20-25 percent higher price compared to our competitors in India'. He credited a sales method the company called Business Value Leverage, which meant talking to clients about what the work would be worth to them rather than about technology.[13] The claim is the founder's alone; no independent price data for the period have been located.

What the filings do show is how fast the firm grew from its small base. Revenue rose from $9.5 million in the year to March 1994 to $68.3 million in the year to March 1998.[14] Over the same years the number of its IT professionals rose from about 480 to about 2,200, and its development centres in India from two to nine.[15] Revenue grew at a compound rate of 63.6 per cent a year.[16]

Part of that growth came from the currency. In the year to March 1998, 90.0 per cent of Infosys's revenue was earned in US dollars, and the filing said that 'a significant portion' of its costs, including pay, would continue to be in rupees. Between December 1994 and December 1998 the rupee lost about 39.5 per cent of its value against the dollar.[17] A firm that earned dollars and paid rupees gained from every fall in the rupee unless it raised salaries to match. Process, Y2K and good management all contributed to the margins of these years. So did the exchange rate.

## Selling the process

To sell work that would be done ten thousand miles from the client, the firms had to show that it would be done properly. They sought two certificates. The international quality standard ISO 9001 was awarded after auditors inspected a firm's documentation, testing and project methods, and the Capability Maturity Model (CMM) of the Software Engineering Institute (SEI) at Carnegie Mellon University graded the 'maturity' of a firm's development process on five levels.[18] In the account of V. Rajaraman, the historian of Indian computing, ISO 9001 certification was 'essential for bidding for software projects in Europe whereas the CMM maturity level is valued more in the USA'.[19]

Motorola's Global Software Group, set up in India in 1991, says that its Indian centre reached Level 5 in 1993 and was 'the first commercial organization in the world' to do so, a claim Rajaraman repeats.[20] A *Business Today* report of January 2003 says only that the Indian unit was the first company in India to be certified, in 1994, at an unstated level, so the world first remains Motorola's own claim.[21]

By the end of the decade Indian firms held a large share of the highest ratings, though the sources do not agree on how large. The researcher AnnaLee Saxenian, writing in 2001, said that in December 1999, 137 Indian companies had ISO 9000 or CMM Level 2 certification, 'and ten companies were certified at Level 5 (the highest level, at which only six U.S. companies are certified.)'[22] Rajaraman gives a different figure for the same year: 'In 1999, 6 out of 12 CMM level 5 certified companies in the world were in India.'[23] Either way, a handful of Indian firms held a large share of the top grade, and the industry said so loudly. 'Quality certification', Saxenian wrote, 'serves as an important marketing device'.[24] The share kept growing. By January 2003, *Business Today* reported, 54 of the 78 organisations assessed at Level 5 worldwide were Indian companies or the Indian operations of multinationals, against 19 American companies.[25] The magazine also recorded what the grade was for. At a Nasscom-Gartner summit in Mumbai in September 2002, one of the chief executives present, whom it did not name, explained how it helped: 'When you tell customers that you are a Level 5 company,' he said, 'they shut up and listen.'[26]

Infosys described its own standing in the February 1999 filing: it had 'been certified at Level 4, a level achieved by only 2% of the more than 1,000 software companies tested under the Capability Maturity Model'.[27] Both the 2 per cent and the word 'certified' are the company's. The SEI's process was an appraisal, and the industry described the result as a certificate.

Rajaraman also explained why process mattered to the firms themselves. Both certificates, he wrote, 'require emphasis on well documented processes which every software engineer in the organization is expected to follow'. And 'The process orientation allowed companies which were recruiting large numbers of employees each year to quickly train them to become productive members of a development team. Staff attrition also could be managed better due to the disciplined software development process.'[28] Rajaraman presents this as a benefit, and it was one. But it also describes what process did to the engineer. A firm that hired thousands of graduates a year, and lost many of them to rivals or to American visas, needed work broken into documented steps that any trained graduate could follow and any other could take over. The certificate reassured the client. The process underneath it made individual engineers easier to replace. Rajaraman does not draw the conclusion, but his sentence points to it: documented, standardised work is also the kind machines learn most easily. Chapter 19 sets that reading against what the firms' own filings later said about tools for coding, testing and documentation.

## The pyramid

The work itself was organised as a pyramid. Infosys's 1999 filing described a typical project: a 'small team of two to five IT professionals' visited the client to set the scope, then its managers went back to India 'to supervise a much larger team of 10 to 50 IT professionals', with the client's systems 'linked via satellite' to the Indian centres.[29] A few experienced people faced the client. Many junior people did the work in India. The filing said the company did about 80 per cent of its project work in India.[30]

The firm described its own model as an industry practice. 'The Indian offshore development model was initiated in the mid-1980's,' the filing said (Chapter 6 tests that dating against the founders' own careers), and it listed what attracted clients: a large pool of English-speaking professionals, 'relatively low labor costs', international quality standards, the 'capability to work on specific projects on a 24-hour basis by exploiting time zone differences', and the ability to run phases of a project in parallel.[31] By 2002 the language had changed. The annual report for the year to March 2002 said that 'Our clients leverage our proprietary Global Delivery Model to achieve higher quality, rapid time-to-market and cost-effective solutions.'[32] In three years an industry practice had become a company brand.

For the industry as a whole, the move offshore was real but slower than the brand suggests. On each of the period's series, more than half of the industry's export work was still done at clients' sites abroad, which is why the story of the H-1B visa (Chapter 13) runs alongside this one.[33]

The pyramid was efficient at turning cheap hours into exports, but by international standards it produced little revenue per head (Chapter 10 gives Saxenian's comparison with Israel and Ireland). Saxenian saw the largest firms, such as Wipro and Infosys, trying to escape that trap: winning larger contracts 'often on a turnkey basis', charging higher rates, and turning what they learned on one project into software components they could reuse for the next.[34] The same pages record the other way out. Indian programmers, aware of what their skills earned abroad, were leaving, many of them on American visas.[35]

The pyramid had a consequence that a senior Infosys manager described in the *Business Today* article, published in January 2001. Sales had more than doubled in the first half of the year to March 2001, and the magazine noted that growth widened the middle and top of the organisation. 'We are growing so fast that many people with two to three years experience are getting into managerial roles,' said Hema Ravichandar, the senior vice-president for human resources.[36] Fast promotion for early recruits depended on a base that grew faster still. That was the book's bargain in miniature: revenue grew with the number of engineers billed, so the base of the pyramid had to keep widening. Not everyone wanted to climb. 'I don't have to become a project manager if I don't want to,' said Sushil, who worked in the company's mobile-commerce practice and is identified in the article only by his first name. 'I can focus on the technology and become a technical consultant to projects.'[37]

## The millennium bug

The work that filled the base of the pyramid in the late 1990s was Y2K. Rajaraman explains the problem simply. Programs written in the 1970s and 1980s, 'mostly in COBOL', stored the year as two digits to save memory, on the assumption that the first two were 19. When the year became 2000 they would give wrong results, and every such program had to be found and corrected. 'This bug fix was labour intensive. There were not enough software engineers in the USA and Europe to fix the bug and it had to be outsourced. This was a godsend opportunity to many fledgling software services companies in India.'[38]

At Infosys, the 1999 filing shows how quickly the work arrived. Y2K projects made up about 7.5 per cent of revenue in the year to March 1997 and 23.3 per cent in the year to March 1998.[39] In the nine months to December 1998 the share was 21.4 per cent.[40] The often repeated figure of 23 per cent 'in 1997' is the same number, since the company's fiscal year 1998 ran from April 1997 to March 1998.[41] Y2K tripled as a share of the business in a single year and had already begun to shrink as a share by the end of 1998.

The company was frank with American investors about what kind of work this was. 'The high demand for these time-sensitive projects results in pricing and margins that are favorable to the Company,' the filing said. It expected demand to 'begin to diminish rapidly after fiscal 1999', and it could not promise to replace the work with other work at the same margins.[42] Then came a sentence about people. 'There is an additional risk that the Company may be unable to retrain and redeploy IT professionals who are currently assigned to Year 2000 conversion projects involving legacy computer systems after such projects are completed.'[43] In a document filed under American securities law, the leading Indian firm said that a wave of demand had trained a cohort of its engineers for work that would soon end, and that it might not find other work for them.

For the industry, the figures come from the National Association of Software and Service Companies (Nasscom), the industry's lobby group, as reported by the trade newsletter *Computergram* in June 1999. Indian software exports in FY1998-99 were $2.65 billion, up 51.4 per cent, and Y2K work accounted for $560 million of that, or 21.1 per cent. Nasscom said that 203 of the Fortune 1000 companies used Indian software services, and that 25 firms earned 63 per cent of all exports.[44] Two weeks earlier the same newsletter had reported a larger Nasscom estimate: that Indian firms had earned $2.3 billion from the bug, might reach $3 billion by the end of 1999, and would earn only 'a few hundred million dollars' from it the following year.[45] The cumulative figure is hard to reconcile with $560 million in the peak year unless it spans several years or other kinds of work; the share of a single year's exports, about a fifth, is the safer number. The same report described the trap that the end of the work would set. Large companies around the world, it said, were holding back from buying new computer systems until the millennium had passed, and were no longer spending much on the bug either, because most of it had been dealt with. Indian firms that had relied on Y2K feared that their profits would fall.[46]

Nasscom already had an answer to the end of the work. Its president, Dewang Mehta, spoke of 'three Es', electronic commerce, enterprise resource planning (ERP, the integrated software that large companies were then installing to run their accounts, stock and staff) and euro conversion, and of an export target of $50 billion by FY2007-08.[47] The euro was a second conversion job. The European Union announced in 1995 that the single currency would be used from 1 January 1999, and banks and other financial institutions had to change their programs before then. In Rajaraman's words, this 'was a labour intensive job and provided software conversion contracts to numerous Indian software companies'.[48]

The millennium arrived without a crisis. In early 2000 the news magazine *Outlook* asked in a headline whether the whole thing had been 'The Rs 1,800 Cr Hoax?'. It put the world's spending on the problem at $600 billion, about $150 billion of it in the United States. It reported Nasscom's estimate that Y2K preparations had cost India Rs 1,800 crore across government and private industry, of which Rs 600 crore was for software and services.[49] The magazine converted the total to $3.6 billion. At the 1999 average exchange rate it was about $420 million.[50] The article also recorded what the night had been like for the firms. Rajeev K. Arora, resident manager of Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), a company that by the magazine's account had written more than 650 million lines of code for Y2K correction, said TCS had bought overseas tickets and arranged visas so that it could fly its engineers to clients if anything went wrong, and had stocked diesel for its generators.[51] Mehta's own verdict, as *Outlook* quoted it, was that 'Y2K was a godsend and might prove to be the turning point for the industry.'[52]

Was it the turning point? The export figures say not. In the series Rajaraman reproduces, Indian software exports had grown by between about a quarter and two-thirds a year in every year from 1990-91 to 1997-98, most of that before Y2K work became large.[53] At its peak Y2K was about a fifth of the industry's exports and about a fifth of the leading firm's revenue, and that firm expected it to fade quickly. What Y2K did, on the best evidence, was open doors. Rajaraman writes that many firms 'earned the goodwill of clients by not only fixing the Y2K bug but also improving the software (when appropriate) at no extra cost', and that 'This opportunity gave many software services companies entry to the Fortune 500 companies and enabled them to get software development contracts later.'[54] N. Chandrasekaran, who had joined TCS in 1987 and became its chief executive in 2009, gave a similar account to the Computer History Museum in 2020, two decades after the event. The Year 2000 work, he recalled, 'gave us scale, because everyone wanted a solution', and clients who saw it done well began to ask what else the firm could do for them.[55] He also gives part of the credit for the quiet rollover to the programmers 'working diligently in India between 1993 and 1999'.[56] That is his judgement, and the *Outlook* article shows that it was not universally shared at the time.[57] The common belief that Y2K made the Indian industry is half right. It accelerated growth that had already begun, and it put Indian engineers inside the systems of large American companies, some of which kept them on for other work.

## Two hundred thousand applications

The engineers on the bus in 2000 had been chosen from a very large crowd: in the year to March 2002 Infosys received about 193,640 applications and about 1,550 people joined, about one in 125, against about one in 55 four years earlier.[58] These are the company's figures, and it used them to advertise itself, but they also show a supply of graduates who wanted these jobs growing far faster than even the fastest-growing firm could take them. Infosys still selected by its own tests and taught its own methods.[59]

The firm explained its appeal in its own terms. In 1999 it told American investors that, because of its stock option plan, it had 'become one of the most sought after employers for Indian engineering graduates', with attrition 'significantly below the industry average'. It added that 'India is home to the world's second largest population of English-speaking technical talent'.[60]

The education that mattered most happened after the degree, in the three-month course that every batch of new engineers took in the training centre the reporter had been shown.[61] The firm selected from a vast pool, taught its recruits its own methods, and placed them into a documented process.

The people inside it were mostly engineers. The magazine counted 4,616 employees on the Bangalore campus in late 2000, and said that apart from the 840 people in the company's staff functions, such as human resources, finance, marketing and administration, everyone was an engineer.[62] The magazine noticed the strain as well as the perks. 'Every time things get a little too much for me,' said an employee who, it reported, 'not infrequently puts in 16 hours a day at work', 'I go out for a smoke, or a walk, or play a few holes of golf.' Muthamma Acharya, 'a twenty-something marketing executive', described the pace of hiring: 'You come in one morning and find the breakfast line 400-people longer'.[63] Suparna Shankar, an assistant manager in marketing for the Asia-Pacific region, summed up the place for the magazine: 'You can create a role for yourself.'[64] These were the voices a magazine chose for a story about the best employer in India.

## Nasdaq

Infosys had listed in India in 1993, in an offering Murthy remembered as 'a very tough time'.[65] Six years later it went to New York. The final prospectus, dated 10 March 1999 and filed the next day, offered 1.8 million American Depositary Shares (ADSs), certificates traded in the United States that each represented half an Indian share, at $34.00 each. The offering raised $61.2 million before an underwriting discount of $1.68 a share. The shares were to be quoted on the Nasdaq National Market under the symbol INFY.[66] The American price was set a little below the equivalent price in Mumbai, and until then, the prospectus noted, there had been no public market for the company's shares in the United States.[67]

Murthy gave a specific reason for the listing. Infosys had prepared its accounts under American accounting rules voluntarily from 1995, so that clients could read them. 'Later on, we said, "Look. We have to create an employee stock option plan in the U.S. currency." Therefore, we wanted ADRs [American Depository Receipts], and that is how we got listed on NASDAQ in 1999.'[68] In his account, the listing was as much about paying staff as about raising money.

Others followed. In June 1999 Mehta of Nasscom said he expected up to ten Indian firms to list in the United States over the next twelve to eighteen months.[69] The next was not a software services firm but an internet company. Satyam Infoway, the internet subsidiary of Satyam Computer Services, priced its ADSs on 18 October 1999 at what the filing gives as $4.50 each, and they began trading on Nasdaq the next day.[70] Satyam Computer Services owned about 52.5 per cent of it in 2002.[71] A rival Indian content provider, Rediff.com, completed its own American offering in June 2000.[72]

## Rupee millionaires

The listing turned paper into wealth for employees because Infosys had given them paper. 'In 1994, the Company established the ESOP, one of the first employee stock option plans in India,' the 1999 filing said. A trust set up for the purpose held warrants for shares, and employees received rights to buy shares at Rs 100 each, $2.35 at the exchange rate of February 1999, which the filing called 'substantially below the market price'. The rights vested over five years.[73] The filing explains the plan at length because under American accounting rules the discount was a cost, and under Indian rules it was not.[74] Stock options were so unusual in India that the government's information technology task force of 1998, among its 108 recommendations, proposed allowing 'sweat equity' and employee stock option plans, which Rajaraman describes as 'alien to other industries in India'. That required a change in company law.[75]

A rupee millionaire, in the magazine's count, held at least Rs 10 lakh (Rs 1 million), about $22,000 at the 2000 exchange rate.[76] That was a large sum for an engineer in his or her twenties, but not a fortune. A dollar millionaire was another matter. Infosys's sales had grown from Rs 88.97 crore in the year to March 1996 to Rs 884.35 crore in the year to March 2000.[77] The new wealth reached the city. 'Indeed, a couple of enterprising Bangalore-based real-estate developers make a living primarily from selling apartments to people who work for Infosys,' the magazine wrote.[78] In 2020 Murthy put the scale of the programme in his own words: Infosys had distributed 19 per cent of its equity to employees through stock options, worth about $9 billion at that time's prices.[79]

The money was very unevenly spread. It went to those who had joined early, at the leading firm, and stayed long enough to vest. A graduate who joined a smaller firm, or who joined Infosys in 2001, was in a different position.

## The bust

The bust looked different depending on where one stood. For investors in Indian internet shares it was a collapse. Satyam Infoway's annual report for the year to March 2002 said that since the offering its ADSs had traded between 'a high of $113 per ADS' and a low of $0.87.[80] The price table in the same report shows a low of $0.72 in the quarter to September 2001.[81] On 5 November 2001 a securities class action was filed in New York on behalf of everyone who had bought its ADSs between 20 October 1999 and 6 December 2000. It named the company, some of its executives and some of the underwriters of its offering, and alleged that the underwriters had failed to disclose commissions and arrangements with investors to whom they allocated shares.[82] In October 2001 Satyam Computer Services announced that it intended to sell its shares in the company.[83] The parent's own later history belongs to Chapter 16.

For the largest services firm the bust was a slower line, not a fall. From the year to March 1998 to the year to March 2002, Infosys's revenue grew at a compound 68.1 per cent a year and its IT staff rose from about 2,200 to about 9,400.[84] But its outlook for the following year was cautious. 'The economic slowdown in the U.S. has impacted the growth prospects of companies that are in the insurance, banking and financial services and telecom segments,' it said, and companies 'may cut their IT spending or postpone decisions regarding new IT expenditures'.[85] The industry's exports kept rising. The Reserve Bank of India recorded software services receipts of $6.3 billion in the year to March 2001 and $7.6 billion in the year to March 2002.[86]
