For new graduates, the bust arrived on campus. In January 2002 *The Hindu Business Line* reported that Anna University had placed 'only around 320 students with various companies, down from 1,200 around the same time last year'. The year before had been a record: 65 per cent of the 70 companies that visited the university had been IT firms. This time about 35 companies came. Wipro and Satyam, which had taken 49 and 23 students the year before, did not come at all. TCS recruited 54 students against 177, Infosys 46 against 126, and Cognizant Technology Solutions 69 against 105.[87] Dr N. Baluswamy, who directed the university's Centre for University-Industry Collaboration, which ran placements, said that some of the previous year's graduates had seen their offers postponed indefinitely, and that the centre had negotiated with the companies. 'A few companies have delayed the date of joining for last year students by over a year,' he said. Some IT companies, 'except big players such as TCS, Infosys and CTS', had cut the pay promised on campus 'by 50-60 per cent'.[88]

At the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) in Madras (Chennai since 1996), a little over 400 of the 719 students registered with the placement centre had been recruited by 51 companies, 30 of them in IT, with ten companies still to come, against about 750 placed the year before. About 30 per cent of students stayed away from campus interviews that year, the paper reported, because of 'shocking stories of lay-offs, delayed appointments and salary cuts' among the previous year's recruits. Most engineering students now wanted 'to consider only engineering companies, rather than shift to IT', and some said they wanted stable jobs.[89] Companies from outside IT were coming back. Maruti Udyog returned after about four years and the Gas Authority of India after fifteen, and NTPC was expected for the first time. At a management institute in Tiruchi, the highest offer came from Citibank, at Rs 6.5 lakh a year, about $13,600.[90]

The pattern matters for the rest of this book. In the placement director's account, the largest firms did not cut the pay they had promised; other firms cut salaries, and some put off joining dates by more than a year. The colleges went on producing graduates while the firms at the end of the pipeline cut their campus intake, the two largest at Anna University by more than half. Later chapters show the same pattern returning.

## Hours and outcomes

One thread runs through the filings of these years and connects them to the end of this book. Most of Infosys's revenue in the mid-1990s had come from time-and-materials contracts, under which the client pays for the hours or months worked, and by 1999 the company said it wanted more fixed-price work.[91] Y2K added a lesson of its own. It paid well because it was urgent: the company said that 'high demand for these time-sensitive projects' brought favourable prices and margins.[92] The risk ran the other way too: the 1999 filing counted 'the accuracy of estimates of resources and time required to complete ongoing projects, particularly projects performed under fixed-price, fixed-time frame contracts' among the causes of uneven results.[93] Under a fixed price, a project that overran cost the firm and not the client.

By 2002 the company reported progress. 'As compare [sic] to the previous year, we have increased the proportion of projects that are undertaken on a fixed-price, fixed-timeframe, rather than a time-and-material basis, which reduce client risk, and if effectively structured and executed, provide opportunities for enhanced margins.'[94] A firm that sells hours earns less when its engineers work faster, unless it uses the saving to win more work. A firm that sells an outcome at a fixed price keeps what it saves. Before 2002 the leading Indian firm had decided that it wanted, where it could, to sell outcomes. When tools arrive that cut the hours needed for coding and testing, the work that Rajaraman says took 70 to 80 per cent of a project's time and was done in India, the way a contract is priced decides who keeps the gain.[95]

In 2002 that question was still far off. The more immediate change was in the size of the machine. In 1991 Infosys had advertised for sixty-four engineers.[96] In 2002 it employed about 10,740 people and had received nearly 200,000 applications in a year.[97] The firms' demand for new engineers had fallen for a season. The supply had not. The next chapter follows the graduates who kept coming, and the companies that learned to hire them by the thousand.


# Chapter 12. The engineer factory (1998-2012)

After one year in his first software job, a young engineer whom the anthropologists Chris Fuller and Haripriya Narasimhan, in their published study, call Raghu earned 200,000 rupees a year (about $4,400). His father, after thirty years as an engineer at the nuclear power station at Kalpakkam, south of Chennai, earned 400,000.[1] Raghu had grown up in Kalpakkam, taken a degree in electronics and communication engineering at a college in Coimbatore, and joined one of India's six largest software companies, which the anthropologists call Indian Computer Services (ICS). When the researchers met him in Chennai he was 22, unmarried and a Tamil Brahman, a member of a community that made up about 2.5 per cent of Tamil Nadu's population and that, in the authors' 'strong impression', dominated many of the city's software firms.[2]

Raghu worked on production support for a British client's system. That is the work of keeping software that is already running in use: fixing what breaks, answering the client's requests, handling the next fault. He told the researchers that every day brought a new problem to solve, so he was never bored. But in their words he 'thinks he is not learning much', except how to turn down demanding foreign clients, and he wanted to leave the industry soon and study for an MBA. In the meantime he enjoyed the money.[3]

Raghu stands near the start of a machine that, between the late 1990s and the early 2010s, turned out software workers on a scale India had never seen. It had two halves. One was a mass of new engineering colleges, most of them private, which multiplied the number of young Indians with an engineering degree. The other was inside the firms: recruiting drives that tested hundreds of thousands of graduates a year, and training campuses that turned engineers of any branch into programmers in a few months. Both halves served the bargain on which the industry ran. The firms sold engineers' time, so their revenue grew with the number of engineers they could bill, and the factory existed to keep that number rising.

## Colleges by the hundred

For forty years after independence India built engineering colleges slowly. The government's statistical compendium counts 31 engineering and technology colleges in 1950-51, 149 in 1980-81 and 289 in 1990-91.[4] Then the pace changed. There were 486 such colleges in 1997-98, 678 in 2000-01, 1,077 in 2001-02 and 1,562 in 2005-06.[5] The country added more engineering colleges in those eight years than in the previous five decades together.

V. Rajaraman, the historian of Indian computing, describes 'a rapid expansion of engineering colleges between 1998 and 2010', and 'a rapid growth of private engineering colleges and colleges offering MCA courses'.[6] The Master of Computer Applications (MCA) was the postgraduate course for graduates in science and commerce, combining computing, mathematics and management. The law made room for the private colleges. On 31 October 2002 eleven judges of the Supreme Court, in *T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka*, overruled the fee and admission scheme the Court had laid down in the *Unni Krishnan* case of 1993 (Chapter 7).[7] For a college that took no government money, 'The decision on the fee to be charged must necessarily be left to the private educational institution'. Capitation fees and profiteering stayed forbidden, but 'a reasonable revenue surplus' for development and expansion was allowed.[8] A share of seats could again be filled by the management.[9] Private corporate bodies were allowed to set up universities in 2002, and under this policy, Rajaraman writes, private universities and private colleges 'proliferated'.[10] The supply of MCAs grew even faster than that of engineers, from about 7,000 graduates in 1998 to 120,000 by 2010.[11]

Quality did not keep pace, and the people who said so were the employers. Rajaraman, writing around 2012, notes that graduates of the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) and the National Institutes of Technology, about 10,000 a year, were excellent, but that 'industry employers opine that the graduates of other institutions are not employable as soon as they graduate and need further training'.[12] The regulators responded with inspection. The All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE), the statutory body that approves technical colleges, set up a National Board of Accreditation, and the University Grants Commission an assessment council to grade institutions.[13]

The expansion was uneven across the map, and the south's colleges fed the south's software cities.[14] In Chennai, Fuller and Narasimhan found that of twenty software engineers under thirty on whom they had information, only three had studied outside Tamil Nadu. The rest could stay at home, because young men and women, Brahmans among them, could now get a good engineering education within the state.[15]

By the early 2010s the building had outrun demand. By 2012-13 AICTE had approved about 1.55 million undergraduate engineering seats, and about 37.6 per cent of them were empty, according to an analysis of the council's data by the education non-profit Avanti Fellows.[16] Approved undergraduate intake peaked at about 1.7 million in 2014-15. By 2016-17 almost half of the seats, 49.5 per cent, had no student in them.[17] The colleges had been built for a market that was already starting to change.

## Sidebar: How many engineers does India really produce?

No figure about Indian education is quoted more often, or more loosely, than the number of engineers the country turns out each year. In the mid-2000s, a study at Duke University found, typical press articles said that in 2004 India had graduated 350,000 engineers and China 600,000, against about 70,000 in the United States.[18] Later, figures of well over a million a year appeared, including in Rajaraman's own history. Neither kind was a like-for-like count of four-year engineering graduates.

The Duke study was an early attempt to check. In December 2005 a team of graduate students led by Gary Gereffi, a sociologist, and Vivek Wadhwa, an executive teaching engineering management, found that the large Indian and Chinese figures 'include not only four-year degrees, but also three-year training programs and diploma holders', and that they had been set against American four-year degrees alone.[19] The figure they used for India in 2004, a projection by the National Association of Software and Service Companies (Nasscom), the industry's lobby group, was 215,000 graduates in engineering, computer science and information technology. Only 112,000 of them held four-year bachelor's degrees; the other 103,000 had three-year diplomas.[20] Per million people, they reckoned, the United States produced about 750 such graduates a year, China about 500 and India about 200.[21]

The team also found something more striking. Nasscom's projections rested on government data published with a 'three- to four-year lag', and 'the most recent official Indian graduation data are from 1993'.[22] Through much of the boom, on the Duke team's account, official counts of the engineers the industry was hiring were erratic and years out of date, and the industry's own lobby group was the 'de facto authority'.[23]

Later figures do not settle the question. Rajaraman gives the best-known growth series: 'In 1998 the number of engineering students was around 135,000 and in 2010 it grew to 1,300,000, a growth of almost 10 times.'[24] Elsewhere in the same history he describes what appears to be the same figure differently: 'Currently India graduates around 1.3 million engineers per year'.[25] Neither passage defines it. A total enrolment of 135,000 in 1998 is far too small for 486 colleges teaching four-year courses, so the 1998 figure is most likely one year's intake. By the same reasoning, 1.3 million in 2010 is most likely intake or approved seats rather than graduates. This book treats it as seats.

In 2014 Aspiring Minds, a company that sells employment tests to employers, wrote of 'the six hundred thousand engineers that graduate annually', without giving a source.[26] If the Duke and Aspiring Minds figures are roughly right, India's output of four-year engineering graduates grew about five times between 2004 and 2013, from about 112,000 to about 600,000. That is broadly in line with the more than threefold rise in college numbers between 1997-98 and 2005-06.[27]

The answer, then, depends on the question. By the early 2010s India approved about 1.5 million undergraduate engineering places a year, and a third or more of them stayed empty.[28] Its output of four-year engineering graduates was about 112,000 in 2004 and perhaps 600,000 by 2013, neither of them an official count. The often-repeated claim that India produces 1.5 million engineers a year matches the seats, not the graduates. The real number grew very fast. It was never as large as the figure that travelled.

## Any branch will do

The second half of the factory explains why so many colleges were worth building. The large software firms did not hire computer scientists in any great number. They hired engineers, and then made them into programmers themselves. Rajaraman sets out the logic plainly: 'The IT companies' common complaint was that there were not enough employable graduates with computer science degrees. Instead they recruited all engineering graduates with aptitude in computing; however they could not be directly placed as members of project teams.'[29] So, he continues, 'All major IT companies had in-house training programmes ranging from 12 weeks to 6 months.'[30]

A mechanical, civil or electrical engineer would do, if he or she could pass the firm's aptitude test. That made a degree in any engineering branch a ticket to the best-paid jobs open to most graduates, and it gave families a reason to pay for one. A Nasscom projection, reported by the Duke team, was that 84.8 per cent of India's four-year engineering graduates in 2004 took branches it classed as IT-related, a broad category that included electrical, electronics and instrumentation engineering as well as computer science.[31]

The scale of recruitment is clearest in the filings of Infosys, the Bangalore (Bengaluru since 2014) software company, made to American securities regulators in much the same categories from year to year. In the year to March 1998 it made about 1,790 offers.[32] Ten years later, in the year to March 2008, it reported screening over 885,000 applications, testing over 227,000 applicants, interviewing more than 97,000 and making about 46,300 offers.[33] Offers had grown about twenty-six times, though the filings do not separate new graduates from experienced recruits.[34] Headcount tells the same story. Infosys had about 9,400 IT professionals in March 2002, about 36,800 employees in March 2005, about 91,200 in March 2008 (of whom about 18,700 worked outside India) and about 150,000 in March 2012.[35] A generation earlier the pattern had been very different. Natarajan Chandrasekaran, who joined Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) in 1986-87, recalled in a 2020 oral history for the Computer History Museum a firm of about 500 to 600 professionals that 'used to hire 20 people or 40 people a year', often by taking a whole class from IIT Bombay or IIT Delhi.[36]

Infosys was not unusual in kind, only in what it published. Rajaraman writes that 'every major software company was recruiting around 8000 graduates each year' in the years from 1998 to 2010, and that with attrition of 15 to 20 per cent and workforces 'of the order of 120,000', 'the replacement numbers themselves were over 15,000 each year'.[37]

How dependent the colleges had become on this hiring was shown by the one year it faltered: after the dot-com bust, campus placements at Anna University in Chennai by January 2002 were less than a third of the year before, as Chapter 11 describes.[38] In Bangalore, many of the engineers interviewed in 2004 and 2005 by the researchers Carol Upadhya and A.R. Vasavi of the National Institute of Advanced Studies (NIAS) described the downturn of 2000-02. Some, the researchers wrote, 'who had been campus recruited were later turned down by the companies, and remained unemployed for months'.[39] Infosys, at least, came back quickly, and on a much larger scale. In the year to March 2004 Infosys alone made about 13,600 offers of employment.[40]

## Mysore

Before there was a training campus, there was a training building. In 2001 the magazine *Business Today* described the Infosys headquarters campus in Bangalore, where in a three-storey chrome and glass centre 'fifty of the country's best software instructors put every batch of engineers recruited by the company through a gruelling three-month training programme'.[41] By 2002, its filing said, Infosys employed 57 faculty members who ran three-month sessions for new recruits, and it had a Leadership Institute for its staff on a 200-acre campus in Mysore (Mysuru since 2014), elsewhere in Karnataka.[42]

The trainee campus came next, and Mysore became the factory floor. In its filing for the year to March 2005, Infosys reported that it had 'recently completed the construction of an employee training facility in Mysore'. The facility could 'house 4,500 trainees at any one time' and train about 12,000 employees a year.[43] The company said it did not fully use new employees on client work while they were in training, 'particularly during our 14-week training course for new employees'.[44] Three years later the capacity was 4,800 at a time and about 15,200 a year.[45] By the year to March 2012 the filing had a new name for it. 'We train the new engineering graduates that join us at our Global Education Center in Mysore,' the company wrote. 'With a total built-up area of 1.44 million square feet, the Infosys Global Education Center can train approximately 14,000 employees at a time.'[46] The course had lengthened too. The same filing describes a '20-29 week training course for new employees'.[47] The filings give capacities and square feet, not the voices of the trainees.[48]

The firm also reached back into the colleges. Through a programme it called Campus Connect, Infosys worked with engineering colleges so that their own teachers could give industry-related training. In the year to March 2012 it reported more than 190 workshops for more than 4,500 college teachers.[49] The boundary between the college and the company, which in 1998 had been the campus interview, was becoming harder to see.

## The pyramid and the bench

The shape of the workforce followed from the shape of a project: a small team at the client's site and a much larger one in India, the pyramid set out in Infosys's 1999 registration statement.[50] Its base had to be refilled every year with new graduates, and the growth of the base was what moved people upward.

The firms measured how much of the pyramid was earning money. Infosys called this utilisation. 'We define employee utilization as the proportion of total billed person months to total available person months excluding support personnel,' its filings said.[51] In the year to March 2012, utilisation of billable staff was 69.0 per cent including trainees and 75.9 per cent excluding them, down from 72.1 and 79.6 per cent the year before, a fall the company told investors had hurt its profitability.[52]

Put the other way round, on average in that year nearly a third of Infosys's billable staff, counting trainees, was not billed to a client. Some were in training. Others were between projects, or waiting for one to start. The industry called this the bench. In the firms' own terms it was not waste. Most work was still billed by the time spent on it: in the year to March 2008 only 31 per cent of Infosys's services revenue came from fixed-price projects, and the rest, 69 per cent, was billed on a 'time-and-materials basis'.[53] A firm paid that way must be able to staff a new contract at once, so it keeps trained people waiting. Here the book's bargain shows at the scale of one firm. Revenue followed the number of people billed, so growth meant hiring ahead of demand, and hiring ahead of demand meant a bench. But the bench is a cost that grows with every hiring wave, and it is the first thing cut when demand falls, as it was in 2001-02 and again in 2008-09.

Billing by time also made the engineer's time the thing to be managed. In Bangalore, Upadhya and Vasavi concluded that 'extracting the maximum amount of time (and "effort") out of software engineers is key to the profitability of services companies', and one respondent described the firms' systems for tracking hours as 'a system of "time slavery"'.[54] In their survey 61 per cent said they worked nine to ten hours a day on average, and staff of large Indian companies reported an average maximum of 13.8 hours, against 12.3 in multinationals.[55] The complaints they recorded were mundane: 'They'll give out work at 5:30 in the evening and expect you to have it done by the next morning, which isn't fair'.[56] One informant explained why flexitime did not shorten the day: 'What's the point of working till late if you aren't seen working?'[57]

Turnover was the other side of the pyramid. Infosys estimated the industry's attrition rate, the share of staff leaving each year, at 'approximately 20%'. Its own rate rose from 9.7 per cent in the year to March 2005 to 17.0 per cent in the year to March 2011.[58] People in Chennai talked about job-hopping constantly. Fuller and Narasimhan found less of it than the talk suggested: among the more senior ICS staff they knew, at least half had spent all or most of their working lives in the company.[59]

## One in twelve

Who passed through the gate? The best evidence for these years comes from the Chennai study. Between August 2003 and February 2005, Fuller, an anthropologist at the London School of Economics, and Narasimhan, who did most of the fieldwork, studied IT professionals in the city.[60] Most of their interviews were at ICS.[61] They interviewed nineteen of its staff and described their sample as 'tiny' and 'the haphazard product of the problems of access' in an industry concerned with security. 'All names used are pseudonyms,' they wrote.[62] Everyone from the study named here is a real informant under a false name given by the authors, and most of their words come to us as the authors reported them.

At ICS the gate was a series of filters on school and college marks. Only students with a consistent record of high examination marks could sit the company's aptitude test and go on to an interview, where one in twelve was offered a job.[63] Starting salaries, in the middle of the range for large software firms, were 'around 15,000 rupees per month' for people in their early twenties (about $330), and could 'easily double within a few years'.[64] That put a new recruit's own income near the level that only about 6 per cent of Indian households reached in 2001-02, according to estimates by the National Council of Applied Economic Research cited by the authors.[65]

The study also shows where these recruits came from. Most of the younger people the authors interviewed had fathers, and occasionally mothers, in professional or managerial posts in government or in public- or private-sector firms; the only exceptions were a few small businessmen and farmers.[66] In this sample, IT did not lift families into the middle class from below. It moved the children of the salaried middle class, many of them the children of government engineers and officials, into a richer, private-sector version of the class they were born into. That is one city and one firm. In Bangalore, Upadhya and Vasavi's survey of 132 software engineers found the same pattern: 84 per cent of their fathers worked in occupations 'that can be identified as solidly middle class'.[67] Together the two studies are the best evidence against the common claim that software created India's middle class.

Inside, the work was organised around appraisal and deadlines. Staff were appraised every six months; those who beat their targets could expect quick promotion, and those who fell short were told they would be 'let go'. Most worked a 40 to 50-hour, five-day week on flexitime, with extra hours when deadlines pressed. The offices were modern and open-plan, and young men and women, many of them unmarried, mixed there more freely than in most social settings in Chennai.[68]

The gate had a keeper. ICS's personnel manager, whom the authors call Ramakrishna, was in his late thirties, held an MCA, and described his job as 'tough and challenging'. In the 'war for talent' among the leading firms, it was his responsibility to make sure ICS recruited enough good people, above all by picking the best graduates from the top colleges. He earned about 70,000 rupees a month, plus stock options, and through much of 2003-04 he was negotiating for a rise while threatening to leave for a job in Bangalore.[69]

A young man the anthropologists call Shoaib shows what the move felt like. He was 29, ran the company's intranet and website, and had a degree in computer science from a Muslim college in Chennai and an MCA. His father had been an engineer in the state electricity board. After his father's early death Shoaib was offered a post at the board, and turned it down. He said he would never work in the public sector, because there you always 'have to bow your head to somebody'.[70] He was also, the authors noted, more worried than most of his colleagues about the future: 'there is no security in this job'.[71]

Older managers in Chennai's manufacturing firms watched the move with some resentment. Sampath, the personnel manager of a bus and lorry maker the study calls Chakra Vehicles, said the IT industry had 'disturbed the social fabric', with its 'quick promotions', 'fancy designations' and 'phenomenal compensation'.[72] One of his colleagues, the authors report, said that at campus interviews by the late 1990s only the weakest men still wanted to join Chakra, because everyone better was chasing IT salaries. Sampath himself, after more than twenty years, probably earned about 60,000 rupees a month, a level a competent IT professional could expect to reach in half the time.[73]

Where the money went is less glamorous than the stereotypes. As far as the authors could tell, most of it went on housing, bought, often with loans, much earlier than their parents had, and for those with children on private schooling.[74] Most of the young people they met had never even considered a government or public-sector job. One ICS assistant manager had turned down a post at the Indian Space Research Organisation because he thought it would be unchallenging and monotonous.[75] The city did not always welcome its new earners. Raghu shared a flat with two other young men in IT, and they were unpopular with their neighbours, who feared they would smoke, drink, cook meat and make a nuisance of themselves. In fact, the authors found, they never cooked at all. They ate every meal out, came home on weekdays only to sleep, and had friends round at weekends to drink beer.[76]

## Marks, English and caste

The Chennai study's most discussed finding is about caste, and the authors were careful with it. ICS, like many other IT companies in the city, 'is said to be dominated by the high-status "Forward Castes"', they wrote, especially Tamil Brahmans, who made up about 2.5 per cent of the state's population, 'and it is our strong impression that this is true'. But 'no accurate figures exist', and the guesses of people in the industry varied widely.[77] In a later paper they repeated that Tamil Brahmans were 'disproportionately well represented' in south India's IT industry, and that 'no figures to confirm this assertion exist', although all the circumstantial evidence pointed that way.[78] The study's terms are the ones used here. In its usage, 'Forward Castes', Brahmans among them, are those that cannot benefit from the reservation system of quotas in education and public employment, which is operated for the 'Backward' (and 'Most Backward') and 'Scheduled' Castes.[79]

The interest of the study lies less in the impression than in the explanation. Many people in Chennai said the reason was reservations. Tamil Nadu reserved 68 per cent of state-sector posts and college seats for the Other Backward Classes and the Scheduled Castes and Tribes, and many said this was why private companies employed so many Brahmans. 'Yet reservations alone cannot fully explain upper-caste predominance in IT companies.'[80]

The authors offered three further reasons. First, Brahmans had become an increasingly urban community, more likely than others to have the social skills and cultural knowledge, fluent English among them, that global IT companies wanted and that their selection tests demanded.[81] Second, the firms' own rules did the sorting. 'Because ICS allows only candidates with consistently high marks to apply for posts, its selection policy in practice favours Forward Caste candidates who, from a tender age, have been motivated to achieve repeated scholastic success.'[82] Third, Brahman families placed a high value on education, notably in mathematics and science, and they were the best-educated community in the state. The authors dismissed as 'fanciful' the popular idea, held by many Tamil Brahmans themselves, that the caste had a special aptitude for software because of its traditional religious learning.[83]

A footnote shows how small the measurable differences were. In 2004 the cut-off mark for admission to electronics and communication engineering at Anna University, the most competitive course in the state, was 293.28 out of 300 for Forward Caste candidates, 290.57 for Backward Castes, 283.67 for Most Backward Castes and 276.13 for Scheduled Castes.[84] The gap at the top was less than three marks in three hundred. The authors' point was that the belief in needing exceptionally high marks shaped how children were raised, even where the arithmetic was less harsh than families thought.[85]

The argument does not need the firms to have looked at caste at all. A selection system that screened on marks, then on an aptitude test, then on an interview in English, reproduced the advantages of urban, educated, upper-caste families on its own. The Chennai evidence is one city and one firm, and it is not a national count.[86] Bangalore points the same way. In Upadhya's account of the NIAS survey, 'Brahmins constituted 48 per cent of our sample', upper castes as a whole 71 per cent, and upper and dominant agricultural castes together 86 per cent. 'Only one respondent said that he belonged to a scheduled community.'[87] The authors warned that 132 engineers, drawn mainly from multinationals and large and medium Indian firms, were 'much too small to be representative'.[88] The mechanism is visible elsewhere. In 2014 Aspiring Minds argued that in screening applications 'the college name is a key signal, and resumes from unknown colleges aren't shortlisted', so that more than half of the graduates who met its benchmark for IT services jobs, studying outside the top 750 colleges, were 'invisible to most employers'.[89] It also estimated that a student from a third-tier college, with the same test score and marks as a student from a first-tier one, had 24 per cent lower odds of getting a job, and if hired was paid 66,000 rupees a year less.[90] The claims come from a firm with an interest in selling another way to find such students. They point in the same direction: a filter that worked by college name fell hardest on students from the new private colleges and the smaller towns.

## Women in the factory

At ICS, 'approximately one-fifth' of new recruits were women, close to the share across the industry.[91] According to Nasscom, 79 per cent of India's software professionals were men in 2001-02, a share it expected to fall to 65 per cent by 2005.[92] In the colleges the gap was narrower. Among undergraduates enrolled in engineering and technology courses at AICTE-approved institutions in 2012, 33.7 per cent were women, according to the council's figures as compiled by the Society of Women Engineers.[93]

What the Chennai researchers heard about women differs from what studies of Western software firms had found. Almost everyone they met, men and women alike, 'insisted to us that both sexes have equal technical skills'.[94] The difference between men and women at ICS lay elsewhere: 'Married women professionals consistently give their families higher priority than their work.'[95] Many men wanted 'home-loving' wives who would not work. So women in IT preferred husbands in IT, and men in IT tended to prefer wives who were not.[96] One leading company, the authors reported, had started an in-house online matrimonial service to encourage its staff to marry each other, and so reduce the number of married women who resigned to follow husbands working elsewhere.[97] The managers of two small software firms, one of them a woman, admitted that they were reluctant to recruit women, because family duties took them away from work.[98]

The study's women show the range. A project manager in her early thirties, whom the authors call Anuradha, had made it a condition of her marriage that she and her husband return from America to Chennai. Her daughter was looked after by both sets of grandparents, and she 'firmly believes that the IT industry has helped to empower women'.[99] Jayashree, about 35, an assistant project manager with an MSc in physics from IIT Madras, had a different experience. Childcare for her two children was 'an endlessly negotiated series of arrangements' among hired help, her parents and her parents-in-law. Her husband, she complained, did not do his share at home; many chores, she joked, had been 'outsourced'. She later resigned from ICS and did contract work for it from home.[100]

Two younger engineers on Jayashree's team, called Sarojini and Parvati, were in their mid-twenties. Sarojini had an electrical and electronics degree from Coimbatore and joined ICS as a trainee in 2002. She told the researchers she found the work exciting and challenging, though her first ambition had been medicine, and she insisted that any husband would have to let her keep working. Her mother also worked, and she appeared, the authors thought, to put her determination down less to the IT industry than to her matrilineal Nayar background. Later in 2004 the company sent her to New Jersey.[101] Parvati, with a BSc in computer science and an MSc in information technology, found her work boring after six months. A year later she was a team leader, determined to get a posting in America. One of her weekly tasks was to search an internet matrimonial site for a husband for her elder sister, and the profiles asking for 'home-loving' wives increasingly irritated her.[102]

The authors' verdict held both halves together. 'Plainly, the IT industry has not revolutionised the position of Indian women.'[103] Yet when they compared their informants with the upper-middle-class Chennai women studied by Patricia Caplan in 1974-75, for most of whom 'employment outside the home is not considered at all desirable', they judged that 'real change has occurred'.[104] Young women in IT appeared to 'command greater respect and have more bargaining power within their families', particularly over whom they married.[105]

## Trainable, not skilled

By the early 2010s a second number had joined the count of engineers. Only a quarter of Indian engineers were employable, it was said, or only a fifth. Both figures can be traced, and both come from parties with an interest.

The 'quarter' comes from the McKinsey Global Institute, the research arm of the consultancy. As the Duke study reported it, 'McKinsey concluded that only 10% of Chinese engineers and 25% of Indian engineers can compete in the global outsourcing arena', citing language, the quality of education, culture and other factors.[106] As quoted, its question was not whether Indian engineers could find work, but how many could compete for outsourced work from rich countries.

The 'fifth' comes from Aspiring Minds. Its 2014 report tested 'more than 1,20,000 engineering students from 520+ engineering colleges' who graduated in 2013, on the company's own test, a test it said was used by more than 650 companies.[107] It found that 'only 18.43% of them are employable for the Software Engineer-IT services role'.[108] These are the shares of a tested sample that met the vendor's benchmark for a role. They are not measures of whether graduates found jobs, and the company that produced them sold the test.

Read for what it measures, though, the report says something precise about the factory. The IT services figure, it explained, was calculated under the firms' 'current hiring philosophy', in which a recruit was not expected to have software skills already but was trained 'over a period of 3 to 6 months'. So 18.43 per cent was the share judged 'trainable into software engineers within a period of 3 to 6 months'.[109] The firms' bar was trainability, not skill. That was the bar Rajaraman described and the one the Mysore campus was built for.

The same report contained an early warning. 'The IT services industry is not growing at the same pace as before and the growth of entry-level jobs is diminishing,' it said. Because firms were hiring fewer people and wanted to cut training costs, there was 'a slow but definite trend towards hiring candidates who already have decent expertise in programming'.[110] It is a vendor's observation, from a firm that sold programming tests, but it is an early documented sign that the factory's demand curve was bending.

The price of a place in the factory points the same way. The figures are rough and measure different things. ICS's starting salary of about 15,000 rupees a month in 2003-05 came to about 180,000 rupees a year.[111] A study by the business website Moneycontrol, relayed by the trade site *HR Katha*, put the median annual pay of freshers at large IT firms in 2012 at about 245,000 rupees.[112] Adjusted for consumer prices, the first is worth about 660,000 rupees at 2024 prices and the second about 480,000.[113] One is a single firm and the other a median, so the comparison can only be suggestive. It suggests that as the gate widened, the price of entry fell.

## Routine work

What were the factory's products made for? Fuller and Narasimhan answered in a sentence that matters for the rest of this book. 'Because software engineering in companies like ICS or TCS has progressively become more routinized and reliant on standard packages, IIT graduates are over-qualified and can secure more technically demanding, better-paid jobs.'[114] Most new recruits in the major firms, they went on, had only a bachelor's degree in engineering, usually from one of the leading colleges in Tamil Nadu.[115]

The people doing the work said similar things. 'Software engineering does not demand exceptional ability, as some experienced people acknowledge,' the authors wrote. Shoaib went further and claimed that any reasonably intelligent school-leaver could learn the job. He was exaggerating, they said, but they had come across several IT professionals bored by work that was too easy.[116] Raghu, keeping a British client's system running, thought he was learning little. Parvati was bored at six months, a team leader at eighteen and set on a posting in America. Sarojini found the work challenging, and was sent to New Jersey.[117] The firms did not need all their recruits to be stretched. They needed them to be trainable, reliable and available. Some managers said so, though not in the way Aspiring Minds' account of firms that looked only at top colleges would suggest. Several large Indian services companies, Upadhya reported, preferred graduates of lower-ranked colleges 'because the best students are not suitable for the kind of routinised work that is on offer'. As one HR manager put it, they required 'guys who can just sit and code and not ask questions'.[118]

Outside observers drew the same line. The Duke team divided engineering graduates into 'dynamic' engineers, capable of abstract thinking and high-level problem solving, and 'transactional' engineers, who might have the fundamentals but were 'typically responsible for rote and repetitive tasks in the workforce'.[119] It was 'the jobs of transactional engineers', the team wrote in 2005, that seemed 'easily outsourced' to relatively low-paid engineers in countries like India.[120] The phrase was American shorthand, and it was unkind to many Indian graduates who did far more than that. But it described the bulk of what the factory was designed to supply.

That was the factory's design, and it fitted the business the Indian firms had built. A client abroad specified a system; a small team onsite fixed the requirements; a large team in India built, tested and maintained it, to documented methods, on standard packages, billed by time. A trained graduate of almost any engineering branch could do most of that work after three months in Mysore, and every graduate the factory turned out was more time to sell. The design succeeded.


# Chapter 13. H-1B (1990-2015)

Reedhar Gunda, an electrical engineer from Bombay (Mumbai since 1995), came to the United States in 1998 on a temporary work visa sponsored by a body shopper, a middleman who hired Indian engineers and rented them out to American companies. When he arrived, the *Dallas Observer* reporter Miriam Rozen wrote that November, he found that the body shopper was taking $22 an hour out of his pay and leaving him $28. To get out he had to find another job and have the new employer petition for his visa all over again, which took several months.[1]

His friend Reddy Bandi, a 27-year-old electrical engineer from Hyderabad, the son of a rice farmer and the first in his family to go to college, had taken a different road. He had come on a student visa, taken a master's degree at Arizona State University within 18 months, and switched to the work visa.[2] He had kept away from body shops. 'I don't like to apply to companies who get people from the outside,' he said. 'I know what their tactics are.' He blamed both sides. Of those who came on the work visa he said, 'Their main intention is just to get in'; once they found they were underpaid, some switched employers 'two, three times a year'.[3] Working through a large American subcontractor, he thought he earned more cash than the permanent staff beside him at the Sabre Group, though they had better benefits and more authority. His wife, a physical therapist, could not work in her field on his visa.[4]

Rozen built her article around a body shop in suburban Plano. Its owner, an engineer from Madras (Chennai since 1996), recruited engineers and programmers in India, signed them to contracts with his firm and hired them out to American companies, often through a further middleman. By Rozen's account he took 'sometimes as much as 40 percent' of their pay.[5] The visa had been closed to new workers for almost five months after the annual quota ran out in May, she wrote, and he was 'making up for lost time'.[6] He said he had brought some 350 engineers and programmers from India since 1993.[7] By his own account, which he would not document, he paid salaries of $45,000 to $60,000; rival recruiters told Rozen he could bill a programmer at $90,000 to $200,000 a year.[8] He would not let her speak to any of his contract workers.[9] He had also begun sending American project specifications to his Madras office, where the work was done at Indian wages and emailed back. 'They are going to lose the whole business to India,' he said.[10] It was the forecast of an interested party, made in a year when the visas had run out by May.

Rozen doubted that the wage rules were much enforced. An enforcement coordinator in the Labor Department's Dallas office told her he received complaints about the visa about once a month; engineers, he believed, moved on rather than pursue a case. Nationally, she reported, prosecutors had filed only eight cases in six years alleging wilful breaches of the prevailing-wage rules for temporary workers.[11]

The body shop was the industry's bargain at its barest. What it sold was an engineer's hour. Its margin was the gap between the rate it billed and the wage it paid, and it could grow only by bringing in more engineers. The visa that made the trade possible was eight years old, and it was called the H-1B.

## A visa with a cap

The Immigration Act of 1990 admitted foreign nationals 'to work temporarily in the United States if hired by a U.S. employer to perform work in a specialty occupation', in the words of the Congressional Research Service (CRS), the research arm of the US Congress. A specialty occupation required at least a bachelor's degree. The visa lasted up to three years and could be renewed for three more.[12] New visas were capped at 65,000 a year. That cap, the CRS noted in 2025, 'is the same now as when it was established in 1990', although Congress raised it for a few years around the turn of the century.[13]

The CRS has described the programme as one that 'epitomizes the tensions' between American employers competing for talent worldwide and the possible harm to American workers of their doing so.[14] The protection for American workers was a promise on paper. Before petitioning for a worker, the employer filed a labour condition application with the Department of Labor, attesting that it would pay 'the greater of the actual wages paid to similar employees or the prevailing wages for that occupation'.[15] The CRS added a dry sentence that explains much of what followed: 'The LCA is a statement of intent rather than a documentation of actions taken'.[16] The department reviewed each application 'for completeness and obvious inaccuracies', and investigated only if someone later complained.[17]

For its first few years the cap did not bind. A table compiled from government data by the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP), a pro-immigration policy group, shows 48,600 new petitions issued against the 65,000 cap in the US fiscal year 1992, and between 54,000 and 62,000 in each of the next four years.[18] Nor was it at first mainly a programmers' visa. The economists Gaurav Khanna and Nicolas Morales cite a 1992 government report finding that computing and related occupations accounted for only 11 per cent of H-1 visas in 1989. By 1999, according to the immigration service, close to two-thirds of H-1B visas went to computer-related occupations.[19] The visa was not free to use. A 2011 survey by the GAO, the US government's audit office, cited by Khanna and Morales, put the legal and administrative cost of each H-1B hire at between $2,300 and $7,500.[20] The new visa also changed the economics of sending Indian programmers to American client sites, the trade Chapter 6 follows. 'In 1993, the shift from B-1 to H-1 visas lowered the incentives to hire Indian engineers for on-site work,' Khanna and Morales write, 'as they were to be paid the prevailing market wage'.[21] The B-1 was a business visitor's visa, meant for meetings and negotiations, not for work. On this reading, one reason the Indian firms moved more of their work offshore in the 1990s was that the visa made on-site labour dearer.[22]

The cap began to bind as the American technology industry grew. Visa numbers ran out by September 1997, and the next year's in May 1998.[23] Both Congress and the Federal Reserve, the CRS wrote, worried 'that a scarcity of labor could curtail the pace of economic growth'.[24] Congress raised the ceiling to 115,000 for fiscal 1999 and 2000, and in 2000 to 195,000 for three years.[25] The government's own counting failed under the strain. The immigration service 'admitted in autumn 1999 that thousands of H-1B visas beyond the 115,000 ceiling were approved in FY1999'.[26] The 1998 law also charged employers $500 a worker, which, the *Observer* reported, would pay for scholarships for low-income students in mathematics, engineering and computer science, with about 5 per cent going to enforce the wage rules.[27] Firms that relied heavily on the visa faced extra duties. An 'H-1B dependent' employer, generally one with at least 15 per cent of its workforce on H-1Bs, had to attest that it had tried to recruit American workers and had not laid any off in the 90 days before or after hiring a visa holder.[28] Then the market turned. NFAP's table shows new petitions falling from 163,600 in fiscal 2001 to 79,100 in 2002 and 78,000 in 2003, against a cap of 195,000.[29] When the limit reverted to 65,000 in fiscal 2005, the CRS wrote, 'that limit was reached on the first day'.[30] In April 2007 the immigration service received about 119,193 petitions for the fiscal 2008 cap on the first two days it accepted them, and chose among them by a computer-generated random draw.[31] From the mid-2000s the visa was allocated by lottery.[32] A young engineer's chance of an American job now depended partly on luck.

## How Indian the visa became

Indians did not dominate the visa at first. The sociologist AnnaLee Saxenian, writing in 2001 and citing a 2000 study of the visa by Lowell, reported that the number of Indian H-1B holders grew steadily from 1989, became the largest national group in 1994, doubled by 1996 and quintupled by 1999. In 1999 Indians received 47 per cent of all H-1B visas issued, 55,047 people; the next largest groups, from Britain and China, had 6 per cent or less each.[33]

The share kept rising, though the published figures measure different things. For fiscal 2005 the CRS reported that India was 'the leading country of origin for newly arriving H-1B workers, comprising almost half (49.0%) of all of the new arrivals', with China a distant second at 9.16 per cent.[34] The same report repeated an undated government estimate that 'nearly three-fourths of all of the systems analysts and programmers are from India'.[35] By 2014, according to immigration service data cited by Khanna and Morales, about 70 per cent of H-1B visas went to Indians; China, the next largest, had received only 8 per cent in 2012.[36] A visa that Congress had written for any skilled foreigner had become, in its largest use, a channel between Indian engineering colleges and American information technology.

Who sponsored those visas is a separate question, and the answer is less simple than the common belief that the visas mostly went to Indian outsourcing firms. In 2013, by Khanna and Morales's tabulation of immigration service reports, Infosys led with 6,298 approvals, just ahead of Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), with Cognizant third; the year before, Cognizant had topped the list with 9,281. Eight more firms had over a thousand approvals each in 2013, among them Accenture, Wipro, IBM's Indian subsidiary and Deloitte.[37]

The authors drew the conclusion from the table: '10 out of the top 11 H-1B firms have Indians as their primary employment base'.[38] Three of those ten had their headquarters outside India: Cognizant and IBM in the United States, Accenture in the Bahamas. The table lists iGate under both the United States and India. Their main workforce, like that of Infosys or Wipro, was in India. Only Deloitte, tenth on the list, employed mainly Americans.[39] The largest sponsors, in other words, were firms built on the offshore services model, whoever owned them.[40]

The sponsors were also only part of the visa's use. Since fiscal 2000, the CRS noted, most H-1B workers had been exempt from the cap, because they were extending an existing status or worked for universities and research bodies.[41] The lottery decided who got in. Extensions, and for some a pending application for permanent residence, decided how long they stayed.[42]

## Who went, and what they had learned

Most temporary visa workers had been educated before they arrived. A 2010 national survey of American college graduates, tabulated by Khanna and Morales, found that among foreign-born workers on temporary work visas whose highest degree was a bachelor's, 94 per cent had earned it abroad. Among those with a master's, 77 per cent had.[43] Since most H-1B holders were Indian, most of that education had been done in Indian colleges, without an American degree in between. Bandi, with his Arizona master's, was the exception.

That was a change from the earlier generation. The Indians already in Silicon Valley in 1990 had mostly come for graduate study. The 1990 census counted 28,520 Indians in the region's workforce, 98 per cent of them immigrants; 87 per cent of the Indians in its high-technology industries had arrived after 1970 and 60 per cent after 1980.[44] National Science Foundation figures that Saxenian cited show that 79 per cent of Indians who received American science and engineering doctorates in 1990-91 were still working in the United States in 1995.[45] Many were graduates of 'the prestigious Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) or Indian Institutes of Science (IISs)', she wrote, and were united by professional as well as ethnic ties; a sizable group had grown up in Africa and never lived in India.[46]

The IITs had been feeding America for decades; one IIT Bombay study found over 40 per cent of a 1970s cohort of its electrical engineering graduates abroad.[47] The pattern outlasted the period of this chapter. A study published in 2023 by Prithwiraj Choudhury, Ina Ganguli and Patrick Gaulé, which followed students who sat the IIT entrance examination, found that 'among the top 1,000 scorers on the exam, 36% have migrated abroad, rising to 62% for the top 100 scorers'.[48] The H-1B also gave Indian students a reason to take an American degree first. The 2004 allowance of 20,000 extra visas for holders of American master's degrees, Khanna and Morales note, 'may incentivize students to obtain their degrees in US universities'.[49]

The two routes together supplied much of America's computing workforce. A national survey of college graduates showed that 55 per cent of foreigners working in computing fields in 2003 had arrived on a temporary work visa or a student visa, and a Department of Commerce estimate for the late 1990s was that 28 per cent of programmer jobs went to H-1B holders.[50] In 1990 immigrants (defined as people born abroad who arrived after the age of 18) made up 11.06 per cent of computer scientists in the United States with a bachelor's or master's degree. By 2000 they were 18.59 per cent, and by 2010 27.82 per cent.[51]

## The pull on the colleges

The most important effect of the visa may have been on the people who never used it. Khanna and Morales built an economic model of students and firms in both countries to test a hypothesis: 'that Indian students enrolled in engineering schools to gain employment in the rapidly growing US IT industry via the H-1B visa program. Those who could not join the US workforce, due to the H-1B cap, remained in India, enabling the growth of an Indian IT sector'.[52] Those who went and came back when their visas expired brought skills and technology with them.[53] As the authors put it, workers who could not get a visa 'or return to India after their visa expires are a ready supply of labor for firms in India'.[54]

Their model's answer is that the visa 'induced Indians to switch to computer science (CS) occupations, increasing the CS workforce in India by 4.9% in 2010'.[55] The same model finds a cost on the other side. The visa 'induced US workers to switch to non-CS occupations, reducing the US native CS workforce by 7%'.[56] Indian IT output was 1.8 per cent higher, and the combined income of the two countries 1.5 per cent higher, than it would have been without the programme.[57] These are estimates from a calibrated model, not counts. They describe a world without the H-1B that never existed. What they offer is a mechanism: the American prospect pulled Indian students towards engineering and computing, and the cap kept most of them at home, where the Indian firms hired them.

Over the same years, according to Nasscom (the National Association of Software and Service Companies), the industry's lobby group, information technology and business process outsourcing grew from 1.2 per cent of India's gross domestic product in 1998 to 7.5 per cent in 2012.[58] The workforce it produced was young. In 2002 Indian software engineers had 'a median age of 26.5 years, and 58% of them had less than three years of experience', according to Nasscom. A Nasscom-Hewitt survey 'found that 88% of firms visited engineering colleges to recruit, and 47% recruited only there'.[59] Drawing on a 2002 study by Arora and Athreye, Khanna and Morales report that the number of engineering doctorates in India fell from about 675 in 1987 to 375 in 1995.[60] The industry, they conclude, was attracting 'some of the brightest young graduates with little experience'.

## Silicon Valley's Indians

By 2000, 53 per cent of Silicon Valley's scientists and engineers were foreign-born, Saxenian reported, and about 20,000 of them were Indian.[61] Many had found their careers stopped short. 'Many Indian engineers complained about a glass ceiling in the region's established companies, and responded by starting their own businesses', she wrote.[62] Prabhat Andleigh, quoted in the *Los Angeles Times* in 1996, put it more sharply: 'Why do you think there are so many Indian entrepreneurs in Silicon Valley? Because they know that sooner or later they will be held back'.[63]

Some of the older arrivals had already built companies. Some time in 1992 a group of Indian businessmen in the Valley gathered to meet a visitor from India, the Secretary of Electronics. His flight was delayed. While they waited, they 'began to informally share complaints about the difficulties of running a business'.[64] Among them were Suhas Patil, a former professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who had founded the chip company Cirrus Logic; Prabhu Goel, founder of Gateway Design Automation; and Kanwal Rekhi, who had started and run the networking firm Excelan until it merged with Novell.[65] Patil and Goel had succeeded 'in spite of their lack of contacts or community support'.[66] Patil put the discovery in a sentence that the *San Jose Mercury News* printed two years later: 'as individuals we are brilliant, but collectively we amounted to nothing'.[67] Satish Gupta, another early member, said much the same in the same article: 'When some of us started our businesses we had nobody we could turn to for help'.[68]

Out of the delayed flight came a club with monthly meetings, called The Indus Entrepreneurs (TiE). Its founders chose 'Indus (rather than Indian)', Saxenian wrote, so that Pakistanis, Bangladeshis and Nepalese could belong too, though the Bay Area members were almost all Indian.[69] TiE's own history dates the founding to December 1992.[70] The first annual conference, in 1994, 'attracted over 500 people'. In 1997 more than 800 came to two days of talks on how to start a company, raise money and take it public.[71] TiE turned to mentoring and, through its members, investing in younger South Asian founders.[72] Its founders belonged to what Saxenian called 'an older generation of Indian immigrants'.[73] The engineers the H-1B brought were younger, trained in India, and hired for a few years rather than for a career.

By Saxenian's 1999 count, firms with Indian chief executives were 7 per cent of the Silicon Valley technology companies founded between 1980 and 1998: 774 firms, with $3.6 billion in sales and 16,598 jobs in 1998.[74] The Indian share of new start-ups rose from 3 per cent in 1980-84 to 9 per cent in 1995-98.[75] Her count, she was explicit, used chief executives as 'a proxy for immigrant-founded businesses'. A later study that counted Indian immigrants among the key founders of 1995-2005 start-ups produced the more often quoted figure of 15.5 per cent.[76] Any share of Indian start-ups is only as good as its definition.

## Drain, then circulation

Saxenian's phrase 'brain circulation' is easily read back into the 1990s. Her own evidence for India in that decade points the other way.

The exception she described in detail was Radha Basu. Basu left 'her conservative South Indian family' for graduate study in computer science at the University of Southern California in the early 1970s and joined Hewlett-Packard.[77] In the mid-1980s, after the Indian government invited her to set up one of the country's first foreign subsidiaries, she spent four years building HP's centre in Bangalore (Bengaluru since 2014). When she went back to California in 1989 it employed 400 people.[78] The first office, she told Saxenian in 1997, 'consisted of a telex machine on her dining room table'.[79] Customs officials could not accept that software could be exported over a satellite link without something physical to inspect, so for five years Basu copied HP's data onto tapes and shipped them to the United States so that the exports could be registered.[80] Doing business in India, she told Saxenian, needed patience: 'You can't just fly in and out and stay in a five-star hotel and expect to get things done like you can elsewhere'.[81] When officials talked of a 'single window of clearance' for foreign trade, she would joke: 'where is the window?'[82]

Basu was unusual. Saxenian wrote in 1999 that 'few Indian engineers choose to live and work permanently in India'; those who went home typically did so for a time.[83] Bangalore software companies reported turnover of 20-30 per cent a year, 'primarily because so many workers jump at the first opportunity to emigrate'. On balance, 'the "brain drain" of skilled workers to the United States continued unabated throughout the 1990s'.[84] The engineers who stayed in America played what she called 'an important, but largely arm's-length, role', persuading their employers to send work to India.[85] The reason was cost. Programmers' wages were 'ten times lower in India', and the fully loaded cost of an engineer there was 35-40 per cent of the American figure.[86]

Much of the work was still body shopping, which Saxenian defined narrowly as programming at the customer's site on 'time and material' contracts billed by the programmer-hour. In the series by Balaji Parthasarathy that she cites, on-site services were about 90 per cent of the value of Indian software exports in 1990 and still 61 per cent in 1995.[87] At the end of the decade much of the work in India was on the year 2000 problem, which earned exports but, in her judgement, created no new intellectual property.[88] The big Indian firms, she judged, 'have been so profitable playing the wage gap that they have had few incentives to address higher value-added segments of the market'.[89] Playing the wage gap was the bargain in another phrase: the firms sold hours, and the hours were cheap.

Writing in 2005, she repeated the point: 'few U.S.-educated emigrants returned to either India or China during the 1980s and 1990s'. It was the technology recession that 'triggered an upsurge in cross-regional entrepreneurship'.[90] In Taiwan and Israel, by contrast, returning immigrants had carried the Silicon Valley model of venture capital home from the early 1980s.[91] Indian entrepreneurs instead mobilised 'thousands of underemployed English-speaking Indian engineers to provide software development services for American corporations'.[92] On her account, India's diaspora had sent work home rather than companies. Inside India, the 1990s turnover did not spread ideas between firms as it did in Silicon Valley. It mainly pushed up wages, by 25-40 per cent a year. Learning happened 'primarily within the firm and through long-distance relationships', not with local universities or laboratories, even in Bangalore, home of the Indian Institute of Science.[93]

By the mid-2000s the trade itself was changing who travelled. In Chennai, the anthropologists Chris Fuller and Haripriya Narasimhan followed a group of engineers. Of their twenty younger software engineers, seven had been or were on overseas assignments in 2005, but only two had spent more than a year in the United States; 'the rest, as is now increasingly common, were away for only a few months'.[94] They argued that 'the very logic of "offshoring"' meant that flows of people might diminish 'as the work travels to the site of labor, instead of the reverse'.[95] For many engineers the American posting became a stint in a career spent in India.

At the Chennai firm they studied, which they called ICS, on-site assignments of several months or a year or two were a normal part of working life.[96] Their individual stories show the range. Ravi (a pseudonym, as are all names in the study), a project manager of 33 at a large Chennai firm, had spent a year on-site in England, 'where he earned plenty of money and got "good exposure"', but came home to be with his elderly father and had no wish to live abroad.[97] Balaram, 37, left the same company in 1995 for Australia, worked there in information technology for eight years, and came back in 2003 because 'the work available in Chennai is far more interesting and challenging, and the industry's growth prospects are much better'.[98] Anuradha, a project manager who had worked for ICS in America from 2000 to 2002, now had a young daughter and refused on-site assignments; she said she did not need any more 'exposure'.[99]

## The parents

Migration also reached into Indian homes. Fuller and Narasimhan found that Chennai was 'said to be full of lonely old folk whose sons and daughters send them dollars, but only ever come on short visits'. Other parents visited their children so often that they became 'bored, exploited childminders marooned in American suburbia under "house arrest", to quote one elderly grandfather'.[100] One informant told them that overseas migration 'damages the proper reciprocal relationship between parents and children in a way that migration within India does not'.[101] Children abroad could send money. They could not provide the daily care that sons and daughters were expected to give their parents.[102]

## The B-1 channel

The H-1B was not the only door. The business visitor's visa that Khanna and Morales described as giving way to the H-1B in 1993 was still in use two decades later. The clearest record of how comes from a legal settlement.

On 30 October 2013 Infosys filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission a settlement agreement with the US Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Texas, the State Department and the Department of Homeland Security. Under it, 'Infosys agrees to pay a full settlement amount of $34,000,000'.[103] The agreement separates what both sides accepted from what the government alleged.

Both sides accepted that 'Infosys failed to maintain accurate I-9 records for many of its foreign nationals in the United States in 2010 and 2011', the forms that record whether an employee may legally work. This included 'a widespread failure to update and re-verify the employment authorization status of a substantial percentage of its foreign national employees'.[104]

The government alleged more, and Infosys denied it. The allegation was that Infosys 'knowingly and unlawfully used B-1 visa holders to perform skilled labor' in jobs that would otherwise have gone to American citizens or to legitimate H-1B holders, for purposes that included 'increasing profits, minimizing costs of securing visas, increasing flexibility of employee movement'.[105] According to the government, invitation letters described trips as 'customer discussions and related business development activities' when the work included 'coding and programming'.[106] It quoted a 'Do's and Don'ts' memorandum given to B-1 travellers: 'Do not mention activities like implementation, design & testing, consulting, etc., which sound like work.' Another line read: 'Please do not mention anything about contract rates'.[107] The government alleged that workers were told to give consular officers the destination named in the labour condition application when they were going elsewhere. In one case, it said, a worker was told to say Seattle when his real destination was Bentonville, Arkansas.[108] And it alleged that on 29 September 2009 Infosys staff were directed by email to convert a time-and-materials contract, which disclosed the names and billing rates of everyone on a project, into a fixed-price contract, which disclosed only the total, in a way that hid the B-1 holders' skilled work.[109]

Infosys's answer, in the same document, was that its use of B-1 visas 'was for legitimate business purposes and not in any way to circumvent the requirements of the H-1B program'. It said the memorandum 'was not intended to deceive U.S. officials' and had been withdrawn in 2011, and that contract changes were 'made to comply with internal Company guidelines and rules regarding billing practices'.[110] Infosys 'denies any allegations of civil or criminal wrongdoing and/or liability'.[111] The settlement resolved the claims without resolving that dispute.

Two points can be made safely. The first is that the older on-site channel had not closed when the H-1B opened, and the agreed facts show that one of the largest sponsors had not kept accurate track of whether its foreign employees in America were authorised to work. The second concerns the contract forms. Whatever happened in that 2009 email exchange, the government's description of the two forms is accurate. A time-and-materials contract names the people and their rates. A fixed-price contract names only the price. The Indian industry grew up on the first kind, the hour sold and billed. Who captures the savings under each kind of contract is a question Chapter 19 takes up.

## Ninety days in Orlando

The other side of the trade has a name and a voice. Leo Perrero had a bachelor's degree in information technology and, by his account, 'twenty years of hard work' in the field.[112] He had worked for Disney in Orlando 'in some capacity for well over ten years', on the point-of-sale system through which visitors paid for food and merchandise.[113] In the holiday season of 2014 he received a meeting invitation from a senior executive and, he later told the Senate Judiciary Committee, his mind 'buzzed with thoughts of a promotion or a bonus'. He walked into a small conference room with about two dozen colleagues.[114] He recalled the executive's words: 'All of you in this room will be losing your jobs in the next 90 days. Your jobs have been given over to a foreign workforce.' Severance pay depended on training their replacements.[115] Later that day, he recalled, he had to tell his children at a church pumpkin sale that the family could not buy one.[116] Only '4 people would be directly rehired by Disney of the hundreds that were lost'.[117]

He described the handover in three stages. In the first, the newcomers sat beside the Disney staff and watched them work. 'Everything was recorded with audio and video. Then the very next day the recordings were put down on paper and read right back to us'.[118] In the second the incumbents worked 'side by side with our replacements'. In the third they watched 'the foreign workers completely take over our jobs'.[119] On 31 January 2015 they handed in their badges and laptops. His desk, chair and computer, he said, went to a worker 'who was just flown in to America weeks before'.[120] Of the severance he had accepted, he said: 'Sadly, I choose the money over America'.[121]

What he described in the first stage was a transfer of knowledge in the most literal sense. The tacit work of a team, what it knew but had never written down, was recorded, transcribed and read back, so that people paid less could do it, first beside the old staff and then without them. A quarter of a century of the visa had refined a method for moving work from one set of people to another by writing it down.

His complaint was aimed at two things together: visa holders 'physically being flown in from foreign countries' and 'the growing use of foreign remote offshore workers'.[122] The firms at the top of the sponsor tables earlier in this chapter ran both. To the worker in the conference room, the H-1B and the offshore centre were one system.


# Chapter 14. Backlash and scale (2002-2011)

In February 2004 N. Gregory Mankiw, a Harvard economist then serving as chairman of the White House Council of Economic Advisers, made a remark about trade that the Princeton economist Alan Blinder would later call a 'textbook' statement. Offshoring, the movement of jobs but not of the people who do them from rich countries to poor ones, was in his words 'the latest manifestation of the gains from trade that economists have talked about at least since Adam Smith'. He added: 'More things are tradable than were tradable in the past, and that's a good thing.'[1] The remark caused what Blinder called a national uproar. 'Democratic and Republican politicians alike excoriated Mankiw', Blinder wrote, while economists lined up to defend him.[2]

The politicians were already acting. On 20 February 2004 the trade paper *Government Computer News* (GCN) reported that a provision in the omnibus budget bill President George W. Bush had signed the month before barred companies that won federal work through competitions under the government's Circular A-76 from shifting that work to other countries.[3] The measure was named the Thomas-Voinovich Amendment after its two Republican sponsors, Senator Craig Thomas of Wyoming and Senator George Voinovich of Ohio. GCN described it as 'part of a swell of legislation' against businesses and governments buying software and IT services from countries such as India and China.[4] For one year, work won by a vendor could not be 'performed by the contractor at a location outside the United States'.[5]

The states went further on paper. The National Conference of State Legislatures had counted 29 bills in 19 state legislatures that would require contractors to hire only American citizens or legal residents, regulate agencies' use of offshore call centres, or otherwise restrict foreign purchases.[6] Justin Marks, the conference's research analyst, said that state legislatures had had to fill a $200 billion budget gap over the previous three years and faced a choice between saving money by outsourcing and keeping jobs at home. Over the years, he said, legislators 'have seen manufacturing jobs go overseas and now they see white-collar jobs going abroad'.[7] The television presenter Lou Dobbs published a book that year with the title *Exporting America*.[8]

Not everyone thought the noise would matter. John Kost, a managing vice-president at the research firm Gartner, told GCN that government agencies had been buying offshore software for years. 'People are naive if they think it is not already happening in large quantities,' he said. 'Once the economy improves and politicians move to a different topic, I doubt it will be a potent political issue.'[9]

In India, the programmers whose work the bills were meant to keep at home were not persuaded. That same month *Wired* published a long report by the journalist Daniel Pink from Hexaware Technologies, a software exporter on the edge of Mumbai that he ranked eighteenth among India's software and services exporters. One of its project managers, Aparna Jairam, an engineering graduate of the University of Pune, wrote embedded software for handheld devices, and her main client was a utility company in the western United States. Her salary, Pink reported, was about $11,000 a year, and he set it beside 'your $70,000-a-year job', the job of the American reader he had in mind.[10] A colleague, Kavita Samudra, rejected the premise of the backlash. 'Back in the US, it's all about cheap, cheap, cheap. It's not only about India being cheap. It's quality services.'[11] The answer did not dispose of the charge. Whatever the quality, the client was buying an engineer's time, and in Mumbai that time cost a fraction of the American price. That is the bargain the rest of this book follows, and the backlash was an argument about its price.

Kost was right that the rules would not stop the work, and wrong about the argument. The federal restriction applied to a narrow class of contracts, and for one year.[12] The industry it was aimed at kept growing, and the argument about which work could be sent abroad did not fade. It became sharper, and one version of it, written in 2006, still sets the terms for the last part of this book.

The decade between the dot-com bust and the end of India's software park tax holiday was the one in which the factory reached full size, a second industry of back offices and call centres grew beside it, and the financial crisis of 2008 tested the model.

## The wire test

Alan Blinder was no protectionist. He had served on the Council of Economic Advisers in 1993-94 and as vice-chairman of the Federal Reserve from 1994 to 1996.[13] In an essay in the March/April 2006 issue of *Foreign Affairs* he agreed with Mankiw's economics and disagreed with his sense of scale.[14]

He began modestly. There were no reliable national data, he wrote, but fragmentary studies suggested that 'well under a million service-sector jobs in the United States have been lost to offshoring to date', less than two weeks of normal gross job losses in the churn of the American labour market.[15] The future was another matter. Improvements in technology and communications, he argued, would bring much more offshoring of what he called 'impersonal services', which he defined as 'services that can be delivered electronically over long distances with little or no degradation in quality'.[16] He called the change 'a third Industrial Revolution'.[17]

His central claim was that the line between safe and exposed work would not follow the line between skilled and unskilled work. 'Janitors and crane operators are probably immune to foreign competition; accountants and computer programmers are not.'[18] Typing, a low-skill job, and security analysis, a high-skill one, were both already being delivered electronically from India, though on a small scale so far.[19] The telephone operator who arranged a conference call, or the clerk who took an airline booking by phone, might already be there. 'He or she may be in India already.'[20] His rough estimate of the American service jobs that could be offshored in the electronic future was two to three times the 14 million then in manufacturing, something like 28 to 42 million jobs. He thought the published estimates too low; one of them, he wrote, counted only 'the currently visible tip of the offshoring iceberg'.[21]
