The usual answer to such fears in rich countries was more education. Blinder thought that answer incomplete, because the dividing line he described was not a line of education. 'The geeks may not inherit the earth after all', he wrote, 'at least not the highly paid geeks in the rich countries.'[22] He told Americans to worry less about China, whose challenge came mainly in manufacturing, and more about India, with its already strong advantage in English.[23]

One passage in the essay matters more to this book than the rest. 'The dividing line between personal and impersonal services will move over time. As information technology improves, more and more personal services will become impersonal services.'[24] Blinder's test, put shortly, was this: if a task can be sent down a wire without losing quality, it is exposed, however skilled the person who does it. The Indian industry had grown by answering yes for a lengthening list of tasks: first code, then accounts, then the voice on the end of a telephone line. Blinder was writing about the movement of work between countries. His test does not care where the work goes, and the last chapters of this book return to it.

## Reconciliations and call centres

Software was half of the industry's story in these years. The other half was business process outsourcing (BPO): the transfer of a company's back-office work, such as accounts, claims, collections and customer calls, to another site or another firm. Its best-known Indian pioneer was Raman Roy, who helped build the Indian operations of American Express and General Electric before founding his own company. He told his story to *Knowledge at Wharton*, the University of Pennsylvania's business journal, in June 2003.[25]

At American Express's Indian division, by Roy's account, the cost per transaction turned out to be 'lower almost by 40% to 50%' than in the company's more advanced markets. Others in the company did not believe it. 'These guys in India obviously don't know how to make their reports; how could these numbers be true?'[26] Roy put the advantage down to the people. An associate doing bank reconciliations in the United States might have just completed high school and earn '$15,000 to $18,000 or perhaps $20,000'. At those salaries, he said, 'I was able to field professionals who were at least college graduates and who sometimes were CPAs', meaning certified public accountants.[27] This was the arbitrage of the software story applied to the back office: Indian graduates doing work that in rich countries was done by people with less schooling, for less money.

The savings were not only in wages. Paying suppliers faster earned American Express discounts for prompt settlement, and Roy once set those against his unit's salary bill. 'You've got us for free', he told it, 'because the incremental discounts that we got alone were more than the salary bill in India.'[28]

The obstacles were physical. When the team asked the Indian telecommunications company VSNL for 100 per cent up-time, 'they looked at us as though we were from some other world because 90% up-time was considered outstanding'.[29] Roy also described a small piece of invention. His Delhi unit reconciled about 12,000 accounts in the spreadsheet program Lotus 1-2-3, where one slip of the hand could throw an account out of balance. Rather than wait fifteen months for head office's standard platform, Roy had an interim tool built by a local firm run by his former head of technology, Sunil Gujral. When the American package proved slower than expected on test data, the Indian tool reconciled the same files: 'It took only 25% of the time to reconcile the file.' Within three months, he said, it had become American Express's global reconciliation platform.[30] Once a process had been moved and written down, the people running it began to improve it.

Roy joined GE in 1996. Its first Indian project was work GE had already sent to Mexico, and Roy had to quote a lower price than Mexico's; his finance chief told him, 'we will probably lose money on every transaction.'[31] His unit became what he called 'the Five Sigma beta site for GE Capital', a testing ground for the company's quality programme.[32] When he proposed handling live customer calls from India, a very senior executive 'pulled out his pen and crossed out the investment', saying that 'call centers would never happen out of India'. Roy borrowed equipment from vendors for three months and found a client to fund part of a trial. 'It was nationalistic pride that drove me to see that a call center came into being,' he said. By 2003 he believed that more than half of GE Capital's Indian revenue came from its call centres.[33] He went on to found Spectramind, which the Indian software company Wipro bought in 2002.[34]

Whatever the dates, the kind of worker the model sought is clear. In the same interview Roy described Indian BPO staff as 'well qualified, highly educated people' who were 'not a transient workforce'. For them, he said, 'BPO is a full-time career', and they expected employers to think seriously about their careers.[35] V. Rajaraman, the historian of Indian computing, put the requirement more plainly. The back office meant accounts receivable, payroll, account reconciliation and similar work, and starting a BPO centre needed little more than overseas clients and 'trainable human resources with good knowledge of English (which was available in reasonable numbers)'.[36] That was the employers' view of the workforce. The workers' own view is harder to find.

## The night shift

The fullest first-hand account of a call-centre floor in these years comes from an anonymous activist, recruited through a German job centre, who spent three months in 2005-06 as a foreign call-centre agent in Gurgaon (now Gurugram), a fast-growing satellite town south of Delhi, and published a report on the libcom.org website in January 2007.[37] It is a political tract, and its figures are the author's. The scholarly studies that follow set it beside other evidence.

The author worked for a research outsourcing firm whose Gurgaon office employed about 800 people, making about 100 outbound calls to companies in Europe in a ten-hour shift.[38] Gurgaon alone, the report estimated, probably had about 150,000 call-centre workers, and one building occupied by Genpact, the former GE Capital operation, held about 12,000.[39] The rules were set by the clients' world: officially, 'the only language allowed for internal communication in the call centre is English'.[40] The agents, mostly in their twenties and about half of them men, had nearly all worked in other call centres nearby.[41]

The report includes short interviews, recorded during breaks and given without names. A 22-year-old woman described her first job interview with a Gurgaon call centre in April 2004, while she was still living in Bhopal; she went to it with her mother. In the next year and a half, by her account, she worked in fourteen call centres and raised her monthly pay from Rs 8,000 to Rs 20,000 (about $180 to $440 at the 2006 average exchange rate) by changing jobs. She had worked six days a week from 2.30 in the morning to 12.30 in the afternoon, calling the United States, Canada and Britain, sometimes on automatic diallers that placed 400 to 500 calls a shift.[42] 'In call centres you mainly learn about working time and discipline,' she said, 'you are physically un-free, but mentally free.'[43]

A 21-year-old woman who had worked on GE Capital's Australian shift, with a cab collecting her at 2.30 in the morning, said she had answered about 100 calls a day and had five minutes to go to the toilet. She had to use an English name. 'I thought it would be fun, but it was more like a prison.'[44] A 22-year-old man from Calcutta (Kolkata since 2001), who described his background as Adivasi (a member of India's indigenous communities), took a technical-support job for Hewlett-Packard in a centre run by Daksh, later taken over by IBM. His training lasted two months and was mainly about using the tools. 'I brought all my software books from the course, because I thought that I would work at IBM now, but I do not need them.'[45]

The same man's basic wage was Rs 10,500 a month. He was expected to sell software and computers to the callers whose problems he had solved; by his account he sold $1,000 to $2,000 worth in a month and received Rs 1,000 to Rs 1,500 in incentives for it.[46] A 24-year-old man who had worked on Citibank's American credit-card process for an outsourcing contractor said the contractor 'made sure that they got the people with the best accent' for that work. Agents on it wore ties, started at Rs 8,500 a month and, he said, could be dismissed for leaving a desk for a minute without logging out.[47]

The report put the basic wage for new agents at about Rs 8,000 a month and the average, with incentives, at Rs 12,000 to Rs 14,000 for a week of about 50 hours on night shifts, which is roughly $265 to $310 at the 2006 average rate.[48] The cleaners and canteen staff in the same building, many of them former small farmers and carpenters from Calcutta and Bihar, were paid about Rs 2,000 a month for 60 to 70 hours a week.[49] The author's impression was that upper-caste surnames were more frequent among the agents, though caste itself was never mentioned.[50] 'Not a single call centre employee I talked to had experience with manual labour,' the report says.[51] The workers were also clear about why the jobs had come: most of those the activists spoke to said that the main reason was wages of about a fifth of those in the United States or Britain, and some said that after five years in call centres you were finished.[52]

Schooling was part of the bargain. The agents were students or former students, several of whom had learned a second foreign language because it paid better, at courses only the upper-middle class could afford.[53] The woman from Bhopal had learned French when she decided that 'only speaking English is not enough of a qualification, because so many people speak English'. She estimated that about 40 per cent of call-centre workers were studying by correspondence, and said that many gave up after a while.[54]

Sociologists recorded the employer's side of that bargain. Carol Upadhya and A.R. Vasavi of the National Institute of Advanced Studies (NIAS) in Bangalore (Bengaluru since 2014), whose fieldwork ran from 2003 to 2006 and included structured interviews with 34 BPO workers, were told by one HR officer that a candidate with a 'very good family background with high percentage of marks in their degree' would not be taken, being likely to be 'looking at call centres as a stopgap arrangement'. One of their respondents had left a postgraduate degree off his c.v. to get a call-centre job.[55] Workers on British projects at one company had to understand 'fourteen different British dialects'.[56] One respondent told them: 'Initially I felt so ashamed that I worked in a call centre that I used to tell people that I'm working for an internet service provider without mentioning any details.'[57]

The pay looked different from inside. Ernesto Noronha and Premilla D'Cruz of the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad interviewed 18 telemarketing agents in Bangalore and Mumbai for a study published in 2007, and quote them without names. One set the pay against the alternatives: 'So repeating 10 lines a day, I will get paid 10000-12000 rupees - amazing, believe me, it is amazing.' Someone working from morning to evening 'in a garment or textile shop', the agent went on, 'wouldn't have been paid even more than 3000 rupees'.[58] Another described the targets that came with the pay: 'everyone knows that for one non-performer, there are five guys outside waiting to replace him.'[59] A third, with an engineering background, had 'got into telemarketing because typical engineering jobs did not pay'.[60]

Not every agent served foreign callers. A domestic industry, much of it answering calls for mobile and other telephone companies, grew beside the export one. Phil Taylor, D'Cruz, Noronha and Dora Scholarios, who surveyed 618 of its employees in 2008, cite a 2008 estimate by the investment bank Avendus Capital of average starting salaries of $2,000 a year there, against $4,500 for agents serving international customers.[61] A team leader at a Chennai outsourcer told them: 'I cannot show that I am under pressure but I have to give this pressure to my agents'.[62]

Some agents organised. UNITES, a union for BPO employees, was formed in September 2005 with backing from the global union federation UNI, and was, in the words of Taylor and his colleagues, 'the first explicit attempt to give BPO employees an independent voice'.[63] Despite attempts in several states, it managed to register only in Karnataka.[64] In 2007 the same researchers surveyed 879 of its members in six cities, a sample of union members rather than of agents at large.[65] A voice agent at a Chennai captive centre, one owned by the client company, told them that 'a technician is supposed to take at least 50-60 calls', that breaks were stopped or postponed, and that 'Once they find that the person has shouted at the customer, he is thrown out of the job.'[66] D'Cruz and Noronha, summarising eight years of fieldwork, found employers blocking the 'bank salary accounts of those absenting themselves' and refusing relieving letters to those who quit, and members who feared 'having one's name blacklisted on NASSCOM's database'.[67]

The night shifts depended on cars. The report describes cab drivers 'tired after seventeen hours shifts' and a colleague killed in a car crash on her way home from work.[68] Transport became a public issue after December 2005, when a woman who worked the night shift for Hewlett-Packard's Bangalore operation was killed, in the words of Taylor and his colleagues, 'by a man purporting to be her driver'.[69] He was a cab driver, and he told her that the car on her usual route was not available and that she would have to travel in his.[70] A fast-track court in Bangalore convicted him in 2010, and the Karnataka High Court upheld the conviction and his life sentence in 2016. In 2023 the Supreme Court, hearing his appeal against sentence, ordered that he serve at least thirty years before he could be released.[71] Its judgment treated the case as one about the industry: 'The issue is of safety and security of women working with such companies.'[72] UNITES won its first tranche of recruits after campaigning for better regulation of transport.[69] One of Upadhya and Vasavi's informants described another risk: 'When a girl gets a drop at some odd hour in the night, neighbours switch on the lights and gaze at her with shock and make comments'.[73] The reviewer Bob Russell writes that Reena Patel's 2010 study of women in the industry found that company transport could 'extend the length of the working day by several hours', and that the mobile phone was used 'to keep track of women who work the night shift'.[74]

## Two million

The industry's own figures for 2008 come from a Nasscom presentation, and they are the claims of an interested party. The number it put first was two million, the 'professionals employed in the sector' directly in FY2007-08, roughly ten times the 200,000 software professionals it had counted, on a narrower definition, for the year to March 1998.[75] The official record of exports, the Reserve Bank of India's balance-of-payments series for software services receipts, rose from $9.6bn in FY2002-03 to $53.1bn in FY2010-11.[76] Rajaraman gives 2.4 million directly employed in IT in 2010,[77] and by the industry's count, which he relays, 166 Indian IT companies had reached level 5, the top level, of the Software Engineering Institute's Capability Maturity Model, and more than 400 of the Fortune 500 companies were clients.[78]

The work was heavily concentrated. Nasscom's map of delivery locations in 2008 gave Bangalore 36 per cent, the New Delhi, Noida and Gurgaon region 17 per cent, Chennai 15 per cent, Mumbai and Pune 15 per cent, Hyderabad 14 per cent and all other places 5 per cent, though its caption said that the industry was 'well spread across multiple locations'.[79] The United States took 61 per cent of exports in FY2006-07, Britain 18 per cent and continental Europe 12 per cent.[80]

The presentation is more revealing about strain than about scale. Its list of the questions clients asked began with attrition and wage inflation: 'is India's talent pool running dry?'[81] Under 'Pressure Points' it listed 'High lateral hiring leading to attrition', meaning the recruiting of experienced staff from rival firms, and 'Tier 3 colleges yields low', and its first point was that talent was trainable but the industry needed 'to make them employable'.[82] Its proposed remedies were an education programme in miniature: an entry-level assessment for BPO and IT recruits, 'finishing schools' to prepare graduates for work, a faculty development programme to make teachers more suitable, and government plans for 20 new Indian Institutes of Information Technology.[83] Nasscom's cost comparison for 2007 put India at about $28,000 against $100,000 for the United States, and projected that India would keep most of that advantage to 2015.[84] That gap was the bargain in a single line, and every pressure point on the list, from wage inflation to lateral hiring, was a threat to it.

The last part of the presentation dealt with a different worry. 'With increasing levels of outsourcing,' it said, 'employees were viewed as a significant weak link'. Nasscom estimated that about 30 per cent of CVs contained false claims, and it noted that India had 'No law addressing privacy or employee rights'.[85] Its answer was the National Skills Registry, a database of employees' verified education and work histories, with photographs and fingerprints, meant, in its words, to 'instill confidence in client about employees'.[86] The industry's workforce had become something its foreign customers wanted to inspect.

## The factory at full size

The largest firms show what this growth meant in practice. Infosys, whose filings with the American Securities and Exchange Commission give the most consistent figures, employed about 25,700 people at the end of March 2004.[87] Its revenue rose from $1,062.6m in FY2003-04, 98.6 per cent of it from exports, to $4,176m in FY2007-08 and $4,663m in FY2008-09.[88] By the FY2008-09 filing its training campus at Mysore (Mysuru since 2014), which Chapter 12 follows, could house 13,500 trainees and train about 40,000 a year, with 476 full-time faculty.[89] One company was running a residential college for tens of thousands of engineers a year, because, as Nasscom put it, the industry needed 'to make them employable'.[82]

## The quarter to March 2009

The financial crisis of 2008 reached the Indian firms through their largest customers, and the clearest record of it is the quarter that closed Infosys's financial year on 31 March 2009. About a third of the company's revenue, 33.9 per cent in FY2008-09, came from the financial services industry.[90] Its filing for that year described 'leading investment banks going bankrupt or being forced to sell themselves in distressed circumstances', and warned that clients might respond with 'contract terminations, deferrals of projects or delays in purchases'.[91]

In that quarter about 66.9 per cent of Infosys's technology professionals, trainees included, were billed to clients, against 70.2 per cent a year earlier.[92] Put the other way, about a third of the technical workforce was on the bench, the pool of trained staff not assigned to paying work, and was being paid without being billed. Pay stood still. 'Until 2009, when we instituted a freeze in salary increases,' the company said, it had reviewed compensation every year.[93] The gate narrowed: Infosys made about 16,900 offers in the year, against about 46,300 the year before.[94] Fewer people left, and attrition fell to 11.1 per cent.[95] Yet the filings show no mass layoffs. Infosys added about 12,400 employees, net of departures, and its headcount rose from about 91,200 in March 2008 to about 104,900 in March 2009 and 113,800 in March 2010.[96]

This was the bargain under strain. A firm that sold engineers' time had hired ahead of demand, and when demand paused it carried the unsold time on its own books rather than shed the people the next upturn would need. Part of the cost fell on the graduates who in a normal year would have been hired, and part on employees whose pay stood still. The FY2009-10 filing reported average rises that year of 8 per cent for offshore staff and 2 per cent for those working at client sites abroad, against 11-13 per cent and 4-5 per cent in FY2008-09, and the annual rise, normally made in April, was postponed to October 2009.[97]

Clients also pushed costs onto their suppliers. In response to smaller client budgets, Infosys said, it was offering more of its work at fixed prices and on fixed timetables, and such projects rose to 35.4 per cent of services revenue in FY2008-09 from 31.0 per cent the year before.[98] The same filing reported 'increased demand from our clients that all risks associated with foreign exchange fluctuations be borne by us'.[99] The filings also described clients consolidating their suppliers to cut costs, and long contracts with benchmarking provisions, under which a client could commission a study comparing the supplier's prices with those of its rivals and seek lower fees.[100]

The pattern had appeared before. In 2004, after the dot-com bust, Infosys had said that 'declines in demand, pricing pressures for our services, appreciation of the rupee against the dollar and increased wage pressures in India' had kept it from 'historical levels of profitability'.[101] On the evidence of its filings, Infosys met the second downturn by slowing hiring, carrying a larger bench, holding down pay and absorbing pressure on prices, while its headcount kept rising. By FY2010-11 utilisation including trainees was back to 72.1 per cent, and in FY2011-12 the company made about 41,460 offers.[102]

The crisis also showed how much of the model still depended on people abroad. At the end of March 2009 most of Infosys's technology professionals in the United States held either H-1B visas, about 8,200 people, or intra-company L-1 visas, about 1,400.[103] About 20,200 of its 104,900 employees worked outside India.[104] Those visa holders were the narrow top of the onsite-offshore pyramid, and the part of it most exposed to American politics (Chapter 13).

## From parks to zones

The state's support for the industry changed form in these years. The tax holiday of the 1990s had been tied to software technology parks: export profits of units in the parks were exempt from income tax. The Finance Act of 2005 introduced a separate holiday for units in designated special economic zones (SEZs) that began providing services on or after 1 April 2005. Such units could deduct all their export profits from taxable income for five years and half of them for a further five, with more relief available on conditions.[105] The Special Economic Zones Act was passed the same year.[106] Rajaraman counts 257 software and services companies set up in SEZs by 2007, and writes that many BPO centres were placed in the zones because profits earned there were tax exempt.[107]

The park holiday was extended and then allowed to end. Infosys reported that the Finance Act of 2009 extended the holiday for park units until 31 March 2011, and that for its remaining park units it would expire by the end of that fiscal year.[108] Four of its centres operated in SEZs by March 2009 and eight by March 2012, and 'many of our proposed development centers are likely to operate in SEZs'.[109] The FY2011-12 filing said that the expiry of tax holidays had already hurt its profit margin.[110]

The change favoured firms large enough to build or lease whole zones, and it moved the industry from office towers into walled campuses. It did not remove the old frustrations. Roy, who had set up centres for three companies, said in 2003 that the government promised a 'single-window clearance', but 'there are 25 single windows you need to go to'. For one new centre in Pune he counted 119 places where he had signed.[111]

By the end of the period the offshore model had largely won. The Reserve Bank's survey for 2010-11 found that about four-fifths of software and IT services export revenue, 79.3 per cent, was earned from work done in India, against 74.6 per cent in 2007-08; the United States took about 63.6 per cent.[112] The same survey put IT-enabled services (ITES) and BPO at about 26.3 per cent of these exports in 2010-11, down from 31.0 per cent the year before.[113] In the 1980s most Indian software export revenue had been earned by engineers working at clients' sites (Chapter 9). Now most of it was earned by engineers and agents in Indian cities, at desks a cab ride from home.

## The other employers

Many of the people in this chapter worked for foreign companies. Roy built his first centres inside American Express and GE, and the Gurgaon call centres in the activist's report worked for Hewlett-Packard, Citibank, American Express and Deutsche Bank, sometimes in centres those companies owned and sometimes through contractors.[114] Nasscom's own chart divided the industry between Indian providers, the captive centres of global companies and global service providers.[115] Foreign companies had also been building engineering centres of their own in India since the mid-1980s, and the next chapter follows that second profession.[116]

Blinder's test applied to all of them, whoever owned the desk. It asked only whether the work could be sent down a wire, and in these years the list of work that could be sent kept growing. Blinder did not pretend to know where it would stop. 'No one knows how far this process will go.'[117]



# Part IV: Beyond services? (1985-2024)

# Chapter 15. The other employers (1985-2024)

On 24 March 1998 Microsoft announced from its headquarters in Redmond, Washington, that it planned to open a software development centre in Hyderabad. The press release was short and hedged. The centre would open in the second half of the year, 'Subject to clearance by regulatory agencies', and an exact date was 'unavailable'.[1] It would work on one narrow problem: making Microsoft's Windows NT operating system and its BackOffice server programs work with computers that did not run Microsoft software. 'The development center initially will employ about 25 people,' the release said, in a company that then had more than 25,000 employees worldwide.[2]

Paul Maritz, the group vice-president for platforms and applications, chose his words with care. 'The majority of our development work will always be based in the United States, but we have a great deal of faith in the IT skills of India,' he said, adding that although the centre was 'initially relatively small', its work would be 'highly valued and strategically important'.[3] Moshe Dunie, a vice-president in the Windows division, called it 'an extension to our product team in Redmond'.[4] Its general manager would be Srini Koppolu, who had spent more than nine years in product development at Microsoft and would move from Redmond to Hyderabad. He would report to S. Somasegar, a director of Windows NT, who stayed at headquarters.[5] The company said the decision came at the end of 'a long evaluation process that began over a year ago', and only once it had found 'a compelling task for the center, the right location and the right management'.[6]

Twenty-five people, one task, a manager moved from the parent and a promise that most development work would stay at home: this was how a foreign product company entered India at the end of the 1990s. Earlier chapters followed the Indian services firms, which sold the hours of Indian engineers to clients abroad. Beside them, and less noticed, grew a second kind of employer: the Indian centres of foreign companies, which hired the same graduates to work on the parent's own products and systems. By 2024, on the count of the National Association of Software and Service Companies (Nasscom), the industry's lobby group, and Zinnov, a consultancy that sells advice to such centres, they employed about 1.9 million people.[7] They began with a satellite dish in Bangalore (Bengaluru since 2014) and ended as the 'global capability centres' of the 2020s. The question is what kind of profession they offered.

## A dish on the roof

The first of them had arrived thirteen years before Microsoft. Texas Instruments (TI), the American chip maker, dates its start in India to 1985, and in a list of milestones published for its twentieth anniversary there it calls itself the first multinational to set up a software design centre in the country. Chapter 8 tells how TI won its satellite link, by working around a long list of government rules, and weighs that claim.[8]

What mattered to the engineers TI hired was the kind of work. None of it was billed by the hour. Within four years of arriving, TI India had a design centre for mixed-signal integrated circuits, chips that handle both analogue and digital signals, and over the next fifteen years it added work on disk-drive and wireless chips before moving, in 2004, into a seven-acre design facility in Bangalore.[9] It was engineering for TI's own products, done by TI's own employees, in India. At the twentieth-anniversary event in August 2005 TI's chairman, Tom Engibous, showed two mobile handsets that the company said were the first designed entirely in India, one developed with the Indian manufacturer BPL.[10]

Hewlett-Packard (HP) came through a returning engineer, Radha Basu, who in the account of the Berkeley scholar of regional development AnnaLee Saxenian spent four years building HP's software centre in Bangalore and left it with 400 people in 1989.[11] Saxenian adds that Indians educated in the United States were 'pivotal' in setting up the Indian facilities of Oracle, Novell, Bay Networks and other Silicon Valley companies.[12] Motorola later claimed that its Indian centre had become, in 1993, the first commercial organisation in the world assessed at Level 5 of the Capability Maturity Model, a scale of software process discipline; Chapter 11 examines the claim.[13] Oracle opened a software development centre in Bangalore in 1994, on the dating of V. Rajaraman, the historian of Indian computing, and SAP (1998) and Intel (1999) are also reported to have opened development centres in India in that decade.[14]

Back offices came at the same time. Raman Roy, later called the father of Indian business process outsourcing, helped American Express and then, from 1996, GE to set up what an interviewer called 'captive shared-service centers' in India: units owned by the parent and working only for it.[15] Rajaraman counts American Express as the first to start back-office work for export in India, in 1994, followed by GE Capital International Services in 1997.[16] The word 'captive' stuck, and it describes the first wave well. These centres were owned by their clients. They did not compete for contracts.

Whether the work in these centres matched the work at headquarters is harder to show. Saxenian, writing in 2001, quoted the chief executive of one American company's offshore development centre in Bangalore, interviewed by another researcher in July 1996. He explained why his company had waited until the 1990s. Earlier, he said, he would have advised 'do anything, bodyshopping, subcontracting, modular work, but don't give full dependability here [in India] because nobody's ever done it.' By the mid-1990s new products and new versions of old products came from Bangalore. 'Technologically, there's zero difference,' he said.[17] It is a manager's claim, reported second-hand, and Saxenian called the evidence for such upgrading 'anecdotal'.[18] But it marks the ambition. Microsoft's Maritz, two years later, was more cautious about where the important work would be done.

## The captive that became a vendor

The most revealing case of the first wave is a company usually counted among the services firms. Cognizant Technology Solutions went public on the Nasdaq stock market in June 1998. Its prospectus opened its corporate history with a plain sentence: 'The Company began its software development and maintenance services business in early 1994 as an in-house technology development center for The Dun & Bradstreet Corporation and its operating units.'[19] Those units included the market researcher A.C. Nielsen and Dun & Bradstreet's own information and software businesses. In November 1996 Dun & Bradstreet spun off a group of businesses, this one among them, to form a new parent company, Cognizant Corporation. During 1996 the development centre also set out to win clients outside the group.[20] The captive had become a vendor.

The prospectus shows who ran it. Its chairman and chief executive, Wijeyaraj (Kumar) Mahadeva, had been Dun & Bradstreet's vice-president for corporate strategy and, from 1993 to 1996, chairman of Dun & Bradstreet in India and China; he had led the team that set up the Indian business in 1994. He held a Harvard MBA and a master's degree in electrical engineering from Cambridge.[21] Its president, Lakshmi Narayanan, had joined the Indian subsidiary as chief technology officer in 1994 after nineteen years at Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), where he had been a regional head.[22] TCS had trained the man who ran the American captive's Indian arm.

The prospectus also shows where the work was done and by whom. At 31 March 1998 Cognizant had about 270 people in North America, at its offices and on clients' sites, of whom only fifteen were 'United States citizens or permanent residents'. It had about 30 in Europe, and 'approximately 870 persons on a full-time basis in its offshore software development centers in India'. Some 245 of its employees in the United States, 93 per cent of them, held H-1B temporary work visas.[23] About 74 per cent of its technical professionals were in India.[24] Its development centres, all in leased buildings, were in Chennai and Calcutta (Kolkata since 2001); its executive office in New York occupied 3,800 square feet.[25] Cognizant explained its model in words any Indian firm might have used: basing technical work in India gave it 'access to a large pool of skilled, English-speaking IT professionals with which to service customers on a cost basis significantly lower than in developed countries'.[26] It also warned investors that 'wages in India are increasing at a faster rate than in the United States'.[27]

The prospectus describes recruitment and training in detail, and it is one of the clearer records of how a foreign-owned employer turned Indian graduates into programmers in the 1990s. Each year the company visited 'approximately 45 premier colleges and technical schools in India'. It judged candidates on academic results, 'a written aptitude test measuring problem-solving skills' and a technical interview, and it also hired experienced staff from other firms.[28] New recruits went through 'an intensive orientation and training program' that taught them the company's own software engineering method, which it called QVIEW.[29] By 2002 Cognizant said it gave newly hired programmers 'five months of combined classroom and on-the-job training'.[30] The degree got a graduate through the door. The employer taught the trade.

Cognizant then grew like the firms it was compared with. At the end of 2002 it had about 1,425 people in North America, 240 in Europe and 'approximately 4,500 persons' in its Indian development centres.[31] At the end of 2007 it had more than 55,400 staff worldwide, 'a majority' of its technical professionals in India.[32] At the end of 2012 it had about 156,700, of whom about 124,100 were in the Asia Pacific region.[33] In 2012 more American H-1B work visas were approved for Cognizant, 9,281, than for any other firm in a ranking two economists compiled from US immigration data.[34]

The lesson is that the line between a foreign company's captive and an 'Indian' services firm was never fixed. A captive could be spun out to sell to others, as Cognizant was. A services firm could be bought by a multinational: IBM acquired the Indian outsourcing firm Daksh.[35] What stayed constant was the work, done by engineers in India for clients or parents abroad.

## A mirror in Bangalore

Product companies came for engineers, not for services. On 13 October 2004 Google's founders, Larry Page and Sergey Brin, spoke to reporters in Bangalore, the third stop of a visit that had taken them to New Delhi and Hyderabad. Google had opened offices in Bangalore and Hyderabad earlier that year.[36] 'One approach we are taking is that Bangalore is where we run a mirror exactly of what we have in the United States in terms of development,' Brin said.[37] Researchers in Bangalore would work with their American colleagues to devise new services and write the software, including search by speech, search in more languages, personalised search and features for the Gmail service.[38] Brin said Google had been 'too late' in tapping Indian talent: 'We would have preferred to do it sooner.'[39]

The man doing the hiring was Krishna Bharat, the engineer who had created Google's news service. 'We don't have a cap (on how many to hire),' he said, in the Associated Press report. 'We will take in as many people as we can, if they meet our global standards.'[40] The phrase 'global standards' marks the difference from Microsoft's careful start six years earlier. Google did not describe its Bangalore office as a satellite with a defined task. It described it, in development at least, as a mirror of the parent.

## January 2007

Two reports three days apart, at the turn of January and February 2007, showed how far the multinationals had come. On 29 January Accenture's chairman and chief executive, William D. Green, told reporters in Bangalore that the consultancy would have 35,000 staff in India by the end of August, up 52 per cent on a year earlier. That would give it more employees in India than in the United States, where it would have just over 30,000.[41] The reporter, John Ribeiro, noted that multinational services companies including IBM, EDS and Capgemini were expanding fast in India, 'helping push up wages and attrition rates' among software and back-office staff.[42]

Three days later *InformationWeek* reported that IBM's 'Indian workforce now stands at 53,000, up from 39,000 a year ago and 23,000 two years ago'. If that rate continued, IBM would have more than 70,000 people in India during 2007, 'almost 25% of its current worldwide workforce of 300,000'.[43] 'IBM workers in India are engaged in everything from routine coding to high-end system design,' the article said; a year earlier the company had decided to consolidate all its development of software for service-oriented architectures, a way of building large systems out of networked services, in Bangalore.[44] India was also IBM's fastest-growing market, with sales up 37 per cent in 2006.[45] For a company that had shut its Indian operations in 1978, the return was complete.[46]

Accenture and IBM were not captives. They were services firms that happened to be American, and their Indian centres did the same kind of work as the Indian firms, for the same kind of clients. They belong in this chapter for another reason. They competed for the same engineers, and by 2007 each employed tens of thousands of people in India. For an engineer leaving college in 2007, 'working for a foreign company' could mean a chip-design team at TI, a product team at Google or Microsoft, a back-office captive at a bank, or a delivery centre at IBM or Accenture. The employers were foreign. The work ranged from research to routine maintenance.

## Counting the centres

The first aggregate count of foreign companies' research and development centres came from Zinnov. In early 2008, according to a summary in the trade paper *EE Times*, it reported about 594 multinational R&D centres in India employing about 146,760 people, more than half of them (312) in Bangalore. It counted 93 new centres opened in 2004 and only 24 in 2007, amid rising costs and attrition of 8 to 20 per cent a year.[47]

Two scholars, Sarosh Kuruvilla and Aruna Ranganathan, who studied the Indian outsourcing industry from fieldwork in 2004-07, give a clearer view of the labour market. On Nasscom's figures, the number of software professionals employed in India rose from 297,000 in 2005 to about 562,000 in 2007.[48] Turnover in 2007 was about 20 per cent a year in software and 50-60 per cent in back-office work.[49] The authors named the multinationals as one cause: 'the entry and expansion of large MNCs such as IBM, Oracle, and Accenture into India have resulted in considerable "poaching" of developers, project managers, and high-level executives'.[50] Their own judgement, which they said rested on no systematic study, was that the main reason software engineers left was not pay but 'the lack of opportunities to work on cutting-edge technology'.[51] That is exactly what the product companies' centres claimed to offer.

In 2004, on a Nasscom survey they cite, the average software professional was about 28 years old, three in four were men, and 69 per cent were engineers.[52] Median pay that year, from a Nasscom-Hewitt survey, was about $6,560 for a software engineer and $30,816 for a project manager, with no separate figure for the multinational centres.[53] At that price the engineer's hour, which the services firms sold and the multinationals' centres used, was cheap. If more than two-thirds of software professionals were engineers, the industry, foreign centres included, was drawing most of its staff from the engineering colleges. The multinationals had come, in Rajaraman's account, 'to take advantage of the availability of high quality computer science graduates at reasonable cost'.[54] Kuruvilla and Ranganathan doubted that the colleges could keep up. Citing an estimate of 2006, they wrote that third-tier colleges produced 88 per cent of India's engineering undergraduates.[55] A manager at a well-known Wall Street firm with its own software support unit in India told them: 'we are really scraping the bottom of the barrel now and are hiring engineers from third and fourth tier schools who have very little engineering knowledge at all'.[56] The employers answered with training, like Cognizant's five months for new programmers, and by hiring experienced staff away from one another. Infosys told American investors in its annual report for the year to March 2009 that it had long faced strong competition for employees from the multinationals setting up in India.[57]

## Captives and careers

Did the other employers offer a different career? The executives' statements describe product work: Brin's 'mirror', TI's chip design, IBM's 'high-end system design'.[58] TI reports that the Indian business magazine *Businessworld* named TI India the 'Best Company to Work for in India' in 2003 and second best in 2004.[59] These are employers describing themselves.

The one comparative study concerns back offices, not engineering. Kuruvilla and Ranganathan distinguished 'captives', 'BPO firms owned by U.S. client firms such as Dell, EDS, and HP that service only their owners', from 'third-party firms' that served many clients, and noted that consolidation was 'eroding the distinction'.[60] They found turnover of 15 to 20 per cent a year in five captive firms, 'although even some captives reported rates as high as 30%'. A survey of seven large third-party call centres found an average of 30 per cent, ranging from 12 to 62 per cent.[61] Their conclusion: 'captive call centers are able to provide more promotions to higher levels than "third-party" call centers, because the market stability they enjoy fosters longer career paths'.[62] A captive's work did not depend on winning the next contract. That stability, on this evidence, made room for a ladder. A pay premium at the multinational development centres is often asserted, but no published comparison of their pay with that of the Indian services firms has been located.[63]

## Sidebar: Why did Eastern Europe become a nearshore rival, and why couldn't it scale?

In January 2007, on the same day he announced that Accenture would soon have more staff in India than in America, William Green looked at the alternatives. 'There will not be another phenomenon like India,' he said, and he expected no other country to overtake India in Accenture's headcount for at least ten years.[64] His colleague Basilio Rueda, a senior managing director of the firm's Global Delivery Network, explained why. Accenture had opened service centres in Eastern European cities such as Prague and Bucharest, but, he said, it was not possible to increase the staff there easily, and the cost of staff was far higher than in India. The Eastern European centres were 'near-shore' locations, chosen to serve European clients from close by with cultural affinity.[65]

The firm that tested the nearshore model most fully was EPAM Systems, a services company listed in New York whose engineers worked mainly in the former Soviet bloc. In its annual report for 2021 EPAM wrote: 'Our largest delivery centers are located in Ukraine, Belarus and Russia'. At the end of that year it had 12,389 delivery professionals in Ukraine, 9,416 in Belarus and 8,933 in Russia, out of 52,617. India came next, with 4,349, followed by Poland, the United States, Hungary and Mexico.[66] EPAM said these countries were well placed for the work, in terms an Indian firm would have recognised: a supply of qualified software engineers, 'established educational infrastructure', an industrial base and government tax incentives.[67]

Then, on 24 February 2022, Russian forces attacked Ukraine.[68] EPAM's annual report for 2024 records the cost. Business continuity plans, relocation, the company's 'humanitarian commitment to our people in Ukraine' and 'the cost of our phased exit from Russia' had 'resulted in materially increased expenses'.[69] The company sold its remaining holdings in Russia on 26 July 2023.[70] And it reported a new fact about itself: 'During 2024, India became our largest delivery location, measured by the number of delivery professionals'. It had 10,072 there at the end of 2024, having added 3,006 during the year. Ukraine, with 8,764, down from 9,113 a year earlier, remained 'a significant delivery location'. EPAM's delivery staff as a whole numbered about 55,100.[71]

What do these figures show? They do not show that Eastern Europe failed a market test. A war is not a market. EPAM's Ukrainian engineers kept working through it, and the company said its operations there had not been significantly affected.[72] They show something narrower. Before 2022, a firm built on Eastern European engineers had about 30,000 of them in three neighbouring countries. When those countries became a risk, the company turned to India to grow, and more than doubled its Indian delivery staff in three years, to the point where India overtook Ukraine. Rueda's remark of 2007 points to one reason: staff numbers in Prague or Bucharest could not be raised easily, and staff there cost far more.[73] The comparison rests on one firm's executives and another firm's filings.[74]

## A new name

In August 2019 Amazon opened a campus in Hyderabad that it described as 'our first owned campus outside USA and the single largest building in terms of area and head count for Amazon globally'. The company's vice-president for global real estate and facilities, John Schoettler, wrote on its Indian blog that the building had '15,000 work points across 1.8 million square feet' of office space, three amenity floors and twelve office floors, and lifts able to move 972 people at once.[75] The largest building of one of the world's largest companies was not in Seattle. It was in the city where Microsoft had started with twenty-five people.

By then the industry had a new name for such places. A 'global capability centre', or GCC, is a foreign company's own unit in India, whether it writes software, designs chips, runs finance and human resources, or analyses data. The term covers the old development centres and the old captives alike. In September 2024 Nasscom and Zinnov published a report on them. As Reuters summarised it, about 1,700 companies had GCCs in India, employing 1.9 million people, and the centres' market size was $64.6 billion in the year to March 2024. The 'revenue' of a GCC needs care. Reuters described the centres as supporting their parent organisations; they do not sell on the open market, so the figure is best read as a measure of the work they do for their parents, not of sales won.[76] Zinnov's own summary counted more than 2,975 separate units, over 400 new centres in five years, and claimed that leading multinationals now did nearly a third of their global engineering in India.[77]

The report also made projections. By 2030, it said, between 2,100 and 2,200 companies would have GCCs in India, employing between 2.5 and 2.8 million people, and the market would be worth $99-105 billion.[78] Those are forecasts by interested parties. A later edition counted 2,117 GCCs employing 2.36 million people in the year to March 2026, with revenue of about $98.4 billion (industry figures, as reported by *Business Today*), close to the figure the 2024 report had projected for 2030.[79]

The 1.9 million needs a denominator. Nasscom, in its review of February 2025, restated the size of the whole Indian technology industry after counting GCCs more fully: about 5.67 million employees in the year to March 2024. It said that the industry's export revenue was now split equally between 'Global MNCs (including GCCs)' and Indian service providers.[80] On these figures, roughly a third of India's technology workforce in 2024 worked for the other employers' own centres, an order of magnitude on the industry's own definition.

The work itself was said to be changing. Zinnov's summary claimed more than 500 centres with artificial intelligence and machine-learning capabilities, 185 of them with dedicated centres for the work, a pool of more than 120,000 people working on AI, and about 6,500 senior 'global roles' held in India, including more than 1,100 held by women.[81] It also pointed to smaller cities, where costs could be 25-30 per cent lower.[82] State governments competed for the centres. Karnataka's GCC policy for 2024-29, as Zinnov summarised it, aimed to double the number of GCCs in the state to 1,000 and to create 350,000 jobs by 2029.[83] The Union Budget of February 2025 announced that a national framework would be drawn up to guide states in promoting GCCs in smaller, 'tier 2' cities.[84]

None of this made the GCC new. The institution goes back to TI's dish in 1985, to HP's 400 people in 1989, to the captives of American Express and GE, and to the 594 R&D centres Zinnov counted in 2008.[85] Cognizant itself began as one. What changed by 2024 was the name, the scale, the spread from software and internet companies to banks and insurers, with retailers, health-care and drug companies expected next, and the claim that senior roles, not only tasks, were now based in India.[86]

## The circle closes

The last document in this chapter is a services firm's annual report. At the end of 2024 Cognizant had 'approximately 336,800 employees', of whom 241,500 were in India and 42,800 in North America; women made up about 38 per cent of the workforce.[87] Seventy-two per cent of the staff of a company that had gone public in 1998 with an executive office in New York of 3,800 square feet now worked in India.[88] Accenture, IBM and EPAM had gone the same way, each in its own measure.[89]

Among its competitors Cognizant now listed, beside Accenture, Infosys, TCS and Wipro, 'clients' in-house technology resources, such as GCCs'.[90] Its risk factors were sharper. 'We face competition from clients' in-house technology resources, such as GCCs, which may provide a lower cost alternative to our services,' it told investors. And for staff: 'We compete for employees not only with other companies in our industry but also with companies in other industries, such as software services, engineering services and financial services companies, as well as our clients' GCCs.'[91]

A company that began in 1994 as one American firm's captive centre in India now named other firms' captive centres as a threat to its business and to its hiring.[92] Clients that had once sent work to Indian vendors were building their own Indian teams, staffed by the same graduates from the same colleges.

This matters for the argument of the rest of the book. A services firm sells its engineers' hours, and the price of an hour is set in a contract with a client. A GCC employs engineers to build and run its parent's own products and systems, and any gain in their output belongs directly to the parent. When tools arrive that let one engineer do the work of several, the two kinds of employer face different questions. The services firm must decide who keeps the saving, and the client will ask for it. The GCC's parent simply keeps it. Chapter 19 returns to that difference.

The multinational centres showed that Indian engineers could do a parent's core work, not only its maintenance; who would answer for the work when it went wrong, a question of trust and governance, is where the next chapter begins, inside the services industry itself and inside the state.


# Chapter 16. Fraud and foundation (2008-2018)

On 7 January 2009 the board of Satyam Computer Services, a software company with its headquarters in Hyderabad, received a letter from its chairman and founder, B. Ramalinga Raju. It began: 'It is with deep regret, and tremendous burden that I am carrying on my conscience, that I would like to bring the following facts to your notice.' The first fact was that the company's balance sheet at 30 September 2008 carried 'Inflated (non-existent) cash and bank balances of Rs.5,040 crore (as against Rs. 5361 crore reflected in the books).'[1] Rs 5,040 crore is Rs 50.4 billion, or about $1.16 billion at the 2008 average exchange rate. On Raju's own account, nearly all the cash the company said it held did not exist.[2]

Copies went to the chairman of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), the market regulator, and to the stock exchanges. Satyam filed the letter the same day with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), because its shares also traded in New York.[3] By the end of that day, according to the order of the Company Law Board two days later, the share price had fallen from Rs 188 to Rs 38.40.[4]

Satyam was not a marginal firm. Its own filings called it the fourth-largest Indian IT services company by export revenue.[5] Its engineers were recruited, trained and deployed in much the same way as those of Infosys, Wipro and Tata Consultancy Services (TCS). The fraud therefore put a question to the whole industry this book describes. If the books of one of its four largest firms could be false for years, what exactly had clients, investors and graduates been buying? The answer that emerged over the next three months was that the work was real and the accounts were not.

The same month, in an unrelated decision, the government of India created an agency to give every resident a unique identity number. Within six months it had hired an Infosys co-founder to run it.[6] Satyam showed what happened when a software company's governance failed. Aadhaar, the identity system, showed what happened when the state borrowed the industry's people and methods for a project of its own, and when the Supreme Court then had to decide what that system could be made to do to Indian citizens.

## The company on paper

The last annual report Satyam filed before the letter was its Form 20-F for the year to March 2008, lodged with the SEC that summer. It described a business growing very fast. 'As of March 31, 2008, we had 50,570 employees, whom we refer to as associates, worldwide as compared to 39,018 associates as of March 31, 2007.'[7] Revenue for the year was reported as $2,138.1 million, and the company said its revenue had grown at a compound rate of 39.1 per cent a year over three years.[8] It had 654 active customers, 'including 185 Fortune Global 500 or Fortune U.S. 500 companies'.[9]

The 20-F is also a record of how such a company made engineers. 'We recruit graduates from the engineering departments of India's leading universities, engineering and technical colleges and management institutes,' it said. It counted 'over 1,500 such institutions' in India, and described a selection process 'involving a series of tests and interviews'.[10] Each new technical recruit, the filing said, went through 'an intensive 12 week initial training program' and then at least 40 hours of training a year.[11] The company reported that 47,405 of its associates were technical staff in IT services, and that 9,941 of them were working onsite, at clients' premises abroad.[12] Attrition in IT services, the share of staff who left in a year, had been 13.1 per cent in the year to March 2008. 'None of our associates are represented by a union,' the filing said.[13]

That was the profession Satyam offered: a campus test, three months of company schooling, a project, perhaps a posting abroad. Nothing in it was unusual for the industry in 2008.

The financial pages were where the fiction lay, though no outside reader could see it. The 20-F reported 'cash and cash equivalents of $290.5 million' at 31 March 2008. It explained that cash used in investing in the year to March 2007 had risen 'primarily due to investment in bank deposits amounting to $745.6 million'.[14] Raju's letter, written five months after the filing, said that cash and bank balances of Rs 5,361 crore in the books included Rs 5,040 crore that did not exist.[15] A company growing at nearly 40 per cent a year, adding more than 11,000 people to its payroll in a year did not look strange from outside. That was the difficulty.

## Riding a tiger

The letter, as filed with the SEC, runs to about two pages.[16] After the cash, Raju listed 'An accrued interest of Rs. 376 crore which is non-existent', 'An understated liability of Rs. 1,230 crore on account of funds arranged by me', and debtors (money owed by customers) overstated by Rs 490 crore.[17] For the quarter to September 2008, he wrote, the company had reported revenue of Rs 2,700 crore and an operating margin of Rs 649 crore, or 24 per cent of revenue. The actual figures were revenue of Rs 2,112 crore and an operating margin of Rs 61 crore, 3 per cent of revenue. In that quarter alone, he said, the false cash and bank balances had grown by Rs 588 crore.[18]

He explained how it had happened. 'What started as a marginal gap between actual operating profit and the one reflected in the books of accounts continued to grow over the years. It has attained unmanageable proportions as the size of company operations grew significantly.' The company, he wrote, had to carry extra staff and assets to justify the higher level of operations it was reporting, which raised its costs further. Every attempt to close the gap had failed. Because the promoters (the founding family) held only a small share of the equity, he feared that poor results would bring a takeover that would expose the gap.[19] Then he wrote: 'It was like riding a tiger, not knowing how to get off without being eaten.'[20]

The letter named the event that had brought the crisis into the open. According to the government's petition, as the Company Law Board summarised it, Satyam's board had recently approved a proposal to buy stakes, at huge cost, in two companies controlled by Raju's near relations; the Board itself recorded that four independent directors had resigned once the decision became public.[21] Raju called the 'aborted Maytas acquisition deal' 'the last attempt to fill the fictitious assets with real ones'.[22]

Much of the letter is Raju's defence of himself. He claimed that neither he nor the managing director, his brother B. Rama Raju, had sold shares in eight years except a small number for charity. He wrote that 'Every attempt was made to keep the wheel moving and to ensure prompt payment of salaries to the associates.' He claimed that 'neither me, nor the Managing Director took even one rupee/dollar from the company', and that none of the board members, past or present, had known. He listed seventeen senior executives who, he said, were also unaware.[23] These are the claims of the man who had confessed. SEBI later held him, his brother and three officials liable for fraud and insider trading, and an appeals tribunal upheld those findings in 2017.[24]

He closed with what he had built. 'I have seen it grow from few people to 53,000 people, with 185 Fortune 500 companies as customers and operations in 66 countries.' And: 'I sincerely apologize to all Satyamites and stakeholders'.[25] He recommended that the bank Merrill Lynch 'can be entrusted with the task of quickly exploring some Merger opportunities'.[26]

## Two days in January

Merrill Lynch had already gone. The same SEC filing carried a letter from Kevan Watts, president of DSP Merrill Lynch, to the chairman of SEBI, dated 7 January. It said the bank had ended its advisory engagement with Satyam the day before. 'In the course of such engagement, we came to understand that there were material accounting irregularities, which prompted our aforesaid decision.'[27] An outside adviser had seen enough to walk away a day before the chairman confessed.

Satyam's own press release that day said its priorities included protecting 'the careers and security of its approximately 53,000 associates'.[28] SEBI appointed an investigating authority the same day to examine dealings in Satyam's shares, including possible fraud and insider trading.[29]

The state then moved quickly. On 8 January the Registrar of Companies for Andhra Pradesh petitioned the Special Judge for Economic Offences in Hyderabad for permission to search Satyam's offices and seize its books, papers and computer records. The judge's order records that the petition was filed 'at 04.30 PM at my residence'. The Registrar, the order says, apprehended that the company appeared to have shown 'artificial and inflated profits for the last several years'. The judge found a prima facie case and allowed the search.[30]

On 9 January the Union of India petitioned the Company Law Board in New Delhi to remove the directors. The petition, as the Board summarised it, described a listed company with about 300,000 shareholders and more than 53,000 employees, the fourth-largest IT company in India, which had 'received a number of awards for best corporate governance'.[31] The Board noted that the promoter group now held less than 4 per cent of the shares and financial institutions about 60 per cent. Its chairman, S. Balasubramanian, wrote that Raju's written admission established 'beyond any shadow of doubt' that there had been 'financial impropriety and jugglery of financial statements'. 'It appears that a serious fraud has been perpetrated on the society as a whole.'[32] He suspended the board with immediate effect and authorised the central government to appoint up to ten 'persons of eminence' as directors.[33]

Two years later the SEC summarised the order bluntly: 'the India government seized control of the company by dissolving its board of directors and appointing new government-nominated directors'.[34]

## The people who did the work

For the engineers, the first question was whether they would be paid. *Business Today*, a business magazine, sent reporters to Satyam's staff in the weeks after the letter and published their accounts in its issue of 8 February 2009.[35] A week after Raju's arrest, the magazine reported, a European client had decided to move a project, with the team working on it, to another Indian vendor. Satyam staff in Europe told the magazine that '95 per cent of the team had agreed to join the competing vendor'.[36]

The rest of the industry did not rush to hire them. T. Sreedhar, managing director of TMI Network, a recruitment firm in Hyderabad, said his office was overrun by Satyam employees. They were, he said, 'stuck between the devil and the deep sea. They cannot quit the job because there is no option being made available by the large companies (who have chosen not to hire them)'. If they stayed, he added, they could not be sure of being paid that month.[37] The magazine reported that Nasscom (the National Association of Software and Service Companies), the industry's lobby group, and Infosys had issued statements against recruiting Satyam's people, 'not because they are tainted but to ensure that the company doesn't suffer because of an exodus'.[38] Rishi Das, chief executive of another recruiter, CareerNet Consulting, estimated that about 35,000 Satyam employees, 70 per cent of the workforce, were already looking for jobs with rivals. That was a recruiter's estimate, not a count.[39]

Some staff were tied in. Insiders told the magazine that about 7,000 employees had been required to give 'Rs 2 lakh bonds' (Rs 200,000) as a deposit under two-year contracts, which they would forfeit if they left.[40] The newest recruits were the most exposed. In 2007, the magazine said, Satyam had issued about 6,000 offer letters on campuses across the country. 'Those offers are not worth the paper they are written on.'[41]

The magazine printed five short first-person accounts, each 'as told to' one of its reporters. N. Kavitha, 22, had studied engineering at the Muthukumaran Institute of Technology near Mangadu, a suburb of Chennai, and had been selected by Satyam in a campus placement in 2007-08. 'I was told that I would get a joining letter by September 2008. This did not happen. The company HR said that I could definitely expect to join in January 2009.' Now, she said, she had lost hope of getting it. But she would still join if it came. 'In this recession, a fresher needs to grab any opportunity. I am not worried too much about Satyam's reputation in the market; I want the work experience first.'[42] Her position was close to the one Chapter 14 traces in the collapse of campus offers in 2009: a campus offer was a promise, not a job, and the graduate carried the risk when the company's plans changed.

S. Mastanamma, 24, had worked at Satyam's Chennai centre for two years after graduating from Newton's College of Engineering in Guntur, Andhra Pradesh. 'I am very positive about the company's future,' she said. She praised the project-level leadership, the employee portal and the training, and said human resources had opened a round-the-clock helpline for staff. 'I am not worried about lay-offs. The existing clients have to be serviced and the new board at Satyam is saying that people are needed to continue to service the clients.'[43]

A consultant in Europe, two years with the firm, who was not named, said the client had arranged to move the whole project team to another vendor. 'We, as employees, are very clear we want to save our livelihoods.' As an employer, the consultant said, Satyam had paid well. 'Raju was always elusive, I have never seen or heard from him in the two years I have been with the firm', except for one mail defending the Maytas deal.[44] A retail consultant five months into the job, also unnamed, said: 'There is a bit of uncertainty in every job.'[45]

In a bracketed note of its own in its issue of 22 February 2009, the magazine reported that employees had started to have their pay credited to their accounts.[46] When the board held a press conference in April, the company said that on 20 March 2009, by its internal data, it had about 42,000 employees on a stand-alone basis (the parent company without its subsidiaries).[47]

## Rs 58 a share

The government's nominees took over a company whose clients were still being served and whose cash was gone. The new directors included Kiran Karnik, who became chairman, and Deepak Parekh.[48] With Goldman Sachs and Avendus Capital as financial advisers, the board ran an auction under the supervision of Justice S.P. Bharucha. Bidders were judged first on technical criteria, including their record in corporate governance and in managing distressed companies, and then on price.[49] On 13 April 2009 the financial bids were opened. They were 'Rs. 58 (Tech Mahindra), Rs. 45.90 (Larsen & Toubro Limited) and Rs. 20 (consortium of WL Ross funds) per share'.[50]

Venturbay Consultants, a company controlled by Tech Mahindra, agreed to buy 31 per cent of the enlarged share capital at Rs 58 a share, putting Rs 1,756 crore into Satyam, which the company converted at about $351 million at a rate of Rs 50 to the dollar. It would then have to offer to buy at least a further 20 per cent from other shareholders.[51] Karnik said the result 'signals a new stage for the Company in its progress towards stabilization and growth'. He hoped it would reassure customers, 'who continue to be happy with Satyam's excellent service delivery'.[52] That was a claim by the chairman of a company being sold, but the bids themselves were evidence of a kind. The process, the company noted, 'has reached this significant stage within three months of the new Board's first meeting'.[53]

The speed of the sale says something about what an Indian services firm was. Its accounts had been falsified for years and its founder had been arrested. Yet within three months two large Indian companies offered real money for control of it. The board told the press that Satyam held about 450 acres of land and that two Hyderabad campuses had been valued at an average of Rs 1,700 crore.[54] But it was the engineers who kept the clients, and the clients who made the company worth buying.

## The auditors

Satyam's auditors were Indian affiliates of PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), and the 20-F carried the consent of Price Waterhouse as its independent registered public accounting firm.[55] In April 2011 the SEC set out what it found they had done. Five Indian affiliates, which it called PW India, had 'repeatedly' conducted deficient audits of Satyam and enabled 'a massive accounting fraud to go undetected for several years'.[56] They agreed to settle and pay 'a $6 million penalty, the largest ever by a foreign-based accounting firm in an SEC enforcement action'. They also agreed not to take new American clients for six months, to train their staff, to revise their audit procedures and to appoint an independent monitor.[57]

The core finding was simple. When an auditor wants to know whether a company really holds the cash it reports, it writes to the banks and asks them to confirm the balances directly to the auditor. According to the SEC's order, PW India staff 'failed to conduct procedures to confirm Satyam's cash and cash equivalent balances or its accounts receivables'. They 'routinely relinquished control of the delivery and receipt of cash confirmations entirely to their audit clients and rarely, if ever, questioned the integrity of the confirmation responses they received from the client by following up with the banks'.[58] The SEC found that this was not limited to Satyam but was 'indicative of a much larger quality control failure throughout PW India'.[59] Robert Khuzami, the SEC's director of enforcement, said: 'PW India violated its most fundamental duty as a public watchdog'.[60]

These were findings in a settled case, not the verdict of a trial. The same day, Satyam itself, now under new management, agreed to settle the SEC's fraud charges, pay a $10 million penalty and carry out internal reforms.[61]

SEBI's own case against the auditors took nine years. In January 2018 it barred the firms practising under the Price Waterhouse name from certifying the accounts of listed companies for two years, and the two engagement partners on Satyam, S. Gopalakrishnan and Srinivas Talluri, for three. It ordered the partners and the Bangalore firm to disgorge Rs 13.09 crore in fees, with interest.[62] On 9 September 2019 the Securities Appellate Tribunal quashed the bans. 'In the instant case, mens rea was not proved,' it held. 'There is no finding that the auditors or the audit firms had knowledge or had intention to connive or collude with the management in the fabrication of the books of account of the company.' It did find a professional lapse, above all the failure to seek direct confirmation of bank balances, which 'amounted to negligence', and it upheld the disgorgement.[63] SEBI appealed. In November 2019 the Supreme Court issued notice and stayed the part of the ruling that limited SEBI's power to bar auditors; no decision on that appeal has been found.[64] The tribunal was ruling on SEBI's powers under the securities laws; the criminal charges against the two partners were a matter for the criminal courts.

## Findings and punishment

The Indian regulators moved more slowly. SEBI passed a final order on 15 July 2014 against Ramalinga Raju, Rama Raju and three officials: V. Srinivas, the former chief financial officer; G. Ramakrishna, a vice-president of finance; and V.S. Prabhakara Gupta, the head of internal audit. It held them liable for fraud and insider trading and barred them from the securities market for fourteen years.[65] On 12 May 2017 the Securities Appellate Tribunal upheld SEBI's findings on the merits but sent back the amounts and the length of the bars.[66] Its summary of SEBI's investigation is the clearest statement in the record of how the fraud worked: 'Investigation carried out by SEBI revealed that Ramalinga Raju as Chairman and Rama Raju as, MD of Satyam were instrumental in creating fictitious invoices, fictitious receipts etc. on the basis of which fictitious monthly bank statements were prepared'.[67]

SEBI's fresh order on the officials, in October 2018, recorded that the tribunal had traced their knowledge of the fraud to meetings with the Raju brothers from about 2001, at which, among other things, 'the need to show inflated results to attract customers/employees' was discussed.[68] The penalties in that order, and in a companion order of November 2018 on the Raju family, did not stand for those who appealed: on 2 February 2023 the tribunal set both aside and sent the amounts and bars back to SEBI.[69] SEBI's new order of 30 November 2023 barred the two brothers from the market until 14 July 2028 and ordered six parties, among them two of the officials, a third brother and the family company, to disgorge about Rs 624 crore in all (Rs 6.24 billion, about $76 million at the 2023 average rate). Because the brothers' and the two officials' appeals against the 2017 ruling were still pending in the Supreme Court, it was to take effect only from a date that court would direct.[70]

The criminal case ran on a separate track. The three charge-sheets of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), India's federal police agency, were tried together, and on 9 April 2015 the XXI Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate-cum-Special Sessions Judge at Nampally, in Hyderabad, convicted ten men and sentenced each to seven years' rigorous imprisonment.[71] They were the Raju brothers; B. Suryanarayana Raju, a director of SRSR Advisory Services; V. Srinivas; the two Price Waterhouse partners, Gopalakrishnan and Talluri; and four former employees of the finance department, among them G. Ramakrishna.[72] Reports of the fines differ.[73]

After a dispute over which court should hear their appeals, settled by the Hyderabad High Court on 30 April 2015 in favour of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge at Nampally, that court on 11 May suspended all ten sentences and granted bail pending the appeals.[74] The CBI, by its own later account, appealed for heavier sentences, and in June 2022 it told the Telangana High Court that the brothers' appeals and its own were still pending.[75] No decision on any of the appeals had been found by October 2026, and in February 2025 the tax department told an income-tax tribunal that no order acquitting Raju existed.[76] Each of the ten, the two auditors among them, was therefore convicted by the trial court in April 2015 and had his sentence suspended in May 2015 pending appeal; for the brothers, the appeals were still undecided in June 2022, the latest record of their status.

## A number for every resident

On 28 January 2009, three weeks after Raju's letter, the Planning Commission issued a notification creating the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI).[77] The project had a longer history, which the Supreme Court later set out from government records. In March 2006 the Department of Information Technology had approved a project called 'Unique Identification for BPL Families', for households below the poverty line, to be carried out by the National Informatics Centre, the government's own computing agency.[78] The notification of January 2009 made the new authority an attached office of the Commission, and the Finance Minister approved Rs 147.31 crore for the first phase of enrolment.[79]

Then the state hired from the industry. By a notification of 2 July 2009, 'Mr. Nandan Nilekani was appointed as the Chairman of UIDAI for an initial tenure of five years in the rank and status of a Cabinet Minister. He assumed charge on July 24, 2009.'[80] Nilekani was a co-founder of Infosys and had been a director since 1981; from 1981 to 1987 he had managed its marketing and development in the United States.[81] When the Supreme Court decided the case about the system in 2018, Justice A.K. Sikri began the majority judgment with a line from the project's own message: 'It is better to be unique than the best.' Aadhaar, he wrote, 'means, in English, "foundation" or "base"'.[82]

## Building it

The first part of the agency to start work was not in Delhi. 'Appropriately, the Technology Centre was the first unit of UIDAI to start functioning in 2009 in Bangalore,' its director general, Vijay Madan, later wrote in the agency's account of its own architecture.[83] *Forbes India*, which profiled the team in November 2010, described a hybrid: civil servants headed the departments and took the policy decisions, aided by experts from the private sector. Nilekani invited Srikanth Nadhamuni, an engineer who had spent fifteen years in Silicon Valley and with whom he had founded a non-profit in 2003 to help municipalities use IT, to head the technology centre. Raj Mashruwala, who had been ahead of Nilekani at IIT Bombay and had founded companies in manufacturing software in the United States, expected to be needed for three months at most. He ended up renting an apartment in Bangalore that doubled as the technology centre in its early days. Pramod Varma, 'an old Infosys hand', was the project's chief software architect.[84] The agency's own document later named Nadhamuni, Mashruwala, Varma, Sanjay Jain, Vivek Raghavan and Jagdish Babu among 'a band of dedicated domain experts' who had worked with the centre.[85]

They worked on unusual terms.
