By the magazine's count, of about 1,000 people who had applied in the project's first sixteen months, 23 had come as unpaid volunteers, 14 on sabbatical from their jobs, and '23 took massive pay cuts to join the Project Management Unit'; another 140 had come from the government. Because the volunteers drew no salaries, the magazine noted, the project had started before its budgets were sanctioned.[86] An industry that had sold its engineers' time by the hour to foreign clients was here lending some of them to the state for less, or for nothing. The magazine reported that MindTree, a Bangalore software firm, had built the enrolment software.[87] The difference between the two worlds was put plainly by K. Ganga, the deputy director general for finance, who came from the government's audit service: 'If an Infosys engineer wrote a program for Burger King, he isn't answerable to the public. I, on the other hand, have to answer parliamentary questions.'[88]

The architects described their aims in the industry's terms. 'The primary technical requirements of the project were of scale and vendor neutrality at all levels,' Regunath Balasubramanian, its principal architect, told a trade magazine in 2011.[89] The agency's document said the system was 'entirely built using open source components'.[90] Nadhamuni later called it 'a massive technology challenge, doing a 1000 trillion biometric matches per day'.[91] What it collected is recorded in Justice D.Y. Chandrachud's opinion in the 2018 case. Besides name, date of birth, gender, address and the names of parents or spouse, every resident would give 'All ten fingerprints, photograph and both iris scans'.[92]

The scheme was launched on 29 September 2010 at Tembhli, a village in Nandurbar district of Maharashtra, 'from where first Aadhaar was issued', according to the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), the government's auditor.[93] 'On 29 September 2011, the Aadhaar project completed one year. An announcement was made of the generation of ten crore enrolments and of more than 3.75 crore Aadhaar numbers', that is, 100 million enrolments and 37.5 million numbers.[94] For seven years the project rested on the Planning Commission's notification of 2009, which, Chandrachud pointed out, made no reference to biometrics at all. The Aadhaar Act came only in 2016, passed as a Money Bill, a form of legislation in which the upper house's part is limited.[95] By the time it was notified, UIDAI had generated about one billion numbers.[96] Twelve years after it was created, the agency itself was small. At the end of March 2021 it had 130 staff at its Delhi headquarters and 219 at its regional offices, and the work 'was being carried out by officers and staffs mostly either on deputation or from outsourced agencies'.[97]

## The right to privacy

The challenge came early. In 2012, while Aadhaar still rested only on an executive notification, Justice K.S. Puttaswamy, a retired judge, and Pravesh Khanna filed a petition in the Supreme Court arguing that the scheme violated the right to privacy of 'innumerable citizens' under Article 21 of the Constitution, which protects life and personal liberty.[98] Two older decisions of the Court had been read as holding that the Constitution did not protect a right to privacy, and the question was referred to nine judges.[99] On 24 August 2017 they answered it unanimously: 'The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution.'[100] The judgment did not decide whether Aadhaar was lawful. It set the test that Aadhaar would have to pass.

## Twenty-sixth of September, 2018

The Aadhaar case itself was decided on 26 September 2018 by five judges. Sikri wrote for Chief Justice Dipak Misra, Justice A.M. Khanwilkar and himself. Justice Ashok Bhushan wrote a separate concurring judgment. Chandrachud dissented.[101]

During the hearings the agency's chief executive, Dr Ajay Bhushan Pandey, had explained its engineering to the judges in a PowerPoint presentation.[102] The Authority claimed that authentication was 'purpose blind', returning only a yes or a no, and that the biometric system 'provides high accuracy of over 99.86%'.[103] Its own figures showed the other side. Of about 616 million Aadhaar numbers used for fingerprint authentication, 6.00 per cent were recorded as failed; for iris authentication the figure was 8.54 per cent. Failures, it said, 'do not mean exclusion or denial from subsidies, benefits or services', because agencies were obliged by law to provide other ways of establishing identity.[104] The CAG later found that 'nearly 4.75 Lakh duplicate Aadhaar numbers were cancelled as of November 2019', about 475,000, and 'instances of issue of Aadhaars with the same biometric data to different residents indicating flaws in the de-duplication process'.[105]

The majority upheld the Act and its central purpose, the use of Aadhaar to deliver subsidies and benefits paid for from the Consolidated Fund of India, and held that it had been validly passed as a Money Bill.[106] It then drew limits. School admission could not require Aadhaar, and 'CBSE, NEET, JEE, UGC etc. cannot make the requirement of Aadhaar mandatory as they are outside the purview of Section 7 and are not backed by any law.'[107] JEE is the Joint Entrance Examination for the engineering colleges. The Court struck down the provision that let 'any body corporate or person' use Aadhaar under a contract, which would have enabled, it said, 'commercial exploitation of an individual biometric and demographic information by the private entities'.[108] The compulsory linking of every bank account and every mobile number to Aadhaar went too.[109]

Chandrachud would have struck the Act down. He held that it was not a Money Bill, and that the programme violated 'essential norms pertaining to informational privacy, self-determination and data protection'.[110] Much of his opinion is about people the system failed. 'For persons, who are engaged in manual labour, and persons who are disabled or aged, fingerprints actually cannot be captured by biometric devices.'[111] He concluded: 'Dignity and rights of individuals cannot be based on algorithms or probabilities. Constitutional guarantees cannot be subject to the vicissitudes of technology.'[112] The majority recorded the government's assurance that no eligible person would lose a benefit because a fingerprint failed to match, and treated such failures as matters of the system's working rather than its validity.[113] Both sides accepted that the system made mistakes. They differed over whether a constitutional system could rest on a machine that was right most of the time.

## Two lessons

The two halves of this chapter look unconnected: a private fraud in Hyderabad, a public database in New Delhi. They are connected by what the Indian software industry had become by 2009. It was large enough that its largest failure needed the state to rescue it, and capable enough that the state turned to it for a project of national scale.

Aadhaar lent the industry's people to a new client. For thirty years Indian programmers had built systems for foreign companies, under foreign contracts and foreign law. Here engineers from the same industry, some of them on reduced pay or none, built a system for the Indian state, meant for every resident. The Supreme Court's judgments of 2017 and 2018 were the first time Indian institutions had to decide, in detail, what Indian software could be made to do to Indian citizens.

Satyam showed where the value of an Indian services firm lay. By SEBI's investigation the books had been inflated from 2001 to 2008, and in the last quarter before the letter, by Raju's own figures, the real operating margin was 3 per cent of revenue.[114] Yet the work went on. Engineers like Mastanamma expected to go on servicing the clients, the new chairman said the customers were still happy with the service, and within three months Tech Mahindra bid Rs 58 a share for control.[115] What the bidder paid for was what the 20-F had described: some 50,000 associates recruited from the colleges, schooled for twelve weeks and placed on clients' work, nearly 10,000 of them at clients' sites abroad.[116] That is the bargain this book follows. The firm sold its engineers' time, so its worth lay in the people it could put in front of a client and the clients who would take them, and because revenue grew with headcount, reported growth was itself something to sell. SEBI's 2018 summary of the tribunal's findings listed 'the need to show inflated results to attract customers/employees' among the matters the officials had discussed with the Raju brothers.[117] That suggests at least one thing the fiction was for. The books failed and the delivery machine did not, because the clients had never been buying the books. They had been buying the people.

The question the next chapter takes up follows from both. An industry that could run a client's systems so reliably that a fraud at the top did not stop them, and that could lend its people to build a national identity platform, had still produced very few software products of its own. Chapter 17 asks why.


# Chapter 17. The product question (1986-2024)

In 1992 Rajesh Hukku, then head of Citicorp Overseas Software, the bank's in-house programming unit in India, spun the unit off from the bank as a company of its own. Fifteen years later, in an interview with Ravi Aron of the Wharton School published in March 2007, he remembered one of the Citibank chiefs asking him, at the start, a blunt question: 'Why should I start the one-thousand-and-first software company in India?'[1] His answer, as he recalled it, was that the new firm would be the first to be wholly focused on understanding its customers' business, so that no banker could say of its staff, 'These guys are great techies, but they don't understand my business.'[2]

In Hukku's account, Citi had decided that writing software for sale was not its business. It invested $400,000 in the venture anyway, and the unit became Citicorp Information Technology Industries Ltd. (CITIL), later renamed i-flex solutions.[3] The bank, as he remembered it, liked the team but would give the new firm no 'management mind-share', and asked one thing more: 'Please don't come back asking for business from Citibank.'[4] In hindsight, he said, it was the best combination, 'because you get the money and you don't get controlled'.[5]

The question the Citibank chief put to Hukku is the question of this chapter, turned round. By 1992 India already had hundreds of software companies, and almost all of them sold the same thing: the time of Indian engineers, billed to foreign clients by the hour, the month or the project. A software product is something different. It is a program that a firm owns and sells many times over, so that the cost of writing it is paid once and the revenue keeps coming. The country that became the world's largest supplier of software labour built remarkably few products of its own. Why that happened, and what changed when it did, is the subject here.

The question matters beyond national pride. A firm that owns a product keeps the gains when its engineers become more productive. A firm that sells hours must negotiate with its clients over who keeps them. That difference decides how the tools of artificial intelligence, which make a programmer's hour more productive, land on the two kinds of firm.

## An accounting package for small business

The longest-lived Indian software product grew from the home market. According to the history page on its own website, Tally Solutions began in 1986 as 'Peutronics Financial Accountant', founded by Bharat Goenka, 'inspired by his father, Shyam Sundar Goenka's vision to simplify business operations'.[6] The company says the firm grew 'from an accounting package for SMEs', small and medium enterprises, into business software for firms of all sizes.[7] Its timeline dates 'code-less accounting' to Tally 3.0 in 1988 and the formal establishment of Tally Solutions Private Limited to 1991.[8]

What the timeline shows clearly is how closely the product followed the Indian state's tax law rather than any foreign client's needs. Tally 6.3, in 1999, added support for several currencies and more advanced inventory management. Tally 7.2, in 2005, 'introduced VAT compliance, aiding businesses with tax regulations'. In 2017 the company launched software compliant with the new Goods and Services Tax (GST), and in 2020 a new generation of the product, TallyPrime.[9] Its buyers were small and medium Indian businesses, and it reached them not through onsite consultants but through a network of partners. It says it is now trusted by more than 2.5 million businesses.[10]

Tally's model was the opposite of the export firms' in almost every respect. It sold a packaged product, not people. Its customers were Indian, not American. It earned in rupees from small businesses rather than in dollars from large ones. Its survival over four decades is evidence that a domestic market for software existed through the years when the export industry was growing much faster. Its modest public profile beside Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) or Infosys is a sign of how small that market was. Goenka himself would become a public critic of how the industry's institutions favoured services.

## Selling to Africa first

i-flex took a different road, out of India and into the world, but not to the countries everyone else was going to. Hukku had studied electrical and electronics engineering at the Birla Institute of Technology and Science (BITS) at Pilani in Rajasthan, a desert campus where, he recalled, students with no television built their own radio station, and had worked for TCS, the export firm F.C. Kohli built, before joining Citicorp's in-house unit.[11]

The new company began poor, selling professional services and consulting and spending as little as it could.[12] It could not afford to chase clients in Britain or America. 'We decided early on that we were not going to go to the U.K. or the U.S. because we couldn't even afford the airfare. We said, "Let's go to Africa. That's all we can handle right now."'[13] The firm took the rights to an older Citicorp banking program called MicroBanker, improved it and sold it to African banks. By 1995, by Hukku's account, MicroBanker was number one in the league tables, sold to 117 banks, most of them in Africa.[14] He remembered a billboard in Nairobi in those years: 'Wanted. IT people, MicroBanker experience essential.'[15]

The services work and the old product paid for a new one. In Hukku's words, 'The money we were making on the services, consulting, MicroBanker, etc., was used to fund the creation of our dream product', which was FLEXCUBE, launched in 1997, an integrated banking package covering consumer, corporate, investment and internet banking and asset management.[16] This is the most important detail in his account for the argument of this chapter. India's best-known early global product was not built in spite of services. It was paid for by them.

Hukku's way of teaching his engineers the business they were automating was itself unusual. 'Right from the beginning, we said 10% to 15% of the staff have to be bankers, because how else will I learn the domain?'[17] The bankers came not from Wall Street but from Indian banks, among them Bank of India and the Reserve Bank of India, and many of them were not computer science graduates. The company asked them to teach.[18] In an industry whose training turned graduates into programmers for foreign clients' systems, i-flex was turning programmers into people who understood banking.

Two of the company's choices ran against the industry as a whole. One concerned markets. Hukku saw that the services business depended on America. 'We said that's a very big limitation for the whole industry to be dependent on one country.'[19] By 2007 i-flex claimed customers in more than 125 countries.[20] The other choice concerned the Y2K boom, the rush to fix two-digit dates in old programs before the year 2000, which brought Infosys about a fifth of its revenue at its height (Chapter 11). 'We're perhaps the only IT company from India who made $0 from Y2K,' Hukku claimed, looking back.[21]

FLEXCUBE climbed quickly. On Hukku's reading of an annual league table compiled by International Banking Systems, a British research firm, it was 16th of 60 or 70 core banking products in 1997, second in 1999 and first 'since 2002'.[22] By early 2007 it had been sold to more than 300 banks in 120 countries.[23] i-flex went public in 2002 on the National Stock Exchange and the Bombay Stock Exchange.[24] By the interviewer's account its shares doubled while almost every other technology stock fell in the dot-com bust, and Hukku put that down to the business model: 'We were a balanced product and services company with a globally hedged customer base.'[25]

The ending was a sale. In 2005 Oracle bought Citicorp's stake: 42 per cent for $592 million, in Wharton's introduction to the interview, or 41 per cent, held by Citigroup Venture Capital International, in Oracle's own announcement of 2 August 2005, which stated no price.[26] Either way, Hukku said, 'No one at the time, including me, ever dreamed that the $400,000 they put in would become almost $600 million in 13 years.'[27]

Hukku was clear that i-flex had never been a pure product company. 'We are a product company. We're also a services company,' he said.[28] As with Cognizant (Chapter 15), a foreign company's captive centre in India had become an independent firm, but this one sold a product, and its largest exit was to an American buyer.

## A product inside the factory

Infosys, the archetype of the services firm, built a banking product of its own. Its annual report to American investors for the year to March 2002 said that, besides its IT services, it marketed and licensed 'our own centralized bank automation software application, known as FINACLE(TM)'.[29] It described Finacle as 'a fully web-enabled, integrated core banking solution that addresses the retail, corporate and trade finance activities of a bank'.[30]

The numbers show where the product sat in the firm. In the year to March 2009 Infosys told investors that it had earned 3.9 per cent of its total revenue from licensing software products, against 3.6 per cent the year before. 'The markets for our primary suite of software products which we call Finacle TM are competitive,' it added, and the costs of developing new products 'may not be recouped'.[31] Three years later the share was a little higher but still small: 4.6 per cent in the year to March 2012.[32]

The product was also sold with services wrapped round it. 'We also provide a core banking software solution, Finacle TM, for the banking industry and provide customization and implementation services around this solution,' the company said in 2009.[33] By March 2012, Infosys said, Finacle was used by 160 banks in 78 countries.[34]

One detail of the 2009 report shows how a services firm thought about its product. The director responsible for Finacle, T.V. Mohandas Pai, who had been chief financial officer from 1994 to 2006, was listed as head of 'Administration, Education and Research, Finacle, Human Resources Development' and the Infosys Leadership Institute.[35] The banking product shared a portfolio with the training machine. Finacle, like FLEXCUBE, was never a pure product business. It was a product nested inside a services company, contributing less than a twentieth of revenue.

## A round table of its own

By 2013 some of the product companies had decided that the industry's lobby did not speak for them. The National Association of Software and Service Companies (Nasscom), the industry's lobby group, had represented the industry for about 25 years, as it grew from $100 million in 1992 to $108 billion in 2012.[36] In March 2013 Knowledge at Wharton reported that a group of 30 software product companies had come together to form the Indian Software Product Industry Round Table, known as iSPIRT, a think-tank for the products segment.[37]

It was a spin-off rather than a walk-out. The round table grew out of Nasscom's own annual product conclave, and its founders were Nasscom members, among them Goenka of Tally and Sharad Sharma.[38] Goenka told the business daily *Business Standard*: 'At Nasscom, the product companies do not have the same weightage as the services companies. The policy interventions Nasscom is trying to make are more in favor of the services industry.'[39] Sharma said: 'We believe that with this think-tank, we will get a louder voice in policy making and other initiatives.'[40]

Nasscom played the split down. Its chairman, N. Chandrasekaran, who was also chief executive of TCS, said: 'When you are on a growth paradigm, you cannot do everything that you want to do. I don't see any conflict.'[41] The association had set up an expert committee the previous July, chaired by N.R. Narayana Murthy, co-founder of Infosys, to chart a roadmap for the industry. Murthy said the industry should aim to reach $300 billion by 2020.[42] Of that, the committee suggested, the internet and mobile could account for $100 billion, the domestic market $75 billion, and software products 'around US$10 billion'.[43] Products were on the list, at about one-thirtieth of the target.

The round table did lobby for its members. In January 2019 it wrote to the prime minister on behalf of start-ups about the 'angel tax', asking that investments of up to Rs 10 crore a year from resident investors in recognised start-ups be exempt, and claiming that the number of angel investors had fallen 48 per cent since 2015.[44] But by then it was best known for something else. It describes itself as 'a non-profit think tank which champions digital public goods', and maintains the website of India Stack, a set of public digital services built around Aadhaar.[45] *Inc42*, a start-up news site, described it in 2023 as 'building the India Stack since 2013'.[46] That closeness to the state drew criticism. In 2017 Sharma, a member of its governing council, admitted to anonymously trolling critics of Aadhaar on Twitter and apologised.[47] The round table formed to speak for product companies had become, above all, an advocate of public platforms.

## The village office

One Indian firm set out to make products from the start. Sridhar Vembu graduated from the Indian Institute of Technology Madras in 1989, took a doctorate at Princeton and worked as a wireless systems engineer at Qualcomm in San Diego. In 1996 he co-founded AdventNet with members of his family and friends, among them Tony Thomas, then at Bell Labs.[48] The company's own timeline begins: 'AdventNet Inc. is born in New Jersey, USA. It all begins with Network Management.'[49] Its first customers, Vembu recalled in 2010, were makers of network equipment such as Cisco.[50] He told *Forbes India* in 2020 what he had seen at the start: 'in India we have perfect talent but we produce almost zero software products.'[51]

On the company's account, the products followed one another: a sister brand, ManageEngine, in 2003, then online applications under the Zoho name, starting with a word processor and a customer relationship management (CRM) program in 2005. In 2009 AdventNet renamed itself Zoho Corporation.[52] It has never taken outside capital, by its own and its founder's statements. 'We have never taken any outside money,' Vembu said in 2010, and the company's website still says it has 'never taken money from investors'.[53] *Forbes India* reported that in 2019 Zoho made profits of Rs 516 crore on revenue of Rs 3,410 crore (Rs 34.1 billion, about $480 million at that year's average rate).[54]

In 2011, the company says, it opened an office in Tenkasi, a district in southern Tamil Nadu, and in 2018 another in Renigunta in Andhra Pradesh.[55] By 2020, *Forbes India* reported, 500 of its 9,300 employees, 8,800 of them in India, worked from those two rural offices, and Vembu himself had moved to Tenkasi in October 2019. 'I always thought that people migrating from villages to cities is not a good idea,' he said.[56]

Zoho also built its own school. Zoho University, which the company dates to 2005 and describes as 'an experiment in providing an alternative to the conventional college education', paid its students a stipend rather than charging fees, and by 2020, *Forbes India* reported, 875 of the firm's 9,300 staff had come through it.[57] Vembu said that 15 to 20 per cent of Zoho's engineers had no engineering degree.[58] One graduate, Saran Babu Paramasivam, told *Forbes India* that in 2005 he could not operate a computer; by 2020 he was a senior product manager, and he said 'a degree is not important anymore'.[59] Where the services firms recruited engineering graduates by the hundred thousand and billed their time, Zoho trained many of its own engineers and put their work into products it owned. When those engineers became more productive, the gain stayed with Zoho.

## The warehouse in Chennai

The next generation of Indian product companies did not sell boxes of software to shopkeepers or core banking systems to banks. They sold subscriptions over the internet, software as a service (SaaS), mostly to small businesses abroad. The best documented is Freshworks, because it listed its shares in the United States and had to explain itself to American investors.

Its founder and chief executive, Girish Mathrubootham, began his letter in the 2021 registration statement with its origins: 'We started in a 700 square foot warehouse in Chennai in 2010. Our simple idea was to create a "fresh" helpdesk in response to a poor customer service experience I had.'[60] He listed the doubts he had heard along the way. Among them were 'You can't find talent in Chennai; you can't win unless you move to Bangalore' and 'You really can't build a global SaaS company from India.'[61]

The company's model needed none of the apparatus of the services industry. 'Freshworks was global from "day one" with our first few customers coming from four different continents,' Mathrubootham wrote. 'Our initial sales came through search-driven online acquisition, powered by robust product-led growth.'[62] Customers found the software by searching the web, tried it and paid for it, without a salesman on a plane. There were no onsite engineers, no visas, no time sheets and no client billing by the hour. By mid-2021, the company said, businesses from more than 120 countries used its products, and it had about 52,500 paying customers.[63]

It also lost money as it grew. Its revenue was $172.4 million in 2019 and $249.7 million in 2020, a rise of 45 per cent, and its net losses in those years were $31.1 million and $57.3 million.[64] The work was done in India. As of July 2021, Freshworks said, it had about 4,300 employees, and about 3,800 of them were in India, 'where most of engineering, product design, sales and marketing, customer support, and general and administrative personnel are located'. Its headquarters were in San Mateo, California.[65]

The rivalry between two Chennai product firms reached an American court. On 17 March 2020 Zoho sued Freshworks in the Northern District of California, alleging the misappropriation of trade secrets and violations of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.[66] In October 2020 the judge refused to dismiss the amended complaint, ruling that Zoho had 'clearly met the standard for pleading trade secret misappropriation', a ruling on the pleading rather than a finding of fact.[67] In December 2021 the companies settled and Zoho dismissed the suit. Freshworks's announcement and its annual report gave no terms. Freshworks said that a now-former sales employee had 'wrongfully accessed and used Zoho confidential information relating to sales leads', and that he had not acted at the company's direction.[68]

By then Freshworks was a public company. On 22 September 2021 the final prospectus fixed the price: 'The initial public offering price is $36.00 per share.' The company offered 28,500,000 shares of Class A common stock for listing on the Nasdaq Global Select Market, about $1.03 billion before any extra shares the underwriters might buy.[69]

The listing settled something that the Chennai warehouse had left open. The most celebrated Indian software-as-a-service company was, legally and financially, an American one: incorporated in Delaware, headquartered in San Mateo and listed in New York, with its engineers in India.[70] The value it created was priced in dollars on an American exchange. Like i-flex's sale to Oracle, the reward for building a product in India was realised abroad.

## Money arrives, and leaves

In Hukku's account, the shortage that had mattered most in 1992 was money. 'Even in 1992, there was not enough capital,' he said in 2007. By then, he believed, the position had reversed. 'So capital is not a problem today.'[71]

Fourteen years later capital arrived on a scale far beyond anything he described, and much of it went to consumer internet businesses rather than to software products in his sense. According to figures from Tracxn, a data firm, reported by *The Week* in January 2025, Indian start-ups raised $25.7 billion in 2022, a fall of 31 per cent on the year before, which implies about $37 billion in 2021.[72] On Tracxn's count, funding then fell by close to 58 per cent in 2023, to $10.8 billion, and rose by about 2 per cent in 2024, to $11.1 billion.[73] The emblem of the bust was Byju's, an education technology company, which by mid-2024 faced insolvency proceedings brought by the Board of Control for Cricket in India over unpaid dues.[74]

## Sidebar: Why was India's most-used software never sold?

By the measure of daily use, the most successful Indian software of the 2010s was not sold by a private firm at all. Aadhaar, the biometric identity number, is one case (Chapter 16). The other is the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), a system run by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) that lets a person pay another directly from a bank account using a phone.

The Reserve Bank of India's statistics show how fast it grew. In the year to March 2017, the year in which UPI was introduced, it carried about 18 million transactions, worth about Rs 6,961 crore (Rs 69.6 billion).[75] Seven years later, in the year to March 2024, it carried 131.13 billion transactions, worth about Rs 199.95 lakh crore (Rs 199.95 trillion, roughly $2.4 trillion at that year's average rate).[76] All India Radio, reporting NPCI's figures, said that in December 2024 alone UPI processed about 16.73 billion transactions worth around Rs 23.25 lakh crore (Rs 23.25 trillion), with the number of transactions about 39 per cent higher than a year earlier.[77]

No private Indian software product in this chapter came near that scale of use. Tally counts its users in millions of businesses, by its own claim; Freshworks counted its paying customers in tens of thousands.[78] UPI counts its transactions in billions each month.

Part of the answer lies in who built it. India Stack's own timeline, on the website iSPIRT maintains, credits the launch of UPI in 2016 to NPCI, and the identity and electronic-signature services beside it to other public bodies.[79] The press gives the volunteers a larger part: *Inc42* counted UPI among the projects iSPIRT 'has been behind'.[80] Either way the builders came from two worlds. The institutions were public, but some of the people around them came from the software industry: Nandan Nilekani, the Infosys co-founder who chaired the identity authority (Chapter 16), was a mentor to iSPIRT.[81]

The rest of the answer, this book argues, lies in what a payments network is. Such a network is worth most when every bank can join it and every phone can use it. A private firm that built one would have had reason to charge for it or close it to rivals. A body that the banks answered to could bring them all in at once.

That is a different answer to the product question. Where private Indian firms built products, they either sold them to small Indian businesses, as Tally did, or sold them abroad and realised their value abroad, as i-flex and Freshworks did. UPI was built for Indians, used at home, and run as infrastructure rather than sold as a product. The country's most-used software was the one piece that no one could sell.

## Products and people

The 'services mindset' is the most common explanation in India for why the country built so few products. It is the participants' own. Hukku said Indian software companies had followed the model F.C. Kohli pioneered at TCS in the 1970s, 'of exporting the Indian brain, or doing software services projects offshore'. Kohli had worked very hard to make it succeed, Hukku said. 'The not-so-great news was that hundreds of companies that came after copied him. Basically it is a human tendency to take the route which is already a proven success.'[82] When Aron asked whether i-flex was 'Made in Spite of India', he replied: 'It's not in spite of India, but it's in spite of whatever was successful when we came into existence.'[83] Goenka's complaint about Nasscom, and Nasscom's own roadmap, said the same thing about the industry's institutions.[84]

These are explanations from people with a stake in them. Several structural explanations fit the same facts. One is capital, which Hukku himself named: there was not enough of it in 1992, and venture funding at scale came only in the following decades.[85] Zoho's founders, by their own account, never raised any. A second is the market. Tally's history suggests that small Indian businesses would pay for software when the state's tax rules required it, but no series of Indian spending on software over the period has been located.[86] Building a product for India was no guarantee of success either. The Simputer, a low-cost multilingual hand-held computer designed in 2000 by a group from the Indian Institute of Science and Encore Software in Bangalore (Bengaluru since 2014), received worldwide attention but was, in the words of V. Rajaraman, the historian of Indian computing, 'not a commercial success'.[87] A third is talent. The services firms offered graduates secure, well-paid jobs with training attached, and a young product firm had to compete with that. Talent also meant knowledge of the customer's trade. i-flex's answer was to hire bankers to teach its programmers banking, and Zoho's was a school of its own.[88] A fourth is the exit. The largest rewards for building products in India were realised through a foreign buyer, as with Oracle and i-flex, or a foreign listing, as with Freshworks.[89] A 'mindset' may be the participants' name for these conditions rather than a separate cause. The question stays open.

What can be measured is the difference in scale, and it cuts both ways. At the end of 2024 Freshworks had about 4,400 employees, and approximately 3,700 of them, 83 per cent, lived in India.[90] Its revenue that year was $720.4 million, up from $596.4 million in 2023 and $498.0 million in 2022.[91] In the same year Cognizant, the American services firm born from a captive centre in India, had about 336,800 employees, 241,500 of them in India.[92] The figures are given only to show orders of magnitude. Freshworks earned its revenue with a workforce less than a fiftieth the size of Cognizant's in India.

The debate in India treated products as the higher path, and on revenue per engineer they were. But the engineer factory was turning out graduates in the hundreds of thousands each year. No set of product companies of the size documented here could have employed them. The services model was not only a habit of mind. It was the model in which the industry's growth turned into mass employment, because a firm that sold hours could grow only by hiring more people to sell.

Hukku had made a prediction in 2007: 'I can guarantee you that five years from now, there will be many famous product companies growing out of India.'[93] By the early 2020s there were some, and a flood of venture money that peaked in 2021. Yet in those same pandemic years the old model did not shrink. The firms that sold engineers' hours went on hiring, in numbers that no product company could match.

Freshworks's annual report for 2024 shows what happened when the product side met the new technology. On 5 November 2024, the company said, it had committed to a plan to realign its workforce 'that resulted in a 13% reduction in force', at a cost of about $9.7 million.[94] The same report described its generative AI offerings. 'Freddy AI Agent offers always-on, autonomous, personalized resolutions to customer and employee queries,' the company told investors, while Freddy AI Copilot provided 'always-on contextual assistance' for support, marketing and sales staff, 'designed to boost productivity'.[95] Among its risks it listed the chance that competitors 'may be able to develop new AI offerings that disrupt our customers' needs and negatively impact demand for our products'.[96]

Read beside Chapter 14, the description is pointed. An Indian-built product company was selling software designed to answer customers' and employees' questions without a person, which is much of what India's call centres and IT help desks had been paid by the hour to do. Products had not escaped the AI question. They met it from the other side, as sellers of the automation that the services firms would have to absorb. It was the services boom, and what it did to the people hired in it, that shaped the lives of most young Indian engineers, and the next chapter follows them.


# Chapter 18. The pandemic boom (2020-2023)

On 21 September 2022 Rishad Premji, the chairman of Wipro, spoke at the convention of the All India Management Association. 'The reality is that there are people today working for Wipro and working directly for one of our competitors and we have actually discovered 300 people in the last few months who are doing exactly that,' he said.[1] Wipro had dismissed them.[2] The practice he described, working for two employers at once, depended on something that had changed two and a half years earlier, when the industry's engineers left their offices.

For thirty years the Indian services firm had sold its clients a place as well as people: secure floors, dedicated links and guarded campuses. In a few weeks of 2020 the place went away and the work carried on. Demand for the industry's services surged, and the firms hired on a scale they had never attempted. Engineers left their jobs at rates the companies called unprecedented, and some took second jobs on the side, while the real pay of a new graduate fell. Then demand turned, and campus recruits found their joining dates pushed back by months and years. The workers who complained began, for the first time in large numbers, to do so through unions. By the end of the period, one sentence in a company filing showed that something new had entered the terms on which India sold its engineers' time.

## The factory goes home

On 25 March 2020 the Indian government put the country under lockdown.[3] Infosys, the second-largest of the Indian software services firms, had moved first.[4] In the annual report it filed with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission two months later, the company wrote: 'By March 20, 2020, we had enabled 93% of our employees to be able to work remotely.'[5] By the time it filed, the campuses in India were, on the company's figures, nearly empty. 'Only essential and critical services for our clients and our own operations are being supported from our campuses in India,' the filing said.[6]

The same report listed what else had changed, from secure laptops and wider bandwidth to 'information security controls for remote working and activity monitoring'.[7] It would 'Continue to monitor the productivity of employees as they work remotely'.[8] Even the training school moved. Infosys's next annual report recorded that 'The early days of the COVID-19 pandemic saw us relocate trainees from Mysuru and continue their training without missing a beat', using an in-house learning platform called Lex.[9] Mysuru (Mysore until 2014) was where the company trained its new graduates before they were placed on projects. Now the trainees were sent away and taught on screens.

The move was not as smooth as the headline figure suggests. Many of the industry's contracts specified where the work would be done. Infosys's annual report for the year to March 2020 warned that its ability to deliver while employees worked from home was 'sometimes constrained by contractual terms with our clients'.[10] Some clients had refused permission, or had been slow to give it: 'Since few of our clients did not give us the required permissions, or there were delays in obtaining them, our service delivery was marginally disrupted'.[11]

Within a year those doubts had mostly gone. 'As of March 31, 2021, we had enabled 99.3% of our employees with a secure remote working environment and 96.5% of our employees were working remotely,' Infosys reported.[12] Staff on critical client projects and on work involving sensitive data still went into the offices.[13]

The filings also recorded what home working cost the people doing it, in the language of risk. 'The productivity of our employees may be negatively impacted due to isolated remote working from home, quarantine requirements, negative social sentiment and personal anxiety,' Infosys wrote in 2020 and repeated in 2021.[14]

What the filings do show is the factory's front door changing. Infosys's recruiters had tested and interviewed candidates in person. In the year to March 2021, the company said, 'All interviews across the Globe in fiscal 2021 were conducted virtually', and the process from application to offer was digitised.[15] The training that followed was online too, and Infosys said it had 'repurposed Lex for over a million college students in India via our InfyTQ app', a platform that, in the company's words a year later, 'brings the best of our Mysuru training to the hands of the learners across the country'.[16] Students who passed its assessments could earn an Infosys certification.[17] The firm's training school, which had once been a campus that graduates travelled to after they were hired, was now partly a phone app that students used before.

These are the company's own descriptions, and they say nothing about how well remote training worked. They do establish the point that matters for the rest of the book. The work of the Indian services firm, and the teaching that prepared people for it, could be done almost anywhere. That opened a door the industry had kept shut: an engineer working at home could work for two employers at once.

## Five million applications

Demand came back faster than the firms had planned for, and the clearest record of it is in the recruiting figures.

Infosys publishes its recruitment funnel every year. In the year to March 2020 (FY2019-20) it made 83,319 offers of employment, and in FY2020-21, the first pandemic year, 48,029.[18] Then came the surge. In FY2021-22 Infosys received 5,866,636 applications and made 222,500 offers.[19] The offers figure counts experienced recruits as well as new graduates, so it is not a count of freshers. Offers rose about four and a half times in a single year.

Headcount followed. Infosys added about 100,000 people in three years, from 242,371 employees in March 2020 to 343,234 in March 2023.[20] The other large firms grew in step. Wipro's rounded totals rose by about a quarter between March 2021 and March 2023.[21] Cognizant Technology Solutions, registered in the United States but with most of its staff in India, added about 66,000 people in the two years to the end of 2022, when 258,500 of its 355,300 employees were in India.[22]

Most of the new hires came from the same colleges that had fed the factory for two decades. A smaller stream came from elsewhere. Infosys said it had 'recruited over 7,280 employees locally in our markets' in FY2020-21, of whom 1,941 were fresh graduates, and that this hiring 'significantly de-risks our operations from regulatory changes related to immigration'.[23] The company ran versions of its foundation training in six countries and a training centre in Indianapolis.[24] Beside the hundreds of thousands hired in India these numbers are small. They show the firms insuring themselves against the visa politics of Chapter 13 by training some of their recruits in the client's own country.

## A third of the workforce, every year

The boom was a labour-market event as much as a demand event. Engineers could leave, and they did.

Cognizant gives the clearest numbers, because, as an American company, it reports attrition (the share of staff who leave in a year) in its annual 10-K filing. Counting both resignations and dismissals, its attrition was 20.6 per cent in 2020, 30.8 per cent in 2021 and 31.7 per cent in 2022. In the last quarter of 2021, on an annualised basis, it reached 34.6 per cent.[25] 'In 2021, we experienced unprecedented attrition, which was considered industry-wide,' the company wrote. 'As a result, we hired over a hundred thousand new employees'.[26] It hired more than a hundred thousand again in 2022.[27] The departures were concentrated at the bottom of the pyramid. 'Our attrition is weighted towards our more junior employees,' Cognizant said, and in 2021 'voluntary attrition constituted the vast majority' of the total. In 2020, by contrast, only about half had been voluntary, because the company's own restructuring programme had raised the number of people it let go while the pandemic held down resignations.[28]

At those rates a large firm had to refill its pyramid almost from scratch every three years. Every departure meant another recruit to find, test, train and place on a project, and every replacement had to be paid more to stay. Cognizant's risk factors put the problem in the plainest terms of the business model: 'While we strive to adjust pricing to reduce the impact of compensation increases on our operating margin, we may not be successful in recovering these increases'.[29] Wipro's filing for FY2021-22 listed the same pressures on its margins: 'strong demand for digital and other niche skills are expected to result in wage inflation', 'Increased hiring and training costs due to higher attrition rates', and a 'Limited ability of the market to accept increase in prices for our offerings'.[30] This was the time-and-materials model under stress. A firm that sells hours at an agreed rate makes money only while the hours cost it less than the rate. When engineers' pay rose faster than clients would pay, the margin was squeezed from both sides.

Infosys gave its rates to investors on its quarterly results calls, whose transcripts it filed with the SEC, and they tell the same story with one caution: the company changed its measure partway through. In the quarter to March 2020 its executives reported voluntary attrition of 15.1 per cent, or 18.2 per cent counting dismissals. A year later voluntary attrition, 'calculated on annualized basis', was 15.2 per cent, and had risen, they said, 'as demand for talent increased'.[31] From FY2021-22 the company reported voluntary attrition over the previous twelve months instead, a measure that moves more slowly. On that basis it was 27.7 per cent in the year to March 2022, 20.9 per cent in the year to March 2023 and 12.6 per cent in the year to March 2024.[32] The first two figures are not strictly comparable with the last three, but the peak is not in doubt: in the year to March 2022 more than one Infosys employee in four chose to leave. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), the largest of the firms by headcount, with 592,195 employees in March 2022, went through the same cycle. As reported in the press, its attrition was 12.1 per cent in the year to March 2020 and 7.2 per cent a year later, then rose to 17.4 per cent in the twelve months to March 2022 and 20.1 per cent in the twelve months to March 2023, before falling back to 12.5 per cent in the year to March 2024.[33]

Women's share of the workforce held steady through the churn, at least at the firms that report it. Cognizant said women made up 36 per cent of its workforce at the end of 2020 and 38 per cent at the end of 2021, the share it reported again for 2023.[34] Infosys said in its annual report for FY2023-24 that women made up 'nearly 40% of our workforce'.[35]

## The price of a new engineer

For engineers who could change jobs, the boom was a seller's market. The demand for talent after the pandemic, *HR Katha* observed, had firms luring people with attractive packages and perks.[36] For those entering the industry, the real price moved the other way. A study by the business website Moneycontrol, published in 2022 and reported by the trade site *HR Katha* and by *Analytics India Magazine*, put the median annual pay of freshers at large IT firms at about Rs 245,000 in 2012 and Rs 355,000 in 2022, a rise of 45 per cent in ten years.[37] At each year's average exchange rate that is about $4,600 and $4,500.[38] Adjusted for Indian consumer prices, the 2022 figure was worth nearly a fifth less than the 2012 one.[39] Over the same decade, the study found, the median pay of chief executives at the large firms rose by 835 per cent.[40]

In this book's reading, these figures are the bargain seen from the bottom of the pyramid. A firm that sold engineers' time at rates its clients were reluctant to raise made its margin on the cheapest hours, the ones worked by new graduates, and it needed more of those graduates every year in order to grow. Whatever the boom did for engineers who changed jobs, on these figures it did not raise the real price of a new one.

## Two employers, one laptop

Home working made a second job easy to hide. An engineer whose office was a bedroom, and whose manager saw her only on a video call, could in principle work for two companies at once. In 2022 the practice, known as moonlighting, became the subject of a public argument among the industry's leaders.

In August 2022 Premji wrote on Twitter that there was a lot of 'chatter about people moonlighting in the tech industry', and that 'it is cheating- plain and simple.'[41] His speech to the management association the next month, quoted at the start of this chapter, turned the complaint into dismissals. *Business Today* reported that Premji regarded the practice as a 'complete violation of integrity in its deepest form'.[2]

The industry did not speak with one voice. Infosys, the magazine reported, had told its staff the week before, in 'a strong and firm message', that moonlighting was not allowed. N. Ganapathy Subramaniam, the chief operating officer of TCS, had warned that employees chasing short-term gains in this way 'might lose out in the long term'.[42] T.V. Mohandas Pai, a former Infosys director, took the other side. 'No, moonlighting is not cheating,' he told the magazine. 'Employment is a contract between an employer who pays me for working for them for 'n' number of hours a day.' During those hours, he said, he was bound by the employer's conditions, including client confidentiality. 'Now what I do after that time is my freedom'.[43]

Infosys then wrote the problem into its annual report. From FY2022-23 its risk factors included a new line: 'Continued remote working exposes the company to the risk of some employees working for multiple employers simultaneously (moonlighting) without obtaining required prior approvals and this may result in potential conflict of interests, confidentiality breach, and reduced productivity.'[44]

The quarrel looks like one about loyalty. It was also about the unit in which the industry sold its work. The services firms billed their clients by the hour or the person-month. Pai's defence turned the same logic around: the employer bought a fixed number of hours, and the rest belonged to the worker. Premji's answer was that an engineer working directly for a competitor was breaking faith whatever the hours. When the work was done on a client's secure floor, the question did not arise, because the office day bounded what an engineer could do. At home that boundary was gone, and both sides found how much of the employment relationship had depended on it. The firms' answer, in the end, was to bring people back. Infosys described 2022 as the year it 'transitioned into a hybrid model of work for our employees and service providers following an extended period of remote work', and from FY2022-23 listed 'Our transition to a hybrid working model' among its risks.[45]

## Packed bags

The turn in demand came in the second half of 2022. Cognizant dated it precisely: 'The rate of attrition began to decrease in the second half of 2022'.[46] For the engineers already employed, that meant fewer outside offers. For the graduates who had been promised jobs during the boom, it meant waiting.

On 5 October 2022 *Business Today* published complaints from new graduates whose start dates at Accenture kept moving. The magazine had already reported similar delays at Wipro, Infosys, HCLTech, Tech Mahindra and Capgemini.[47] The graduates it quoted were not named. One said: 'I was placed in Accenture as Associate Software Engineer (ASE) via campus placement in November 2021. I received my offer letter in the last week of April this year.' Since then, the start date had been 'pushed time after time'; the latest, 30 September, had now become 'somewhere in 2023'.[48] Another described a postponement two days before the joining date: 'I had packed my bags and booked all tickets to move to the new city, just two days before joining, they postponed the date again. When will they finally make me join, who will pay for my expenses in the meanwhile?'[49] A third had turned down other employers: 'I am riddled with depressive feelings because I rejected TCS, Wipro, and HCL for a job in Accenture.'[50] Others worried about the record it would leave: 'It's a year since I have been waiting to get onboarded. It is going to reflect as a gap year in my CV.'[51]

The graduates also blamed their colleges. The placement cell, the office that had invited the companies to campus and organised the tests, was the link between the college and the factory. 'The college placement cell should have helped us in this tough time,' said a graduate of CV Raman Global University in Bhubaneswar. A graduate of Galgotias University in Greater Noida said the placement office had stopped answering once students had graduated: 'they don't care for me anymore.'[52] For the colleges, a campus offer was a result to be counted at the end of the year. What happened after graduation was no longer their business.

None of this was new. The bust of 2001-02 had left recruits at Anna University waiting for deferred joining dates, and the collapse of Satyam in 2009 had stranded a batch of its campus hires (Chapters 11 and 16). This was the third time in about twenty years that the factory's newest products took the first shock of a turn in demand.

At Infosys the numbers turned with unusual speed. Offers of employment fell from 222,500 in FY2021-22 to 114,374 in FY2022-23, and to 26,975 in FY2023-24, a fall of about 88 per cent in two years. Applications fell from 5.9 million to 2.4 million.[53] Headcount, which had peaked at 343,234 in March 2023, fell to 317,240 a year later.[54] Wipro's rounded total fell from more than 250,000 to more than 234,000 over the same year.[55] Cognizant ended 2023 with about 347,700 employees, 7,600 fewer than a year before, and with 254,000 in India.[56] Its own measure of voluntary attrition in its technology services business fell from 25.6 per cent in 2022 to 13.8 per cent in 2023.[57] The engineers who had changed jobs freely in 2021 now stayed put.

## Outside the factory laws

The people who took the delayed recruits' complaints to the government belonged to organisations that had barely existed a few years earlier. The industry had grown without unions, and partly under exemptions from the labour laws that governed factories.

A note published in November 2017 by Arvind Gurumurthy of the law firm Kochhar & Co. set out the position. The Industrial Disputes Act of 1947 required employers with more than 100 workers to get the labour commissioner's approval before retrenching staff, 'but this does not cover IT industry'.[58] The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act of 1946 required industrial employers to publish certified terms of employment covering hours, shifts, leave and dismissal. 'However, by a notification published on January 25, 2014 the Karnataka government exempted IT companies from applicability of Standing Orders Act for a period of five years.'[59] The engineer factory, in other words, was not in law a factory. The note suggested that the exemptions might have been meant to help the industry grow, and recorded that many employees' leaders saw them as giving firms room to treat layoffs as they liked.[60]

On Sunday 20 August 2017 close to 200 IT workers gathered at the YWCA Hall in Koramangala, Bengaluru, to found the Karnataka State IT/ITeS Employees Union (ITeS stands for IT-enabled services), known as KITU. *The News Minute* reported that the meeting came amid 'reports of large-scale layoffs in the IT sector'.[61] The union's general secretary was Vineeth, a testing lead at the Bengaluru software firm MindTree. He was also part of the IT Employees Centre, an association that had worked for IT employees' rights in Bengaluru for eight years and had received complaints about layoffs and maternity leave, but had never been registered as a union. 'What is currently happening is that if an employee is facing a problem, they have to fight in their individual capacity and the companies may not listen to them,' he told the reporter. 'The trade union will help them negotiate and bargain with the management, and even fight.'[62]

Others at the meeting spoke in the same terms. Sethumadhavan, a Wipro employee, said: 'As per our Constitution, we have the right to join a union.' The industry, he said, was facing many challenges, among them layoffs and automation, and 'This is the right time to form an organisation'.[63] Akshaya, an IBM employee on the union's executive committee, described the hours: 'sometimes we are given a project that requires us to work 15 hours a day and we are paid just Rs 25 per extra hour.'[64] The union's president, Amanullah Khan, answered the charge that unions held the country back: 'Trade unions are generally seen as anti-social or anti-national.' He said that neither the National Association of Software and Service Companies (Nasscom), the industry's lobby group, nor the government would be pleased. 'But we are not individuals anymore.'[65] The report noted that Mohandas Pai, among others, had opposed unions in the IT sector, on the grounds that they would harm a service industry.[66]

On 7 November 2017 the Karnataka labour commissioner certified KITU's formation under the Trade Unions Act of 1926.[67] Kochhar & Co. called it 'the first trade union in India, officially registered and recognised by the labour department, which is dedicated to the information technology ("IT") sector', with about 250 members by its own claim.[68] The same note acknowledged that 'unrecognised groups' had already existed, and the IT Employees Centre had been working for eight years before KITU was founded.[69] What is documented is narrower: KITU was the first IT employees' union registered in Karnataka, home to the city the reporter called India's Silicon Valley.

The pandemic gave such organisations work. A second body, the Nascent Information Technology Employees Senate (NITES), based in Pune, took up the cause of more than 2,000 graduates whom Infosys had recruited on campus in 2022 and had still not brought in.[70] It complained to the Union Ministry of Labour and Employment on 20 August 2024, and by the union's account Infosys issued about 2,000 offer letters with October joining dates on 2 and 3 September.[71] In February 2025 several hundred of those recruits, by then trainees at Mysuru, were let go after the company's internal assessments, over 300 by Infosys's count and 700 by NITES's, as the prologue tells.[72]

How many members either union had in these years is not on record. Their influence is easier to see than their size: complaints that would once have been one graduate's grievance against one company were now reaching a ministry in Delhi.

## Offices, and the people in them

The bust brought restructuring as well as slower hiring. In the second quarter of 2023 Cognizant began what it called its NextGen programme, 'aimed at simplifying our operating model, optimizing corporate functions and consolidating and realigning office space to reflect the post-pandemic hybrid work environment'.[73] In 2023 it cost $229 million, about half of it for employee separations and the rest for leaving offices and other items.[74] The company warned that 'Our NextGen program and the associated reductions in headcount and consolidation of office space could disrupt our business'.[75]

The pandemic's lesson about place had come round again. In 2020 the firms had learned that the work could leave the campus. In 2023 one of them was giving up offices because hybrid working meant it needed fewer of them, and was cutting staff in the same programme.

## The sentence in the risk factors

The most important single sentence of these years for the rest of this book appeared in Infosys's annual report for FY2023-24, filed in June 2024. In its risk factors, among the familiar warnings about competition and pricing, the company repeated a line it had carried in each annual report since 2020: 'due to competitive market conditions and pricing pressures, we are committing to higher productivity improvements in our contracts with our clients.' Then it added a new one: 'Due to the attention created by the code generation capabilities of AI technologies, clients have demanded higher commitments around productivity improvements.'[76] If those promised gains did not materialise, the filing said, the company's profitability could suffer.[77]

The sentence is short, and it is easy to read too much into it. It does not say that artificial intelligence had cut Infosys's hiring, and the same filing pointed elsewhere when it described pressure on demand, warning that clients 'may become cautious and reduce their discretionary spending in the short term or delay their decision-making process'.[78] Whether the fall in offers from 222,500 to 26,975 owed anything to AI is weighed in Chapter 19, which also follows how the sentence changed in later reports.

What the sentence does show is narrower and, for the book's argument, sharper. Clients had read about software that writes code. They had asked their Indian suppliers to commit, in contract, to doing the same work with less effort, and the supplier bore the risk if the gains did not come. Under time-and-materials billing, a productivity gain that the client captures means fewer billable hours. Under a fixed-price contract, it means a lower price for the same result. Either way the first share of the gain goes to the client, and the firm keeps something only if it beats its own promise.

The pandemic years had shown three things about the engineer factory. Its intake was set by clients' discretionary spending, not by the number of graduates: offers at one firm had risen four and a half times in a year and then fallen by nearly nine-tenths in two. Its workers, for a brief period, had the upper hand, and used it by leaving, by moonlighting and, in small numbers, by organising. And its work no longer needed a particular place. By 2024 the clients were asking whether it needed the same number of hours. For forty years the Indian services firms had grown by selling their engineers' time. Now they were being asked, in writing, to promise that the time would shrink.



# Part V: The break (2022-2026)

# Chapter 19. The machines learn to code (2022-2026)

## One sentence, three years

In June 2024 Infosys filed its annual report on Form 20-F with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, a document in which a misleading statement carries legal risk. Among its risk factors, in a passage about wages and productivity, was a new sentence: 'Due to the attention created by the code generation capabilities of AI technologies, clients have demanded higher commitments around productivity improvements.'[1] The sentence came back the next year and the year after, changed each time in small ways, and the changes trace the arrival of the problem. In the report filed on 1 July 2025 one phrase changed: clients 'have started demanding higher commitments around productivity improvements'.[2] In the report filed on 15 June 2026, for the year to March 2026, the cause was widened. The sentence now began 'Due to the attention created by evolving AI technologies', and the clients were still demanding.[3]

The sentences on either side explain what the demand meant. Before it, in both later reports, Infosys said that 'due to competitive market conditions and pricing pressures, we are committing to higher productivity improvements in our contracts with our clients'. After it, the company warned that failing to deliver those improvements 'may impact our profitability'.[4] Read together, the three sentences describe a mechanism. Clients hear that machines can write code. They ask for contracts that assume fewer hours of human work. The vendor promises the savings in advance and carries the loss if they do not arrive.

The 2026 report added a passage that had not appeared before. In its review of operations, Infosys described what its clients were doing: 'large technology platforms continue to expand their service layers, while clients themselves are selectively insourcing capabilities as AI improves productivity and reduces dependency on external labor-based models'.[5] An 'external labor-based model' is a fair description of what Infosys had sold since its founding in 1981. Here the company named, in a regulatory filing, the threat this chapter is about.

Its competitors' filings moved the same way. Wipro's report for the year to March 2026 added a risk factor: 'AI-driven automation, efficiency gains and increased client self-service may reduce demand for certain services we provide and may adversely affect pricing, margins, service levels or the mix of services delivered.'[6] It listed 'outcome-based pricing', meaning charging for a result delivered rather than for the hours spent on it, among the strategies firms were likely to adopt, and predicted that 'Hiring will shift from volume to skills, emphasizing AI fluency, domain expertise, and productivity-based workforce models'.[7] Cognizant, which is registered in the United States but employs most of its staff in India, wrote in its annual report for 2025 that 'demand for some services that we currently perform for our clients may be reduced' as AI evolved.[8] All three also told investors, at length, that AI would create new kinds of work. But risk factors are written for lawyers rather than customers, which is why they are useful here. By 2026 three of the largest employers of Indian software engineers had told an American regulator that the machines threatened the volume of work they sold.

That volume was the whole of the bargain this book has followed. For forty years the Indian software industry had sold the time of people who write code, priced by the hour and the head, and the colleges had grown to supply the heads. This chapter covers the years in which machines learned to write usable code, from 2022, when the pandemic hiring boom ended, to the autumn of 2026. When code became cheap to produce, both halves of the arrangement were exposed at once. The evidence for what happened is recent, thin in places and contested on the point that matters most, which is cause.

## The tools on the desk

The same filings record which tools the engineers were given. Infosys's report for the year to March 2025 named one, GitHub Copilot, and claimed that Infosys was 'among the top GSIs in adoption', a GSI being a global systems integrator.[9] A year later the list was longer: 'We utilize leading AI solutions like Github Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code and Devin to name a few.'[10] All four are commercial products that use AI models to write or change code. Claude Code is made by Anthropic, which also makes the AI model that assisted with the research and drafting of this book, and the reader should weigh this chapter with that in mind; here it is treated like the other three, as a tool a company reported using. Infosys said it had 'infused AI throughout our software development lifecycle' and used its own platforms for what it called 'Agentic software engineering', meaning software agents that carry out programming tasks over several steps.[11]

Wipro gave a count. In the year to March 2025, 'over 20,000 associates' in its delivery teams were 'leveraging AI developer tools, boosting our overall productivity'.[12] A year later the same sentence said 'over 60,000'.[13] Wipro reported more than 240,000 employees at 31 March 2026, so on its own figures about a quarter of its workforce was using such tools; how the productivity was measured, the filing does not say.[14] Cognizant gave its staff 'leading vibe coding tools', meaning tools that let a person describe a program in ordinary language and have a model write it, and reported that they had produced 'more than 30,000 prototypes'.[15] The phrase thus entered an American annual report as a way of training a workforce of whom about 256,900, out of roughly 351,600 at the end of 2025, were in India.[16]

Every company also claimed that its workforce was being trained in AI, and none defined what training meant. The largest claim came from the National Association of Software and Service Companies (Nasscom), the industry's lobby group, which said that 2 million of the industry's 5.95 million direct employees had been 'upskilled in AI'.[17] The companies' own counts ran into the hundreds of thousands.[18] They show what the firms wanted investors and clients to believe, which was that their workforces were being remade rather than replaced.

## The price of an hour

By 2026 the business press had a name for what Infosys had set out in 2024. Payal Ganguly's report for *Forbes India* on 11 May 2026 called it 'AI-led deflation, characterised by a productivity-based pricing structure demanded by customers and the passing on of productivity benefits to enterprises'.[19] She quoted HCL Technologies' (HCLTech's) chief executive, C. Vijayakumar, on his company's earnings call: 'A $100 million deal would be much less today, maybe $80 million, just on a rough ballpark.' Winning the same revenue, he added, took 'at least 25-30 percent more effort'.[20] K. Krithivasan, chief executive of Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), was more hopeful on his own call: 'Our expectation is AI will be net accretive.'[21] Salil Parekh of Infosys said that his company was signing multi-year deals priced on productivity.[22]

Who gained from a saved hour depended on the contract. A time-and-materials contract names the people and their rates; a fixed-price contract names only the price. Under the first, a saving in hours passes to the client, because the client pays for fewer hours. Under the second, the vendor keeps it, which is why Infosys had set out before 2002 to win more fixed-price work (Chapter 11). The evidence from 2026 suggests that both forms were being squeezed. Clients would not pay for hours that a machine could save, and under the productivity commitments Infosys described, the vendors had to promise the savings before they had made them.

There was a third form, and it was growing. Global capability centres (GCCs), the Indian offices that multinational companies own and staff themselves, employed about 2.36 million people by the year to March 2026, by the count of Nasscom and the consultancy Zinnov, and their revenue was already close to what the two had projected for 2030.[23] Those figures come from an industry body and from a consultancy that sells its services to GCCs, and they are not measured on the same basis as Nasscom's totals for the industry. What they suggest is a shift in who employed India's engineers. The client was moving its work in house, and the house was often in Bengaluru (Bangalore until 2014) or Hyderabad. That was the 'selectively insourcing' of which Infosys had warned, seen from the other side. A parent company that does the work in its own centre keeps whatever saving the tools produce, where the client of a services firm has to bargain for it.

This, in the book's reading, is where the bargain began to come apart. A firm that sells hours earns more only by selling more of them, which is why the industry had to keep hiring. A tool that shortens the hour does not merely make the firm more efficient. It hands the client a reason to buy fewer hours, and a captive centre a reason not to buy them from outside at all. Writing and testing code had passed early the test that the economist Alan Blinder proposed in 2006 (Chapter 14): work that can be sent down a wire without losing quality is exposed, however skilled the person who does it, and that is how so much of it came to India. The filings of 2024 to 2026 show the same work being repriced in the light of what machines could do.

## The class of 2026

The colleges asked a simpler question: would the entry-level job survive? The evidence is mixed, and it is easy to read too much into it.

At Infosys, offers of employment, which include experienced hires as well as graduates, had collapsed to 26,975 in the year to March 2024, when 2,436,929 people applied, about 90 applicants for each offer. They recovered to 83,207 and then 87,286 in the next two years, while applications rose to 4,457,748 and 5,884,480, about 54 and 67 for each offer on the book's calculation.[24] In April 2026 *Business Standard* reported that TCS had given 'a fresher hiring number of 25,000' for the year to March 2027, against the roughly 40,000 that the paper said TCS usually took from engineering colleges.[25] Krithivasan's own words, to the Press Trust of India earlier that month, put the figure in a different light: 'We have made 25,000 offers for freshers in FY27. Clarity on demand will lead to more hiring.'[26] On his account the 25,000 were offers already made, not a ceiling, and TCS had reportedly hired more than 44,000 freshers the year before.[27]

The other firms were uneven. Infosys said in April 2026 that it would add 20,000 freshers in the coming year, keeping its annual target, a plan for graduate hires that measures something different from its offers of all kinds.[28] Wipro's chief human resources officer, Saurabh Govil, declined to give a figure: 'Hiring will be as per demand.'[29] HCLTech's chief people officer, Ramachandran Sundararajan, said: 'Given the current environment, it is difficult to provide a number.'[30] Krithivasan added, in the newspaper's paraphrase, that freshers take 'up to nine months to come on the floor, while a lateral can deliver immediately'.[31] The complaint that graduates arrive unready is as old as the industry. What may have changed was that some of the junior work a fresher used to learn on was the work for which the companies now described AI tools. Infosys's 2024 report spoke of 'a code assistant' for 'tasks like coding, testing, and documentation'.[32] This is the kind of documented, standardised work Chapter 11 described, and the kind the tools were built for.

The dates, though, warn against a simple story. Infosys's offers had already collapsed in the year to March 2024, and the delayed joining dates began in 2022.[33] Yet the company's first annual report to mention the 'code generation capabilities of AI technologies' was the one filed in June 2024, and the first coding tool it named in a filing, GitHub Copilot, appeared in the report filed in July 2025; Wipro's first count of staff using such tools covered the year to March 2025.[34][35] On the companies' own records, the slowdown in graduate hiring began before AI coding tools were a reported part of their work. *Business Standard* itself blamed the conflict in West Asia for the gloomy outlook of 2026.[36] On the evidence available AI is at most one of several possible causes, alongside the end of the pandemic boom, weak demand from clients and geopolitics. On this book's reading, what the tools changed was the reason to expect the rung to come back.

What the slowdown felt like on a campus is documented by Yashraj Sharma of *Rest of World*, in a report published on 9 December 2025. Rishabh Mishra joined the Indian Institute of Information Technology, Design and Manufacturing in Jabalpur in 2022 with what the reporter called 'the most predictable dream in global tech': to 'study computer science, write code, and one day make it to Silicon Valley'.[37] His course was due to end in May 2026. Among his 400 classmates, according to the article, fewer than 25 per cent had secured job offers.[38] 'It is really bad out there,' Mishra said.[39] Some classmates were thinking of further study before looking for work. He was doubtful: 'But after one year, if you return to the job market, your degree is even more irrelevant.'[40] Another student named in the report, Nishant Kaushik, who had studied computer science at a well-ranked college in eastern India, had decided to look for jobs in sales or marketing instead.[41] *Rest of World* framed its report around AI and cited a finding by the consultancy EY that Indian IT services firms had cut entry-level roles by 20-25 per cent because of automation and AI.[42] One college in one year is a single data point. It is also a real student, in his own words, at the moment the argument about AI reached the campuses.

Those who did get jobs found that the starting salary had barely moved. Udit Hinduja of *ThePrint* reported in September 2025 on an unnamed TCS fresher in Ahmedabad who shared a room with three colleagues he had met in training, on a monthly salary of Rs 24,000 (about $270 at the year's average rate). 'I'm lucky that I had some savings to buy a bike, otherwise I would have to walk to work,' he said.[43] Neeti Sharma, chief executive of the staffing firm TeamLease Digital, told the same reporter that starting salaries for science and engineering graduates had been Rs 2-2.5 lakh a year in 2014 and were Rs 3-3.5 lakh (about $3,400-4,000) 'today', 'not even enough to cover inflation over the last decade'.[44] The entry-level hour had always been the cheapest the industry sold. On the argument of this chapter, it was also the one a machine could most easily replace.

## A stall, not a collapse

The fear in 2025 and 2026 was that the machines would empty the offices. The headcount figures do not show that. They show a stall after the boom and bust of the pandemic years.
