Infosys had 317,240 employees at 31 March 2024, 323,578 a year later and 328,594 at 31 March 2026.[45] Wipro reported 'more than' 232,000, 230,000 and 240,000 at the same dates.[46] At Cognizant, voluntary attrition in technology services, the share of staff who chose to leave in a year, fell from 25.6 per cent in 2022 to 15.9 per cent in 2024 and 13.9 per cent in 2025, figures consistent with fewer outside offers.[47] Nasscom estimated 135,000 net additions across the industry in the year to March 2026, taking direct employees to 5.95 million, while revenue rose 6.1 per cent to $315 billion: the non-linearity with which the prologue began.[48] Nasscom's figures are an industry body's estimates and are revised.[49]

TCS was the exception. Avik Das of *Business Standard*, compiling the companies' results in April 2026, reported that the five largest firms' combined headcount fell by 6,981 in the year to March 2026, after rising by 12,718 the year before. TCS's net headcount fell by 23,460, while Infosys, Wipro and HCLTech added people.[50] Part of that fall was the result of a decision announced on a Sunday the summer before.

## July 2025

On Sunday 27 July 2025 TCS said, in a statement printed by *Business Standard*, that it was 'on a journey to become a future-ready organisation'. Its initiatives included 'deploying AI at scale for our clients and ourselves' and 'realigning our workforce model'. 'We will be releasing associates from the organisation whose deployment may not be feasible,' it said. 'This will impact about 2 per cent of our global workforce, primarily in the middle and the senior grades, over the course of the year.'[51] The paper put the number at about 12,260 of TCS's 613,069 employees.[52] The company said it would provide, in *Deccan Herald*'s paraphrase, 'appropriate benefits, outplacement, counselling, and support' to those affected.[53]

Krithivasan explained the decision to the business website Moneycontrol. Reuters quoted him: 'This is not because of AI giving some 20% productivity gains. We are not doing that. This is driven by where there is a skill mismatch, or, where we think that we have not been able to deploy someone.'[54] *Outlook Business*, relaying the same interview, reported him saying that 'Some people, especially at senior levels, find it difficult to transition to tech-heavy roles', and that 'This is not a question of demand. It is about us being future-ready.'[55] He described a move away from 'waterfall' project management, in which a project passes through fixed stages under layers of managers, towards agile methods that needed fewer such layers.[56] Shritama Bose and Ujjaini Dutta of Reuters Breakingviews wrote that he was seeking to play down fears of an 'AI-induced jobs armageddon', and offered a reading of their own: TCS's headcount had risen 36 per cent since 2020, and while revenue per employee had risen 20 per cent, costs per employee had risen by a quarter.[57] On this reading the cut was about cost after over-hiring. The IT & ITES Democratic Employees Association (IIDEA), a union, offered a third: 'What we are witnessing is not transformation but cost-cutting masquerading as future-readiness.' It accused TCS of targeting experienced, better-paid staff.[58]

The three explanations are not exclusive, and AI could sit behind any of them. A skill mismatch can arise because clients want AI work; costs matter more when clients demand AI-driven discounts. No published record shows which roles were cut, or why, in enough detail to decide between them. Whether AI caused the TCS cuts remains an open question.

## The bench

What the cut felt like is known from reporting in Bengaluru, almost entirely through employees who would not give their names. Anisha Reddy of *South First* reported on 2 August 2025 that more than 100 TCS employees had approached unions in the previous week.[59] Lenil Babu, secretary of the Karnataka State IT/ITeS Employees Union (KITU), told her: 'So far, we have filed complaints with the Additional Labour Commissioner of Karnataka on behalf of 15 employees who were already let go. But another 100 have approached us after being put on the bench.'[60]

The bench is where an engineer waits, still employed and paid, between projects. In the industry's long boom, time on the bench was a normal part of a career and a cost the firms absorbed, because a firm that sells hours needs people ready to bill. *South First* reported that a new TCS policy, in force from 12 June 2025, allowed an employee at most 35 days a year without a project and required at least 225 billable days.[61] The reporter saw an email sent to one employee: 'Your prolonged un-allocation without any productive assignment is a matter of concern to the company and the company views this matter very seriously.'[62] The Nascent Information Technology Employees Senate (NITES), a union based in Pune, said the policy 'frames lack of allocation as a personal failure of the employee'.[63] TCS told *South First* that the restructuring was being planned with due care so that service to clients would not be affected.[64]

Korah Abraham of *The News Minute* reported on 7 August 2025 how the resignation meetings worked, again from anonymous accounts. A Bengaluru employee in middle management alleged: 'They offered three months' pay as an incentive to resign. But if someone refuses, they're told they'll be terminated without compensation, and won't receive a relieving letter.'[65] A relieving letter is the document an Indian employer gives a departing employee, and the next employer usually asks to see it. Two employees said they had been asked to switch off their phones and leave them on the table before meeting human resources staff.[66] A woman who had resigned said she would have fought the case if she could have afforded to: 'I come from a financially poor background.'[67] One employee estimated that more than 300 people had been made to resign from a single Bengaluru campus in a week.[68]

TCS denied that it had forced people out. When NITES wrote to the chief minister of Maharashtra in the autumn, claiming that about 2,500 employees in Pune had been made to resign or abruptly removed, the company replied: 'The misinformation shared here is inaccurate and purposefully mischievous. Only a limited number of employees have been affected by our recent initiative to realign skills in our organisation.' Those affected, it said, 'have been provided due care and severance'.[69]

KITU had taken its case to the state. It filed an industrial dispute on 29 July, two days after the announcement, accusing TCS of illegal mass retrenchment. Its argument was that the company was pushing people to resign so as to avoid the government approval that the Industrial Disputes Act requires before a firm with more than 100 employees retrenches workers.[70] Karnataka's labour minister, Santosh Lad, told reporters that his department was looking into the union's letter, but added: 'We cannot act in a hurry.'[71] On Wednesday 6 August two managers from TCS's human resources department sat down at the Labour Office in Bengaluru across from three KITU officials, among them its general secretary, Suhas Adiga, and its president, V.J.K. Nair. The Additional Labour Commissioner, G. Manjunath, presided as conciliation officer. The meeting ended without agreement, and a further round was set for 8 September.[72]

The company's own figures, two months later, sharpened the dispute. On the investor call after its results for the quarter to September, TCS's new chief human resources officer, Sudeep Kunnumal, said that 'the 20,000 headcount (reduction) is a factor of voluntary and involuntary attrition'; and, as *Deccan Herald* reported, he hinted that the involuntary part was 6,000 employees who had been 'released'. Headcount had fallen from 613,069 at the end of June to 593,314 at the end of September.[73] KITU and two other unions read that as a confession: 'By openly accepting that it has retrenched 6,000 employees, TCS has admitted to a violation of the Industrial Disputes Act'.[74] The company called the departures realignment; the unions called them retrenchment by another name. The word that decided which law applied was the one the two sides could not agree on.

## The regulator's answer

The All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE), the regulator that approves engineering colleges, responded with announcements. On 23 December 2024 it declared 2025 the 'Year of Artificial Intelligence', with a campaign called 'AI for All', AI laboratories and workshops for teachers across what it said were more than 14,000 colleges with 40 million students.[75] On 6 June 2025 its chairman, T.G. Sitharam, told the Press Trust of India that AI would be brought into the model curricula of every branch of engineering, information technology and management. 'A committee of experts has been constituted to suggest necessary revisions in the model curriculums,' he said.[76] No circular making AI part of every branch, and no revised model curriculum, has been located. The regulator announced the change; whether the colleges carried it out is not on record.

## The state builds a model

The Indian state answered the AI question as it had answered identity and payments, by building. The IndiaAI Mission was launched in March 2024 with an outlay of Rs 10,372 crore (Rs 103.7 billion, about $1.25 billion at the year's average rate), for computing capacity, data, models and research.[77] It selected twelve organisations and consortia to build foundation models, the large general-purpose models on which applications are built.[78] The first was Sarvam AI, founded in August 2023 by Vivek Raghavan and Pratyush Kumar, both graduates of the IITs.[79] On 26 April 2025, according to the trade journal *tele.net*, Sarvam was chosen to build 'an open source 120 billion parameter' model (parameters are the adjustable values in a model, a rough measure of its size).[80] The minister for electronics and information technology, Ashwini Vaishnaw, said: 'We are confident that Sarvam's models will be competitive with global models.'[81]

At the India AI Impact Summit in February 2026 Sarvam unveiled two models, Sarvam-30B and Sarvam-105B, the larger of them smaller than the 120 billion parameters announced in 2025.[82] Debarghya Sil of *Inc42* judged the models competitive in their size class and strong on Indian languages, but behind the frontier models of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta in 'raw reasoning depth'.[83] Raghavan called the launches a 'significant first step'.[84] The state was not trying to replace the services industry with a model of its own. It was trying to make sure that the country that had supplied so much of the world's programming labour owned some of the machines that were starting to do it.

## More coders than ever

In October 2025 GitHub, the code-hosting service, projected in its annual *Octoverse* report, as *The Register* reported it, that India would have 57.5 million or more developers on the platform by 2030, overtaking the United States, and said that 80 per cent of new users began using its AI coding assistant in their first week.[85] A GitHub account is not a job, and the projection is not a count of engineers. But the two numbers belong together. More Indians were writing code than at any point in the history this book has traced, and most of the newest of them were writing it with a machine at their elbow. The industry built on selling their hours had told its regulator that clients would buy fewer of them. For half a century the problem had been how to make enough engineers. Now it was who would pay for their time.

## As of October 2026

The account above rests on documents that will date quickly. What follows records where the numbers, the forecasts and the American visa stood when the book went to press.

In the year to March 2026 two of the largest firms shrank in dollar terms. According to *Forbes India*, TCS's revenue fell 0.5 per cent in US dollars and Wipro's 0.32 per cent.[86] At the same time the companies reported growing AI revenue: TCS an annualised figure above $2.3 billion by the end of the year, HCLTech $620 million of what it called 'Advanced AI' revenue, and Infosys $275 million in a single quarter.[87] Nasscom made its first estimate of the industry's AI revenue, at $10-12 billion.[88] Each company defines AI revenue its own way, so the figures cannot be added up or compared, and Gaurav Vasu of the research firm UnearthInsight put it at under 5-7 per cent of the top five firms' revenue.[89] Vijayakumar spoke of a deflationary effect of 3 to 5 per cent on HCLTech's guidance for the year to March 2027.[90] The brokers were blunter. A report by Motilal Oswal Financial Services, dated 4 May 2026, estimated that 12-15 per cent of the sector's revenue faced 'direct AI-driven displacement risk', and said: 'The cost of delivering an outcome has fallen sharply; these savings are currently being extracted almost entirely by enterprise buyers through productivity demands and vendor price pressure.'[91] Kotak Securities expected the industry's revenue growth to stay 'range-bound at 3 percent'.[92]

The route to America narrowed at the same time. On 19 September 2025 President Donald Trump signed Proclamation 10973, which said the H-1B programme, the visa that had carried Indian engineers to client sites since the 1990s, had been 'deliberately exploited to replace, rather than supplement, American workers', and that 'Information technology (IT) firms in particular have prominently manipulated the H-1B system'.[93] From 21 September, for twelve months, it barred the entry of H-1B workers whose petitions were not 'accompanied or supplemented by a payment of $100,000'.[94] The traffic was already falling: the National Foundation for American Policy, a pro-immigration research group, counted 4,573 initial-employment approvals in the US fiscal year 2025 for the top seven Indian-based companies, 70 per cent fewer than in 2015.[95] On 18 September 2026 Proclamation 11069 extended the restriction for another year, and claimed that 'the largest IT staffing and outsourcing firms' had cut 'their combined H-1B registrations from 24,946 to 2,055, a 92 percent decrease'.[96] Those are a party's figures, offered to justify the policy.

The courts then stopped the fee without striking down either proclamation. On 8 June 2026 Judge Leo T. Sorokin of the federal district court in Massachusetts, in a suit brought by twenty states, held that the agencies' policy 'imposes a tax on H-1B petitions without the requisite delegation by Congress' and vacated it.[97] The First Circuit refused to suspend his order pending appeal.[98] A federal court in Washington, DC, had upheld the fee in 2025, and that ruling too was on appeal.[99] On 30 September 2026 Judge Haywood S. Gilliam Jr. in the Northern District of California barred the agencies from enforcing their policies under both proclamations until they had gone through the formal process of public notice and comment.[100] By mid-October the $100,000 could not be collected, three appeals were pending, and the Department of Homeland Security had proposed a fee of about $103,000 through the process the courts said had been skipped.[101]

The factory, meanwhile, had not stopped. By TCS's quarterly results as reported, about 14,000 freshers joined in the April-June quarter of 2026 and about 10,000 in July-September, and its headcount had risen for three quarters in a row, to 598,056.[102] Its chief human resources officer put the policy in five words: 'We are hiring for demand'.[103] In the long boom the firms had carried the bench as the cost of always being ready to bill. Now the largest of them was hiring only for the work in hand.


# Epilogue. India in 2035

Rishabh Mishra's course at the Indian Institute of Information Technology, Design and Manufacturing in Jabalpur was due to end in May 2026. He had joined in 2022 to study computer science, write code and, in the words of the *Rest of World* reporter who told his story, 'one day make it to Silicon Valley'. By December 2025, according to the article, fewer than a quarter of his 400 classmates had job offers. 'It is really bad out there,' he said.[1] Earlier that year, at the other end of the same pipeline, the trainee whom the prologue called Gayatri had been let go from Infosys's training campus in Mysuru, four months after a joining date she had waited nearly two years for. 'They wasted two and a half years of my career,' she said.[2] Between them they stand at the two ends of the book's present: a graduate who cannot get in, and a recruit who got in and was sent home.

What their degrees will be worth by 2035 is the question this epilogue takes up. The furthest official projection is a NITI Aayog report of October 2025, *Roadmap for Job Creation in the AI Economy*, prepared by the Indian government's policy think-tank with the National Association of Software and Service Companies (Nasscom), the industry's lobby group, and the consultancy BCG.[3] It offers two endpoints for 2031. In what it calls a business-as-usual case, 'the headcount in the tech services sector could go down from 7.5 to 8 million in 2023 to 6 million by 2031'. If India acted on the report's advice, the total 'could swell to 10 million'.[4] The numbers need caution. On one page the report calls its base the employment of the tech services industry, and on another a 'total tech workforce' that includes 'tech jobs in other sectors', which is not the industry headcount that Nasscom publishes.[5] And the report was written to argue for a new national programme of AI teaching and retraining, so its two paths are framed to show the cost of not adopting it.[6] That makes the numbers advocacy, published under a government's name and co-written by the industry that would benefit from the spending. The 2035 of this epilogue's title is therefore the book's own horizon, about ten years from the time of writing.[7]

## What the history shows

The book began with a working argument. India's software profession, it proposed, was shaped less by technology than by three constraints: scarce foreign exchange, a surplus of English-educated engineers, and an American labour market hungry for them. The result priced engineering by the hour and grew by adding people, and AI attacks exactly that model. On the evidence of the chapters, the verdict is mixed.

The first constraint holds best. In the 1970s the Department of Electronics allowed computers to be imported 'exclusively meant for software export'.[8] The policy of 1986 still required an importer to 'earn 250% of the cost of the imported computer within 4 years', and the budget of July 1991 extended a tax concession to software so that 'the exports of this industry should register rapid growth'.[9][10] Selling programmers' time abroad was the export the rules made easiest. But scarcity built skills as well as exporting labour: because software could not be imported, in the account of V. Rajaraman, the historian of Indian computing, Indian hardware firms wrote their own, and 'a large number of systems programmers in India became experts in UNIX development and usage'.[11] And a trade justified by dollars kept fewer of them than its headline figures suggested: the development scholar Richard Heeks put net earnings at around 40 per cent of the gross.[12]

The second constraint is where the strongest counter-evidence lies. In the early 1990s the World Bank found not a surplus but a shortage: 'the demand for trained software personnel far outstrips the supply'.[13] The surplus came later, and it was built: on one reading, by decades of public investment in science and engineering in Bangalore (Bengaluru since 2014), and then by private colleges that multiplied the supply until, by 2016-17, on an analysis of the regulator's data by the education charity Avanti Fellows, 49.5 per cent of approved undergraduate engineering seats had no student in them.[14][15] On this book's reading, the surplus was less a starting condition than something the industry's demand called into being.

The third constraint is real, but it did not stay a demand for people. The economists Gaurav Khanna and Nicolas Morales built a model in which Indian students enrolled in engineering 'to gain employment in the rapidly growing US IT industry via the H-1B visa program', with those the visa cap kept out 'enabling the growth of an Indian IT sector'.[16] The share of work done at the client's site then fell from 90 per cent in 1988 to 56 per cent in 2000.[17] The constraints set the price of the work; the wire decided how much of it could be done in India.

The middle of the argument is the best supported. Heeks wrote in 1998 that in custom software services 'earnings are directly proportional to the number of people working in the industry', and the pyramid, the bench and the training campuses were built on that arithmetic.[18] Even in the year to March 2008, fixed-price projects brought Infosys only 31 per cent of its services revenue.[19] Whether AI ends that model is the last clause, and the one the rest of this epilogue weighs.

## The book's judgement

What follows is the book's own argument, built from the evidence of its chapters. It is that the hourly bargain is ending as a way to grow; that what replaces it depends on who keeps the hour a machine saves; and that the cost falls first on the bottom rung.

The first part rests on the companies' own words. In three successive annual reports to the American regulator, from 2024 to 2026, Infosys said that clients were demanding higher commitments around productivity because of what AI could do, and that it was promising those improvements in its contracts in advance.[20] In 2026 it added that clients were 'selectively insourcing capabilities as AI improves productivity and reduces dependency on external labor-based models'.[21] Wipro predicted that 'Hiring will shift from volume to skills', and TCS's head of human resources said in October 2026 that the company was 'hiring for demand'.[22] Nasscom's own figures show the result: in the year to March 2026 the industry's revenue rose 6.1 per cent and its jobs 2.3 per cent.[23] For fifty years revenue and headcount had risen together because revenue was, roughly, heads multiplied by a billing rate. A gap between them is small, but it is the bargain coming apart. It does not mean the offices empty. By 2026 headcount had stalled, not collapsed. It means that growth no longer requires the factory to keep hiring at the old pace.

The second part is the pricing mechanism the book has traced since the Y2K years. Under time-and-materials billing a saved hour belongs to the client, who simply pays for fewer of them. Under a fixed price the vendor keeps what it saves, which is why Infosys told investors in 1999 that it wanted more fixed-price work and reported in 2002 that the share of such work had risen.[24] In a captive centre owned by the client there is nothing to bargain over: the parent keeps the saving outright (Chapter 15). And a product firm can sell the saving itself. Freshworks, an Indian-built software company with most of its staff in India, told investors that its Freddy AI Agent 'offers always-on, autonomous, personalized resolutions to customer and employee queries', which is much of what India's help desks had been paid by the hour to do.[25] Each of these owners would produce a different industry. In 2026 the evidence pointed one way. The vendors had promised the savings before making them, deals for the same work were worth, by HCLTech's chief executive's rough estimate, about a fifth less, and a broker's report said the savings were 'currently being extracted almost entirely by enterprise buyers through productivity demands and vendor price pressure'.[26] For now, the client owns the saving.

The companies' answer deserves its strongest statement. They argue that AI creates more work than it removes, and they had numbers to show for it. By the end of the year to March 2026 TCS reported AI revenue at an annualised rate above $2.3 billion, HCLTech reported $620 million for the year and Infosys $275 million in a single quarter, and Nasscom made a first estimate of the industry's AI revenue at $10-12 billion. 'Our expectation is AI will be net accretive,' TCS's chief executive said.[27] Each firm defines AI revenue its own way, and one analyst put it at under 5-7 per cent of the five largest firms' revenue.[28] The new work is real. But on the evidence so far it is small beside the old work being repriced, and Wipro expected the industry to move towards 'outcome-based pricing', charging for a result rather than for the hours spent on it.[22] New work sold that way is the point of the judgement, not an exception to it.

The third part follows from the second. The hours a client is most willing to stop paying for are the junior ones: the coding, testing and documentation that the book's chapters followed from the Y2K years, broken into documented steps that any trained graduate could follow. Those are the tasks for which Infosys described its code assistant in 2024, and the tasks the NITI roadmap expects to go first: in an IT services company, it says, AI 'typically translates to a shrinking of entry-level roles involving QA and support'.[29][30] The report illustrates this with invented characters, a junior test engineer in Pune and a support agent in Chennai.[31] The starting salary had barely moved in a decade, and TCS's chief executive said, in a newspaper's paraphrase, that freshers take 'up to nine months to come on the floor, while a lateral can deliver immediately'.[32] Infosys's offers had recovered from their trough, but in the year to March 2026 they were still well under half the 222,500 of the boom year to March 2022.[33] The rung is still there. It is narrower, and the reason to expect it to widen again is weaker than it was.

The machines have been forecast to take this work before, and the forecast was wrong for thirty years. In 1994 the World Bank's study of the Indian industry warned that 'Demand for these skills is likely to be eroded by tools that automate many of these tasks', and added that 'a long-term decline in demand for routine or low-level programmers has been forecasted'.[34] In 1998 Heeks named 'automation from new technology' among the risks to the trade and saw a trap in it: clients sent work offshore only when it was tightly specified, and such projects were 'more amenable to automated software tools'.[35] Instead exports kept growing fast, and by 2026 Nasscom counted 5.95 million direct employees.[36][23] The warnings were wrong because demand absorbed the productivity. Each tool that made an engineer faster made software cheaper, cheaper software found new buyers, and a firm that sold hours could use the saving to win more work. The book's one documented case of the pattern in India is small but exact. When the railway booking office in New Delhi was computerised in 1986, Rajaraman records, there was 'no reduction of staff; in fact there was an increase as more counters were operated with more clerks working simultaneously'.[37] On the book's reading, the machine raised each clerk's output and demand that the queues had held down absorbed it.

For that to happen again, three things would have to be true. Demand for software at the new, lower price would have to grow faster than the hours needed for each piece of it fall. The saving would have to stay with someone who reinvests it in hiring, rather than being taken by the client in advance. And the new work would have to reach the firms and the graduates the factory was built to supply. On the evidence of 2026 the first is uncertain: the industry still grew, but HCLTech said winning the same revenue took 'at least 25-30 percent more effort', TCS's and Wipro's revenue fell in dollar terms, and one broker expected growth to stay 'range-bound at 3 percent'.[38] The second points the other way, for as long as the clients keep the saving. The third is partly true: Indian engineers were still being hired in large numbers, but increasingly by the captive centres, which by the year to March 2026 employed about 2.36 million people by an industry count, and the graduates still had to get past a narrower bottom rung.[39] The book's reading is that demand may again absorb much of the productivity, and that Indian engineers may again be employed in large numbers, but not through the bargain that built the factory. Heeks's trap has closed on the hourly vendor, and most tightly at the bottom rung.

## Four things to watch

The four futures that follow are signposts, not forecasts. They are not exclusive, and they are not equally likely. The evidence in this book currently favours the third, in which the client moves in, and the first, in which the pyramid thins, because both follow from the client keeping the saving. It gives least support to the second, which needs the price of each engineer to rise while the price of each deal falls. The fourth is real but small.

## The thinning pyramid

An Indian services firm has long been described as a pyramid, with a wide base of junior engineers billed at rates well above their pay. In this future the base shrinks. The firms survive, smaller at the bottom and older on average, and the colleges keep producing graduates trained for a base that is narrowing, so that the prologue's waiting fresher becomes the normal case. The evidence for it is the pricing evidence above. The supply side had begun to adjust before the tools arrived: by the Avanti Fellows analysis, approved undergraduate intake peaked at about 1.7 million seats in 2014-15 and fell to about 1.25 million by 2021-22, with roughly a third of the seats left empty.[40] The counter-evidence is that by 2026 the pyramid had not visibly thinned: Infosys's offers had tripled from their trough, TCS was still taking freshers by the tens of thousands, and Nasscom still reported net hiring, while the delayed joining dates began in 2022, two years before Infosys's filings first mentioned AI code generation.[41][42] The signposts are fresher offers as a share of headcount at the five largest firms falling year after year, revenue per employee rising while headcount stays flat, and the share of engineering graduates in engineering jobs falling, which is why the missing placement data matter.

## The diamond

In this future the shape becomes a diamond: fewer people at the bottom and a wide, better-paid middle that directs and checks what the tools produce. The image is the staffing executive Kamal Karanth's, in a Reuters Breakingviews column's paraphrase.[43] The NITI roadmap expects 'the price-per-FTE for the industry to grow 5-8% annually over the next few years', FTE meaning one full-time person's working time.[44] The weight of the evidence is against it for now. Price per worker and value per deal measure different things, but the deflation reported seven months after NITI's estimate points the other way, and nothing published by 2026 settles which is right.[45] For education this future is kinder but harder: it needs fewer graduates who can follow a specification and more who can judge whether a system is right. The signposts would be revenue per employee and average pay rising together, lateral hiring outpacing campus hiring, and a revised curriculum actually taught: the All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE), the regulator, declared 2025 its 'Year of Artificial Intelligence', but no revised model curriculum had appeared by the time of writing.[46]

## The client moves in

In this future multinationals stop buying Indian engineers' time from Indian vendors and employ the engineers themselves, in global capability centres (GCCs), the Indian offices that a foreign company owns and staffs. It has a long history, from the software design centre that Texas Instruments, by its own account, began operating in Bangalore in 1985 to the centres of Chapter 15.[47] It is the future the evidence most clearly shows arriving. By the year to March 2026, on Nasscom and Zinnov's count, GCC revenue was already close to what the two had projected for 2030; Infosys listed clients 'setting up or expanding their own GCC in India' as a risk; and Karnataka set a target of 500 new GCCs by 2029.[39][48][49] Indian engineers keep their jobs but change employers, and the national champions matter less. The counter-evidence is about the numbers themselves: every GCC figure comes from Nasscom and from Zinnov, a consultancy that sells advice to GCCs, and Nasscom has restated its counts before.[50] The signposts would be GCC headcount growing while the services firms' stays flat, services firms earning more from building and running centres for clients, and states beyond Karnataka adopting their own policies under the national framework that the 2025-26 Union Budget promised.[51]

## The builder state

In this future barriers abroad and ambitions at home turn the industry inward. The H-1B route was contested by 2026: a $100,000 fee proclaimed in September 2025, the administration's claim of a 92 per cent fall in the largest outsourcing firms' registrations, and courts that had stopped the fee being collected without striking down the proclamations.[52] The Indian firms' approved petitions had begun to fall before the fee, by the count of the National Foundation for American Policy, a pro-immigration research group.[53] At home the state that had built Aadhaar, the biometric identity system, and UPI, the payments network, had launched the IndiaAI Mission and backed Sarvam's first foundation models, and Nasscom expected domestic revenue to grow faster than the industry as a whole.[54][55] The counter-evidence is serious. *Inc42* judged that Sarvam's models trailed the leading foreign ones in 'raw reasoning depth', and the NITI report records that India's share of granted AI patents fell from 8-10 per cent in 2010 to under 5 per cent in 2023.[56][57] Building identity and payments systems was a feat of engineering and organisation; building frontier AI needs far more capital. The signposts would be spending on AI sustained beyond one budget cycle, Indian-language models in use in state services, and a rising share of graduates hired by domestic product firms and public bodies. GitHub's projection of Indian developers on its platform counts accounts on one company's service, not jobs, but a rising number of Indians writing code for Indian users would show up there first.[58]

## Reading the signposts

Several of these signposts are numbers that India does not collect well. AICTE's data on graduates placed in jobs are unusable, by the Avanti Fellows analysis; Nasscom's headcount is an industry body's estimate; GCC counts come from parties that sell to GCCs; AI revenue has no common definition.[59] Projections in this industry have also been overtaken within a few years: Nasscom and Zinnov's GCC projection for 2030 was nearly reached by 2026, and NITI's rising price per engineer was contradicted by reported deflation seven months later.[60][61] A reader in 2030 who wants to know which future is arriving will need, first, an independent count of software employment, a placement series for engineering graduates, and revenue per employee for the large firms on comparable terms.

## The joining date

The book began with a joining date that kept moving. For Gayatri the date came after nearly two years, and the job lasted four months. She told the reporter it had been her dream job.[62] For Rishabh Mishra and his classmates in Jabalpur, the reporting ends before any date. Some of them were thinking of further study instead. Mishra was doubtful: 'after one year, if you return to the job market, your degree is even more irrelevant'.[63]

His sentence is about education as much as about jobs. For half a century the engineering degree in India was a ticket to a particular kind of work: billable hours, learned first on a company training campus and then sold to a client by the month. The colleges, the entrance examinations, the coaching towns and the company campuses were built around that ticket. If the book's judgement is right, the ticket will still buy work in 2035, but less often at the bottom, more often from a client's own centre, and on terms set by whoever keeps the hour the machine saves. The engineer factory was built on purpose, by the state and the companies and millions of families, in answer to the questions of its time. The question for the next ten years is what a joining date means when the factory's product is no longer hours.

This timeline lists 162 dated events that the chapters describe, from the founding of the Indian Statistical Institute in 1931 to the autumn of 2026. Each entry gives the date as the chapters state it, a short description, the chapters in which the event appears, and the source IDs from the book's source register, where full references are given. Where the sources disagree on a date, the entry follows the chapter and notes the other date. Indian fiscal years run from April to March and are written FY1997-98. Figures from Nasscom, the industry's lobby group, from Zinnov, a consultancy that sells to global capability centres, and from companies about themselves are labelled as theirs.

# Data appendix

This appendix describes the 27 data files built for this book. Each section says what a file measures, how it is defined, what years it covers, where the figures come from and what limits them, and gives a short table of selected values. The full files, with a source ID and usually a confidence grade on every row, are in the book's repository under `book/research/data/`, together with notes on gaps (`notes/`) and the scripts that rebuild them (`scripts/`). Source IDs refer to the source register, `book/research/sources.md`. A few conventions apply throughout. Indian fiscal years run from April to March and are written FY2023-24 (the year to 31 March 2024); where a file gives a single year for a fiscal year, it is the calendar year in which the fiscal year ends. Lakh (100,000) and crore (10 million) are converted to international units. Rupee amounts are converted to US dollars at annual average rates from `inr_usd.csv` (calendar years) and `inr_usd_fy.csv` (fiscal years). Real values are deflated as each file states: rupee series by an Indian consumer price index (`cpi_india_cy.csv` or `cpi_iw.csv`), dollar series by the US CPI-U (`us_cpi_u.csv`), with the base year given in the column name. Series with different definitions are kept in separate columns and never joined. Figures from Nasscom, the industry's lobby group, from Zinnov, a consultancy that sells to the global capability centres it counts, from Aspiring Minds, which sells the test it reports on, and from the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP), a pro-immigration group, are marked as such, as are projections.

## Reference series

### Rupees per US dollar, calendar year (`inr_usd.csv`)

**What it measures.** The annual average exchange rate of the Indian rupee against the US dollar, used for every calendar-year conversion in the book.

**Definition and unit.** Rupees per US dollar. Three independent series sit in separate columns: the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Handbook (1987-2025), the Federal Reserve's G.5A noon buying rates (1973-2025) and the Penn World Table (1950-2023). A preferred column takes RBI where available, then the Federal Reserve, then the Penn World Table.

**Coverage.** 1950-2025 (76 years).

**Sources.** S0155, S0320, S0319.

**Caveats.** The series agree within 0.3 per cent in the overlap years checked. The rupee was pegged for much of the period, and the regime dates in the file's header (fixed parity from 1949, devaluation of June 1966, sterling link, basket peg, unified market rate from 1993) are from background knowledge and not yet sourced. Annual averages hide the within-year jumps of 1966 and July 1991.

| Year | Rupees per dollar (preferred) | Series used |
|---|---|---|
| 1950 | 4.76 | Penn World Table |
| 1960 | 4.76 | Penn World Table |
| 1966 | 6.36 | Penn World Table (devaluation in June) |
| 1970 | 7.50 | Penn World Table |
| 1975 | 8.41 | Federal Reserve |
| 1980 | 7.89 | Federal Reserve |
| 1985 | 12.33 | Federal Reserve |
| 1991 | 22.69 | RBI (devaluations of 1 and 3 July) |
| 2000 | 44.94 | RBI |
| 2010 | 45.73 | RBI |
| 2020 | 74.10 | RBI |
| 2025 | 87.17 | RBI |

Full file: `book/research/data/inr_usd.csv`.

### Rupees per US dollar, fiscal year (`inr_usd_fy.csv`)

**What it measures.** The exchange rate averaged over the Indian fiscal year, and the rate at its end, used for converting fiscal-year flows such as export earnings and company revenue.

**Definition and unit.** Rupees per US dollar, annual average and end-year (31 March) rate, as published in RBI Handbook Table 133.

**Coverage.** FY1986-87 to FY2025-26.

**Sources.** S0155.

**Caveats.** The basis changes from official rates (to FY1991-92) to indicative market rates and then RBI and FBIL reference rates. Averages are used for flows, end-year rates for stocks. No RBI series was obtained for fiscal years before FY1986-87.

| Fiscal year | Average | End-year (31 March) |
|---|---|---|
| FY1986-87 | 12.78 | 12.89 |
| FY1991-92 | 24.47 | 31.23 |
| FY1995-96 | 33.45 | 34.35 |
| FY2000-01 | 45.68 | 46.64 |
| FY2005-06 | 44.27 | 44.61 |
| FY2008-09 | 45.99 | 50.95 |
| FY2013-14 | 60.50 | 60.10 |
| FY2015-16 | 65.47 | 66.33 |
| FY2020-21 | 74.23 | 73.50 |
| FY2022-23 | 80.36 | 82.22 |
| FY2024-25 | 84.58 | 85.58 |
| FY2025-26 | 88.31 | 94.65 |

Full file: `book/research/data/inr_usd_fy.csv`.

### Consumer prices in India, calendar year (`cpi_india_cy.csv`)

**What it measures.** A long consumer price index for India, used to deflate calendar-year rupee figures and any figure before FY1993-94.

**Definition and unit.** OECD Main Economic Indicators series for India, index 2015 = 100. A multiplier column converts a nominal rupee value of a given year into 2024 rupees.

**Coverage.** 1957-2024.

**Sources.** S0321 (OECD via FRED).

**Caveats.** The OECD documentation was not read. The series moves with the Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW) rather than the newer CPI Combined, and is treated here as CPI-IW-based. Base changes in the underlying national index (1960, 1982, 2001, 2016) are linked by the OECD by a method not documented in the file.

| Year | Index (2015 = 100) | Multiply by, for 2024 rupees |
|---|---|---|
| 1960 | 1.70 | 91.71 |
| 1970 | 3.09 | 50.41 |
| 1975 | 5.40 | 28.89 |
| 1980 | 6.55 | 23.81 |
| 1985 | 10.23 | 15.25 |
| 1991 | 17.59 | 8.87 |
| 1995 | 25.40 | 6.14 |
| 2000 | 36.57 | 4.27 |
| 2005 | 44.44 | 3.51 |
| 2010 | 67.29 | 2.32 |
| 2015 | 100.00 | 1.56 |
| 2024 | 155.99 | 1.00 |

Full file: `book/research/data/cpi_india_cy.csv`.

### Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers, fiscal year (`cpi_iw.csv`)

**What it measures.** The Labour Bureau's CPI-IW, the index the book's house rules prefer for deflating fiscal-year rupee series.

**Definition and unit.** All-India general index, fiscal-year average, as reproduced in RBI Handbook Table 34. The file gives the value on the base in force each year and a series linked to 2016 = 100 with the published linking factors (4.63 and 2.88), plus a multiplier into FY2025-26 rupees.

**Coverage.** FY1993-94 to FY2025-26.

**Sources.** S0156 via S0155.

**Caveats.** Bases change in FY2005-06 and FY2020-21. Values on the older bases are published as whole numbers, so the linked series carries rounding error of up to about 0.2 per cent. Earlier years are not in this table; `cpi_india_cy.csv` covers them by calendar year.

| Fiscal year | Base | Published value | Linked (2016 = 100) | Multiply by, for FY2025-26 rupees |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY1993-94 | 1982 | 258 | 19.35 | 7.60 |
| FY1995-96 | 1982 | 313 | 23.47 | 6.26 |
| FY2000-01 | 1982 | 444 | 33.30 | 4.41 |
| FY2005-06 | 2001 | 117 | 40.62 | 3.62 |
| FY2008-09 | 2001 | 145 | 50.35 | 2.92 |
| FY2010-11 | 2001 | 180 | 62.50 | 2.35 |
| FY2013-14 | 2001 | 236 | 81.94 | 1.79 |
| FY2015-16 | 2001 | 265 | 92.01 | 1.60 |

## The industry

### Software and services exports (`software_exports.csv`)

**What it measures.** India's export earnings from software and related services, in three families of series that measure different things.

**Definition and unit.** US$ million, nominal, with real columns in 2025 dollars (deflated by `us_cpi_u.csv`). Family one is early gross foreign-exchange earnings from software: Heeks (citing his own research and Dataquest) and Bhatnagar (via Rajaraman). Family two is Nasscom's industry exports, whose scope widens over time from 'software exports' to 'IT-BPO exports' to 'technology industry' exports including business process management and engineering services. Family three is the RBI: a survey of software and IT services exporters (2009-11) and the balance-of-payments 'software services' receipts (from FY2000-01).

**Coverage.** 1980 to FY2025-26, with gaps (no series for FY1998-99 to FY1999-2000 except one Nasscom point). Heeks rows for 1980-1987 are calendar years; all others are fiscal years.

**Sources.** S0085, S0001, S0109, S0107, S0140, S0306, S0106, S0155 (six editions of the RBI Handbook).

**Caveats.** The families are not reconciled and must not be joined. Heeks's figures are gross; net foreign-exchange earnings were estimated at about 40 per cent of gross. Nasscom's figures are a lobby group's and change definition; its FY2025-26 figure is an estimate. The RBI balance-of-payments series is compiled with Nasscom data as a controlling total, so it is not wholly independent. The FY2025-26 RBI value is preliminary. Revisions between RBI editions were small.

**The 1990s: two series compared.** Two series cover the decade of the reforms. One, compiled by Subhash Bhatnagar and reproduced by V. Rajaraman, gives $128 million in 1990-91, $164 million in 1991-92, $225 million in 1992-93, $330 million in 1993-94, $450 million in 1994-95, $734 million in 1995-96, $1,100 million in 1996-97 and $1,759 million in 1997-98 (S0001, p. 48, Table 2). The other, Richard Heeks's, drawn from his own research and the trade magazine *Dataquest*, gives $131.2 million, $173.9 million, $219.8 million, $314.0 million, $480.9 million, $668.0 million, $997.0 million and $1,650.0 million for the same years (S0085, p. 2, Table 1). The two differ by up to about a tenth in some years: Bhatnagar's figure is about 10 per cent higher in 1995-96 and 1996-97, and Heeks's about 7 per cent higher in 1994-95. Both show annual growth of between about a quarter and two-thirds (Bhatnagar 28 to 63 per cent, Heeks 24 to 65 per cent). On Heeks's longer series, growth ran at 29 to 51 per cent a year in 1988-90, slowed to 24 to 33 per cent in 1990-93, and from 1993-94 ran at 39 to 65 per cent, faster than in 1990-93 and at least as fast as in the late 1980s (S0085, p. 2). Heeks notes that these 'headline' figures are gross foreign-exchange earnings (S0085, p. 2); as the caveat above says, net earnings were a much smaller share. The narrative chapters give one figure from these series and cite it.

| Period | Heeks | Bhatnagar | Nasscom (lobby) | RBI survey | RBI balance of payments | RBI BoP, 2025 dollars |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1980 | 4.0 | | | | | |
| 1984 | 25.3 | | | | | |
| FY1990-91 | 131.2 | 128 | | | | |
| FY1995-96 | 668.0 | 734 | | | | |
| FY1997-98 | 1,650.0 | 1,759 | | | | |
| FY1998-99 | | | 2,650 (software exports) | | | |
| FY2000-01 | | | | | 6,341 | 11,771 |
| FY2005-06 | | | | | 23,600 | 38,592 |
| FY2010-11 | | | | 47,600 | 53,100 | 77,784 |
| FY2015-16 | | | | | 74,153 | 100,406 |
| FY2020-21 | | | | | 99,997 | 122,945 |
| FY2025-26 | | | 246,000 (estimate) | | 203,675 (preliminary) | |

The TCS figures for FY2019-20 to FY2023-24 are as reported in the press, not taken from the company's fact sheets; those for FY2020-21, FY2022-23 and FY2023-24 rest on one trade publication (*HR Katha*). ### Global capability centres (`gcc.csv`)

## The H-1B visa

### Cap and policy events (`h1b_policy.csv`)

**What it measures.** The annual cap on new H-1B visas, how many new petitions were issued against it, and the main policy changes.

**Definition and unit.** Petitions, US fiscal years (October-September). Numeric rows are NFAP's table of new petitions issued against the cap; other rows are dated events.

**Coverage.** 1990-2026.

**Sources.** S0105 (Congressional Research Service), S0338 (NFAP), S0335, S0136, S0137, S0300.

**Caveats.** NFAP is a pro-immigration group; its table is compiled from government data. The start year of the extra 20,000 places for holders of US master's degrees is not in the sources read (Chapter 13 gives 2004). Rulings of June and September 2026 on the $100,000 fee are summarised differently by different law firms, and the court orders were not read; the 2026 events postdate the research cut-off.

| US fiscal year | Cap | New petitions issued against the cap |
|---|---|---|
| 1992 | 65,000 | 48,600 |
| 1995 | 65,000 | 54,200 |
| 1997 | 65,000 | 65,000 (cap first reached, September 1997) |
| 1999 | 115,000 | 115,000 |
| 2000 | 115,000 | 115,000 |
| 2001 | 195,000 | 163,600 |
| 2002 | 195,000 | 79,100 |
| 2003 | 195,000 | 78,000 |
| 2004-2026 | 65,000 | 65,000 (cap reached every year) |

Events in the file: the Immigration Act of 1990 creates the visa; the FY2005 cap is reached on the first day of filing; the FY2008 cap is reached in two days in April 2007 (about 119,193 petitions); denial rates for initial employment fall from 24 per cent (FY2018) to 13 per cent (FY2020); the first lottery by electronic registration is held for FY2021; Proclamation 10973 of 19 September 2025 requires a $100,000 payment for new petitions; a DHS rule of 29 December 2025 weights selection towards higher wage levels; a Massachusetts court rules the fee unlawful on 8 June 2026; Proclamation 11069 of 18 September 2026 extends the fee to September 2027; and a California court vacates the implementing policies on 30 September 2026. Full file: `book/research/data/h1b_policy.csv`.

### H-1B approvals by country of birth (`h1b_country.csv`)

**What it measures.** The share of approved H-1B petitions that went to workers born in India.

**Definition and unit.** Approved petitions and per cent, by beneficiary's country of birth; initial (new employment), continuing (extensions) or all, as labelled.

**Coverage.** October 1999-February 2000; FY2005 (new arrivals); FY2023; FY2024. USCIS reports for FY2000-22 exist but could not be reached.

**Sources.** S0104, S0105, S0336 (USCIS FY2023 report), S0335 (USCIS FY2024 report, via a verified mirror).

**Caveats.** Petitions are not people: one worker can appear more than once. The FY2005 row counts new arrivals, a different measure. The USCIS FY2024 report gives two slightly different totals for India.

The Lok Sabha record dates the decision to 1964 and the first installation to November 1965 (*Lok Sabha Debates*, 24 November 1966, col. 5287). A short biographical note on Ajoy Dasgupta, a leader of the insurance employees, dates the insurance workers' 'struggles against computerisation' earlier, to 1959-61, and says that 'the computers were installed step by step and the agitation died down' (Indian Labour Archives, 'Ajoy Dasgupta', p. 2). The two dates may describe two waves of protest, one against earlier office machinery and one against the computer itself; the record does not settle which.

The first policy paper on this was published in 1974' (Rajaraman, *History of Computing in India* (2012), p. 28). William Aspray dates a Software Export Scheme to a 1972 bill sponsored by the DoE that eased hardware imports for companies that would use them to produce software for export (Aspray, 'The Role of Policy' (2010), section 'Trade, industrial regulation, and foreign investment policy'). No primary text of either has been located; the two dates may describe an announcement and a formal policy.

Nandan Nilekani, who joined Patni in January 1979 and left in July 1981, recalled that Patni 'did a lot of work for clients in the U.S.', and that he spent almost a year at Data General, living in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and taking the bus to its offices in Westborough to work on the company's own software (Computer History Museum, 'Oral History of Nandan Nilekani' (2020), pp. 7-8; title page dated 8 January 2019; CHM reference X9234.2020). Upadhya and Vasavi, citing Balaji Parthasarathy, call bodyshopping 'the primary form of outsourcing in the 1980s' (Upadhya and Vasavi, *Work, Culture, and Sociality in the Indian IT Industry* (2006), p. 10, n. 12, citing Parthasarathy 2005, p. 208). The filings count all 'offers of employment' without separating new graduates from experienced recruits, so the growth in fresher hiring alone cannot be read from them. Offers are the steadier measure. The number of applications behaves oddly: the year to March 2005 shows about 1,348,800, more than the 885,000 of three years later, even though offers more than tripled in between. Both filings use 'screened' in one place and 'received' in another for the same figure, so the change of wording does not explain the fall.

# Index term list

This list gives 487 terms for the index: people, organisations, places, laws and policies, events and concepts. Each term is followed by the parts of the book in which it appears: the Prologue, Chapters 1 to 19 (by number) and the Epilogue. The locations were found by searching the text of each chapter, excluding its endnotes, so they record mentions rather than page numbers; page references will be added when the book is typeset. Names are given as the text gives them, with people listed surname first. Where a place or body has more than one name, the variants are merged under one heading, with the current name first and the older one in brackets, as in Mumbai (Bombay); the entry covers mentions under either name. Pseudonyms given by the sources are marked as such. Abbreviations used in the text follow the full name in brackets.
